MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS
OF DEFENDANT THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN
Defendant the National Center of Missing & Exploited Children [“NCMEC”], by and
through undersigned counsel and pursuant to the Rules and Orders of this Honorable Court,
hereby respectfully set forth the following Memorandum in Support of NCMEC’s Motion to
Dismiss Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint. The Motion should be granted, on the grounds
that Plaintiff’s claims are barred by litigation privilege, as the allegedly-defamatory language
was set forth in a response to a subpoena; because NCMEC enjoys qualified statutory immunity
under federal law; because Plaintiff fails to plausibly allege that the language in question is not
true; because the language utilized cannot support a defamation by imputation claim; because
Plaintiff has failed to plausibly allege that the subpoena response was sufficiently outrageous to
support a claim of intentional infliction of emotional distress; and because Plaintiff’s claims of
conspiracy are predicated on conclusory, illogical allegations. In further support, NCMEC states
as follows:


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

I.

Document 11

Filed 08/12/26

Page 2 of 17 PageID# 212

FACTUAL SETTING/BACKGROUND
The above-captioned lawsuit is Plaintiff’s second effort as to NCMEC, having previously

filed and voluntarily dismissed a prior lawsuit based on the same facts while a motion to dismiss
was pending. See Ballentine v. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, et al.,
Case No. 1:26-cv-01341 (E.D. Va.).1
Plaintiff alleges that on April 9, 2026, Plaintiff sent two letters to NCMEC’s legal
department, which contained subpoenas seeking documents from NCMEC. See First Amended
Complaint [“FAC”] at ¶¶ 55, 56. Copies of those letters are attached hereto as Exhibits A and B.
In the identical schedules of requested documents that were attached to the subpoenas, Plaintiff
instructed NCMEC
[t]o produce a document sufficient to show whether [NCMEC] received or
maintains any CyberTipline report, referral, or submission concerning (1)
Marvelle J. Ballentine; (2) Jay Ballentine; and/or (3) the account-level identifier
jaychizza@icloud.com for the period July 2, 2022 through the date of compliance.
Ex. A and B at Schedule A. Schedule A to the subpoenas went on to instruct that NCMEC was
not to produce:
(a) the contents of any CyberTipline Report;
(b) any narrative text;
(c) attachments;
(d) images, video, or media;
(e) investigative materials; or
(f) any material beyond what is necessary to show the existence or non-existence
of a CyberTipline report, referral, or submission.
Id. On April 22, 2026, NCMEC responded to the subpoenas without awaiting formal service via
two substantively-identical letters signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel
for NCMEC. In those letters, NCMEC represented:
Dear Mr. Ballentine:
1

A hearing on the Motion to Dismiss was scheduled to occur on August 7, 2026.

2


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

Document 11

Filed 08/12/26

Page 3 of 17 PageID# 213

In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for
Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) provides its written responses as
detailed below.
NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J.
Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier
jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.
See Letters from NCMEC to Plaintiff (4/22/206) (attached hereto as Exhibits C and D). In other
words, NCMEC responded precisely as requested, mirroring the language utilized by Plaintiff in
the Schedules accompanying the subpoenas. Notwithstanding that the information was requested
in precisely the manner requested, Plaintiff alleges that the letters were defamatory, and that he
vomited and experienced recollections of childhood sexual abuse, lived in “acute fear of
imminent arrest and prosecution, [etc.]” upon receipt of the letters. FAC at ¶ 231.
Plaintiff further alleges that NCMEC and counsel for Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc.
engaged in a conspiracy “to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from continuing to attend [two other
federal lawsuits he has filed] … as a party and from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully as a
prospective witness in those pending federal proceedings…” Id. at ¶ 158.
Plaintiff alleges six counts: Defamation Per Se and Defamation by Implication (Count I,
as to Defendants NCMEC and Hall); Defamation Per Se and Defamation by Implication (Count
II, as to Defendants NCMEC and Hall); Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress (Count III,
as to Defendants NCMEC and Hall); Conspiracy to Deter a Party and Witness, by Intimidation,
from Attending and Testifying in Courts of the United States—42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) (Count IV, as
to all Defendants); Common-Law Conspiracy (Count V, as to all Defendants); and Insulting
Words—Va. Code § 8.01-45 (as to Defendants NCMEC and Hall). Plaintiff seeks
$42,820,260.00 (Forty Two Million Dollars) in compensatory damages, and punitive damages.

3


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

II.

Document 11

Filed 08/12/26

Page 4 of 17 PageID# 214

STANDARD OF REVIEW
A motion to dismiss pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6) tests the legal sufficiency of a

complaint to determine whether a plaintiff has properly stated a claim. In reviewing a dismissal
for failure to state a claim, the Court is to accept as true all factual allegations contained in the
complaint and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the plaintiff. E.I. du Pont de Nemours
& Co. v. Kolon Indus., Inc., 637 F.3d 435, 440 (4th Cir. 2011). To survive a motion to dismiss, a
complaint “must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that
is plausible on its face. A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual content
that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the
misconduct alleged.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Bell Atlantic Corp. v.
Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007). A claim has facial plausibility “when the plaintiff pleads
factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that defendant is liable for
the misconduct alleged.” Id. While Courts are to construe pro se complaints liberally, a pro se
plaintiff must nevertheless allege sufficient facts to state a plausible cause of action. Hardnett v.
M&T Bank, 204 F. Supp. 3d 851, 856 (E.D. Va. 2016) (internal citations omitted). Further,
conclusory allegations are not entitled the presumption of truth, nor is the Court required to
“accept as true unwarranted inferences, unreasonable conclusions, or arguments.” Wahi v.
Charleston Area Med. Ctr., Inc., 562 F.3d 599, 616 FN26 (4th Cir. 2009) (quoting Kloth v.
Microsoft Corp., 444 F.3d 312, 319 (4th Cir. 2006)).
Where a plaintiff fails to introduce a pertinent document as part of his complaint, the
defendant may attach the document to a motion to dismiss, and the Court may consider the same
without converting the motion into a motion for summary judgment, especially where the
plaintiff has referred to the document in the complaint. See Goines v. Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd.,

4


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

Document 11

Filed 08/12/26

Page 5 of 17 PageID# 215

822 F.3d 159, 166 (4th Cir. 2016); Davis v. George Mason Univ., 395 F.Supp.2d 331, 335 (E.D.
Va. 2005); Hoffman v. Daimler Trucks N. Am., LLC, 940 F. Supp. 2d 347, 354 (W.D. Va. 2013);
Orlando v. Smith, 2024 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 210073, *5 FN 1 (W.D. Va 2024) (internal citations
omitted) (same).
III.

ARGUMENT
A. Counts I, II, III, and VI are Barred by the Litigation Privilege.2
At a minimum, Plaintiff’s defamation and intentional infliction of emotional distress

claims are barred by the litigation privilege. Under Virginia law, litigation privilege “is broad in
scope and applies to communications made in proceedings pending in a court or before a quasijudicial body.” Lindeman v. Lesnick, 268 Va. 532, 537 (2004). It is an absolute privilege,
meaning “the maker of an absolutely privileged communication is accorded complete immunity
from liability [even if] the communication is made maliciously and with knowledge that it is
false.” Id. (quoting Spencer v. Looney, 116 Va. 767, 774 (1914)). The reason for the rule is “to
encourage unrestricted speech in litigation.” Lindeman, 268 Va. at 537 (internal citations
omitted). Virginia courts have “extended the application of the absolute privilege well beyond
the actual courtroom,” such as applying the privilege to protect a third party whose statements
were republished by another during a deposition. Id. (citing Watt v. McKelvie, 219 Va. 645, 651
(1978)). “Words spoken or written in a judicial proceeding that are relevant and pertinent to the
matter under inquiry are absolutely privileged.” Donahoe Constr. Co. v. Mt. Vernon Assocs., 235
Va. 531, 537 (1988).
While undersigned counsel has not identified any clear holding by the Fourth Circuit or

It does not appear that Defendant Hall has been served with the FAC in this matter. As such, the Motion
is filed by NCMEC, only. However, unless otherwise specified, the arguments set forth apply equally to
Defendant Hall, as she at all times relevant was an employee of NCMEC.
2

5


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

Document 11

Filed 08/12/26

Page 6 of 17 PageID# 216

its member districts as to whether subpoena responses are subject to absolute privilege, this
Court has recognized that the privilege would apply to comments made in response to a police
investigation. Fields v. Sprint Corp., 2017 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 147654, *18 (E.D. Va. 2017).
Other courts have extended the privilege in that manner. See, e.g., United States Dep’t of Educ.
v. NCAA, 481 F.3d 936, 939 (7th Cir. 2007) (noting that “[d]efamation based on material
contained in a response to a subpoena, as in other statements made in a judicial proceeding, is
absolutely privileged.”) (internal citations omitted); Parrino v. SunGard Availability Servs. LP,
2012 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 32137, *9 (E.D.N.Y. 2012) (noting that “certain communications, such as
the act of responding to a subpoena, may not serve as the basis for a defamation action”)
(internal citations omitted, applying New York law); Willis v. Centennial Mortg. & Funding, Inc.,
2004 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 18666, *25 (D. Minn. 2004) (holding that defendant’s actions, in
responding to subpoena, were absolutely privileged in defamation suit); Farooq v. Std. Chtd.
Bank, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 10392, *7-8 (E.D. Tex. 2026) (noting that “[u]nder Texas law, the
bank’s response to the subpoena is shielded by an absolute privilege and could not form the basis
of a tort claim”); United States v. Westinghouse Elec. Corp., 638 F.2d 570, 574 FN4 (3rd Cir.
1980) (noting absolute privilege extends to disclosure of records in response to subpoena).
The FAC emphasizes repeatedly that the subpoenas in question were not formally
served pursuant to Rule 45. However, this Court may take judicial notice of the fact that
parties routinely waive formal service of subpoenas, and routinely produce information in
response to a subpoena without requiring formal service. To wit, in both Virginia state courts
and the Fourth Circuit, even service of process can be waived, despite the service requirements
set forth under the relevant frameworks. A failure to serve is not a prohibition against response;

6

it simply means that compliance may not be compelled, unless service is waived. See, e.g.,
Hanwha Azdel, Inc. v. C&D Zodiac, Inc., 2013 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 96690, *13 (W.D. Va. 2013)
(noting that objections as to formal service of a subpoena can be waived).
B. NCMEC Has Statutory Immunity to Several of Plaintiff’s Claims.
Second, NCMEC enjoys qualified statutory immunity that bars Counts I, II, and
V. 18 U.S.C. § 2258D provides that in light of NCMEC’s
clearinghouse role as a private, nonprofit organization and its mission to help find
missing children, reduce online sexual exploitation of children and prevent future
victimization… a civil claim… against NCMEC, including any director, officer,
employee, or agent of NCMEC, arising from the performance of any
CyberTipline responsibilities or functions of NCMEC… may not be brough in
any Federal or State Court.
18 U.S.C. § 2258D(a). The statutory immunity is not absolute—it does not apply where
NCMEC engaged in intentional misconduct (§ 2258D(b)(1)), or acted with actual malice,
reckless disregard a substantial risk of causing injury without legal justification, or for a
purpose unrelated to the performance of any responsibility or function under § 2258D, § 2258A
(requiring reports to CyberTipline), or Section 404 of the Missing Children’s Assistance Act (§
2258D(b)(2)). Further, the statutory immunity does not apply to an act or omission relating to an
“ordinary business activity, including general administration or operations, the use of motor
vehicles, or personnel management.” § 2258D(c).
Additionally, 34 U.S.C. § 20505 provides that unless a plaintiff can show actual malice,
or that NCMEC provided information or took action for a purpose unrelated to an activity
mandated by federal law, NCMEC “including any of its officers, employees, or agents, shall not
be liable for damages in any civil action for defamation, libel, slander, or harm to reputation
arising out of any action or communication by [NCMEC]… in connection with any
clearinghouse, hotline, or complaint intake or forwarding program…”
7

Page 8 of 17 PageID# 218

NCMEC respectfully submits that the statutory immunity applies, at a minimum, to
Plaintiff’s defamation counts (Counts I, II, and VI). Plaintiff sent subpoenas to NCMEC seeking
information it received and maintains pursuant to its statutory charge, and NCMEC responded
precisely as requested. None of the exceptions are applicable; no facts are alleged, nor can any
reasonable inference be derived from any factual allegations, that NCMEC engaged in
“intentional misconduct,” or acted with “actual malice” or “reckless disregard.” “Actual
malice,” in the context of a defamation claim, requires “knowledge that [the statement] was false
or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.” Fleming v. Moore, 221 Va. 884, 891
(1981) (quoting New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254, 280 (1964)). Plaintiff’s
allegations as to malice are conclusory; no factual allegations are set forth to establish that
NCMEC or its employee, Defendant Hall, acted with actual malice, and the complained-of
activity clearly relates to NCMEC’s clearinghouse role. As such, Plaintiff’s defamation counts
should be dismissed.
Further, given the lack of factual support for Plaintiff’s claims of intentional misconduct,
NCMEC respectfully submits that its statutory immunity should properly apply to all counts.
C. The Statements are True, and Thus Not Actionable.
Third, assuming arguendo that no privilege or immunity applies, the Complaint fails to
state a claim upon which relief may be granted, as Plaintiff does not assert that the factual
representations in the letter are inaccurate, and Plaintiff’s theory of defamation by implication is
not actionable. Under Virginia law, “a private individual asserting a claim of defamation first
must show that a defendant has published a false factual statement…” Dangerfield v. WAVY
Broadcasting, Inc., 228 F. Supp. 3d 696, 701 (E.D. Va. 2017) (quoting Hyland v. Raytheon Tech.
Servs. Co., 277 Va. 40, 46 (2009) (emphasis added)).

8

Document 11

Filed 08/12/26

Page 9 of 17 PageID# 219

Plaintiff has not alleged that the allegedly-defamatory statements are not, in fact, true—
that NCMEC received two CyberTipline reports relating to any of the three search terms
specified in the subpoena. In other words, Plaintiff would need to establish that the statement
was false; that NCMEC did not, in fact, receive two CyberTipline reports for the search terms
specified by Plaintiff during the time period specified by Plaintiff. He cannot plausibly assert
that is the case, because he does not have access to those reports. While it is certainly
understandable that a person would be upset to learn that they, or a person with the same name,
or their e-mail address—is linked with a report to NCMEC, that does not render an accurate
factual recitation of that fact actionable.
Plaintiff asserts in the Complaint that he “has not engaged in conduct constituting, or
reasonably appearing to constitute, a violation of any statute enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.”
FAC at ¶ 102. NCMEC takes no position on that allegation, as it cannot know whether or not
that is true. However, the fact remains that NCMEC did not accuse Plaintiff of any such
conduct; NCMEC simply responded that two reports were received regarding the identifiers
requested by Plaintiff in the subpoenas. Plaintiff has not, and cannot, plausibly allege that
statement is false, and as such, the statement is not actionable.
D. The Allegedly-Defamatory Meaning Cannot be Imputed from the Language Used.
Further, Plaintiff’s defamation claims are not actionable, because his theory of
defamation by implication relies on a tortured interpretation of the allegedly-defamatory letters.
Virginia recognizes the theory of defamation by implication, so long as the implication is
“reasonably drawn from the words actually used.” Webb v. Virginian-Pilot Media Cos., 287 Va.
84, 49 (2014). Whether such an implication may reasonably be drawn is a question of law. Id. at
90. The meaning of the allegedly defamatory language “cannot, by innuendo, be extended

220

Page 10 of 17 PageID#

beyond its ordinary and common acceptation.” Id. at 89 (quoting Carwile v. Richmond
Newspapers, Inc., 196 Va. 1, 9 (1954)).
In the case at hand, Plaintiff attempts to do just that—impermissibly extend the language
in the letters, by arguing that NCMEC, by advising of the existence of the reports, was implying
that Plaintiff had violated child exploitation statutes that gave rise to those reports. That is not an
implication that can reasonably be drawn. All NCMEC stated was that it had received two
CyberTipline reports relating to the search terms provided by Plaintiff; NCMEC did not express
any opinion as to the validity of those reports, nor express in any way those reports were or were
not credible (and as noted supra, Plaintiff expressly instructed NCMEC to not provide any
information beyond what NCMEC provided).
Dangerfield is instructive. In that matter, the plaintiff sued a news organization for, inter
alia, reporting that Plaintiff had been accused of rape. The court concluded that was factually
accurate, and noted “Defendants’ broadcast stated that Plaintiff was ‘accused of rape.’ Plaintiff
may not extrapolate beyond the ‘plain and natural’ meaning of words to claim that Defendants’
broadcast stated that Plaintiff was a ‘rapist.’” Dangerfield, 228 F. Supp. 3d at 702 (internal
citations omitted).
Here, Plaintiff is attempting to do precisely what the Court prohibited in
Dangerfield; extend factually-accurate representations that the identifiers he identified had been
referenced to the CyberTipline to claim that NCMEC stated he had engaged in child exploitation
or other conduct that would be appropriately reported to NCMEC. NCMEC advised of reports;
NCMEC took no position as the validity of the reports, or expressed anything relating to the
conduct that lead to the reports. Rather, NCMEC provided only the information requested—the

existence or nonexistence of any CyberTipline reports as to the search terms identified by
Plaintiff.
Further, defamation by implication requires Plaintiff to plausibly allege “that the
challenged language not only imparts a ‘false innuendo’ but also suggests that the author intends
or endorses the inference.” Malone v. WP Co., LLC, 2023 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 176018, *18 (W.D.
Va. 2023) (quoting Chapin v. Knight-Ridder, Inc., 993 F.2d 1087, 1092 (4th Cir. 1993)).3 That
element is clearly missing in this matter; NCMEC reported a factual statement in response to the

simply responded to Plaintiff’s subpoena, in the manner requested.
E. Count VI (Insulting Words) Fails for the Same Reasons.
Virginia’s insulting words statute was originally enacted to prevent duels. Malone, 2023
U.S. Dist. LEXIS 176018 at *19. The statute is treated “the same as ‘an action for slander or
libel, for words actionable per se, with one exception, namely that no publication is necessary.’”
Id. (quoting Carwile, 196 Va. at 1). As such, defamation and insulting words claims “must
ineluctably rise or fall together.” Potomac Valve & Fitting Inc. v. Crawford Fitting Co., 829 F.2d
1280, 1284 (4th Cir. 1987).
Defendants do not impute to Plaintiff any serious crime involving moral turpitude; nor
that he has a contagious disease, nor that the is unfit to perform his duties, nor that prejudice him
in his profession or trade. Again, Defendants simply responded to Plaintiff’s subpoenas, and
accurately advised him of the existence of two CyberTipline reports using search terms selected

defamatory inference can reasonably be drawn, the libel is not established. But if the communication…
supplies additional, affirmative evidence suggesting that the defendant intends or endorses the defamatory
inference,” the communication is actionable.) (emphasis in original).

by Plaintiff. That fact is not actionable, any more than accurately stating that a person has been
accused of a crime.
F. Plaintiff Has Failed to Allege Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress.
In Count III, Plaintiff alleges that NCMEC intentionally inflicted emotional distress on
Plaintiff by responding to the subpoenas using the language instructed. Plaintiff fails to plausibly
state a claim as to Count III.
In order to establish intentional infliction of emotional distress under Virginia law, a
plaintiff must show four elements of proof: (1) the conduct was intentional or reckless; (2) the
conduct was “outrageous or intolerable;” (3) there was a casual connection between the conduct
and the resulting emotional distress; and (4) the resulting emotional distress was severe.
SuperValu, Inc. v. Johnson, 276 Va. 356, 370 (2008); Almy v. Grisham, 273 Va. 68 (2007); Young
v. Wilson, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 147023, *10 (E.D. Va. 2026) (quoting Almy). “[O]nly where
the conduct has been so outrageous in character, and so extreme in degree, as to go beyond all
possible bounds of decency, and to be regarded as atrocious, and utterly intolerable in a civilized
community” can a claim survive. Young, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS at *10 (quoting Russo v. White,
241 Va. 23, 27 (1991)). This is an exacting standard—as noted by the Virginia Supreme Court in
Russo v. White, even if a defendant intended to inflict emotional distress, and acted in a fashion
that could support an award of punitive damages for another tort, the conduct must still be utterly
intolerable. 241 Va. 23, 27 (1991).
Plaintiff cannot plausibly claim that the conduct was intentional or reckless. Plaintiff sent
subpoenas to NCMEC, and NCMEC responded precisely as instructed. That is not reckless; and
Plaintiff’s theory that the conduct was intentional requires a tortured journey through conclusory
allegations that are unsupported by any factual allegations (as discussed infra under the

“outrageous” element). Regardless of Plaintiff’s alleged response to the letters, the Complaint
does not plausibly allege that the act of responding to the subpoenas, in the matter requested by

Plaintiff’s theory for intentionality, or outrageousness, appears to be as follows: in

California in which, in a footnote, he advised that he was a survivor of childhood sexual abuse.

was a victim of childhood sexual abuse. Id. at ¶ 61. Additionally, NCMEC either reviewed the

what he hopes occurred in order to better position potential claims. However, that conclusory
and imaginary chain of events is what Plaintiff deems shows that sending the letters was
outrageous. As the Court is not bound by conclusory allegations, there is nothing in the FAC to
provide so much as a hint of an inference that NCMEC, in responding to the subpoenas, acted in
a manner that was “intolerable in a civilized community.”
While it is not clear from the FAC, Plaintiff may attempt to argue that the “content
defects” in the April 22, 2026 subpoena responses show intent, or outrageous conduct beyond all
possible bounds of decency. However, each identified “content defect” tracks Plaintiff’s
subpoena exactly. For example, Plaintiff complains that the letters “did not identify any report

necessary to carefully review the pleadings in the matter in order to respond to what seemed to be two

number, report date, or reporting electronic provider.” FAC at ¶ 91. That is true—likely because
Plaintiff instructed as much in the subpoenas. See, e.g., Ex. A at Schedule A, exclusion (f)
(prohibiting the production of “any material beyond what is necessary to show the existence or
nonexistence of a CyberTipline report, referral, or submission.” Plaintiff complains that the
letters “linked Plaintiff’s three identifiers in the disjunctive using ‘and/or’…” FAC at ¶ 93. That
again is true—because Plaintiff’s subpoenas linked the identifiers using “and/or.” Ex. A at

G. Plaintiff’s Conspiracy Claims are Void of Any Factual Support.
Finally, Plaintiff has two conspiracy claims. Count IV alleges a conspiracy by all
defendants to intimidate him from participating in/testifying in federal court in violation of 42
U.S.C. § 1985(2), while Count V alleges common-law conspiracy to cause Plaintiff “presumed
damages, humiliation, embarrassment,” etc. Both counts are predicated exclusively on
conclusory allegations, with no factual support whatsoever, and should be dismissed as such.
Where a conspiracy is alleged, a plaintiff “must plead facts amounting to more than
‘parallel conduct and a bare assertion of conspiracy… Without more, parallel conduct does not
suggest conspiracy, and a conclusory allegation of agreement at some unidentified point does not
supply facts adequate to show illegality.” A Society Without a Name, for People Without a
Home, Millenium Future-Present v. Virginia, 655 F.3d 342, *346 (4th Cir. 2011), cert. denied,
2012 U.S. LEXIS 3028 (U.S. 2012) (quoting Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556-57). Put another way,
“[t]he factual allegations must plausibly suggest agreement, rather than being merely consistent
with agreement.” Society Without a Name, 655 F.3d at 346. “Indeed, we have specifically
rejected section 1985 claims whenever the purported conspiracy is alleged in a merely
conclusory manner, in the absence of concrete supporting facts.” Simmons v. Poe, 47 F.3d 1370,

14


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

225

Filed 08/12/26

Page 15 of 17 PageID#

1377 (4th Cir. 1995); Davidson v. Whitbeck, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 58977, *18 (E.D. Va. 2026)
(dismissing § 1985 conspiracy claim predicated on “conclusory assertions of conspiracy
unsupported by factual allegations”).
Here, Plaintiff’s claimed conspiracy is entirely conclusory. Plaintiff alleges that at some
point between April 9 and April 22, Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. and Defendant Hall “reached
an understanding that Hall would issue correspondence asserting the existence of CyberTipline
reports associated with one or more of Plaintiff’s identifiers before service of the intended
subpoenas and while motions directed at the same discovery remained pending.” FAC at ¶ 124.
Plaintiff’s support is exceedingly difficult to logically follow, but it seems as though Plaintiff
concludes that an agreement must have been reached for a variety of reasons, including that
NCMEC did not await formal service before responding to the subpoenas, provided separate
responses (one for each subpoena), and because “depositions covering the report-existence
question were imminent,” etc. See, e.g., id. at ¶¶ 126-134. Such allegations are conclusory, and
do not provide an inference, much less a logical conclusion, that an agreement existed with a
common goal to intimidate Plaintiff. Plaintiff sent NCMEC subpoenas, NCMEC responded
without awaiting formal service. It cannot be said that a logical conclusion follows that NCMEC
and Meta Platforms, Inc. must have had a secret conspiracy to humiliate Plaintiff or intimidate
him from testifying.
The same rationale applies to the common-law conspiracy claim. Under Virginia state
law, conclusory or general allegations of conspiracy are insufficient to withstand a motion to
dismiss. Firestone v. Wiley, 485 F. Supp. 2d 694, 703 (E.D. Va. 2007) (internal citations
omitted). It is not enough to merely state that a conspiracy took place. Id. “… Virginia requires
a plaintiff to allege ‘some details of time and place and the alleged effect of the conspiracy.’” Id.

15

at 704; Chipper Pro, LLC v. Bandit Indus., 616 F. Supp. 3d 525, 537 (W.D. Va. 2022) (same).
Plaintiff has not alleged sufficient facts to plausibly assert the existence of a conspiracy; rather,
Plaintiff has effectively hypothesized that such a conspiracy existed, based on illogical
reasoning, such as (as noted above) that NCMEC did not require formal service of the subpoenas
to respond, and responded exactly as instructed. At best, these allegations are parallelism,
twisted to imply some sort of concerted action, and the Complaint fails to state a claim upon
which relief may be granted as to the alleged conspiracy counts.5
Finally, Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy fails if Plaintiff cannot establish that an
underlying tort was committed. See Almy v. Grisham, 273 Va. 68, 80 (2007).
IV.

CONCLUSION
For the reasons set forth above, Defendant NCMEC respectfully submits that dismissal is

necessary and appropriate in this matter. Counts I, II, III, and VI are barred by litigation
privilege; Counts I, II, and V are barred by NCMEC’s statutory privilege; Counts I, II, and VI are
barred, as Plaintiff fails to plausibly allege that the allegedly-defamatory language is not true,
and takes an indefensible position as to how the language represents defamation by imputation;
Count III fails, as Plaintiff falls well short of the requisite standard for pleading intentional
infliction of emotional distress; and Counts IV and V are barred because the Complaint fails to
set forth any facts on which to establish the existence of any conspiracy.
At its core, this is a simple case. Plaintiff sent subpoenas to NCMEC; NCMEC
responded, without waiting for formal service, in precisely the manner instructed, and using
precisely the language instructed. Perhaps Plaintiff anticipated that NCMEC would respond that
no such reports were received, and Plaintiff now regrets sending the subpoena/phrasing the
While not relevant to the Court’s determination of a Motion to Dismiss, NCMEC denies any conspiracy
or even coordination with the alleged co-conspirators.

amendment would be futile, NCMEC respectfully requests that dismissal be with prejudice, and

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document16- Filed 08/20/26 Page 1 of 7 PagelD# 243
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
08/20/2026
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
V. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge
Rossie D. Alston Jr.
KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,
Defendants.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION UNDER
FEDERAL RULE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE 26(d)(1) FOR LEAVE TO SERVE
THREE LIMITED INTERROGATORIES ON NCMEC BEFORE THE RULE 26(f)
CONFERENCE
INTRODUCTION

NCMEC has moved to dismiss. ECF No. 10. One ground of its motion is truth. Section C of
its Memorandum in Support (ECF No. 11) is titled “The Statements are True, and Thus Not
Actionable.” In that section, NCMEC tells the Court why Plaintiff cannot contest the defense:

He cannot plausibly assert that is the case, because he does not have access to those

reports.

That sentence supplies the reason for this Motion.

NCMEC holds the two CyberTipline reports its April 22, 2026 letters described. Plaintiff
does not. NCMEC asks the Court to accept the truth of the April 22 statement, and it points to
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document16- Filed 08/20/26 Page 2 of 7 PagelD# 244
Plaintiff’s lack of the two reports as the reason Plaintiff cannot contest that truth. NCMEC’s motion
does not merely identify the missing information; it relies on Plaintiff’s inability to obtain that
information as a reason to dismiss the case.

Plaintiff asks for three interrogatories, directed to one Defendant, concerning two identified
records. Each asks whether one of Plaintiff’s three identifiers appeared in either report as originally
received by NCMEC. Each permits three answers: “Yes,” “No,” or “Unable to determine after
reasonable inquiry.” Plaintiff does not seek the reports.

The answers matter because NCMEC’s own brief concedes that the April 22 letters do not
say who the reports are about. NCMEC writes that a person would understandably be upset to learn
“that they, or a person with the same name, or their e-mail address—is linked with a report to
NCMEC.” That is NCMEC’s formulation, and it identifies three different things a report might
concern: Plaintiff himself; a stranger who shares his name; or an email string. The letters do not say
which. Only the reports can supply that source-level answer, and only NCMEC has them. The three
interrogatories ask which.

Plaintiff does not ask the Court to open discovery. He asks the Court to authorize three
answers about the two records NCMEC itself has made material to its request for dismissal.

BACKGROUND

On April 22, 2026, NCMEC issued two letters, each keyed to one of Plaintiff’s pending
federal actions. Each letter stated: “NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning
(1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier
jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.” The three identifiers are joined by
“and/or.” The letters do not state which identifier appears in either underlying report.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document16- Filed 08/20/26 Page 3 of 7 PagelD# 245

On August 12, 2026, NCMEC moved to dismiss. ECF No. 10. Section C of its
Memorandum in Support (ECF No. 11) is titled “The Statements are True, and Thus Not
Actionable.” The Memorandum argues that Plaintiff “would need to establish that the statement
was false; that NCMEC did not, in fact, receive two CyberTipline reports for the search terms
specified by Plaintiff during the time period specified by Plaintiff.” It then states that “[h]e cannot
plausibly assert that is the case, because he does not have access to those reports.”

In the same section, NCMEC writes: “While it is certainly understandable that a person
would be upset to learn that they, or a person with the same name, or their e-mail address—is linked
with a report to NCMEC, that does not render an accurate factual recitation of that fact actionable.”
NCMEC’s own sentence separates what the letters merged. A report may concern Plaintiff. It may
concern a different person who shares his name. It may concern nothing more than an email
address. Those are three materially different facts, and the difference between them is the
difference between a true statement about Plaintiff and a false one. What the Memorandum does
not say, anywhere, is that either report concerned Plaintiff.

LEGAL STANDARD

Rule 26(d)(1) bars discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference “except . .. when authorized
by these rules, by stipulation, or by court order.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1). The Court may therefore
authorize discovery now. Discovery must be relevant to a claim or defense and proportional to the
needs of the case. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1). District courts have broad discretion over the scope and
timing of discovery.

This District has exercised that authority to permit limited discovery before the Rule 26(f)
conference. See Shenzhenshibairihongmaoyiyouxiangongsi v. Novoluto GmbH, No. 3:25-cv-
00844 (E.D. Va. Mar. 9, 2026). That case arose in the preliminary-injunction setting and applied a
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document16- Filed 08/20/26 Page 4 of 7 PagelD# 246
modified preliminary-injunction test requiring a strong showing on the merits and likely
irreparable harm absent expedited discovery. Plaintiff does not contend that the modified
preliminary-injunction test governs this Rule 12 posture. The decision is relevant here for the
narrower proposition that the Court may authorize circumscribed pre-Rule 26(f) discovery and
limit that discovery to information necessary for an imminent adjudication where material
information is asymmetrically held.

ARGUMENT
I. NCMEC Has Made the Unresolved Referent Material to Its Request for
Dismissal.

NCMEC’s dismissal argument uses Plaintiff’s lack of access to the reports twice. First,
NCMEC invokes it as the reason Plaintiff cannot contest truth: he “cannot plausibly assert” falsity
“because he does not have access to those reports.” Second, NCMEC treats the resulting silence as
support for dismissal on the truth ground itself. Rule 26(d)(1) permits the Court to authorize the
limited discovery necessary to test the premise NCMEC has made material.

NCMEC did not merely deny an allegation; it advanced truth as an affirmative ground for
dismissal. The three interrogatories are directed to the precise factual proposition NCMEC made
material: whether either report, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise
identified each of Plaintiff’s three identifiers. That proposition is relevant to a defense NCMEC
raised, Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1), and NCMEC cannot rely on Plaintiff’s lack of access to bar
Plaintiff from testing the premise while relying on the same lack of access to establish it.

The ordinary answer to a request for pre-conference discovery is: wait for ordinary
discovery. NCMEC is not waiting. Its motion asks the Court to dismiss the action with prejudice
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Documenti16 Filed 08/20/26 Page 5 of 7 PagelD# 247
now, in part on the ground that the April 22 statement was true. The need for the three answers
exists now because NCMEC has chosen to litigate truth now.

In Shenzhenshibairihongmaoyiyouxiangongsi, the Court found expedited discovery
justified in part because a pending adjudication would otherwise require a party to litigate while
lacking information necessary to that adjudication, and it emphasized the imbalance of information
while limiting discovery to what was necessary. No. 3:25-cv-00844. The procedural posture
differs, but those practical considerations are present here. Plaintiff does not contend that every
pending motion to dismiss entitles a plaintiff to discovery. Five features combine here and will
rarely combine elsewhere:

(1) an affirmative truth theory;

(2) two specifically identified source records;

(3) exclusive control of those records by the movant;

(4) the movant’s express reliance on the opposing party’s lack of access; and

(5) a request limited to three closed answers.

II. The Three Interrogatories Are Directed Only to That Ambiguity.

Each interrogatory asks a single closed question: whether one identified term — “Marvelle
J. Ballentine,” “Jay Ballentine,” or jaychizza@icloud.com — appeared in, or was otherwise
identified by, either of the two CyberTipline reports referenced in NCMEC’s April 22, 2026 letters,
as originally received by NCMEC. Each interrogatory excludes information Plaintiff supplied,
information from court filings and public sources, and information obtained or added after original
receipt by NCMEC, so each answer addresses the report as NCMEC originally received it.

The interrogatories are directed only to the ambiguity NCMEC’s own Memorandum
describes. NCMEC identified three possible referents — Plaintiff, a person with the same name, or
an email address — without stating which is true. The three interrogatories ask NCMEC to answer
that question from the records it holds, and nothing else.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Documenti16 - Filed 08/20/26 Page 6 of 7 PagelD# 248

III. The Requested Discovery Is Minimal and Does Not Commence General

Discovery.

Plaintiff seeks three interrogatories, directed only to NCMEC, concerning only the two
reports NCMEC has already identified, requiring review only of those reports as originally
received by NCMEC, and permitting only three responses: “Yes,” “No,” or “Unable to determine
after reasonable inquiry.” Plaintiff does not seek production of either report or any portion of either
report. He does not seek any additional interrogatory, document request, deposition, third-party
discovery, communication, metadata, report number, submitter identity, date, narrative, or follow-
up discovery. Answering three closed questions about two identified records in the answering
party’s possession imposes a burden that is minimal and sharply bounded. The request is
proportional to the needs of the case. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1).

A “Yes” establishes only that the identified term appeared in, or was otherwise identified
by, at least one report as originally received by NCMEC. A “No” establishes only that the
identified term did not appear in, or otherwise identify, either report under the stated exclusions. An
“Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry” establishes only that NCMEC cannot presently
make that source-level determination after reasonable inquiry. Every permitted answer reduces
uncertainty on the question NCMEC made material. None adjudicates liability, and Plaintiff does
not ask the Court to treat any answer as adjudicating liability.

The Court need not choose between opening general discovery and leaving ordinary
discovery closed. The proposed order leaves ordinary discovery closed and authorizes only the
three interrogatories identified in the Motion. It preserves three answers made presently material
by NCMEC’s own dispositive filing without commencing general discovery.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Documenti6 - Filed 08/20/26 Page 7 of 7 PagelD# 249

The Fourth Circuit has recognized that dispositive relief ordinarily should not rest on facts

within the moving party’s exclusive control when the opposing party has been denied any

opportunity to test them. Harrods Ltd. v. Sixty Internet Domain Names, 302 F.3d 214, 244—47 (4th

Cir. 2002). NCMEC asks the Court to resolve a fact-dependent truth argument against Plaintiff on

the basis of Plaintiff’s lack of access to records NCMEC controls; the three answers requested are

the least discovery that could test that argument. Harrods arose under Rule 56, and Plaintiff does
not contend that the Court cannot rule on NCMEC’s motion without discovery.

CONCLUSION

This Motion asks for three answers. NCMEC asks for dismissal. NCMEC says its April 22

statement was true. NCMEC will not say whom the statement was about. It told the Court the

reports may concern Plaintiff, a person with his name, or an email address. Only the reports can

supply that source-level answer. NCMEC has them. Plaintiff does not. NCMEC relies on that fact

to argue Plaintiff cannot dispute truth at all. A party should not obtain dismissal on a fact-dependent

truth theory by relying on records it alone controls while refusing the limited discovery necessary

to test that theory. The Court should not decide truth on records one side holds and the other side

has never seen. Three closed questions cure that. Rule 26(d)(1) permits them. The Motion should

be granted.

Date: August 20, 2026 Respectfully submitted,

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847

Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503

jayballentine@protonmail.com

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 1 of 14 PagelD# 261
8/20/2026
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
V. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge
Rossie D. Alston Jr.
KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,
Defendants.
PLAINTIFF’S PROTECTIVE OPPOSITION TO THE MOTION TO DISMISS
OF DEFENDANT NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING &
EXPLOITED CHILDREN
Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine files this opposition protectively: it demonstrates that the
First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) states its claims on the facts already pleaded, without awaiting,
and without prejudice to, Plaintiff’s forthcoming motion for leave to file a supplemental pleading
under Rule 15(d). Citations to “Mem.” refer to NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 Memorandum in
Support.
I. INTRODUCTION
“You got exactly what you asked for.”
Counsel for the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children wrote those words to
Plaintiff on August 13, 2026. That same day, Plaintiff had asked three closed questions: whether
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 2 of 14 PagelD# 262
the two CyberTipline reports NCMEC invoked identified him by his legal name, by the name he
uses, or by an email identifier. Counsel answered none of them. What counsel wrote instead went
to a Plaintiff whose pleaded injuries NCMEC had recited in its own memorandum one day earlier.

The refusal matters because it is the motion. NCMEC’s April 22 letters stated that two
CyberTipline reports concerned “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” “Jay Ballentine,” “and/or” an email
identifier. NCMEC’s motion says less. It tells the Court the reports may be linked to Plaintiff, “a
person with the same name,” or an email address—while emphasizing that Plaintiff “does not have
access to those reports.” NCMEC holds the records that resolve that ambiguity. NCMEC declines
to resolve it. NCMEC now asks the Court to convert Plaintiff’s lack of access to NCMEC’s own
records into dismissal with prejudice.

The same posture appears on the other coast. In Plaintiff’s California action, Meta
Platforms, Inc. filed a motion the same day invoking its child-safety enforcement policy while
omitting that Meta is a named and served defendant here under the first clause of 42 U.S.C. §
1985(2). Meta cites this case but omits its role in it. NCMEC invokes the reports but will not say
whom they concer. Each defendant claims the protection of the same child-safety apparatus.
Neither will answer the identity question their own positions have made dispositive.

The answer NCMEC will not give is the answer its truth argument requires. Without it, the
motion reduces to one question: whether the First Amended Complaint states claims on the facts
actually pleaded. It does. The motion should be denied.

Il. ISSUES TO BE DECIDED

1. NCMEC asks the Court to dismiss this case on litigation privilege and statutory
immunity. Those defenses depend on facts. May NCMEC obtain dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6)
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 3 of 14 PagelD# 263
when the First Amended Complaint does not establish the predicates those defenses require — and
pleads facts bringing the April 22, 2026 letters within the statutory exceptions?

2. NCMEC says its letters were true. May NCMEC establish truth at the pleading
stage with the letters alone, when the Complaint pleads that their imputation is false and the letters
never identify which person or identifier either report concerns?

3. Do the pleaded facts — what the letters said, the CyberTipline context in which they
said it, when they issued, to whom they went, and what came before them — plausibly state
Plaintiff’s claims for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and conspiracy?

Il. LEGAL STANDARD

A motion under Rule 12(b)(6) tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint. The Court
accepts well-pleaded factual allegations as true, draws all reasonable inferences in Plaintiff’s favor,
and does not resolve disputed facts. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Kolon Indus., Inc., 637 F.3d
435, 440 (4th Cir. 2011).

An affirmative defense ordinarily cannot be resolved on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion. The
exception is rare, and it exists only when all facts necessary to establish the defense clearly appear
on the face of the complaint. Goodman v. Praxair, Inc., 494 F.3d 458, 464 (4th Cir. 2007) (en
banc). This Court applied that rule in SkyBell Technologies, Inc. v. Alarm.com, Inc., No. 1:25-cv-
01105-RDA-WBP (E.D. Va. Mar. 4, 2026), ECF No. 32, declining to resolve a defense that turned
on facts the pleadings did not settle.

IV. ARGUMENT

A. NCMEC Cannot Establish Privilege, Statutory Immunity, or Truth on This

Pleading.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 4 of 14 PagelD# 264

NCMEC’s first three arguments share one structure: each asks the Court to adopt a
predicate that the Rule 12 record does not establish. The subsections below identify each predicate
in turn.

1. Litigation Privilege

Virginia’s absolute judicial privilege reaches some communications made outside the
courtroom and can reach qualifying communications preliminary to contemplated litigation.
Mansfield v. Bernabei, 284 Va. 116, 727 S.E.2d 69 (2012). A court in this district has resolved the
privilege at the pleading stage. Daniczek v. Spencer, 156 F. Supp. 3d 739 (E.D. Va. 2016). The
question is whether, accepting the FAC’s facts as true, Virginia law establishes that these particular
communications fall within the absolute privilege. It does not.

NCMEC acknowledges that its counsel has identified no clear holding of the Fourth Circuit
or its member districts extending absolute privilege to subpoena responses. Mem. at 5. And on the
pleaded facts, the letters were not part of compelled judicial process: no subpoena had been served,
no court order required a response, Plaintiff had not waived service or requested an early answer,
and the announced notice period had not run. FAC {fj 71, 73. The letters were voluntary
correspondence sent to Plaintiff alone, filed with no tribunal, and copied to no counsel of record,
FAC 4 78; each opened by invoking compulsory force that did not then exist, FAC 4 70; and each
issued while motions directed at the same discovery remained pending, FAC { 72. The FAC
predicates no liability on any court filing. FAC 4 25. The absence of service matters not because
service is an element of the privilege, but because it separates these letters from compelled judicial
process — and from the subpoena-response authorities NCMEC assembles from other
jurisdictions.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 5 of 14 PagelD# 265

NCMEC answers with waiver: recipients may respond to a subpoena without formal
service, and a failure to serve “is not a prohibition against response.” Mem. at 6. That answers a
different question. Permission to respond is not the question. Absolute immunity from tort liability
is. The proposition that NCMEC was free to volunteer information does not establish the separate
proposition that Virginia law makes the resulting communication absolutely privileged. On the
pleaded facts, and on the authority NCMEC itself describes, the privilege is not established.

2. Statutory Immunity

Immunity under 18 U.S.C. § 2258D is qualified, as NCMEC’s own Memorandum
recognizes. Mem. at 7. It reaches claims arising from the performance of CyberTipline
responsibilities or functions, and it yields to exceptions for intentional misconduct; for actual
malice or reckless disregard of a substantial risk of causing injury without legal justification; for
action taken for a purpose unrelated to the specified statutory functions; and for ordinary business
activity. 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(a)-(c).

The FAC does not concede the predicate. It pleads that neither letter was a CyberTipline
report, a referral or disclosure to law enforcement, or any reporting, preservation, or disclosure
function described in 18 U.S.C. §§ 2258A—2258C — that the challenged act was voluntary legal
correspondence issued without any served subpoena or court order. FAC 4 79. It pleads, in the
alternative, facts within the statutory exceptions: a knowingly false invocation of compulsory
process, issuance without obligation of any kind, wording Hall selected and controlled, and timing
keyed to pending motions and imminent depositions. FAC {{ 70-74, 79, 85-86.

The sequence matters. NCMEC must show that the challenged conduct falls within the
protected statutory function. The FAC pleads facts distinguishing that function from the
correspondence at issue and pleads exception facts in the alternative. NCMEC’s contrary
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 6 of 14 PagelD# 266
characterization requires the Court to choose NCMEC’s version of the letters over the version
pleaded. Goodman forecloses that choice. The Court need not classify the conduct now. It need
only decline to accept NCMEC’s classification as fact.

Immunity under 34 U.S.C. § 20505 is worded differently and must be answered on its own
terms. It bars specified reputational claims arising from actions or communications “in connection
with” a clearinghouse, hotline, or complaint intake or forwarding program, unless the plaintiff
shows actual malice or that the information or action was provided or taken for a purpose unrelated
to an activity mandated by federal law. 34 U.S.C. § 20505. It contains no ordinary-business
exception and no separately stated reckless-disregard exception. The FAC pleads facts within both
of the exceptions it does contain. It alleges actual malice: Hall invoked a subpoena that had not
been served and that compelled nothing, and she selected wording associating Plaintiff personally
with the reports although the identifiers were supplied by Plaintiff, linked disjunctively, and
accompanied by no report-specific match or disambiguation. FAC {ff 85, 191-192. And it alleges a
purpose unrelated to any activity mandated by federal law: the letters implemented no reporting,
referral, preservation, or disclosure function, and their alleged purpose was to deter Plaintiff from
attending and testifying in the two federal actions. FAC § 79, 156, 162. On those allegations, §
20505, like § 2258D, is not established on the face of the pleading.

3. Truth

NCMEC reframes the falsity alleged. The FAC does not depend on proving that NCMEC
possessed no records responsive to any one of three search terms. It alleges that NCMEC falsely
published a person-level association between Plaintiff and child-exploitation reports. FAC J 99-—
101, 189, 210.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 7 of 14 PagelD# 267

The letters stated that NCMEC had received two CyberTipline reports “concerning”
Plaintiff’s legal name, the name he uses, “and/or” an email identifier. They did not identify which
listed identifier corresponded to either report. FAC §] 92. They did not state whether any identifier
appeared in a provider-submitted report or was instead drawn from Plaintiff’s own April 9
materials. FAC 4 77, 95. They did not state that the three identifiers describe one person, and “Jay
Ballentine” is not alleged to be unique. FAC {| 94, 96. The FAC pleads that the personal
imputation each letter conveyed is false. FAC ¥ 101.

At this stage, the Court credits a pleaded allegation of falsity unless it is conclusory or
contradicted by a document properly before the Court. See Dangerfield v. WAVY Broadcasting,
LLC, 228 F. Supp. 3d 696, 701-02 (E.D. Va. 2017). No underlying CyberTipline report is before
the Court. The April 9 materials NCMEC attaches establish what Plaintiff asked; the April 22
letters establish what NCMEC published; neither establishes which person or identifier actually
appears in either source report. And Goines forecloses the use NCMEC makes of the letters.
Consideration of a document at Rule 12 does not mean the plaintiff adopts the truth of its contents
— a rule that exists precisely because treating every attached writing as true would let the allegedly
libelous publication plead the plaintiff out of court. Goines v. Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd., 822 F.3d
159, 167-69 (4th Cir. 2016). The letters establish what NCMEC published. They do not establish
that what NCMEC published was true. NCMEC’s own Memorandum states that Plaintiff “does not
have access to those reports” while describing the possible referent as Plaintiff, “a person with the
same name,” or an email address. Mem. at 9. The truth theory presents a disputed factual predicate,
not a basis for Rule 12 dismissal.

B. The Pleaded Words and Context State Defamation and Insulting-Words

Claims.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 8 of 14 PagelD# 268

The letters state:

“NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J.

Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier

jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.”

The question is whether those words, read in the pleaded context, are reasonably capable of
the meaning the FAC alleges. The FAC supplies that context. Reports to the CyberTipline concern
apparent violations of enumerated federal child-exploitation statutes. FAC { 97-98. The
statement says the reports are “concerning” the listed names and identifier; it does not say that a
search of records produced results. Plaintiff’s full legal name appears first on the list. The
disjunctive “and/or” never identifies the actual match, and nothing in either letter separates
Plaintiff from the reports or attributes them to a different person. FAC {{ 92, 95-96. The FAC
pleads the resulting imputation and its falsity. FAC 4 99-101.

Dangerfield does not carry the weight NCMEC assigns it. There, the court could determine
what the words “accused of rape” communicated, and the incorporated warrant materials showed
that the accusation had in fact been made. 228 F. Supp. 3d at 701-02. Here, NCMEC’s own
Memorandum preserves the ambiguity the letters created, describing the referent as Plaintiff, a
person with the same name, or an email address. Mem. at 9. That ambiguity does not itself establish
liability. It defeats NCMEC’s contention that the publication is incapable, as a matter of law, of the
pleaded implication. As to authorial intent, the FAC alleges that Hall selected the wording; that she
invoked a subpoena as the basis for the response when that subpoena had not been served and
compliance had not been compelled; and that the identifiers were supplied by Plaintiff, linked
disjunctively, and accompanied by no report-specific match or disambiguation — circumstances
from which intent to convey the implication is inferred. FAC § 85, 191-192, 212-213.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 9 of 14 PagelD# 269

Count VI requires little more. NCMEC argues that the insulting-words claim rises or falls
with the defamation theory. Mem. at 11. Accepting that premise for purposes of this Motion, the
conclusion follows: because NCMEC has not established that the defamation theory fails, its
derivative argument against Count VI fails with it.

C. Count III Plausibly Alleges Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress.

NCMEC reduces Count III to the act of “responding to the subpoenas.” Mem. at 12. Rule
12 requires the Court to evaluate the conduct actually pleaded, and the FAC pleads a combination
of circumstances, not a subpoena response.

Hall was NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel. FAC § 80. The FAC alleges that she understood
the criminal and law-enforcement significance of associating a named individual with
CyberTipline reports, FAC {{ 61, 224; that before the letters issued she had reviewed, or received
from participants in the two actions, materials disclosing that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood
sexual abuse who had already been injured by association with the language of child exploitation,
FAC 49 39-45, 60, 225; and that she possessed the case-specific materials identifying the two
actions, the identifiers, and the discovery at issue, FAC 9 59, 87. On that footing, the FAC alleges,
Hall issued two case-keyed letters with no subpoena served, no waiver, no court order, and no
request for an early answer — one day after motions directed at the same discovery and before any
ruling on them — transmitted to Plaintiff alone, opening with a false invocation of compulsory
process, and substituting an unsworn, source-free assertion for the sworn examination then days
away. FAC ff 68, 70—73, 76, 78, 226.

The distress pleaded is concrete. Upon reading the letters, Plaintiff vomited, experienced
recurrent involuntary recollections of his own childhood sexual abuse, lived in acute fear of
imminent arrest and prosecution, distanced himself from his own children because he expected to
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 10 of 14 PagelD#
be taken into custody by law enforcement, could not maintain ordinary sleep or eating, could not
sustain attention on litigation materials, and refrained from dismissing his two federal actions only
by deliberate effort. FAC § 171-173, 229, 231. That exceeds a bare assertion of severe distress.

Virginia confines this tort to conduct that is outrageous and intolerable, and the standard is
not satisfied lightly. SuperValu, Inc. v. Johnson, 276 Va. 356, 370 (2008). But whether the pleaded
combination — directing at a disclosed survivor of childhood sexual abuse a false, source-
unidentified assertion tying his name to child-exploitation reporting, under color of compulsory
force that did not then exist, timed to the same discovery then pending — crosses that threshold is
answered on the allegations as pleaded, taken together, not on NCMEC’s shortened description of
them. FAC 4 226—227. Count III states a claim.

D. The Conspiracy Counts Plead Agreement Through Particular Facts, Not

Labels.

The rule NCMEC cites is not in dispute: parallel conduct plus a bare assertion of agreement
does not state a conspiracy claim. A Soc’y Without a Name v. Virginia, 655 F.3d 342, 346 (4th Cir.
2011). That rule does not describe this pleading.

The FAC alleges particulars. As of April 9, 2026, NCMEC and counsel for Meta and
Accenture had received identical case-specific materials identifying the same two federal actions,
the same three identifiers, and the same discovery objective. FAC {J 57-58, 124. On April 21, the
defendants in those actions moved to stop the identified discovery. FAC §§ 63-67, 125.
Depositions covering the report-existence question were noticed for April 28 through April 30.
FAC 4 50-52, 126. On April 22 — under no compulsion of any kind — Hall issued two separate
letters, each keyed by caption and case number to one of the two actions, before service, before the
requested ruling dates, and before the depositions. FAC §§ 68, 127-129. The letters supplied,
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 11 of 14 PagelD#
outside the discovery process, an unsworn and source-free assertion on the exact question
scheduled for sworn examination. FAC §f 131, 133. And the identities and communications that
would establish the details of the agreement rest in Defendants’ records, not Plaintiff’s. FAC { 134.

These allegations do not prove agreement, and at this stage they need not. They are concrete
circumstances from which agreement may plausibly be inferred. NCMEC’s argument asks the
Court to select NCMEC’s innocent explanation over the inference Rule 12 requires the Court to
draw in Plaintiff’s favor.

The FAC also pleads the statutory object of Count IV. It alleges that the purpose of the
agreement was to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from continuing to attend the two federal actions
as a party and from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully as a prospective witness in them, with the
April 22, 2026 letters as the means. FAC ff 156-157, 162, 235.

The common-law count follows. The FAC pleads combination, underlying tortious
conduct, overt acts, time and sequence, purpose, and resulting injury. FAC §§ 156, 163-166, 243—
248. Because the underlying defamation claims survive this Motion, NCMEC cannot obtain
dismissal of Count V by declaring the alleged agreement implausible. See Almy v. Grisham, 273
Va. 68, 80 (2007).

E. Dismissal With Prejudice Would Be Unwarranted.

NCMEC requests dismissal with prejudice, citing the prior action and the single
amendment here. Mem. at 17. The prior action ended in a voluntary dismissal without any merits
adjudication. The present FAC reflects one amendment, not repeated failures to cure deficiencies
identified by any court. NCMEC’s claim that amendment would be futile depends on the same
Rule 12 arguments addressed above. If the Court were to identify a curable deficiency, dismissal
with prejudice would require a recognized basis under Rule 15 — such as repeated failure to cure
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 12 of 14 PagelD#
272
by amendments previously allowed — that this record does not present. Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S.
178, 182 (1962).
V. CONCLUSION
The Motion should be denied. In the alternative, any dismissal should be without prejudice
and with leave to amend.
Date: August 20, 2026 Respectfully submitted,
Marvelle J. Ballentine
Plaintiff, pro se
