MEMORANDUM OF LAW IN SUPPORT OF DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS,
INC.’S MOTION TO DISMISS PLAINTIFF’S FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT
I.

INTRODUCTION

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine brings this action against Defendants Katie Hall (“Hall”), the
National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC” and, together with Hall, the
“NCMEC Defendants”) and Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”), based on two letters that Hall sent to
Plaintiff, on behalf of NCMEC, in response to a notice of intended subpoenas that Plaintiff himself
sent to NCMEC. The proposed subpoenas were sent in connection with two cases Plaintiff filed
against Meta in the Middle District of Florida and asked NCMEC to confirm whether NCMEC
had received any CyberTipline reports associated with the following identifiers: (1) Marvelle J.
Ballentine; (2) Jay Ballentine; and/or (3) jaychizza@icloud.com (the “Identifiers”). Despite
expressly requesting this information from NCMEC (and having previously sought similar
information from Meta via discovery in other litigation), Plaintiff contends that NCMEC’s

1


response indicating that it had received two CyberTipline reports associated with the Identifiers is
somehow tortious.
As to Meta, based solely on suppositions, conclusory allegations, and despite Meta refusing
to respond to similar discovery requests directed at it, Plaintiff alleges that Meta “conspired” with
the NCMEC Defendants to get them to respond to Plaintiff’s subpoena early to “intimidate” him
into dismissing the underlying lawsuits against Meta and/or to defame him. Based on these
allegations, Plaintiff brings two conspiracy-based causes of action against Meta, each of which
fails.
First, Plaintiff’s claim that Meta and the NCMEC Defendants engaged in a conspiracy to
deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from attending and testifying in courts of the United States in
violation of 42 U.S.C § 1985(2) fails for three independent reasons. To start, the FAC contains no
factual allegations supporting the existence of a conspiracy between Meta and the NCMEC
Defendants. Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim separately fails because the FAC does not include
any allegations of any violent or threatening conduct whatsoever, much less any such conduct that
was intended to deter Plaintiff from pursuing his other litigation against Meta. Further, the FAC
does not plead the requisite injury, i.e., that Plaintiff was actually hindered from pursuing litigation
or testifying.
Second, Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy to defame claim fails for similar reasons. As
was true for his Section 1985(2) claim, Plaintiff fails to plausibly allege the existence of any
agreement between Meta and the NCMEC Defendants, much less one to engage in an unlawful
purpose or to defame Plaintiff. Indeed, Plaintiff does not allege any wrongful conduct by Meta at
all. And, as explained in their motion to dismiss, Plaintiff does not and cannot state the underlying
claim for defamation against NCMEC or Hall, which is a prerequisite to bringing a conspiracy

2


claim. Among other reasons, the defamation claims are barred by the litigation privilege because
they arise out of responses to subpoenas, and the NCMEC Defendants have statutory immunity
from such claims arising out of CyberTipline reports.
Because the FAC fails to state any claim for relief against Meta, it should be dismissed.
II.

BACKGROUND
A. Procedural History
The instant action arises from discovery Plaintiff sought in connection with a series of

meritless complaints against Meta and a host of other parties, across several different courts based
on the alleged disablement of Plaintiff’s Facebook account. Plaintiff filed his first complaint
against Meta and Accenture, LLP (“Accenture”) in the United States District Court for the
Northern District of California on September 9, 2025, based on allegations that Meta disabled
Plaintiff’s Facebook account and Accenture affirmed the disablement because of Plaintiff’s race.
See Complaint, Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc. et al., No. 3:25-cv-7671-CRB (N.D. Cal. Sept.
9, 2025), Dkt. No. 1 (“Ballentine 1”). After the court declined to allow Plaintiff to seek discovery,
including discovery “clarifying whether any CyberTipline report exists,” (Ballentine 1, Dkt.
No. 36 at 2) pending resolution of Meta’s and Accenture’s motions to dismiss, Plaintiff voluntarily
dismissed this action and re-filed his claims in the Middle District of Florida. See Complaint,
Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc. et al., No. 6:26-cv-376 (M.D. Fla. Feb. 17, 2026), Dkt. No. 1
(“Ballentine 2” or the “376 Action”).
In Ballentine 2—the “376 Action” referenced in the FAC—Plaintiff raised substantially
similar claims as those raised in Ballentine 1, based on essentially identical factual allegations.
Ballentine 2, Dkt. No. 1. Plaintiff also again sought discovery regarding the existence of a
“CyberTipline report,” including filing a motion to serve a Request for Admission to Meta targeted

3


at this information. See Ballentine 2, Dkt. No. 7 at 5 (explaining that the “answer to this request”
regarding whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff “will materially affect the
scope and direction of . . . subsequent proceedings”); see also FAC ¶ 35 (alleging that “Plaintiff’s
first substantive act in the 376 Action was a motion for leave to serve a single early request for
admission directed to whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff’s account”).
After failing to get the discovery regarding any “CyberTipline report” from the parties in
Ballentine 2, Plaintiff filed a “Notice of Intent to Serve Subpoena” on NCMEC in that action,
explaining that Plaintiff “transmitted to NCMEC . . . advance notice of a[] . . . subpoena concerning
whether a CyberTipline report . . . was filed in connection with the Facebook account associated
with Plaintiff and terminated on or about July 4, 2022.” Ballentine 2, Dkt. No. 82 at 1; FAC ¶¶ 5556 (describing “Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas” sent to NCMEC and attached request).
Meta moved to dismiss and moved to transfer the 376 Action to the Northern District of California,
and the court granted Meta’s Motion to Transfer, transferring the action to the Northern District of
California where it remains pending.
This action is also not the first time that Plaintiff has sued Meta for conspiring to defame
him based on the conduct of its co-defendants (or their lawyers) who simply responded to
Plaintiff’s legal claims. Around the same time as he filed Ballentine 2, Plaintiff filed an additional
action in the Middle District of Florida, asserting defamation claims against Accenture and its
counsel and a conspiracy to defame claim against Meta based on language in Accenture’s Motion
to Dismiss in Ballentine 1. See Complaint, Ballentine v. Accenture, LLP et al., No. 5:26-cv-472
(M.D. Fla. Feb. 9, 2026), Dkt. No. 1 (“Ballentine 3” or the “286 Action”). In Ballentine 3—the
“286 Action” referenced in the FAC—Plaintiff again sought discovery regarding the existence of
a CyberTipline report, among other items. See FAC ¶ 3. The 286 Action was dismissed by the

4


Court based on Plaintiff’s failure to comply with a court order requiring “disclosure of the use of
Artificial Intelligence” with respect to Plaintiff’s filings. Ballentine 3, Dkt. No. 80.
While these cases were pending, Plaintiff filed yet another action in Florida, his fourth
distinct action against Meta and Accenture and several other defendants, including Accenture’s
counsel. See Complaint and Notice of Removal, Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc. et al., No. 5:26cv-213 (M.D. Fla. Mar. 25, 2026), Dkt. No. 1, removed from No. 35-2026-CA-000494 (Cir. Ct.
Lake Cnty.) (“Ballentine 4”). Plaintiff’s complaint in Ballentine 4 effectively combined the
allegations of Plaintiff’s two sets of prior actions and asserted claims under Florida state law based
both on the alleged disablement of his Facebook account and on the allegedly defamatory language
in Accenture’s Motion to Dismiss in Ballentine 1. Plaintiff voluntarily dismissed Ballentine 4.
Finally, Plaintiff first raised the claims at issue in this lawsuit in a separate action against
the NCMEC Defendants. See Complaint, Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for Missing & Exploited Children,
No. 1:26-cv-1341 (E.D. Va. May 19, 2026) (“Ballentine 5”). After the NCMEC Defendants moved
to dismiss Plaintiff’s complaint (See Ballentine 5, Dkt. No. 4), Plaintiff moved for leave to amend
his complaint, seeking to add conspiracy claims against Meta. Ballentine 5, Dkt. No. 18. After
NCMEC and Hall opposed Plaintiff’s motion for leave to amend, Plaintiff, in a transparent attempt
to circumvent Fed. R. Civ. P. 15, opted to voluntarily dismiss his action and re-file as a new action
in this court. See Ballentine 5, Dkt. No. 21 at 1 (Notice of Voluntary Dismissal) (noting that because
“Defendants declined to consent to Plaintiff’s proposed amended and supplemental complaint, . . .
Plaintiff has elected to commence a new action asserting the expanded claims . . . rather than await
[a] hearing” on his motion to amend). Plaintiff then filed his complaint in the above-captioned
action and shortly thereafter filed the FAC. Dkt. Nos. 1, 5.
B. Plaintiff’s Allegations

5


In the FAC, Plaintiff alleges that, during the pendency of the 286 and 376 Actions in the
Middle District of Florida, Plaintiff sought early discovery regarding “whether Meta filed a
CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff’s [Facebook] account.” FAC ¶ 35; Ballentine 2, Dkt. No. 7
at 3 (explaining that “Plaintiff first raised this issue in the original complaint filed . . . on September
9, 2025” and despite “pursu[ing] multiple procedural vehicles to obtain this information” he had
not yet obtained responsive information). After the Court in the 376 Action denied his request to
serve an early request for admission relating to the existence of a CyberTipline report, Plaintiff
“served a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition notice on Accenture” that included the existence of a
CyberTipline report as a topic. FAC ¶¶ 35; 51-52. Plaintiff similarly noticed a deposition of
Accenture’s counsel in the 286 Action. FAC ¶ 53. In response to Plaintiff’s attempts to open
discovery in both cases, Defendants in the 286 and 376 Actions filed motions to stay discovery.
FAC ¶¶ 64; 66. Additionally, Accenture and its counsel filed motions for protective orders in both
cases, in light of Plaintiff’s noticed deposition of Accenture and its counsel. FAC ¶¶ 65; 67. The
Court granted the motions for protective orders in both cases, temporarily staying discovery
pending resolution of the motions to stay discovery. FAC ¶ 76.
Frustrated by his inability to get the discovery he sought in the 286 and 376 Actions, the
FAC alleges that “[o]n April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted to NCMEC’s Legal Department a letter”
which “identified the 376 Action and the 286 Action ” and “enclosed . . . draft subpoenas”
addressed to NCMEC. FAC ¶ 55. The FAC alleges that “Schedule A to each draft subpoena”
requested “a document sufficient to show whether NCMEC received or maintains any
CyberTipline report concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the
account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com.” FAC ¶ 56.

6


The FAC alleges that, “[o]n April 22, 2026,” prior to Plaintiff formally serving the
subpoenas on NCMEC, “Hall issued two letters on NCMEC letterhead;” one each for the 286
Action and the 376 Action, stating that “[i]n response to your subpoena . . . NCMEC has received
two (2) CyperTipline reports concerning” the identifiers supplied by Plaintiff. FAC ¶¶ 69-71; 77.
The FAC alleges that “[e]ach letter was addressed to Plaintiff alone” and was not sent to any other
individual or filed in either the 286 Action or the 376 Action. FAC ¶ 79. The FAC alleges that
NCMEC’s letter “did not state that Meta . . . submitted either report, that either report concerned
Plaintiff’s Facebook account, or that either report” concerned the alleged disablement of Plaintiff’s
Facebook account. FAC ¶ 92.
Based on the FAC’s allegations that (1) Meta was aware that Plaintiff had sent the proposed
subpoenas to NCMEC (FAC ¶ 58); (2) Defendant Hall had access to the publicly filed documents
in both the 286 and 376 Actions (FAC ¶ 61); (3) Meta and the other Defendants moved to stay
discovery in the 286 and 376 Actions on April 21, 2026 (FAC ¶¶ 64; 66); and (4) Defendant Hall
issued the correspondence at issue in this litigation on April 22, 2026 (FAC ¶ 69), the FAC
concludes that Meta and NCMEC “reached an understanding that Hall would issue correspondence
asserting the existence of CyberTipline reports associated with one or more of Plaintiff’s
identifiers,” as explicitly requested by the subpoena, “while motions directed at the same discovery
remained pending” in the 286 and 376 Actions. FAC ¶ 124. Plaintiff alleges that “[t]he purpose of
the understanding” between Meta and NCMEC was to “deter Plaintiff . . . from continuing to
attend the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party.” FAC ¶ 158.
Based on these allegations, the FAC raises two causes of action against Meta:
(1) conspiracy to deter a party from attending and testifying in courts of the United States under
42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) (Count IV) and (2) Common Law Conspiracy (Count V). The FAC also

7


alleges causes of action for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress (“IIED”), and
“insulting words” against NCMEC and Hall alone.
III.

LEGAL STANDARD
“To survive a motion to dismiss under Federal Rule 12(b)(6), a [p]laintiff must ‘provide

the grounds of his entitlement to relief,’ including ‘enough facts to state a claim to relief that is
plausible on its face.’” Schmidt v. Synchrony Bank, No. 22-cv-344, 2022 WL 18635838, at *1 (E.D.
Va. June 14, 2022) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007)). When
determining whether the complaint plausibly states a claim, the court may also “consider
documents attached to the complaint, . . . as well as ‘documents incorporated into the complaint
by reference, and matters of which the court may take judicial notice.’” Barry v. Novartis Pharms.
Corp., No. 3:22-cv-196, 2022 WL 2373452, at *5 (E.D. Va. June 30, 2022) (quoting Tellabs, Inc.
v. Makor Issues & Rts., Ltd., 551 U.S. 308, 322 (2007)); see also Fed. R. Evid. 201; In re Ironnet,
Inc., No. 1:22-cv-449, 2023 WL 5110932, at *4 n.7 (E.D. Va. Aug. 9, 2023) (noting “U.S.
government documents, and ‘documents found on government websites’ are ‘the proper subject of
judicial notice’” (citation omitted)).
“Although allegations in a pro se complaint are construed liberally, a pro se complaint must
still allege a plausible claim for relief.” Leggo v. M.C. Dean, Inc., No. 1:22-cv-374, 2023 WL
1822383, at *1 (E.D. Va. Feb. 7, 2023).
IV.

ARGUMENT
A. Plaintiff Fails to State a Claim Under Section 1985(2)
In relevant part, 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) prohibits “two or more persons” from conspiring “to

deter, by force, intimidation, or threat, any party or witness in any court of the United States from
attending such court, or from testifying to any matter pending therein, freely, fully, and truthfully.”

8


42 U.S.C. § 1985(2). To establish a claim under the first clause of Section 1985(2)—the clause
Plaintiff invokes here (FAC ¶ 11)—a plaintiff must allege (1) a conspiracy, (2) to deter attendance
in court or testimony by force or intimidation and (3) injury to the plaintiff. See Glynn v. Impact
Sci. & Tech., Inc., 807 F. Supp. 2d 391, 422 (D. Md. 2011). Plaintiff fails to sufficiently plead a
single element.
1. Plaintiff Fails to Plausibly Allege Any Agreement
To start, the FAC fundamentally fails to plausibly allege a conspiracy between Meta and
either NCMEC or Hall in non-conclusory terms. Under Fourth Circuit law, to allege a conspiracy,
a plaintiff “must plead facts amounting to more than ‘parallel conduct and a bare assertion of
conspiracy.’” A Society Without a Name v. Virginia, 655 F.3d 342, 346 (4th Cir. 2011) (citation
omitted). To establish a conspiracy, “[t]he factual allegations must plausibly suggest agreement,
rather than being merely consistent with agreement.” Id. The pleading burden for such claims are
high—the Fourth Circuit has noted that it has “rarely, if ever, found that a plaintiff has set forth
sufficient facts to establish a section 1985 conspiracy.” Simmons v. Poe, 47 F.3d 1370, 1377 (4th
Cir. 1995).
Here, the FAC’s allegations of an agreement between Meta and the NCMEC Defendants
are exactly the type of conclusory allegations that do not plausibly suggest an agreement. Indeed,
the FAC does not even allege parallel conduct; it alleges contradictory conduct—namely, that Meta
engaged in motion practice on April 21, 2026, to try to prevent the exact discovery that Hall and
NCMEC provided on April 22, 2026. FAC ¶¶ 127; 130. Based solely on these contradictory
actions, and Meta’s alleged knowledge of the subpoenas and the NCMEC Defendant’s alleged
knowledge of the 286 and 376 Actions, the FAC jumps to the conclusion that Meta conspired with

9


the NCMEC Defendants to have Hall issue correspondence asserting the existence of CyberTipline
reports associated with one or more of Plaintiff’s identifiers. FAC ¶¶ 137-38.
This plainly does not suffice to meet Plaintiff’s burden to plead an agreement. See, e.g.,
Johnson v. Henrico Cnty Bd. of Supervisors, 751 F. Supp. 3d 627, 647 (E.D. Va. 2024) (dismissing
conspiracy claim as “’highly conclusory” where plaintiff alleged defendants conspired to harass
him, noting that “the fact that a bus drove by his property when he was there and honked” is merely
“parallel conduct that does not adequately support an allegation of conspiracy”). Even putting
aside the contradictory nature of Meta’s and the NCMEC Defendant’s conduct (with Meta seeking
to stay discovery and NCMEC providing it), the coincidental timing of the joint motion to stay
discovery and the NCMEC letters is perfectly consistent with independent, non-conspiratorial
conduct. As Plaintiff notes, Meta (and the co-defendants in the relevant actions) filed the joint
motion to stay discovery on April 21 in part to halt the “imminent” depositions Plaintiff noticed,
which were scheduled for April 28-30. FAC ¶ 128. In turn, NCMEC’s response to Plaintiff was
sent roughly two weeks after Plaintiff sent NCMEC the subpoena, a reasonable amount of time for
NCMEC to review the subpoena’s discrete request and collect responsive information.
FAC ¶¶ 126; 130. Especially in light of these reasonable explanations for the parallel timing,
Plaintiff’s conclusory assertion that the filing of the joint motion to stay discovery and NCMEC’s
letter must be the product of an agreement is untenable. See, e.g., Feeley v. Total Realty Mgmt.,
660 F. Supp. 2d 700, 712 (E.D. Va. 2009) (dismissing conspiracy claims where “[n]othing in the
[complaint] elevates the allegations from possible parallel conduct to an indication that there was
an actual meeting of the minds”); see also Azimi v. Zug, No. 3:25-cv-00041, 2026 WL 701680, at
*5 (W.D. Va. Mar. 12, 2026) (“The Fourth Circuit has instructed that ‘[a]llegations of parallel

10


conduct and a bare assertion of a conspiracy are not enough for a claim to proceed.’” (quoting
Thomas v. Salvation Army S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632, 637 (4th Cir. 2016))).
2. Plaintiff Fails to Allege Any Use of “Force, Intimidation or Threats,” Much
Less to Deter his Lawsuits
Plaintiff also fails to allege any “use of force, intimidation or threats” by Meta or others,
much less any such use of force, intimidation, or threats intended to deter Plaintiff from continuing
participation in his various lawsuits, as is necessary to state a Section 1985(2) claim. See Kegege
v. Breitenstein, No. 20-1066, 2025 WL 2306528, at *3 (D. Md. Aug. 11, 1025) (quoting Scott v.
Mountain Mission Sch., Inc., 809 F.2d 786, 1987 WL 36169, at *2 (4th Cir. 1987)).
Here, Plaintiff alleges only that the NCMEC Defendants responded to subpoenas that he
sent them and provided him with exactly what he asked for, albeit allegedly prematurely. Compare
FAC ¶¶ 55-56 (admitting he “transmitted . . . Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas” that
requested “a document sufficient to show whether NCMEC received or maintains any
CyberTipline report concerning” two variations of his name and his email address), with id. ¶ 77
(admitting that NCMEC provided two letters that provided exactly that information). That is not a
threat, it is professional courtesy. And the FAC does not allege that Meta communicated with
Plaintiff at all regarding the subpoenas or NCMEC’s responses. See FAC ¶¶ 158-64. Accordingly,
Plaintiff’s failure to identify any force, intimidation, or threats by anyone is independently fatal to
his Section 1985(2) claim. See Glynn, 807 F. Supp. 2d at 422 (dismissing Section 1985(2) claim
premised on defendant allegedly “pursu[ing] its counterclaims against [plaintiff] in a retaliatory
and heavy-handed manner” because “legal claims possessing a reasonable basis . . . do not
constitute the ‘force or intimidation’ necessary to satisfy § 1985(2)” (citation omitted)); see also
Grezak v. Ropes & Gray, LLP, No. 3:15-CV-02111, 2018 WL 4289338, at *14 (M.D. Pa. May 16,

11


2018) (allegation that defendant “left a phone call” with Plaintiff which “made [plaintiff] nervous
to attend” court proceeding was insufficient to allege claim under Section 1985(2)).
3. Plaintiff fails to plead injury
Even assuming that Plaintiff could theoretically be injured by receiving discovery that he
himself requested, Plaintiff fails to plead any facts showing that the discovery actually impacted
his ability to testify or pursue his claim. To sufficiently plead injury for a Section 1985(2) claim,
Plaintiff needs to plead facts that show “he was actually hindered from providing truthful testimony
or that the intimidation had any impact at all on his potential testimony or the federal proceeding.”
Kimberlin v. Hunton & Williams LLP, No. GJH-15-723, 2016 WL 1270982, at *6 (D. Md. Mar.
29, 2016); see also Kegege, 2025 WL 2306528, at *3 (dismissing §1985(2) claim because none
“of the alleged conduct . . . can be fairly construed to constitute deterring court attendance or
testimony . . . or injuring someone for having attended or testified in court”). Here, Plaintiff does
not and cannot do so.1 Indeed, Plaintiff admits he continued to pursue both actions, FAC ¶ 178,
and his conclusory allegation that he did so “at materially diminished capacity” has no factual
support. Id. Indeed, judicially noticeable documents show that he has continued to aggressively
pursue both actions.2
Because the FAC fails to plausibly allege that any of Meta’s alleged conduct was intended
to unlawfully deter from pursuing his claims against Meta, his Section 1985(2) claim fails.

1

Moreover, to the extent that “attending [federal] court” for purposes of Section 1985(2) is interpreted as requiring
physical presence at a court proceeding, and not merely the filing of a lawsuit, Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim
would fail for that reason as well. See, e.g., Ho v. City of Long Beach, Pub. Works, No. 2:19-cv-09430, 2020 WL
695887, at *9 n.6 (C.D. Cal. Jan. 15, 2020) (“[T]o the extent § 1985(2) requires Defendants to have acted to deter
Plaintiff from . . . attending . . . an actual proceeding, then Plaintiff cannot state a claim, because the prior action was
dismissed without any such proceedings.”).
2
In the 376 Action, following transfer to the Northern District of California, Plaintiff filed a Motion for Leave to
File a Second Amended Complaint, which the Court granted, and Defendants there have once again moved to
dismiss his Second Amended Complaint. Ballentine 2, Dkt. Nos. 141, 151, 152. In the 286 Action, following the
court’s dismissal of Plaintiff’s Complaint for failing to comply with a standing order, Plaintiff appealed the dismissal
to the 11th Circuit and has already filed his opening brief. See Ballentine 3, Dkt. Nos. 80, 82.

12


B. Plaintiff’s Common Law Conspiracy Claim Fails
Plaintiff’s claim for common law conspiracy against Meta fails for similar reasons. To state a
claim for common law conspiracy under Virginia law, “a plaintiff must allege sufficient facts to
show (1) an agreement between two or more persons (2) to accomplish an unlawful purpose or to
accomplish a lawful purpose by unlawful means, which (3) results in damage to the plaintiff.”
Adkins v. Whole Foods Mkt. Grp., Inc., No. 1:16-cv-00031, 2016 WL 1367170, at *2 (E.D. Va.
Apr. 5, 2016). “[T]o satisfy the ‘unlawful’ element” under Virginia law “at least one member of
the conspiracy must commit an ‘underlying tort.’” Kissinger-Stankevitz v. Town of Tappahannock,
750 F. Supp 3d 590, 624 (E.D. Va. 2024) (quoting Firestone v. Wiley, 485 F. Supp. 2d 694, 703
(E.D. Va. 2007)).
First, as was the case for his Section 1985(2) claim, Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy
claim fails because he fails to allege any non-conclusory facts showing an agreement between
Meta and the NCMEC Defendants sufficient to plausibly allege a conspiracy. See supra at Section
IV.A.1; Moschetti v. Nixon Peabody, LLP, No. 3:23-cv-389, 2024 WL 2750010, at *12 (E.D. Va.
May 29, 2024) (dismissing common law conspiracy where “the Complaint lacks factual allegations
of an agreement between the conspirators” and is instead “littered with conclusory language”);
Johnson v. Kaugars, 14 Va. Cir. 172, 1988 WL 619378, at *3 (Va. Cir. Ct. 1988) (“[I]t is not enough
merely to state that a conspiracy took place.”).
Second, Plaintiff also fails to allege the requisite unlawfulness for his common law
conspiracy claim because the FAC fails to adequately allege any underlying tort. See Am. Airlines,
Inc. v. Shahi World & Travels, LLC, No. 1:20-CV-17, 2023 WL 3952332, at *8 (E.D. Va. June 12,
2023) (holding that conspiracy claims require “proof that an underlying tort was committed”
(citation omitted)). Even setting aside that Plaintiff has failed to plead any overt act by Meta or

13


any conspiracy with NCMEC or Hall, Plaintiff’s conspiracy claim fails because he fails to
adequately plead either defamation claim against NCMEC and Hall, which are the alleged
predicate torts. See FAC ¶¶ 246-51 (identifying Counts I and II as the alleged underlying torts).
Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy claim identifies the FAC’s defamation claims as its
predicate torts. See FAC ¶ 246. But, as explained in NCMEC and Hall’s Motion to Dismiss, the
alleged defamation claims fail for multiple independent reasons. See Dkt. No. 11. Among other
reasons, the defamation claims are barred by the litigation privilege because Plaintiff’s claims seek
to impose liability based on information contained in a response to subpoenas. See Lindeman v.
Lesnick, 268 Va. 532, 537 (2004) (holding that the litigation privilege “is broad in scope and
applies to communications made in proceedings pending in a court”). And, the NCMEC
Defendants also have statutory immunity from Plaintiff’s defamation claims pursuant to 18 U.S.C.
§ 2258D. See 18 U.S.C. § 2258D (barring “civil claim[s] . . . against NCMEC, including any
director, officer, employee, or agent of NCMEC, arising from the performance of the CyberTipline
responsibilities or functions”).
Because the FAC fails to plausibly allege the existence of any conspiracy to accomplish an
unlawful purpose or to accomplish a lawful purpose through an unlawful means, and fails to
plausibly allege any underlying tort, Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy claim fails.
V.

CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court dismiss the FAC with

prejudice.

14

PLAINTIFF’S PROPOSED SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT TO FIRST AMENDED
COMPLAINT
PURSUANT TO FED. R. CIV. P. 15(d)

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine, pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d),
supplements Count III of the operative First Amended Complaint with events occurring after that
pleading was filed. The First Amended Complaint remains unchanged. This Supplemental
Complaint adds no defendant, no cause of action, and no category of relief, and is directed solely to
Count III.

I. INCORPORATION AND SCOPE

1. Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement,

Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections of the First Amended
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 26-1 Filed 08/21/26 Page 2 of 8 PagelD#
Complaint; Sections A, B, C, G, H, I, J, M, and R of the Facts of the First Amended Complaint; and
Count III of the First Amended Complaint, as if fully set forth herein.

2. The allegations below supplement Count III only. They concern post-filing
knowledge, state of mind, acknowledged distress, continuation of the course of conduct alleged in
Count III, and Defendants’ present awareness that the person-level uncertainty created by the April
22, 2026 letters remains unresolved.

3. No independent cause of action is predicated on the filing of NCMEC’s August 12,
2026 memorandum or on the August 13, 2026 communication alleged below. Consistent with the
Scope of Allegations section of the First Amended Complaint, those post-filing events are alleged
solely as facts bearing on knowledge, state of mind, intent or recklessness, continuation of the
conduct alleged in Count III, and awareness of continuing injury.

II. POST-FILING EVENTS

4. On August 12, 2026, NCMEC filed its memorandum in support of its motion to
dismiss the First Amended Complaint. ECF No. 11. The memorandum was filed on behalf of
NCMEC and stated that, unless otherwise specified, its arguments applied equally to Defendant
Hall because she was at all relevant times an employee of NCMEC.

5. NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum expressly addressed the First Amended
Complaint’s allegations that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse; that, after receiving
the April 22, 2026 letters, Plaintiff vomited; that Plaintiff experienced recollections of childhood
sexual abuse; and that Plaintiff experienced fear of arrest and prosecution.

6. By August 12, 2026, NCMEC had actual knowledge of Plaintiff’s disclosed survivor
history and of the severe emotional distress Plaintiff alleged resulted from the April 22, 2026
letters.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 26-1 Filed 08/21/26 Page 3 of 8 PagelD#

7. In addressing Plaintiff’s falsity allegations, NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum
stated both that Plaintiff “does not have access to those reports” and that the asserted CyberTipline
linkage could concern Plaintiff, “a person with the same name,” or an email address.

8. NCMEC thereby acknowledged that the April 22, 2026 letters did not resolve whether
either asserted CyberTipline report concerned Plaintiff personally, another person with the same
name, or an email identifier.

9. NCMEC possesses the two CyberTipline reports underlying the April 22, 2026 letters.

10. Plaintiff does not possess or have access to those reports.

11. The April 22, 2026 letters do not identify which listed person or identifier
corresponds to either report.

12. As of August 12, 2026, the resulting person-level uncertainty remained unresolved
from Plaintiff’s perspective.

13. NCMEC knew that the uncertainty remained unresolved.

14. On August 13, 2026, Plaintiff sought clarification concerning the unresolved identity
question by asking counsel for NCMEC and Hall whether either CyberTipline report, as received
from the reporting provider, contained or identified: (1) Plaintiff’s full legal name, “Marvelle J.
Ballentine”; (2) the name “Jay Ballentine”; or (3) the email identifier jaychizza@icloud.com.

15. Counsel did not provide an answer resolving whether any of those identifiers
appeared in either provider-submitted report.

16. On August 13, 2026, one day after NCMEC filed its memorandum, counsel
representing NCMEC and Hall wrote to Plaintiff: “I read your email as being upset with the
language used in the memorandum—I did not intend to offend you with the phrasing, but my point
was you got exactly what you asked for, using the language you provided.”
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 26-1 Filed 08/21/26 Page 4 of 8 PagelD#

17. When counsel made the August 13, 2026 statement: NCMEC had demonstrated
actual knowledge of Plaintiff’s survivor history and of the emotional injuries pleaded in the First
Amended Complaint; counsel expressly acknowledged that Plaintiff was upset; the April 22, 2026
letters remained unretracted and uncorrected; NCMEC continued to possess the two underlying
CyberTipline reports; Plaintiff continued to lack access to those reports; and the person-level
uncertainty described in NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum remained unresolved.

18. The unresolved question whether either asserted CyberTipline report concerns
Plaintiff personally remained a continuing consequence of the April 22, 2026 letters after the filing
of the First Amended Complaint and continued to sustain the apprehension alleged in Count III.

Ill. SUPPLEMENT TO COUNT III
INTENTIONAL INFLICTION OF EMOTIONAL DISTRESS
(Against Defendants Katie Hall and NCMEC)

19. Plaintiff incorporates the preceding allegations of this Supplemental Complaint and
the allegations incorporated into Count III of the First Amended Complaint as though fully set forth
herein.

20. By August 12, 2026, NCMEC had actual knowledge of Plaintiff’s disclosed survivor
history and of the severe emotional distress Plaintiff alleged the April 22, 2026 letters caused. The
following day, counsel representing NCMEC and Hall acknowledged that Plaintiff was upset and
stated that Plaintiff “got exactly what you asked for, using the language you provided.”

21. The post-filing sequence — actual knowledge of the pleaded injuries,
acknowledgment of Plaintiff’s distress, continued possession of the information capable of
resolving the person-level uncertainty, continued knowledge that Plaintiff lacked access to that
information, and the August 13, 2026 statement — further supports Count III’s existing allegations
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document eet Filed 08/21/26 Page 5 of 8 PagelD#
that the course of conduct was intentional or reckless and was continued with knowledge of its
effect on Plaintiff.

22. NCMEC also knew that Plaintiff lacked access to the reports and that the April 22,
2026 letters had left unresolved whether either asserted report concerned Plaintiff personally,
another person with the same name, or an email identifier. Because that uncertainty remained
unresolved, the apprehension alleged in Count III continued after the filing of the First Amended
Complaint. Considered with the conduct already alleged in Count III, the post-filing events further
support the existing allegations concerning intent or recklessness, outrageousness, and continuing
injury.

IV. RELIEF

This Supplemental Complaint seeks no relief different from or additional to the relief
requested under Count III of the First Amended Complaint. Plaintiff respectfully requests that the
Court read this Supplemental Complaint together with the operative First Amended Complaint and
award the relief requested therein.

PLAINTIFF’S PROPOSED SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT TO FIRST AMENDED
COMPLAINT
PURSUANT TO FED. R. CIV. P. 15(d)

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine, pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d),
supplements Counts III and IV of the operative First Amended Complaint with events occurring
after that pleading was filed. The First Amended Complaint remains unchanged. This
Supplemental Complaint adds no defendant, no cause of action, and no category of relief, and is
directed solely to Counts III and IV.

I. INCORPORATION AND SCOPE

1. Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement,

Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections of the First Amended
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 26-2 Filed 08/21/26 Page 2 of 10 PagelD#
Complaint; Sections A, B, C, G, H, I, J, M, and R of the Facts of the First Amended Complaint; and
Counts III and IV of the First Amended Complaint, as if fully set forth herein.

2. The allegations below supplement Counts III and IV only. The allegations concerning
NCMEC and Hall concern post-filing knowledge, state of mind, acknowledged distress,
continuation of the course of conduct alleged in Count III, and awareness of continuing injury. The
allegations concerning Meta Platforms, Inc. concern post-filing knowledge, notice, state of mind,
and Meta’s demonstrated awareness of the relationship between this action and the Northern
District of California proceeding identified in Count IV.

3. No independent cause of action is predicated on the filing of NCMEC’s August 12,
2026 memorandum, on the August 13, 2026 communication by counsel for NCMEC and Hall, or
on the August 13, 2026 filing by Meta Platforms, Inc. and its co-defendants in the Northern District
of California alleged below. Consistent with the Scope of Allegations section of the First Amended
Complaint, those post-filing events are alleged solely as subsequent facts bearing on the existing
claims. The NCMEC and Hall events bear on knowledge, state of mind, intent or recklessness,
continuation of the conduct alleged in Count III, and awareness of continuing injury. Meta’s filing
bears on knowledge, notice, state of mind, and Meta’s awareness of the relationship between this
action and the Northern District of California proceeding, under Count IV.

II. POST-FILING EVENTS

A. NCMEC’S AUGUST 12, 2026 MEMORANDUM AND THE AUGUST 13, 2026

COMMUNICATIONS

4. On August 12, 2026, NCMEC filed its memorandum in support of its motion to
dismiss the First Amended Complaint. ECF No. 11. The memorandum was filed on behalf of
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 26° Filed 08/21/26 Page 3 of 10 PagelD#
NCMEC and stated that, unless otherwise specified, its arguments applied equally to Defendant
Hall because she was at all relevant times an employee of NCMEC.

5. NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum expressly addressed the First Amended
Complaint’s allegations that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse; that, after receiving
the April 22, 2026 letters, Plaintiff vomited; that Plaintiff experienced recollections of childhood
sexual abuse; and that Plaintiff experienced fear of arrest and prosecution.

6. By August 12, 2026, NCMEC had actual knowledge of Plaintiff’s disclosed survivor
history and of the severe emotional distress Plaintiff alleged resulted from the April 22, 2026
letters.

7. Inaddressing Plaintiff’s falsity allegations, NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum
stated both that Plaintiff “does not have access to those reports” and that the asserted CyberTipline
linkage could concern Plaintiff, “a person with the same name,” or an email address.

8. NCMEC thereby acknowledged that the April 22, 2026 letters did not resolve whether
either asserted CyberTipline report concerned Plaintiff personally, another person with the same
name, or an email identifier.

9. NCMEC possesses the two CyberTipline reports underlying the April 22, 2026 letters.

10. Plaintiff does not possess or have access to those reports.

11. The April 22, 2026 letters do not identify which listed person or identifier
corresponds to either report.

12. As of August 12, 2026, the resulting person-level uncertainty remained unresolved
from Plaintiff’s perspective.

13. NCMEC knew that the uncertainty remained unresolved.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 26-2 Filed 08/21/26 Page 4 of 10 PagelD#

14. On August 13, 2026, Plaintiff sought clarification concerning the unresolved identity
question by asking counsel for NCMEC and Hall whether either CyberTipline report, as received
from the reporting provider, contained or identified: (1) Plaintiff’s full legal name, “Marvelle J.
Ballentine”; (2) the name “Jay Ballentine”; or (3) the email identifier jaychizza@icloud.com.

15. Counsel did not provide an answer resolving whether any of those identifiers
appeared in either provider-submitted report.

16. On August 13, 2026, one day after NCMEC filed its memorandum, counsel
representing NCMEC and Hall wrote to Plaintiff: “I read your email as being upset with the
language used in the memorandum—I did not intend to offend you with the phrasing, but my point
was you got exactly what you asked for, using the language you provided.”

17. When counsel made the August 13, 2026 statement: NCMEC had demonstrated
actual knowledge of Plaintiff’s survivor history and of the emotional injuries pleaded in the First
Amended Complaint; counsel expressly acknowledged that Plaintiff was upset; the April 22, 2026
letters remained unretracted and uncorrected; NCMEC continued to possess the two underlying
CyberTipline reports; Plaintiff continued to lack access to those reports; and the person-level
uncertainty described in NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum remained unresolved.

18. The unresolved question whether either asserted CyberTipline report concerns
Plaintiff personally remained a continuing consequence of the April 22, 2026 letters after the filing
of the First Amended Complaint and continued to sustain the apprehension alleged in Count III.

B. META’S AUGUST 13, 2026 NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

FILING

19. On August 13, 2026, Meta Platforms, Inc., Accenture LLP, Genpact Limited, and
TaskUs, Inc. jointly filed a consolidated motion to dismiss Plaintiff’s Second Amended Complaint
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 262 Filed 08/21/26 Page 5 of 10 PagelD#
in Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D. Cal.), ECF No. 152. That
proceeding is the Northern District of California action referenced in Count IV of the First
Amended Complaint.

20. The August 13, 2026 filing expressly cited the present action by case number:
Ballentine v. Katie Hall, et al., No. 1:26-cv-02331 (E.D. Va.).

21. At page 4, footnote 3, ECF No. 152 characterized the present action as “a complaint
against the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) and its corporate
counsel in the Eastern District of Virginia based on allegedly defamatory language in a letter sent
by NCMEC to Plaintiff in response to a subpoena.”

22. When the August 13, 2026 filing was made, Meta was a named defendant in the
present action; Meta had been served in the present action on July 31, 2026; and the operative First
Amended Complaint asserted Count IV under the first clause of 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) against Meta
and other defendants.

23. Count IV alleges interference with Plaintiff’s participation as a party and prospective
witness in federal proceedings that include the litigation now pending as Ballentine v. Meta
Platforms, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D. Cal.).

24. Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing identified the present action. It did not identify Meta as
a defendant in the present action. It did not identify the claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) alleging
interference with Plaintiff’s participation in the Northern District of California proceeding in
which the filing was made.

25. Meta’s affirmative citation of the present action in the Northern District of California
proceeding demonstrates that, by August 13, 2026, Meta had actual knowledge of the existence of
the present action, of the relationship between the present action and the Northern District of
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 26-2 Filed 08/21/26 Page 6 of 10 PagelD#
California proceeding, and of the allegations asserted against Meta concerning Plaintiff’s
participation in that proceeding.

Ill. SUPPLEMENT TO COUNT III
INTENTIONAL INFLICTION OF EMOTIONAL DISTRESS
(Against Defendants Katie Hall and NCMEC)

26. Plaintiff incorporates the preceding allegations of this Supplemental Complaint and
the allegations incorporated into Count III of the First Amended Complaint as though fully set forth
herein.

27. By August 12, 2026, NCMEC had actual knowledge of Plaintiff’s disclosed survivor
history and of the severe emotional distress Plaintiff alleged the April 22, 2026 letters caused. The
following day, counsel representing NCMEC and Hall acknowledged that Plaintiff was upset and
stated that Plaintiff “got exactly what you asked for, using the language you provided.”

28. The post-filing sequence — actual knowledge of the pleaded _ injuries,
acknowledgment of Plaintiff’s distress, continued possession of the information capable of
resolving the person-level uncertainty, continued knowledge that Plaintiff lacked access to that
information, and the August 13, 2026 statement — further supports Count III’s existing allegations
that the course of conduct was intentional or reckless and was continued with knowledge of its
effect on Plaintiff.

29. NCMEC also knew that Plaintiff lacked access to the reports and that the April 22,
2026 letters had left unresolved whether either asserted report concermed Plaintiff personally,
another person with the same name, or an email identifier. Because that uncertainty remained
unresolved, the apprehension alleged in Count III continued after the filing of the First Amended
Complaint. Considered with the conduct already alleged in Count III, the post-filing events further
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 26-2 Filed 08/21/26 Page 7 of 10 PagelD#
support the existing allegations concerning intent or recklessness, outrageousness, and continuing
injury.

IV. SUPPLEMENT TO COUNT IV
CONSPIRACY TO DETER A PARTY AND WITNESS, BY INTIMIDATION,
FROM ATTENDING AND TESTIFYING IN COURTS OF THE
UNITED STATES — 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2)

30. Plaintiff incorporates the preceding allegations of this Supplemental Complaint and
the allegations incorporated into Count IV of the First Amended Complaint as though fully set
forth herein.

31. Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing expressly invoked the present action in the Northern
District of California proceeding identified in Count IV. The filing demonstrates Meta’s actual
post-filing knowledge of the relationship between the two proceedings. The filing was made while
Meta was a named and served defendant in the present action, and after Count IV had alleged
interference with Plaintiff’s participation in the Northern District of California litigation.

32. The August 13, 2026 filing is pleaded as a subsequent fact bearing on Meta’s
knowledge, Meta’s state of mind, Meta’s awareness of the relationship between the present action
and the Northern District of California proceeding, and the existing circumstantial allegations
supporting Count IV. Liability under Count IV remains predicated on the conduct alleged in the
First Amended Complaint.

V. RELIEF

This Supplemental Complaint seeks no relief different from or additional to the relief

requested under Counts III and IV of the First Amended Complaint. Plaintiff respectfully requests
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 26-2 Filed 08/21/26 Page 8 of 10 PagelD#
317

that the Court read this Supplemental Complaint together with the operative First Amended
Complaint and award the relief requested therein.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF'S MOTION FOR LEAVE
TO FILE SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT PURSUANT TO
FEDERAL RULE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE 15(d)
INTRODUCTION
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d) permits a party, on motion and reasonable notice, to
serve a supplemental pleading setting out events that happened after the date of the pleading to be
supplemented. Every event pleaded in Exhibit A occurred after the First Amended Complaint was
filed.
As to Count III, Exhibit A pleads that NCMEC's August 12, 2026 memorandum
demonstrated actual knowledge of Plaintiff's pleaded injuries and disclosed survivor history and
acknowledged that the person-level referent of the April 22, 2026 letters remains unresolved; that
on August 13, 2026, counsel for NCMEC and Hall acknowledged that Plaintiff was upset and


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

Document 27

Filed 08/21/26

Page 2 of 6 PageID# 321

stated that Plaintiff "got exactly what you asked for"; and that the unresolved uncertainty
continued.
As to Count IV, Exhibit A pleads that on August 13, 2026, Meta Platforms, Inc. and the
other Northern District of California defendants filed a consolidated motion to dismiss, ECF No.
152, that expressly cited this action; that the filing described this matter as litigation against
NCMEC and its corporate counsel; that Meta was already a named and served defendant here; that
Count IV asserts a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) against Meta concerning interference with
Plaintiff's participation in that Northern District of California proceeding; and that the filing did
not identify those facts. The event is pleaded as evidence of Meta's knowledge, state of mind, and
awareness of the relationship between the two proceedings.
The Motion is narrow. It involves the same parties, the same causes of action, and the same
requested relief. It supplements two existing counts and leaves the First Amended Complaint
otherwise unchanged. Leave should be granted.
BACKGROUND
A.

The First Amended Complaint

The First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) is the operative pleading. Count III asserts
intentional infliction of emotional distress against Defendants Hall and NCMEC. Count IV asserts
a claim under the first clause of 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) concerning alleged interference with
Plaintiff's participation as a party and prospective witness in federal proceedings, including the
proceeding now pending as Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D.
Cal.).
B.

The August 12-13, 2026 NCMEC and Hall Events


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

Document 27

Filed 08/21/26

Page 3 of 6 PageID# 322

On August 12, 2026, NCMEC filed its memorandum in support of its motion to dismiss.
ECF No. 11. The memorandum expressly addressed the First Amended Complaint's allegations
that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse and that Plaintiff vomited, experienced
recollections of childhood sexual abuse, and feared arrest and prosecution after receiving the April
22, 2026 letters. The memorandum stated that Plaintiff "does not have access to those reports" and
described the asserted CyberTipline linkage as one that could concern Plaintiff, "a person with the
same name," or an email address.
On August 13, 2026, Plaintiff asked counsel for NCMEC and Hall whether either report, as
received, contained or identified his legal name, the name he uses, or his email identifier. Counsel
did not provide an answer resolving the question, and wrote: "I read your email as being upset with
the language used in the memorandum-I did not intend to offend you with the phrasing, but my
point was you got exactly what you asked for, using the language you provided." The person-level
uncertainty remains unresolved.

C.

Meta's August 13, 2026 Northern District of California Filing

On August 13, 2026, Meta Platforms, Inc., Accenture LLP, Genpact Limited, and TaskUs,
Inc. jointly filed a consolidated motion to dismiss in No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL. ECF No. 152. The
filing expressly cited the present action and described it as "a complaint against the National Center
for Missing & Exploited Children ('NCMEC') and its corporate counsel in the Eastern District of
Virginia based on allegedly defamatory language in a letter sent by NCMEC to Plaintiff in
response to a subpoena." ECF No. 152 at 4 n.3. When the filing was made, Meta was a named
defendant in this action, served on July 31, 2026, and Count IV asserted a claim under 42 U.S.C. §
1985(2) against Meta concerning Plaintiff's participation in the Northern District of California


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

Document 27

Filed 08/21/26

Page 4 of 6 PageID# 323

litigation. The filing did not identify Meta's status as a defendant here and did not identify that
Count IV allegation.
LEGAL STANDARD
Rule 15(d) provides that, on motion and reasonable notice, the Court may, on just terms,
permit a party to serve a supplemental pleading setting out any transaction, occurrence, or event
that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented. Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d).
A supplemental pleading concerns matters occurring after the filing of the pleading being
supplemented. The standards governing amendment under Rule 15(a) and supplementation under
Rule 15(d) are nearly identical: leave should be freely granted, and denial requires a good reason,
such as prejudice to the opposing party. Franks v. Ross, 313 F.3d 184, 198 n.15 (4th Cir. 2002).
ARGUMENT
I.

The Proposed Supplement Properly Pleads Subsequent Events Directly
Related to Existing Claims.

A.

The August 12-13 Events Directly Supplement Count III.

The August 12 and 13, 2026 events occurred after the First Amended Complaint was filed.
They concern the Defendants already named in Count III. They concern those Defendants' postfiling knowledge of the injuries already pleaded, their acknowledged awareness that Plaintiff
remained distressed, their continued possession of the information capable of resolving the
uncertainty already alleged, and the continuing injury already pleaded. The supplement uses the
post-filing events to bear on existing allegations concerning knowledge, intent or recklessness,
outrageousness, and continuing injury. Exhibit A does not allege that the August 12 memorandum
or the August 13 communication independently satisfies the elements of intentional infliction of
emotional distress.


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

B.

Document 27

Filed 08/21/26

Page 5 of 6 PageID# 324

Meta's August 13 Filing Directly Supplements Count IV.

Count IV already concerns alleged interference with Plaintiff's participation in federal
proceedings, including the Northern District of California litigation. Meta's August 13, 2026 event
occurred inside that same litigation. Meta affirmatively invoked the present action there. Meta was
already a defendant here, and already faced Count IV, when it made the filing. The event therefore
supplies a subsequent fact concerning Meta's actual knowledge and its awareness of the
relationship between the two proceedings. The proposed Supplemental Complaint does not seek
liability based on Meta's filing of ECF No. 152 or on any statement contained in that filing. The
filing is alleged as evidence bearing on knowledge, notice, state of mind, and the existing
circumstantial allegations supporting Count IV.
II.

The Proposed Supplement Causes No Prejudice and Does Not Expand the

Action.
Six facts define the scope of the request. The supplement adds no new party. It adds no new
cause of action. It adds no new relief. It supplements only Counts III and IV. The subsequent events
it pleads were created by or on behalf of the existing Defendants -NCMEC's own memorandum,
its counsel's own communication, and Meta's own filing- so their existence presents no surprise
to any Defendant. And Plaintiff sought supplementation promptly after the events occurred. The
First Amended Complaint remains otherwise unchanged. The proposed supplementation permits
the existing controversy to be adjudicated on a factual record that includes subsequent events
directly related to existing claims.


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

III.

Document 27

Filed 08/21/26

Page 6 of 6 PageID# 325

The Pending Rule 12 Posture Does Not Make Supplementation Futile.

Rule 15(d) expressly permits subsequent events to be added to an existing pleading. The
presence of pending Rule 12 motions does not change the temporal character or the relevance of
those subsequent events.
Exhibit A does not create independent causes of action from the post-filing litigation
statements. For Count III, the subsequent events bear on existing issues of knowledge, state of
mind, intent or recklessness, and continuing injury. For Count IV, Meta's filing bears on existing
issues of knowledge, awareness, state of mind, and circumstantial evidence.
The question this Motion presents is whether the subsequent events may be pleaded, not
whether Counts III and IV ultimately succeed. The Court can grant leave without resolving the
merits of either count.
CONCLUSION
The Court should grant Plaintiff leave under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d) to file
the Proposed Supplemental Complaint attached as Exhibit A.

Date: August 20, 2026

Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine
Plaintiff, pro se

PLAINTIFF’S RULE 15(d) MOTION

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine respectfully moves to continue the September 25, 2026
hearing on the Motion to Dismiss of Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
(“NCMEC”) until after the Court resolves Plaintiff's Motion for Leave to File Supplemental
Complaint pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d).

NCMEC filed its Motion to Dismiss on August 12, 2026 and has noticed that motion for
hearing on September 25, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. Plaintiff is separately moving under Rule 15(d) for
leave to supplement Count III with events occurring after the First Amended Complaint was filed
and is noticing that motion for hearing on September 25, 2026.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 29 Filed 08/20/26 Page 2 of 5 PagelD# 331

The Rule 15(d) motion bears directly on the pleading that will govern adjudication of Count
III. NCMEC’s pending Motion to Dismiss expressly seeks dismissal of Count III for failure to
plead intentional or reckless conduct and sufficiently outrageous conduct. Plaintiff’s proposed
supplemental pleading adds post-filing allegations directed to NCMEC’s subsequently
demonstrated knowledge, acknowledged distress, intent or recklessness, continuation of the
alleged course of conduct, and awareness of continuing injury.

Under Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d), if supplementation is permitted, the Court may also order the
opposing party to plead to the supplemental pleading within a specified time. Resolving the Rule
15(d) motion first will therefore establish whether the supplemental allegations are properly before
the Court and permit the Court to determine what further response, if any, should precede oral
argument on NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss.

Plaintiff does not seek an extension of the briefing schedule on NCMEC’s Motion to
Dismiss or withdrawal of that motion. Plaintiff requests only that oral argument on the Motion to
Dismiss be continued until the Court has resolved the Rule 15(d) motion and established the
resulting pleading and briefing posture.

Local Civil Rule 7(G) provides that a continuance of a hearing date requires Court action
and is not accomplished merely by agreement of the parties. E.D. Va. Loc. Civ. R. 7(G).

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court continue the September 25,
2026 hearing on NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss pending resolution of Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave
to File Supplemental Complaint under Rule 15(d), while leaving the September 25, 2026 hearing
on Plaintiff’s Rule 15(d) motion undisturbed, and reset oral argument on NCMEC’s Motion to
Dismiss as appropriate thereafter.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 32 Filed 08/26/26 Page 1 of 5 PagelD# 363
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
Alexandria Division

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE, )

THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR

OPPOSITION OF DEFENDANT THE NATIONAL CENTER
FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN
TO PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT

Defendant the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”), by and
through undersigned counsel and pursuant to the Rules and Orders of this Honorable Court,
hereby respectfully opposes the pro se Plaintiff’s “Motion for Leave to File Supplemental

Complaint Pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d)” [Doc. 26] on the basis of futility.

In further support, NCMEC states as follows:
I. PROCEDURAL HISTORY & FACTUAL SETTING

Pro Se Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine filed a substantively-identical Complaint against
NCMEC (and its employee, Ms. Katie Hall, Esq.) in Ballentine v. NCMEC, et al., Case No. 1:26-
cv-01341-MSN-WPB in this Court on May 19, 2026. On July 17, 2026, the Honorable Judge
Nachmanoff granted a motion to stay discovery in that matter, staying discovery pending
resolution of NCMEC’s then-pending motion to dismiss. On July 27, 2026, Plaintiff filed a
motion for leave to amend his Complaint in that matter, which was opposed on the grounds of
futility by NCMEC on July 29, 2026. On the same day as NCMEC’s Opposition was filed,
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 32 Filed 08/26/26 Page 2 of 5 PagelD# 364
Plaintiff filed a notice of voluntary dismissal, and filed the original Complaint in this matter on
July 30, 2026. On August 6, 2026, Plaintiff filed a First Amended Complaint [Doc. 5]. On
August 12, 2026, NCMEC filed a Motion to Dismiss. [Doc. 10] That Motion has been set for a
hearing on September 25, 2026.

Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File Supplemental Complaint appears to be predicated on
the concept that Plaintiff seeks to add allegations related to arguments set forth in NCMEC’s
August 12 Motion to Dismiss; a communication between undersigned counsel and Plaintiff on
August 13, 2026; and a Motion to Dismiss filed by co-defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (along
with numerous other defendants) in Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Case No. 3:26-cv-
005939-RFL (N.D. Cal.).

A. August 12, 2026 Motion to Dismiss

As for this issue, Plaintiff alleges that NCMEC—in arguments in NCMEC’s
Memorandum in Support of its Motion to Dismiss— showed “actual knowledge of Plaintiff’s

i pleaded injuries and disclosed survivor history, acknowledged... that the person-level referent of
the April 22, 2026 letters remains unresolved...” It is unclear from Plaintiff’s Motion, or his
Memorandum in Support [Doc. 27] how arguments in NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss have any
relevance to the matter. Neither the Motion to Dismiss, nor Memorandum in Support, revealed
any new information—the motion simply argues that Plaintiff has failed to state a claim upon
which relief may be granted. Nor does Plaintiff provide any explanation as to why NCMEC’s
counsel—addressing allegations in the First Amended Complaint—would have any impact on
the knowledge of NCMEC or any other defendant. For example, acknowledging that Plaintiff
alleges he experienced distress does not introduce any new facts into evidence, nor demonstrate
“actual knowledge of Plaintiff’s pleaded injuries...” Nor do arguments in motions practice, as a

2
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 32 _ Filed 08/26/26 Page 3 of 5 PagelD# 365
general rule, create any basis for legal action. Plaintiff sets forth no authority to suggest that is
the case—and sets forth no cognizable explanation as to why the Motion to Dismiss would have
any bearing on substantive claims in this matter.

B. August 13, 2026 Communication

Next, Plaintiff alleges that on August 13, 2026, undersigned counsel wrote to Mr.
Ballentine and attempted to make clear that no offense was intended to Mr. Ballentine for
language used in the Memorandum in support of NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss. See Doc. 27 at
p. 3. Plaintiff had expressed displeasure with that phrasing in a prior email. Undersigned
counsel responded to voluminous correspondence from Plaintiff, set forth his clients’ position as
to requests from Mr. Ballentine, and advised him that no offense was intended.! Again, it is
entirely unclear how that could form the basis for any liability on the part of NCMEC—r how it
informs any claim as to what NCMEC, or its employee, is claimed to have done.

C. Meta August 13, 2026 Filing

; While NCMEC is aware of Plaintiff’s ongoing litigation in other districts, NCMEC is not
tracking the filings in those matters. Plaintiff appears to be upset with the manner in which co-
defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. described this litigation, in parallel litigation pending in the U.S.
District Court for the Northern District of California. Again, Plaintiff does not articulate how
that filing impacts any claims or defenses in this matter—it certainly would not appear to
implicate NCMEC in any way.
1 To the extent the Court would like to review the email exchange, undersigned counsel would be happy to
submit it as an exhibit upon the Court’s request. However, given that such an innocuous attempt at polite
discourse is being utilized to serve as the basis for amendment of pleadings, undersigned counsel is
reluctant to introduce new grounds for grievance by Plaintiff, unless requested by the Court.
3
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 32 Filed 08/26/26 Page 4 of 5 PagelD# 366

Il. ARGUMENT

Rule 15(d) provides in relevant part that “[o]n motion and reasonable notice, the court
may, on just terms, permit a party to serve a supplemental pleading setting out any transaction,
occurrence, or event that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented...”
“(D]istrict courts use ‘nearly identical’ standards of review when ruling on motions to amend
pleadings versus motions to supplement them.” Cole v. Lucid USA, Inc., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS
158618, *3 (W.D. Va. 2025) (internal citations omitted). “In either situation, leave should be
freely granted, and should be denied only where good reason exists... The court may also ‘deny
leave to supplement or amend where the proposed supplement is clearly insufficient or frivolous
on its face.” Id. (quoting Anand v. Ocwen Loan Serv’g, 754 F.3d 195, 200 (4th Cir. 2014)).
Stated somewhat differently, “[m]Jotions to amend or supplement ‘should generally be denied in
instances of futility, undue delay, bad faith or dilatory motive, [etc.]...” Wood v. Yancey, 2025
U.S. Dist. LEXIS 168390, *4-5 (E.D. Va. 2025) (internal citations omitted).

: NCMEC respectfully submits that Plaintiff’s request to supplement the First Amended
Complaint is frivolous and futile. Undersigned counsel can find no authority to suggest that Rule
15(d) is intended to be used to enable a litigant to complain about language utilized in a motion,
while the matter is underway—or for an attempt at professionalism to discourage perceived
offense. (Similarly, the manner in which a separate defendant—trepresented by separate
counsel—characterizes the litigation would seem to have no importance, either.) Flatly put, the
supplementation requested does not appear to have any impact whatsoever on the claims asserted
in the First Amended Complaint, nor on the arguments set forth in NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss.
It remains entirely unclear how the supplementation would in any way inform the central theme
of Plaintiff’s claiam—that NCMEC allegedly defamed Plaintiff by imputation by responding as

4
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 32 Filed 08/26/26 Page 5 of 5 PagelD# 367
requested to subpoenas. Rather, it certainly appears that this is a further attempt to prolong what
NCMEC believes is frivolous litigation. Given the lack of any meaningful explanation as to why
supplementation is necessary, and given the events Plaintiff claims give rise to the need for
supplementation, NCMEC respectfully submits that Plaintiff's Motion should be denied.

Respectfully submitted,
JORDAN COYNE LLP

Fairfax, VA 22030

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 33 Filed 08/26/26 Page 1 of 5 PagelD# 368
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
Alexandria Division
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE, )
Plaintiff,
V. Case No. 1:26-CV-02331-RDA-IDD
THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR
MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN, _ )
ETAL., )

Defendants.

OPPOSITION OF DEFENDANT THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING
& EXPLOITED CHILDREN TO PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE
TO SERVE LIMITED DISCOVERY UNDER RULE 26(d)(1)

Defendant the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (““NCMEC”), by and
through undersigned counsel and pursuant to the Rules and Orders of this Honorable Court,
hereby respectfully opposes the pro se Plaintiff’s “Motion for Leave to Serve Three Limited

; Interrogatories on NCMEC before the Rule 26(f) Conference.” [Doc. 15] NCMEC respectfully
submits that the Motion should be denied, on the basis that Plaintiff has yet to establish the
existence of a claim upon which relief may be granted as to NCMEC, and Plaintiff has not
demonstrated any unusual circumstances or other grounds for the imposition of premature
discovery in this matter. In further support, NCMEC states as follows:

I. PROCEDURAL HISTORY

This matter arises out of three subpoenas that were sent by Plaintiff to NCMEC, inquiring
as to whether NCMEC had received CyberTipline reports, and requesting “a document sufficient
to show whether NCMEC received or maintains any CyberTipline report concerning (1)
Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account level identifier
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 33 Filed 08/26/26 Page 2 of 5 PagelD# 369
jaychizza@icloud.com.” Amend. Compl. [Doc. 5] at § 56. NCMEC, without awaiting formal
service, responded to Plaintiff, and advised that “NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline
reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level
identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.” Jd. at 77. Plaintiff
alleges that this response was tortious and actionable as defamation by imputation, and alleges a
conspiracy between the defendants hereto.

The Amended Complaint in this matter is the third iteration of a claim against NCMEC
(and its employee, Ms. Katie Hall, Esq.). Plaintiff initially filed a substantively-identical
complaint against NCMEC and Ms. Hall in Ballentine v. NCMEC, et al., Case No. 1:26-cv-
01341-MSN-WPB in this Court on May 19, 2026. On July 17, 2026, the Honorable Judge
Nachmanoff granted a motion to stay discovery in that matter, staying discovery pending
resolution of NCMEC’s then-pending motion to dismiss. On July 27, 2026, Plaintiff filed a
motion for leave to amend his Complaint in that matter, which was opposed on the grounds of

1 futility by NCMEC on July 29, 2026. On the same day as NCMEC’s Opposition was filed,

Plaintiff filed a notice of voluntary dismissal, and filed the original Complaint in this matter on
July 30, 2026. On August 12, 2026, NCMEC filed a Motion to Dismiss. [Doc. 10] That Motion
has been set for a hearing on September 25, 2026. Plaintiff has filed a “Protective Opposition” to
that motion, alleging that the Opposition demonstrates that NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss is
without merit, “without awaiting, and without prejudice to, Plaintiff’s forthcoming motion for
leave to file a supplemental pleading under Rule 15(d).” Doc. 20 at p. 1.
Il. PLAINTIFF’S MOTION UNDER RULE 26(d)(1)

Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to conduct early discovery in this matter appears to be
predicated on an argument set forth in NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss—namely, that Plaintiff

2
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 33 Filed 08/26/26 Page 3 of 5 PagelD# 370
cannot plausibly allege that the allegedly-actionable statements are not, in fact, true. That is
entirely accurate; the CyberTipline system is not publicly-accessible for obvious reasons, and
while Plaintiff can allege that the representations as to its contents are untrue, he has no factual
basis for doing so. In other words, that claim is conclusory. While not expressly stated in
Plaintiff’s Motion, it appears his request for discovery is to ascertain whether he has a viable
claim.

lil. ARGUMENT

Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1) provides that “[a] party may not seek discovery from any source
before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f), except in a proceeding exempted
from initial disclosure under Rule 26(a)(1)(B), or when authorized by these rules, by stipulation,
or by court order.” (Plaintiff was advised that to the extent Plaintiff desired to have a Rule 26(f)
conferral in this matter prior to the Court’s ruling on NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss, NCMEC
would move to stay that requirement pending resolution.) The Court has “wide latitude in

: controlling discovery.” Rowland v. Am. Gen. Fin., Inc., 340 F.3d 187, 195 (4th Cir. 2003).

Plaintiff has not set forth good cause, or any other cognizable basis, on which
discovery—albeit limited—is appropriate at this stage in the proceeding. Rather, Plaintiff’s
Motion makes it clear that he is unaware as to whether he has any legitimate claim in this matter;
he cannot plausibly assert that the allegedly-defamatory letters from NCMEC are, in fact, false
(among numerous other deficiencies in Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint). There is no
“ambiguity” to resolve; Plaintiff simply cannot possibly know what CyberTipline Reports have
been received by NCMEC, and as such cannot plausibly allege that the statements are, in fact,
false. It is not NCMEC’s burden to establish a plausible claim on the part of Plaintiff.

3
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 33 Filed 08/26/26 Page 4 of 5 PagelD# 371

Further, Plaintiff has recently moved to supplement his First Amended Complaint,
apparently complaining of statements made in NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss. Given that
Plaintiff appears to have not yet settled on an operative Complaint—despite the prior litigation
and the fact that he has already amended his Complaint in this matter once—discovery certainly
appears premature at this stage.

In United States v. Ebrahimi, the defendant asked this Court for leave under Rule
26(d)(1) to serve a subpoena on the National Archives. The Court denied that motion
(apparently without awaiting an opposition from the plaintiff), noting that the defendant “has not
argued that ‘unusual circumstances or conditions exist that would likely prejudice’ him from
seeking discovery, once it has been authorized.” 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 200610, *2 (E.D. Va.
2025) (collecting cases). Plaintiff, in this matter, has not set forth any unusual circumstances or
conditions that would prejudice him from his ability to set forth a legally-coherent and
cognizable claim, to the extent he presently has any such claim (or good-faith basis for such a

i claim).

Respectfully, NCMEC submits that early discovery is inappropriate in this matter, and
should not be allowed. At the essence of this dispute is this fact: Plaintiff sent but did not serve
subpoenas on NCMEC. NCMEC responded as requested, without forcing Plaintiff to deal with
the expense and trouble of formal service. For that, NCMEC has been exposed to two separate
lawsuits, multiple iterations of Complaints, and multiple motions. NCMEC respectfully requests
that Plaintiff demonstrate that he has any valid cause of action to assert against NCMEC before
NCMEC is subjected to any discovery, regardless of how limited the discovery is claimed to be.

4
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 33 Filed 08/26/26 Page 5 of 5 PagelD# 372
WHEREFORE, for the reasons set forth above, Defendant NCMEC respectfully opposes
Plaintiff’s Motion for Discovery, and requests that the Court deny the Motion, and for such
additional relief as this Court may deem necessary and appropriate.
Respectfully submitted,
JORDAN COYNE LLP

Fairfax, VA 22030

I. NCMEC OPPOSES A CLAIM PLAINTIFF DID NOT PLEAD

Plaintiff’s proposed supplement states its purpose on its face. The August 12 filing and the
August 13 communication are not independent causes of action. Plaintiff pleads them as post-
filing facts. They bear on Count III. Count III already exists. Plaintiff said so in the pleading
NCMEC opposes.

NCMEC reads that pleading otherwise. Most of its Opposition explains why the August 12
filing and the August 13 communication do not create liability on their own. Plaintiff does not
dispute that. Plaintiff never pleaded it. NCMEC answers an argument Plaintiff did not make.

Remove that argument, and little of the Opposition remains. The supplement adds no
defendant. The supplement adds no cause of action. The supplement adds no category of relief.
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 35 _ Filed 08/26/26 Page 2 of 4 PagelD# 376
The events occurred on August 12 and August 13. Plaintiff moved on August 20. NCMEC
identifies no prejudice. NCMEC identifies no delay. NCMEC identifies no discovery to reopen.
NCMEC identifies no deadline to disturb. NCMEC invokes futility. NCMEC never measures the
supplemental allegations against Count III.

NCMEC’s final substantive paragraph completes the error. NCMEC argues that the
supplement does not inform Plaintiff’s claim that NCMEC “defamed Plaintiff by imputation.”
Count III is not a defamation claim. Count III is the only count Plaintiff seeks to supplement.
NCMEC analyzed a count Plaintiff did not move to supplement.

NCMEC therefore opposes a claim Plaintiff did not plead. NCMEC opposes that claim
under a theory Plaintiff disclaimed. NCMEC closes by analyzing a count Plaintiff did not
supplement. The Opposition supplies no reason to deny the narrow supplementation Plaintiff
requested.

The Motion should be granted.
