MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR TARGETED
VACATUR OF ECF NOS. 64 AND 84, WITHDRAWAL OR MODIFICATION OF THE
MAGISTRATE-JUDGE REFERRAL, AND RELATED INTERIM RELIEF
I. THE REQUESTED CORRECTION

Two signed financial disclosure reports of Magistrate Judge Davis list “FB common stock”
at year-end 2024 and year-end 2025, each with a value of $15,001 to $50,000. Ex. A at 2; Ex. B at
4. FB common stock is the common stock of Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. Two orders entered
during the Magistrate Judge’s participation in this action carry continuing procedural effects. ECF
No. 64 conditioned consideration of the proposed Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint
on a comparison document due within two days. ECF No. 84 denied the amendment motion for
nonproduction of that document and denied two discovery motions, one directed to Meta, on the
stated ground that discovery had not begun.

1
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 14 PagelD# 958

This Motion asks the District Judge to remove those continuing effects and to adjudicate
the affected motions on the submissions already of record. Two questions are presented, and they
are different. Whether participation violated 28 U.S.C. § 455 is the statutory question. Whether the
affected orders should be vacated is the remedial question. The disqualification motion before the
Magistrate Judge presents the first. This Motion presents the second, together with the referral and
interim questions that only the District Judge can decide. The merits of the underlying claims are
not argued here. They are argued in the Rule 72(a) objections and the amendment briefing, which
this Motion preserves.

II. AUTHORITY AND PROCEDURAL POSTURE

A. Referral and district-judge review.

A district judge may designate a magistrate judge to determine pretrial matters, and may
“reconsider any pretrial matter under this subparagraph (A) where it has been shown that the
magistrate judge’s order is clearly erroneous or contrary to law.” 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). Rule
72(a) implements that review on timely objection. The referral itself remains within the District
Judge’s control; the statute designates and the District Judge may withdraw or modify the
designation. Plaintiff does not invoke 28 U.S.C. § 636(c)(4), which governs consensual civil-trial
referrals, and does not contend that its standard applies to this ordinary pretrial referral. The Fourth
Circuit treats a ruling that “relies on erroneous factual or legal premises” as an abuse of discretion
correctable on Rule 72(a) review. Wall v. Rasnick, 42 F.4th 214, 217, 220 (4th Cir. 2022).

B. Interlocutory revision under Rule 54(b).

An order “that adjudicates fewer than all the claims . . . may be revised at any time before
the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). The Fourth Circuit reads
that text to give “broader flexibility to revise interlocutory orders before final judgment as the
litigation develops and new facts or arguments come to light,” and permits revision where there is

2
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 3 of 14 PagelD# 959
“substantially different evidence,” a change in applicable law, or clear error causing “manifest
injustice.” Carlson v. Boston Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). That discretion “is not
limitless,” and a party may not use Rule 54(b) to repeat evidence or arguments the court has already
considered. Id. at 325-26. Plaintiff invokes Rule 54(b) as additional authority for the District
Judge’s revision of ECF Nos. 64 and 84. Plaintiff does not invoke it to revive any reconsideration
request to the Magistrate Judge, and does not contend that it extends any Rule 72(a) deadline. The
financial disclosure reports are evidence that no court in this action has considered. They are not a
repetition of anything previously presented.

C. The retrospective remedy.

Section 455 “neither prescribes nor prohibits any particular remedy for a violation of that
duty.” Liljeberg v. Health Servs. Acquisition Corp., 486 U.S. 847, 862 (1988). The remedial
inquiry considers “the risk of injustice to the parties in the particular case, the risk that the denial of
relief will produce injustice in other cases, and the risk of undermining the public’s confidence in
the judicial process.” Id. at 864. Liljeberg applied that inquiry to a final judgment under Rule 60(b)
(6). The orders targeted here are interlocutory. Plaintiff does not invoke Rule 60(b)(6). The three
considerations govern the remedial question whatever the procedural vehicle, and the District
Judge’s authority over interlocutory orders under § 636(b)(1)(A) and Rule 54(b) supplies the
vehicle.

ECF No. 64 is already before the District Judge on timely objections submitted September
13, 2026. ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68. Those objections challenge the informational premise, the baseline,
and the deadline. This Motion adds the financial-conflict evidence as a separate basis for relief
from ECF No. 64. It does not suggest that the period to object to ECF No. 64 has restarted, and it
does not depend on that period.

Ii. THE FINANCIAL PREDICATE AND THE PERIOD REQUIRING REVIEW
3
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 4 of 14 PagelD# 960

The chronology is short. Judge Davis certified the 2024 report on August 18, 2025. Ex. B at
1, 8. He certified the 2025 report on May 14 and May 26, 2026. Ex. A at 1. Plaintiff filed this action,
naming Meta, on July 30, 2026. ECF No. 1. Meta appeared, moved to dismiss, and filed its
corporate disclosure statement on August 21, 2026. ECF Nos. 21, 22, 24. Judge Davis entered ECF
No. 64 on September 9, 2026 and ECF No. 84 on October 7, 2026. Plaintiff was unaware of the
reported financial interest when ECF No. 84 was entered and promptly presented the issue after
learning of it. Ballentine Decl. { 2.

Section 455(b)(4) requires disqualification where the judge “knows that he, individually or
as a fiduciary, or his spouse or minor child residing in his household, has a financial interest in the
subject matter in controversy or in a party to the proceeding.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4). A financial
interest is “ownership of a legal or equitable interest, however small.” Id. § 455(d)(4). “It is well-
established that the ownership of stock constitutes a ‘financial interest.’” Shell Oil Co. v. United
States, 672 F.3d 1283, 1289 (Fed. Cir. 2012); accord Cent. Tel. Co. of Va. v. Sprint Commc’ns Co.
of Va., Inc., 715 F.3d 501, 515 (4th Cir. 2013). Subsection (b)(4) requires knowledge. Liljeberg,
486 U.S. at 859. The fund exception in § 455(d)(4)(i) applies where shares are held through a
mutual or common investment fund managed without the judge’s input. Cent. Tel., 715 F.3d at 516.
The reports list the FB holding as common stock and list funds and an IRA as separate line items.
Ex. A at 2-3; Ex. B at 4-6. Whether the holding is in fact held through a qualifying arrangement is
a fact for determination.

Section 455(a) requires disqualification “in any proceeding in which his impartiality might
reasonably be questioned.” The inquiry is objective and does not require knowledge. Liljeberg, 486
U.S. at 859-60. Whether an objective observer would question impartiality depends on the
circumstances, including the judge’s knowledge before the action was filed, “what happened while

4
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 5 of 14 PagelD# 961
the case was pending before him, and what he did when he learned” of the interest. Id. at 856.
Plaintiff does not contend that § 455(a) applies without regard to those circumstances. Plaintiff
contends that those circumstances must be determined and that, on the facts the reports support, an
informed observer would question the impartiality of a judge deciding discovery directed to a
company whose stock the judge reported holding five months earlier.

Section 455(f) relieves a judge of disqualification where the interest is discovered after
assignment, substantial judicial time has been devoted to the matter, the interest could not be
substantially affected by the outcome, and the judge divests. 28 U.S.C. § 455(f). Each condition is
factual. Divestiture requires that the interest be “sold or given away”; placement in a blind trust
does not qualify. Centripetal Networks, Inc. v. Cisco Sys., Inc., 38 F.4th 1025 (Fed. Cir. 2022).
Whether divestiture cures earlier participation depends on how far the litigation had advanced and
what decisions were rendered in the interim. Litovich v. Bank of Am. Corp., 106 F.4th 218 (2d Cir.
2024). Plaintiff does not contend that § 455(f) is categorically unavailable. Plaintiff contends that
its conditions must be determined on the record, and that a present disposition of the interest, if one
has occurred or occurs, does not by itself resolve the effect of participation before it. The
retrospective determination requested here remains live whether or not present recusal becomes
unnecessary.

IV. THE THREE LILJEBERG CONSIDERATIONS SUPPORT VACATUR

A. Risk of injustice to the parties.

The concrete effect of the two orders is procedural. ECF No. 64 supplied a condition on
consideration of ECF No. 59. ECF No. 84 used nonproduction of the conditioned document to
exclude the proposed pleading from consideration and, separately, rejected the discovery requests
on the stated ground that discovery had not begun. The result is that three dismissal motions will be
decided against a pleading Plaintiff moved to replace, without seven closed answers about records

5
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 6 of 14 PagelD# 962
only Defendants hold. Plaintiff does not contend that losing a motion establishes injustice. The
injustice identified is adjudication of those motions by a judge who, on the evidence, held a
financial interest in the party whose discovery request he denied, with the consequence that the
completed submissions were never reached on their merits.

The proposed correction preserves completed briefing. Every submission on ECF Nos. 15,
54, and 59, including Defendants’ oppositions at ECF Nos. 33, 73, 74, and 83 and the reply
accepted by ECF No. 82, remains of record and is determined as it stands. No party begins again.
Defendants have an interest in retaining favorable rulings and in prompt resolution. Independent
determination on the existing submissions addresses that interest: it supplies a decision by a judge
whose participation is not questioned, on the same papers, without treating the challenged rulings
as controlling. The Federal Circuit, reviewing a judgment of this District, rejected the argument
that a judge’s prior rulings should stand because they were decided before he learned of his wife’s
interest, and rejected the argument that vacatur requires a showing of actual bias. Centripetal, 38
F.4th 1025. “Unlike § 455(a), [§ 455(b)(4)] is not triggered by an appearance of impropriety, but by
a known financial interest, which creates not only an appearance of impropriety but impropriety
itself.” Id.

B. Risk of injustice in other cases.

The second consideration asks whether denial of relief “will produce injustice in other
cases.” Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 864. A remedy confined to prospective recusal leaves every order
entered during the disqualification in force. The statute’s duty to inform, § 455(c), and its bar on
waiver of subsection (b) grounds, § 455(e), assume that participation during a known financial
conflict has consequences beyond the judge’s future participation. Vacatur where the statutory and
remedial findings are made “may prevent a substantive injustice in some future case by
encouraging a judge or litigant to more carefully examine possible grounds for disqualification.”

6
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 7 of 14 PagelD# 963
Id. at 868. The remedy requested is not discipline. It addresses the legal effect of judicial
participation during an established disqualification, and it addresses nothing else.

C. Public confidence.

The third consideration is the objective concern created by adjudication involving a
corporate party in which a qualifying interest was held. The Federal Circuit ordered vacatur under
§ 455(b)(4) where “there [wa]s neither an allegation nor suggestion that the judge was unduly
influenced by his wife’s financial interest, which no one argues was substantial.” Shell Oil, 672
F.3d at 1291. The statute “simply requires recusal whenever financial conflicts of interest exist,
regardless of whether those conflicts affect the outcome of the case.” Id. Plaintiff makes no claim
of actual influence, no claim that this action is economically significant to Meta, and no claim of
improper intent. The concern is the one the statute identifies: a judge deciding whether a party may
be required to answer three questions about its own records, while reporting ownership of that
party’s stock.

Liljeberg leaves room for harmless error. 486 U.S. at 862. Not every violation requires
vacatur of every order, and the Federal Circuit has stated the rule the same way: “mandatory
recusal does not require mandatory vacatur.” Shell Oil, 672 F.3d at 1293. Plaintiff addresses
harmlessness in Part V rather than avoiding it.

V. THE FINANCIAL-CONFLICT VACATUR DECISIONS AND THE QUESTION

OF HARMLESSNESS

Three decisions apply the separate disqualification and remedy inquiries to financial
conflicts. Shell Oil held that a trial judge whose spouse held stock in the parent of two parties was
required to disqualify himself “from the entire proceeding,” that severing the affected parties did
not satisfy that requirement, and that vacatur was the appropriate remedy on the Liljeberg factors.
672 F.3d at 1290-93. Centripetal arose in this District. The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of a

7
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 8 of 14 PagelD# 964
recusal motion, vacated every order entered after the judge learned of his wife’s interest in a party,
and remanded for proceedings before a different judge, observing that “[a]llowing the same judge
to reaffirm his own rulings would severely undermine § 455.” 38 F.4th 1025. Litovich vacated a
judgment under § 455(a) where the judge’s spouse had divested her stock before the decision
issued, because the length of participation during the conflict and the substantive motions decided
in that period made the divestiture insufficiently curative. 106 F.4th 218. Centripetal and Shell Oil
are decisions of the Federal Circuit and Litovich is a decision of the Second Circuit. They are
persuasive authority, not binding Fourth Circuit law. Plaintiff does not read Litovich to hold that
every former holding creates continuing disqualification. He reads it to hold that divestiture after
substantive participation does not automatically eliminate the need for a remedy.

Harmlessness is addressed on the orders’ own terms. The discovery ruling in ECF No. 84
rests on a legal premise, that discovery cannot be authorized before a Scheduling Order, that the
District Judge can correct independently on the Rule 72(a) objections. The amendment ruling is
different. It rests on a case-specific finding of “ample opportunity” and on the selection of denial as
the consequence of nonproduction, with no determination of the pending requests for relief from
the deadline. ECF No. 84 at 2. A finding and a choice of consequence made by a judge whose
participation is questioned are not cured by a reviewing court’s confirmation that some
consequence was available. Plaintiff does not contend that review by the District Judge is legally
incapable of correcting either ruling. Plaintiff contends that the appropriate correction is
independent adjudication of the restored motions on their existing submissions, which the District
Judge can provide on the Rule 72(a) objections, and that vacatur removes the challenged rulings as
the baseline against which that adjudication would otherwise occur.

VI. ORDER-SPECIFIC APPLICATION AND PRESERVATION
8
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 9 of 14 PagelD# 965

ECF No. 84 should be vacated in full. It contains the denials of all three motions to be
restored, and no part of it operates independently of the challenged participation.

ECF No. 64 should be vacated as to the comparison requirement and the expired September
11 deadline. That requirement is the predicate ECF No. 84 enforced. Vacating the enforcement
while leaving the predicate in place would leave ECF No. 59 subject to the same condition and the
same consequence. ECF No. 64 is separately before the District Judge on the September
objections, which challenge it on grounds that do not depend on the financial evidence. ECF Nos.
66, 67, 68. If the evidence establishes disqualification as of October 7 but not as of September 9, the
independent challenge to ECF No. 64 remains pending on those grounds, and Plaintiff does not
represent that both orders were necessarily entered during the same proven conflict.

ECF Nos. 63, 65, and 82 are not targeted. Their hearing and certification provisions are not
prerequisites to the relief requested here, and Plaintiff’s objections to those provisions in ECF Nos.
66 and 67 remain pending. The acceptance of ECF Nos. 78 and 78-1 under ECF No. 82 is
preserved. ECF No. 62 is not targeted; ECF No. 26 remains withdrawn. The organizing principle is
procedural correction, not preservation of orders because they favored Plaintiff. Should the Court
consider broader vacatur necessary, Plaintiff requests that all authorized briefing be independently
preserved or re-accepted so that no party is required to resubmit it.

VII. TIMELINESS AND CONSIDERATION OF THE EVIDENCE

The financial ground was not included in the September objections or in the original
drafting of the Rule 72(a) objections because Plaintiff was unaware of the reported interest.
Ballentine Decl. { 2. He presented the ground promptly after learning of it, in three coordinated
applications submitted the same day. The Fourth Circuit requires that a disqualification motion be
raised “at the earliest moment after knowledge of the facts,” and applies that requirement to §
455(b) as well as § 455(a). Kolon Indus. Inc. v. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., 748 F.3d 160, 169—

9
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 9¢ Filed 10/13/26 Page 10 of 14 PagelD#
71 (4th Cir. 2014). The judge’s independent obligation under 8 455(c) and the nonwaiver provision
of § 455(e) do not eliminate the litigant’s obligation; “waiver and timeliness are distinct issues.” Id.
Plaintiff does not argue otherwise. The showing here is that no interval of knowing delay exists.

Plaintiff requests express consideration of Exhibits A and B and the Declaration in deciding
this Motion, and, to the extent needed, in connection with the pending objections. The District
Judge’s authority to revise interlocutory orders on substantially different evidence, Carlson, 856
F.3d at 325, and the statute’s delegation of the remedy to the judiciary, Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 862,
each supply a basis for considering the evidence. The retrospective remedy should not depend
solely on whether the evidence is received within the ordinary scope of Rule 72(a) record review.
VHI. RESTORATION, AFFIRMATIVE ADJUDICATION, AND INTERIM

PROTECTION

Restoration is not the endpoint requested. Vacatur supplies the procedural correction. Rules
15(a)(2), 15(d), and 26(d)(1) supply the separate bases for granting ECF Nos. 59, 15, and 54 on
their briefed merits, and the Rule 72(a) objections present those merits. Plaintiff requests that the
District Judge proceed, following vacatur, to grant those motions on the existing submissions, or
alternatively to direct their prompt independent determination.

The interim relief has four parts. First, suspension of further substantive action under the
challenged referral while the disqualification motion is determined and any administrative transfer
is effected. Second, suspension of further reliance on the nonproduction condition in ECF No. 64
while ECF Nos. 66 and 67, the Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 84, and this Motion are
determined. Third, determination of the amendment and financial-conflict issues before, or
expressly within, any claim-terminating disposition of ECF Nos. 10, 21, or 45 that relies on the
exclusion of the proposed pleading. Fourth, express provision that the District Judge may grant

10
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Pecument 34 Filed 10/13/26 Page 11 of 14 PagelD#
independently warranted relief on the Rule 72(a) objections without awaiting resolution of every
financial-conflict question.

A pause “calls for the exercise of judgment, which must weigh competing interests and
maintain an even balance,” and the applicant “must make out a clear case of hardship or inequity in
being required to go forward.” Landis v. N. Am. Co., 299 U.S. 248, 254-55 (1936). The burden
rests on the party seeking the pause. Williford v. Armstrong World Indus., Inc., 715 F.2d 124, 127
(4th Cir. 1983). Defendants have an interest in prompt disposition of their dismissal motions. The
hardship asserted is specific: claim-terminating adjudication on a pleading Plaintiff moved to
replace, under a condition imposed and enforced by a judge whose participation is questioned on
documentary evidence, while that question is pending before two judges of this Court. Defendants’
briefing is preserved in full. Each protection has a defined terminating event: determination of the
disqualification motion and completion of any transfer; determination of the identified objections
and this Motion; and entry of the order on the amendment and financial-conflict issues. Plaintiff
does not request a pause tied to the remaining hearing or certification disputes, and does not request
an indefinite stay.

PLAINTIFF’S RULE 72(a) OBJECTIONS TO ECF NO. 96 AND MOTION TO SET
ASIDE OR MODIFY THAT ORDER, DETERMINE REASSIGNMENT AUTHORITY,
AND GRANT LEAVE TO SUPPLEMENT ECF NO. 93

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine objects under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 72(a) and 28
U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A) to the Order entered October 22, 2026 (ECF No. 96). Plaintiff moves to set
aside or modify that Order, to determine the authority under which this action was reassigned and
the procedure by which the successor Magistrate Judge was designated, and for leave under Local
Civil Rule 7(F)(1) to file the supplement to ECF No. 93 attached as Exhibit A. A Memorandum in
Support accompanies this Motion under Local Civil Rules 7(F)(1) and 72. Plaintiff incorporates it
by reference.
I. THE DISPOSITION CHALLENGED

1. The docket for October 22, 2026 records two actions. An unnumbered entry
states: “Case Reassigned to Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick. Magistrate Judge Ivan D.
Davis no longer assigned to the case.” ECF No. 96, signed by Magistrate Judge Davis, addresses

1
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF Document97_ Filed 10/23/26 Page 2 of 10 PagelD# 978
Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis Under 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) and
§ 455(a), and for Priority Determination (ECF No. 86). The docket entry for ECF No. 96 states
that the matter “can be resolved without oral argument,” orders that the Motion “is DENIED AS
MOOT,” and states: “The case has been reassigned to Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick.”

2. The quotations in this Motion and in the Memorandum in Support are taken from
the October 22, 2026 docket entry for ECF No. 96.

3. Both actions are dated October 22, 2026. ECF No. 96 describes the reassignment
as completed. The available entries do not establish the relative timing of execution, issuance,
entry, and the effective termination or modification of the relevant designation.

4. These Objections are directed to ECF No. 96. The administrative reassignment
entry is addressed through the District Judge’s authority over the referral under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)
and Local Civil Rule 72.

IL. TIMELINESS

5. Rule 72(a) requires objections within 14 days after service of the order. ECF No.
96 was entered October 22, 2026. These Objections are filed within 14 days of that date and are
timely under Rule 72(a).

6. These Objections do not extend, restart, or replace any period to object to any
other order. Plaintiff’s pending submissions concerning ECF Nos. 63, 64, 65, and 84 (ECF Nos.
66, 67, 76, 89, 90, 91, 93, 94) remain pending on their own terms. Plaintiff maintains each of them
by this reference.

Il. OBJECTIONS

Objection One: Authority to adjudicate ECF No. 86.

7. Predicate. ECF No. 96 states that the case “has been reassigned.” The reassignment
entry states that Magistrate Judge Davis is “no longer assigned to the case.” The record does not

2
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF Document97_ Filed 10/23/26 Page 3 of 10 PagelD# 979
identify the designation under which Magistrate Judge Davis acted on October 22, 2026, the scope
of the reassignment, or any authority retained over ECF No. 86.

8. Ground. A magistrate judge’s authority to hear and determine a pretrial matter
derives from a designation under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A) and Local Civil Rule 72. Plaintiff
objects to the disposition of ECF No. 86 if, when ECF No. 96 was issued, the reassignment had
terminated the authority necessary to adjudicate that motion and no applicable statutory, standing,
or case-specific authority permitted the disposition. Plaintiff requests identification of the
operative authority and the effect of reassignment on it. The objection does not rest merely on the
absence of a separately docketed referral order.

9. Relief. Determination of the operative authority and the effect of the reassignment
on it. If the authority necessary to adjudicate ECF No. 86 had ended and no other authority
permitted the disposition, vacatur of ECF No. 96.

10. This objection does not depend on whether a financial interest in Meta Platforms,
Inc. was held on any date.

Objection Two: Permissible administrative action after recusal or during required

disqualification.

11. ~~ Predicate. ECF No. 96 disposes of the whole of ECF No. 86, including the requests
in ECF No. 86, Parts V and VII(A2), for determinations of fact. The record does not state whether
the reassignment reflected a recusal, another disqualification determination, or another
administrative basis.

12. Ground. A judge who has recused takes no action in the case beyond the ministerial
steps needed to transfer it. Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC v. NTE Carolinas I, LLC, No. 22-2168,
slip op. at 52-54 (4th Cir. Aug. 5, 2024) (published), reported at 111 F.4th 337; Arnold v. Eastern
Air Lines, Inc., 712 F.2d 899, 904—05 (4th Cir. 1983) (en banc). The same limit applies during a

3
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF Document97_ Filed 10/23/26 Page 4 of 10 PagelD# 980
period in which 28 U.S.C. § 455 requires disqualification. McCuin v. Texas Power & Light Co.,
714 F.2d 1255, 1261 (Sth Cir. 1983); In re BellSouth Corp., 334 F.3d 941, 949-50 & n.4 (11th
Cir. 2003). Plaintiff contends that disposing of ECF No. 86 after the relevant authority ended
would exceed implementation of a transfer. Plaintiff objects to ECF No. 96 to the extent it
constitutes adjudication after an established recusal or during a period in which § 455 required
disqualification.

13. Relief. Determination whether ECF No. 96 was authorized adjudication,
permissible administrative closure, or action beyond the authority remaining. If the latter, vacatur
of ECF No. 96 and independent disposition of ECF No. 86’s prospective request by the District
Judge.

14. —_ The two objections are independent. Each identifies its own predicate, ground,
and relief.

IV. RELATED REQUESTS
A. Request Concerning the Successor Designation and Conditional Corrective
Relief.

15. Plaintiff requests identification of the authority and procedure that produced the
successor designation. If the designation resulted from discretionary selection by a disqualified
officer or another unauthorized process, Plaintiff requests correction under the Court’s governing
assignment procedures, administered without the disqualified officer’s participation. Plaintiff
requests Clerk-administered random selection to the extent authorized by those procedures. If the
existing designation complied with the governing procedure, Plaintiff requests that determination.

16. ‘Plaintiff does not allege that Magistrate Judge Davis selected Magistrate Judge
Fitzpatrick. Plaintiff raises no objection to Magistrate Judge Fitzpatrick personally. Plaintiff does
not seek the reinstatement of Magistrate Judge Davis.

4
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF Document97_ Filed 10/23/26 Page 5 of 10 PagelD# 981

B. Alternative Relief: Define ECF No. 96’s Effect in Determining ECF No. 93.

17. ECF No. 96 disposed of ECF No. 86 on mootness grounds following
reassignment. It did not determine whether the challenged earlier participation complied with 8
455 and did not adjudicate ECF No. 93. Plaintiff requests that the District Judge decide ECF No.
93 on its own grounds, resolving the statutory facts to the extent necessary to that decision, or
granting independently warranted relief without reaching unnecessary questions.

18. Plaintiff does not contend that ECF No. 96 purports to decide ECF No. 93. The
request is for the District Judge to define the effect of ECF No. 96 when adjudicating the pending
retrospective application.

C. Leave to Supplement ECF No. 93.

19. The October 22, 2026 developments postdate ECF No. 93 and bear on the relief it
requests. Plaintiff requests leave under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) to file the Proposed Supplement
attached as Exhibit A, which is confined to those developments and their effect on ECF No. 93 §
10(R1) through (R7), with such opportunity for the Defendants to respond as the Court directs.
V. RELIEF REQUESTED

20. Plaintiff requests an order, in the form of the accompanying Proposed Orders:

(1) granting leave to file Exhibit A;

(2) retaining in the District Judge the determination of the Objections and related
requests, and placing on the record, in the decision itself, through a statement of the Clerk, or from
existing records, the following: the effective scope of the reassignment and, where material and
available, its timing relative to ECF No. 96; whether authority over ECF No. 86 remained and the
source of that authority; whether the reassignment reflected recusal, another disqualification
determination, or another administrative basis relevant to the Objections; and the governing
successor-selection procedure and whether that procedure was followed;

5
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF Document97_ Filed 10/23/26 Page 6 of 10 PagelD# 982

(3) affording the parties an opportunity to address any newly supplied material
factual information before it becomes a basis for decision;

(4) upon sustaining Objection One or Objection Two, vacating ECF No. 96 and
disposing independently of ECF No. 86’s prospective request, with the material statutory questions
addressed as necessary in deciding ECF No. 93;

(5) in the alternative, leaving the prospective mootness disposition in place,
identifying its limited effect as stated in paragraph 17, and determining ECF No. 93 on its own
grounds;

(6) identifying the authority and procedure that produced the successor designation
and, if that designation resulted from an unauthorized process, correcting it as stated in paragraph
15;

(7) determining the Objections in coordination with ECF Nos. 66, 67, 76, 89, 90, 91,
93, and 94, distinguishing in the order the relief granted, the requests that remain pending, and the
requests rendered unnecessary by complete relief; and

(8) providing that no relief granted returns any referred matter to Magistrate Judge
Davis.

21. Plaintiff does not contend that the filing of these Objections stays any order or
makes ECF No. 59-1 the operative pleading. Vacatur of ECF No. 96 would not by itself vacate
ECF No. 64 or ECF No. 84 or grant ECF No. 59. Those requests are stated in ECF Nos. 66, 67,
89, 90, 91, 93, and 94 and are determinable on their own grounds.

VI. SUBMISSION

22. Local Civil Rule 72 provides that an objection under Rule 72(a) “shall be
considered a motion and is subject to the briefing and notice requirements on Local Civil Rule 7.”
Plaintiff waives oral argument on this Motion only and requests that the Court direct its submission

6
Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF Document97_ Filed 10/23/26 Page /7 of 10 PagelD# 983
on the papers under Local Civil Rules 7(E) and 7(J) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 78(b). A
Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument and Request for Submission on the Papers accompanies this
Motion. The waiver does not withdraw the objections stated in ECF Nos. 66 and 67 to provisions
of ECF Nos. 63 and 65.

23. Plaintiff submits with this Motion: the Memorandum in Support; Exhibit A;
Proposed Orders A, B, and C; and the Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument and Request for
Submission on the Papers. Plaintiff relies on the existing record, including ECF Nos. 86 through
94 and their attachments.

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter Proposed Order A and,
upon determination of these Objections, Proposed Order B or, in the alternative, Proposed Order
C.

I certify that on October 23, 2026, I submitted the following documents to the Clerk of

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF'S RULE 72(a) OBJECTIONS TO ECF
NO. 96 AND MOTION TO SET ASIDE OR MODIFY THAT ORDER, DETERMINE
REASSIGNMENT AUTHORITY, AND GRANT LEAVE TO SUPPLEMENT ECF NO.
93

I.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

The October 22, 2026 docket records reassignment of this action to Magistrate Judge
Fitzpatrick and states that Magistrate Judge Davis is no longer assigned. ECF No. 96, signed by
Magistrate Judge Davis, disposes of Plaintiff's disqualification motion on the ground that the case
has been reassigned. The quotations from ECF No. 96 in this Memorandum are taken from its
October 22, 2026 docket entry. Plaintiff objects to that adjudication to the extent it occurred after
the authority necessary to decide ECF No. 86 had ended or exceeded the administrative action
permissible after recusal or statutory disqualification.
The available record does not establish the effective scope of the reassignment, whether
authority over ECF No. 86 remained, or the procedure used to designate the successor. Plaintiff

1


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 99
1007

Filed 10/23/26

Page 2 of 16 PageID#

requests determination of those matters and vacatur if the challenged disposition lacked authority
or constituted prohibited participation.
Independently, Plaintiff requests that the District Judge determine the October 22
developments' effect on pending ECF No. 93. At minimum, the completed prospective
reassignment must remain distinct from the unresolved requests concerning ECF Nos. 64 and 84.
ECF No. 96 does not determine the financial-conflict facts or the retrospective application.
Plaintiff requests adjudication of that application on its own grounds, with factual determinations
to the extent necessary, and without delaying independently warranted relief on the existing
objections.
II.

PROCEDURAL HISTORY AND GOVERNING REVIEW

A.

Chronology

On September 9, 2026, ECF No. 64 required Plaintiff to file by September 11, 2026 a
redlined comparison of the proposed Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint (ECF No.
59-1) against the original Complaint (ECF No. 1). On September 13, 2026, Plaintiff submitted
Rule 72(a) objections to ECF Nos. 63, 64, and 65 and a motion to set aside ECF No. 64 (ECF Nos.
66, 67, 68). On October 7, 2026, ECF No. 84 denied ECF Nos. 15 and 54 as premature and denied
ECF No. 59 for nonproduction of the comparison.
On October 13, 2026, Plaintiff filed three coordinated applications, each entered October
14, 2026. ECF No. 86 moved before Magistrate Judge Davis for disqualification under 28 U.S.C.
§ 455(b)(4) and § 455(a), supported by a Declaration and by Exhibits A and B, the Financial

Disclosure Reports for calendar years 2025 and 2024 (ECF Nos. 86-1 through 86-3). ECF Nos.
89, 90, and 91 presented Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 84 before the District Judge. ECF Nos.
93 and 94 moved before the District Judge for targeted vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84, withdrawal
or modification of the referral, and interim relief.

2


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 99
1008

Filed 10/23/26

Page 3 of 16 PageID#

On October 22, 2026, the docket recorded the reassignment of this action to Magistrate
Judge Fitzpatrick and the entry of ECF No. 96. Both actions are dated October 22, 2026. ECF No.
96 describes the reassignment as completed. The available entries do not establish the relative
timing of execution, issuance, entry, and the effective termination or modification of the relevant
designation.
B.

The allocation of issues among the October 13 filings

ECF No. 86 asked the Magistrate Judge to state on the record whether the asset reported as
"FB common stock" is common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.; whether that interest was held on
July 30, 2026 and on each date on which ECF Nos. 62, 63, 64, 65, 82, and 84 were entered; the
date and manner of any divestiture; whether the interest is held directly or through a fund within
28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4)(i); and any other fact material to§ 455(f). ECF No. 86, Part V. It requested
disqualification upon those determinations and, upon disqualification, "the ministerial steps
necessary to return or transfer the referred matters through the Court's assignment procedures." Id.,
Parts V, VII{Al)-(A4). It stated that the companion filings "seek the retrospective and casemanagement remedies" and that "[t]his Motion does not." Id., Part VI. It reserved review under
Rule 72(a) of any order disposing of it. Id.
ECF No. 93 requests the retrospective and referral relief. ECF No. 93 ,i 10 states seven
requests: {Rl) withdrawal or modification of the referral, with affected matters retained by the
District Judge or reassigned through the Court's assignment procedures; (R2) vacatur of ECF No.
84 and of the comparison requirement and deadline in ECF No. 64 upon the statutory findings
identified in its paragraph 5; (R3) restoration of ECF Nos. 15, 54, and 59 to pending status; (R4)
affirmative adjudication of those motions or prompt independent determination; (RS) interim
protection; (R6) coordinated determination with the existing objections; and (R7) a decision
record. ECF No. 93 ,i 2 states that it does not extend or restart any period to object.

3


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

C.

Document 99
1009

Filed 10/23/26

Page 4 of 16 PageID#

ECF No. 96

The docket entry for ECF No. 96 identifies ECF No. 86 as the matter before the Court,
states that the matter "can be resolved without oral argument," orders that the Motion "is DENIED
AS MOOT," and states: "The case has been reassigned to Magistrate Judge William E.
Fitzpatrick." The entry records no determination on any item in ECF No. 86, Part V. It does not
refer to ECF No. 93. It does not identify the basis for the reassignment or the authority under which
ECF No. 96 was entered after the reassignment it describes.

D.

Governing review

The district judge "must consider timely objections and modify or set aside any part of the
order that is clearly erroneous or is contrary to law." Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a); 28 U.S.C. § 636(b){l)
(A). Whether a magistrate judge possessed authority to decide a matter is a question of law. A
disposition entered without that authority is contrary to law. Plaintiff does not seek de novo
reconsideration under Rule 72(b). Wall v. Rasnick, 42 F.4th 214 (4th Cir. 2022) (No. 21-6553, slip
op. at 3), states the Rule 72(a) framework. It does not decide when a reassignment terminates a
magistrate judge's authority, and Plaintiff does not cite it for that proposition.
A district judge "may designate a magistrate judge to hear and determine any pretrial matter
pending before the court," subject to the exceptions stated in § 636(b){l){A). In this District,
"[m]agistrate judges . . . are authorized and specially designated to perform all duties authorized
or allowed to be performed by United States magistrate judges by the United States Code and any
rule governing proceedings in this Court," and "[d]uties and cases may be assigned or referred to
a magistrate judge by an order entered in the action or on the instructions of a district judge." E.D.
Va. Loe. Civ. R. 72. The same rule provides that a Rule 72(a) objection "shall be considered a
motion and is subject to the briefing and notice requirements on Local Civil Rule 7." Id. The
District Judge controls the scope of the referral. The present record concerns an ordinary pretrial

4


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 99
1010

Filed 10/23/26

Page 5 of 16 PageID#

referral, and Plaintiff does not invoke the standard for vacating a consensual reference under §
636(c)(4).
ECF No. 93 invokes Rule 54(b) for revision of ECF Nos. 64 and 84. Plaintiff maintains
that authority there. Plaintiff does not invoke Rule 60(b )( 4) and does not contend that any order is
void. Timely objection under Rule 72(a) is the vehicle for review of ECF No. 96.
III.

AUTHORITY TO ISSUE ECF NO. 96

A.

The issue

Magistrate Judge Davis remained a magistrate judge of this District on October 22, 2026.
The question is whether, when ECF No. 96 was issued, he retained authority to adjudicate ECF
No. 86 in this action.
Plaintiff objects to the disposition of ECF No. 86 if, when ECF No. 96 was issued, the
reassignment had terminated the authority necessary to adjudicate that motion and no applicable
statutory, standing, or case-specific authority permitted the disposition. Plaintiff requests
identification of the operative authority and the effect of reassignment on it. The objection does
not rest merely on the absence of a separately docketed referral order.

B.

What the record does and does not establish

ECF No. 96 gives one reason for its disposition: the case "has been reassigned." The
reassignment entry states that Magistrate Judge Davis is "no longer assigned to the case." The two
entries together describe a completed reassignment and a disposition that relies on it. They do not
establish the relative timing of execution, issuance, entry, and the effective termination or
modification of the designation. They do not state whether the reassignment withdrew every matter
then pending before Magistrate Judge Davis in this action or preserved any specified matter.
Plaintiff does not assert that the reassignment entry terminated every possible source of
authority. Plaintiff does not assume that a motion under advisement remained with Magistrate

5


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 99
1011

Filed 10/23/26

Page 6 of 16 PageID#

Judge Davis. Those are competing propositions. The docket does not resolve them. Local Civil
Rule 72 permits referral "on the instructions of a district judge" without an entered order, and an
instruction of that kind would not appear on the docket. For that reason the objection asks the
Court to identify the operative authority, in whatever form it took, and to determine whether the
disposition of ECF No. 86 fell within it.
C.

The record request

Plaintiff requests that the District Judge place on the record, in the decision itself, through
a statement of the Clerk, or from existing records, four matters:
1.

The effective scope of the reassignment and, where material and available, its

timing relative to ECF No. 96.
2.

Whether authority over ECF No. 86 remained and the source of that authority.

3.

Whether

the

reassignment

reflected

recusal,

another

disqualification

determination, or another administrative basis relevant to the Objections.
4.

The governing successor-selection procedure and whether that procedure was

followed.
Plaintiff requests an opportunity to address any newly supplied material factual information
before it becomes a basis for decision. Plaintiff does not request a deposition of any judicial officer,
access to chambers communications, inquiry into judicial mental processes, or the production of
timestamps that may not exist. The request is for the source of administrative authority, which the
Court can state.

6


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

IV.

RECUSAL,

Document 99
1012

STATUTORY

Filed 10/23/26

DISQUALIFICATION,

Page 7 of 16 PageID#

AND

PERMISSIBLE

ADMINISTRATIVE ACTION
A.

Three distinct circumstances

The second objection is independent of the first. It requires the Court to distinguish three
circumstances. The first is an established recusal. The second is an established statutory duty to
disqualify under 28 U.S.C. § 455. The third is the mere pendency of a motion requesting
disqualification. The filing of a § 455 motion does not establish the alleged financial interest. It
does not eliminate the judge's ability to decide the motion. The statutory conditions in § 455(b)
(4), § 455( d)( 4), and § 455(f) must be addressed before a duty to disqualify is established. The
issue under this objection is whether ECF No. 96 was an authorized administrative disposition or
prohibited adjudication under the circumstances the Court determines to exist.
B.

Participation after recusal

In Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC v. NTE Carolinas II, LLC, No. 22-2168, slip op. at 52-54
(4th Cir. Aug. 5, 2024) (published), reported at 111 F.4th 337, a district judge recused under a
prophylactic policy, the Clerk reassigned the case and recorded "conflict" as the reason, and the
case later returned to the same judge. The Fourth Circuit held that once a judge recuses himself
from a case he should remain recused, even though the recusal may not originally have been
required. Id. at 4, 52-54. The court relied on Arnold v. Eastern Air Lines, Inc., 712 F.2d 899, 90405 (4th Cir. 1983) (en bane), for the rule that a recused judge is "out of service insofar as that case
is concerned" and "should take no action which would possibly affect the outcome of [the] case."
Duke Energy, slip op. at 53 (quoting Arnold, 712 F .2d at 904-05).
Duke Energy supports the rule against a recused judge acting in the same case. It does not

hold that every same-day reassignment and docket-closing order is invalid. Its facts involved a
clerk-recorded reassignment based on a conflict, which shows that the absence of a document

7


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 99
1013

Filed 10/23/26

Page 8 of 16 PageID#

labeled "recusal" is not dispositive of whether a recusal occurred. Timing alone does not establish
that the reassignment here was a recusal. The record does not say what it was. That is the third
matter in the record request.

C.

Permissible administrative action

In re BellSouth Corp., 334 F.3d 941, 949-50 & n.4 (11th Cir. 2003), distinguishes

substantive participation from administrative transfer. The district judge there did not rule on the
merits and did not designate a successor. He referred the matter to the Clerk for random
reassignment and stayed the matters before him. The Eleventh Circuit held that the referral was
ministerial and contrasted cases in which a judge continued to enter substantive orders after the
duty to recuse arose. Id. at 949-50. The court also recognized that technical error of this kind does
not invariably warrant vacatur, and it applied the Liljeberg factors in that assessment. Id. at 949
n.4. BellSouth arose on a petition for mandamus. Its mandamus standard does not govern this Rule
72(a) application. Its distinction between substantive participation and administrative transfer
does.
McCuin v. Texas Power & Light Co., 714 F.2d 1255, 1261 (5th Cir. 1983), holds that a

disqualified judge "has no authority to sign such an order, or any other judicial order, pertaining
to a proceeding in which he is disqualified." The Fifth Circuit vacated the disqualified judge's
order assigning the cases to a named successor. Id.
Plaintiff contends that disposing of ECF No. 86 after the relevant authority ended would
exceed implementation of a transfer. The Court should determine whether ECF No. 96 was
authorized adjudication, permissible administrative closure, or action beyond the authority
remaining. Its title and dispositive verb do not alone resolve that question.

8


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

D.

Document 99
1014

Filed 10/23/26

Page 9 of 16 PageID#

Plaintiff's prior request

ECF No. 86 requested determination of the statutory question and supporting facts before
further substantive action, followed, upon disqualification, by transfer through the Court's
procedures. ECF No. 86, Part VII(A3)-(A4). Plaintiff does not object merely because Judge Davis
addressed a motion directed to him. The present objection concerns the authority and permissible
scope of the disposition in light of the completed reassignment described in ECF No. 96.

E.

The statutory grounds are maintained

The record on which ECF No. 86 rests remains before the Court. The Financial Disclosure
Reports for calendar years 2025 and 2024 report "FB common stock" at Part VII, line 6, with a
gross year-end value of $15,001 to $50,000 and no reported transaction on that line. ECF No. 862 at 2; ECF No. 86-3 at 4. The public filings establishing the relationship between "FB" and Meta
Platforms, Inc. are identified in ECF No. 87, Part II.B. Section 455(b)(4) requires disqualification
where the judge knows that he has a financial interest in a party. Section 455(d)(4) defines a
financial interest as ownership of a legal or equitable interest "however small," with the exception
in§ 455(d)(4)(i) for an interest held through a mutual or common investment fund. Section 455(f)
permits divestiture to cure a disqualification discovered after substantial judicial time has been
devoted to the matter. Section 455(a) applies independently.
The reports establish the holding at year-end 2024 and year-end 2025. They do not establish
the holding on any date in 2026. ECF No. 86, Part II; ECF No. 93 , 5. ECF No. 96 did not
determine the factual questions identified in ECF No. 86, Part V. Those questions remain relevant
to the extent necessary to decide the statutory grounds and retrospective relief presented in ECF
No. 93. Plaintiff requests that the District Judge address them in that proceeding rather than treat
the completed reassignment as resolving them. A mootness disposition supplies no finding on
ownership, knowledge, divestiture, or statutory compliance. The inclusion of requested findings

9


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 99
1015

Filed 10/23/26

Page 10 of 16 PageID#

in ECF No. 86 does not by itself require the Court to make every finding after the prospective
request has become unnecessary. Fed. R. Civ. P. 52(a)(3). Plaintiff requests a factual and legal
basis sufficient to decide the relief still sought, and no more.
V.

SUCCESSOR DESIGNATION AND CONDITIONAL CORRECTION

A disqualified judge may not select the judge who will succeed to the case. McCuin, 714
F.2d at 1261. Permitting that selection "would violate the congressional command that the
disqualified judge be removed from all participation in the case" and "might, in addition, create
suspicion that the disqualified judge will select a successor whose views are consonant with his."
Id. Referral to the Clerk for assignment under the court's procedures is permitted. BellSouth, 334
F.3d at 949-50. The application of McCuin depends on facts not established here. The record does
not identify who directed the reassignment or under what procedure, and the absence of a publicly
described selection mechanism is not proof that the selection was unauthorized.
Plaintiff requests identification of the authority and procedure that produced the successor
designation. If the designation resulted from discretionary selection by a disqualified officer or
another unauthorized process, Plaintiff requests correction under the Court's governing
assignment procedures, administered without the disqualified officer's participation. Plaintiff
requests Clerk-administered random selection to the extent authorized by those procedures. If the
existing designation complied with the governing procedure, Plaintiff requests that determination.
This request bears on the first objection and on the pending referral relief in ECF No. 93 ,i
lO(Rl). If the officer who issued ECF No. 96 also directed the successor designation, the authority
for both acts rests on the same determination. ECF No. 93 ,i lO(Rl) requests that affected matters
be reassigned "through the Court's assignment procedures." Identification of the procedure
actually used answers whether that request has been satisfied.

10


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 99
1016

Filed 10/23/26

Page 11 of 16 PageID#

Plaintiff claims no right to a different magistrate judge. A procedure conducted under the
Court's rules may designate Magistrate Judge Fitzpatrick. Plaintiff raises no objection to
Magistrate Judge Fitzpatrick personally and does not seek the reinstatement of Magistrate Judge
Davis.
VI.

ECF NO. 96'S EFFECT ON PENDING ECF NO. 93; ALTERNATIVE RELIEF
ECF No. 96 disposed of ECF No. 86 on mootness grounds following reassignment. It did

not determine whether the challenged earlier participation complied with § 455 and did not
adjudicate ECF No. 93. Plaintiff requests that the District Judge decide ECF No. 93 on its own
grounds, resolving the statutory facts to the extent necessary to that decision, or granting
independently warranted relief without reaching unnecessary questions.
Plaintiff does not contend that ECF No. 96 purports to decide ECF No. 93, and Plaintiff
does not ask the Court to restore every determination requested in ECF No. 86 as a standalone
controversy. The live relief is the requested correction of ECF Nos. 64 and 84 and the pending
referral questions. The determinations necessary to that relief belong in the District Judge's
resolution of the pending applications, on an appropriate factual record. Plaintiff does not request
that any inquiry be returned to Magistrate Judge Davis.
Liljeberg v. Health Services Acquisition Corp., 486 U.S. 847, 862-64 (1988), separates the

question whether a judge should have disqualified himself from the question what remedy follows
for past participation. The Court identified three considerations for the remedial question: the risk
of injustice to the parties in the particular case, the risk that denial of relief will produce injustice
in other cases, and the risk of undermining the public's confidence in the judicial process. Id. at
864. Liljeberg arose on a Rule 60(b )(6) motion for relief from a final judgment. The present
application concerns interlocutory orders, and the grounds invoked in ECF No. 93, including Rule
54(b) and§ 636(b){l){A), supply the vehicle. Vacatur does not follow automatically from a§ 455

11


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 99
1017

Filed 10/23/26

Page 12 of 16 PageID#

violation. The remedial question, where reached, is decided on the Liljeberg considerations and on
the record the Court develops.
The District Judge may grant complete relief from ECF Nos. 64 and 84 on the procedural
grounds independently briefed in ECF Nos. 66, 67, 89, 90, and 91 without deciding every financialconflict question. Plaintiff preserves that route and does not make any collateral determination a
prerequisite to it.
VII.

CONSEQUENCES, COORDINATED DETERMINATION, AND LEAVE TO
SUPPLEMENT
A.

Consequences

The consequence of any defect in ECF No. 96 must be assessed separately from the
continuing effects of ECF Nos. 64 and 84. An authorized district-judge determination that
considers the preserved grounds and supplies appropriate relief may eliminate any remaining
consequence of the October 22 disposition. Reassignment alone does not perform that review.
Rule 61 directs the Court to disregard errors that do not affect a party's substantial rights, and
Plaintiff requests correction matched to the consequence established, not reversal for its own sake.
Fed. R. Civ. P. 61.
Leaving necessary issues unresolved while the challenged orders control the operative
pleading can matter on review. In Wall v. Rasnick, 42 F.4th 214 (4th Cir. 2022) (No. 21-6553, slip
op. at 3, 9-10), timely and specific Rule 72(a) objections remained reviewable when the final
judgment implicitly rejected them, and the court vacated because the underlying issues had been
left unresolved by the magistrate judge and were material to the result. Plaintiff does not contend
that every omitted finding, unexplained ruling, or implicit denial is reversible. Plaintiff states the
issues here with the specificity that Rule 72(a) and Rule 46 require so that the Court can decide
them.

12


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 99
1018

Filed 10/23/26

Page 13 of 16 PageID#

Plaintiff maintains by reference the requests concerning ECF No. 64 (ECF Nos. 66, 67;
ECF No.93110(R2)), ECF No. 84 (ECF Nos. 89, 90, 91; ECF No.93110(R2)-(R4)), and ECF
No. 59 (ECF No.93110(R3)-(R4)). This Memorandum does not repeat their merits. This package
does not restart any period to object.
B.

Coordinated determination

Plaintiff requests that the District Judge retain determination of the authority and
assignment questions and coordinate them with ECF No. 93 and the pending objections. ECF No.
931 10(R6). Plaintiff maintains the request in ECF No. 931 l0(RS)(c) that the amendment and
financial-conflict issues be determined before, or expressly within, any disposition of ECF Nos.
10, 21, or 45 that would terminate a claim and that relies on the exclusion of the proposed pleading.
Plaintiff does not request a stay. The pendency of these Objections does not prevent the Court from
granting independently warranted relief on the amendment and discovery objections, and Plaintiff
requests that relief without awaiting resolution of every assignment question. ECF No. 93 1
10(R6).
C.

Leave to supplement

Local Civil Rule ?(F)(l) provides that "[n]o further briefs or written communications may
be filed without first obtaining leave of Court." The October 22 developments postdate ECF No.
93 and bear on its requests (Rl), (RS), and (R6). The Proposed Supplement, Exhibit A, is confined
to those developments and their effect on ECF No.93110. It repeats no argument from ECF No.
94 and adds no ground. Plaintiff requests leave to file it, with such opportunity for the Defendants
to respond as the Court directs. Rule 15(d) governs supplemental pleadings and is not invoked.
VIII. CONCLUSION
Plaintiff requests that the Court (1) grant leave to file Exhibit A; (2) retain determination
of the Objections and place on the record the four matters identified in Part 111.C; (3) determine

Document 99
1019

Filed 10/23/26

Page 14 of 16 PageID#

Objections One and Two and, if either is sustained, vacate ECF No. 96 and dispose independently
of ECF No. 86's prospective request; (4) in the alternative, define the limited effect of ECF No.
96 and determine ECF No. 93 on its own grounds; (5) identify the authority and procedure that
produced the successor designation and correct it if it was unauthorized; and (6) coordinate these
determinations with the pending applications, distinguishing relief granted, requests pending, and
requests rendered unnecessary.

DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO
PLAINTIFF’S MOTION TO SET ASIDE THE AMENDMENT AND DISCOVERY
DENIALS (DKT. NO. 90) AND MOTION FOR TARGETED VACATUR OF ECF NOS. 64
AND 84, WITHDRAWAL OR MODIFICATION OF THE MAGISTRATE-JUDGE
REFERRAL AND RELATED INTERIM RELIEF (DKT. NO. 93)

Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc., (“Meta”) by and through its undersigned counsel, hereby
respectfully opposes Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine’s Rule 72(a) Objections to ECF No. 84 and
Motion to Set Aside the Amendment and Discovery Denials (Dkt. No. 90), and Motion for Targeted
Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84, Withdrawal or Modification of the Magistrate Judge Referral, and
Related Interim Relief (Dkt. No. 93). In support of its response, Meta states the following:
I.

PROCEDURAL HISTORY
Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) seeks to hold Defendants National Center

for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) and Katie Hall (collectively, the “NCMEC
Defendants”) liable for responding to draft subpoenas that Plaintiff sent to NCMEC. The FAC also
seeks to hold Meta liable for purportedly conspiring with the NCMEC Defendants to send the
responses to the draft subpoenas. After NCMEC and Meta filed Motions to Dismiss the FAC (Dkt.
1


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 101
1033

Filed 10/27/26

Page 2 of 9 PageID#

Nos. 10 and 21), Plaintiff filed a Motion for Leave to File a Supplemental Complaint, seeking to
add allegations based on NCMEC’s Motion to Dismiss and a Motion to Dismiss filed by Meta
(along with 3 co-defendants) in a separate action filed by Plaintiff. See Dkt. No. 26. Plaintiff
subsequently withdrew that Motion to file a renewed version, attaching a proposed Second
Amended Complaint to his Motion for Leave to File Supplemental Complaint. Dkt. No. 59.
Separately, while Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss remained pending, Plaintiff also filed Motions
for Leave to Serve Interrogatories prior to a Rule 26(f) conference on both NCMEC (Dkt. No. 15)
and Meta (Dkt. 54), seeking to serve similar interrogatories on both NCMEC and Meta relating to
the existence of CyberTipline reports associated with 3 identifiers provided by Plaintiff.
On September 9, 2026, Magistrate Judge Davis ordered Plaintiff to “provide a redlined
version of the Amended Complaint. . . no later than September 11, 2026” to allow the Court to
review the changes and additions in the proposed amended complaint. Dkt. No. 64. Rather than
comply with this order, Plaintiff filed Rule 72(a) objections and a motion to set aside the
requirement that he submit a redlined version of the amended complaint. See Dkt. Nos. 66, 67. On
October 7, 2026, nearly a month after ordering Plaintiff to submit a redlined version of his
proposed Second Amended Complaint, Magistrate Judge Davis denied Plaintiff’s Motion for
Leave to File his Second Amended Complaint based on his failure to comply with the order. Dkt.
No. 84. In that same order, Magistrate Judge Davis also denied Plaintiff’s requests for leave to
serve interrogatories as premature, because the District Judge has not yet issued a scheduling order
in the matter.
In response to the Magistrate Judge’s order denying his motions, Plaintiff filed: (1) a
motion to disqualify Magistrate Judge Davis under 28 U.S.C. § 455 (Dkt. No. 86), (2) Rule 72(a)
objections and a corresponding motion to set aside the order denying his Motions (Dkt. Nos. 89

2


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 101
1034

Filed 10/27/26

Page 3 of 9 PageID#

and 90), and (3) a motion for vacatur of both the order denying his request and the order requiring
Plaintiff to submit a redlined version of his proposed amended complaint. Dkt. No. 93. The matter
has since been reassigned to Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick and Plaintiff’s Motion to
Disqualify Magistrate Judge Davis has been denied as moot. Dkt. No. 96.
II.

LEGAL STANDARD
Rule 72(a) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure allows a magistrate judge to hear and

decide non-dispositive motions” and “permits a party to submit objections to a magistrate judge’s
ruling on non-dispositive matters, such as discovery orders.” Bruce v. Hartford, 21 F. Supp. 3d
590, 593 (E.D. Va. 2014). For non-dispositive matters, “the review of a magistrate’s order is []
governed by the clearly erroneous or contrary to law standard of review.” Id. (internal quotations
omitted). Under Rule 72(a), the “Court will [] review the factual portions of the Magistrate Judge’s
order under the clearly erroneous standard, but will review legal conclusions to determine if they
are contrary to law.” Id.
III.

DISCUSSION
A. Magistrate Judge Davis Did Not Err in Denying Plaintiff’s Leave to Serve
Interrogatories or to File a Supplemental Complaint
Magistrate Judge Davis properly denied Plaintiff’s request for early discovery as

premature, because “discovery has not officially begun in this case” where “currently there is no
Scheduling Order in this case.” Dkt. No. 84 at 1-2; see Bui v. Smyth, No. 1:23-cv-1224, 2023 WL
11691500, at *1 (E.D. Va. Oct. 24, 2023) (denying request for early discovery because “the parties
have not conferred as required by Rule 26(f) and the Court has not issued a scheduling order
authorizing the parties to begin engaging in discovery” and “Defendants have filed their motions
to dismiss”); see also Rowland v. Am. Gen. Fin., Inc., 340 F.3d 187, 195 (4th Cir. 2003) (“A district
court has ‘wide latitude in controlling discovery’”).

3


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 101
1035

Filed 10/27/26

Page 4 of 9 PageID#

Plaintiff appears to fault Magistrate Judge Davis’s order for failing to consider whether his
requested early discovery should have been authorized by a court order pursuant to Rule 26(d).
Dkt. No. 91 at 4. In denying Plaintiff’s request for leave to serve interrogatories, however,
Magistrate Judge Davis expressly construed Plaintiff’s “Motions as requests for expedited
discovery.” Dkt. No. 84 at 1. And, for the reasons stated in Meta’s Opposition to Plaintiff’s Motion
for Leave to Serve Four Interrogatories on Meta, Plaintiff has failed to identify any justification
warranting expedited discovery here. See Dkt. No. 73 (arguing that expedited discovery was
unwarranted here because case-dispositive motions to dismiss were pending, plaintiff’s proposed
discovery would not be helpful in resolving the motions to dismiss, and, if plaintiff’s claims
survive dismissal, he could seek the discovery later in the case). Plaintiff’s objections do not
effectively refute any of Meta’s arguments, instead reiterating arguments from his original motion
for leave to serve interrogatories.
Plaintiff’s objections to Magistrate Judge Davis’s denial of his Motion for Leave to File a
Second Amended Complaint are similarly meritless. Plaintiff largely takes issue with the
requirement that he submit a redlined version of the proposed amended complaint and the denial
of his motion based on non-compliance with that requirement. See Dkt. No. 91 at 8-11. In ruling
on Plaintiff’s motion for leave to amend, Magistrate Judge Davis found that the Court “does not
possess sufficient information to” rule on Plaintiff’s request without a redline showing “the
changes, deletions, and additions” made to the Complaint. Dkt. No. 64. Courts in the Fourth Circuit
routinely require parties seeking to amend their pleadings to file redlines showing applicable
changes. See, e.g., Vogel v. RMAC Trust, No. 1:24-cv-2182, 2025 WL 1095370, at * 1 (E.D. Va.
Apr. 11, 2025) (providing that if plaintiffs “wish to seek leave to file an amended Complaint” they
may file a motion to amend with “a redlined copy of the proposed amended Complaint against the

4


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 101
1036

Filed 10/27/26

Page 5 of 9 PageID#

original Complaint”). “Filing a redline version of the Amended Complaint is not an empty
exercise” but rather “provides essential notice. . . as to the new claims.” Oyola v. Wash. Metro.
Area Transit Auth., No. 8:21-cv-540, 2021 WL 6884624, at *1 (D. Md. Nov. 12, 2021). Over a
month after the Court ordered Plaintiff to submit a redlined version of his amended Complaint,
Plaintiff failed to complete this essential exercise, warranting denial of his motion for leave to
amend.
Moreover, granting Plaintiff leave to file the proposed Second Amended Complaint would
be futile. As explained in Meta’s Opposition to Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to Amend his
Complaint (Dkt. No. 83), the new allegations in Plaintiff’s proposed Second Amended Complaint
relate only to Meta’s alleged awareness of this action based on language in Meta’s Motion to
Dismiss in a separate action brought by Plaintiff, and have no relevance to Plaintiff’s conspiracy
claims against Meta. Nothing in Plaintiff’s Rule 72(a) objections refute this argument, and instead
merely reiterate his assertion that his new allegations relate to “Meta’s knowledge, Meta’s state of
mind, Meta’s awareness of the relationship between this action,” and separate litigation Plaintiff
filed against Meta, without explaining how these allegations support his conspiracy claims against
Meta. Dkt. No. 91 at 22-23.
B. Vacatur of Magistrate Judge Davis’s Orders Is Not Warranted
Plaintiff’s objection requesting the vacatur of Magistrate Judge Davis’s orders based on the
alleged violations of 28 U.S.C. § 455 is similarly without merit. See Dkt. Nos. 91 at 24; see also
Dkt. No. 94. As an initial matter, there has been no finding of any violation of 28 U.S.C. § 455
here. But even assuming there was a violation of 28 U.S.C. § 455, vacatur of Magistrate Judge
Davis’s prior orders is unwarranted.

5


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 101
1037

Filed 10/27/26

Page 6 of 9 PageID#

In determining whether vacatur of prior orders is appropriate based on a violation of 28
U.S.C. § 455, courts consider: (1) the risk of injustice to the parties in the particular case, (2) the
risk that the denial of relief will produce injustice in other cases, and (3) the risk of undermining
the public confidence in the judicial process. Here, even assuming any conflict subject to 28 U.S.C.
§ 455 exists here, the weighing of these three factors counsels against vacatur of Magistrate Judge
Davis’s orders. First, giving continued effect to Magistrate Judge Davis’s orders does not pose any
risk of injustice or prejudice to Plaintiff. See Brock, 2022 WL 1231044, at *4 (denying motion to
vacate orders based on district judge’s “failure to recuse in light of his wife’s stock ownership in
Facebook” even though “the second and third factors weigh in favor of vacatur” because “the risk
of injustice to the parties is exceedingly low”). Neither of the two orders issued by Magistrate
Judge Davis dismissed any of Plaintiff’s claims nor did they address the merits of any of Plaintiff’s
claims or the arguments raised in Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss. See Chesher v. 3M Co., No.
3:15-cv-2123, 2022 WL 88328, at *2 (D.S.C. Jan. 6, 2022) (denying motion for vacatur of
judgment based on order on defendant’s motion to exclude plaintiff’s expert because the recused
judge “made no substantive rulings as to the” relevant entities).
Moreover, neither order provides any final judgment nor do they foreclose Plaintiff from
renewing his requests at a later stage in the action. Indeed, with respect to Plaintiff’s requested
discovery, Magistrate Judge Davis found only that Plaintiff’s request for discovery was
“premature,” leaving open the possibility that Plaintiff can seek the sought discovery later in the
case, if his claims survive Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss. And, with respect to Plaintiff’s
proposed amended complaint, nothing in Magistrate Judge Davis’s order expressly precludes
Plaintiff from renewing his request to amend by curing his failure to comply with the Court’s order
requiring Plaintiff submit a redlined version of the proposed amended complaint. Accordingly, any

6


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 101
1038

Filed 10/27/26

Page 7 of 9 PageID#

potential injustice caused by the orders is mitigated by the fact that Plaintiff may pursue his
requests again at a later stage of the litigation.
Second, that denial of Plaintiff’s requested relief will risk future injustice is minimal here.
Plaintiff filed timely objections to Magistrate Judge Davis’s orders and had an opportunity to seek
reassignment, and the case has since been re-assigned to Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick. See
Dkt. No. 96; see also ExxonMobil Oil Corp. v. TIG Ins. Co., 44 F.4th 163, 174 (2d Cir. 2022)
(finding that the “risk of harm in future cases is minimal. . . because the district court disclosed the
conflict as soon as [the judge] became aware of it and because [challenging party] has had ample
opportunity to challenge [the judge’s] rulings”).
Finally, vacatur is not warranted here to protect against any risk of harm to public
confidence in the judicial process because the challenged orders will be independently reviewed
by the District Judge. As noted above, Plaintiff has filed Rule 72(a) objections to the order
requiring him to submit a redlined version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint (Dkt. No.
66) and the order denying his leave to serve discovery and file his Second Amended Complaint.
(Dkt. No. 90). These objections ensure that Magistrate Judge Davis’s orders will be reviewed by
the District Judge and if there are any errors in those orders, they can be remedied through that
review, rather than by vacating the orders. See ExxonMobil Oil Corp., 44 F.4th at 174 (concluding
that “declining to vacate the judgment poses little additional risk to the public’s confidence the
judiciary” where party “had ample opportunity to challenge [conflicted judge’s] rulings” before
unconflicted judges, noting that “public also has an interest in speedy adjudication of disputes, an
interest that would not be furthered by forcing the parties to re-brief the same issues”); Waldon,
2022 WL 4552673, at *2 (denying motion to vacate judge’s prior orders based on alleged conflict
of interest because appellate court reviewed and affirmed judge’s decision, showing “that there is

7


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 101
1039

Filed 10/27/26

Page 8 of 9 PageID#

no risk of injustice to [plaintiffs] from [district judge’s] failure to recuse”). Indeed, “there need
not be a draconian remedy for every violation of §455(a)”—let alone every alleged violation of
§455(a). See Brock v. Zuckerberg, No. 21-1796, 2022 WL 1231044, at *3 (2d Cir. Apr. 27, 2022)
(quoting Liljeberg v. Health Servcs. Acquisition Corp., 486 U.S. 847, 862 (1988)).
IV.

CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court overrule Plaintiff’s

Rule 72(a) Objections to ECF No. 84 and deny his Motion to Set Aside the Amendment and
Discovery Denials (Dkt. No. 90) and Motion for Targeted Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84,
Withdrawal or Modification of the Magistrate Judge Referral, and Related Interim Relief (Dkt.
No. 93).

Defendants.

PLAINTIFF'S CONSOLIDATED REPLY IN SUPPORT OF ECF NOS. 90 AND 93

Plaintiff replies to Meta's opposition, ECF No. 101, to Plaintiffs Rule 72(a) objections to
ECF No. 84 (ECF Nos. 89, 90, 91) and to Plaintiffs motion for targeted vacatur (ECF Nos. 93,
94). Plaintiff seeks correction of the challenged rulings and determination of the remaining relief
on the existing submissions.
I.

ECF NO. 84 RESTS ON A LEGAL PREMISE RULE 26(d)(l) DOES NOT
PERMIT.
ECF No. 84 states that "the Court cannot issue an order concerning Plaintiffs Motions

because discovery has not officially begun in this case." ECF No. 84 at 1-2. Rule 26( d)(l) bars
discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference "except ... when authorized by these rules, by
stipulation, or by court order." Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(l). ECF Nos. 15 and 54 asked for that order.
ECF No. 84 identifies the absence of ordinary discovery and a Scheduling Order as preventing the
requested authorization. Rule 26( d)(l) expressly permits authorization by court order. The

1


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 102
1042

Filed 10/28/26

Page 2 of 10 PageID#

objection is to the legal reason the order gives. A court abuses its discretion when it "relies on
erroneous factual or legal premises." Wall v. Rasnick, 42 F.4th 214, 220 (4th Cir. 2022) (quotation
omitted).
Meta answers that the Magistrate Judge "expressly construed Plaintiffs 'Motions as
requests for expedited discovery."' ECF No. 101 at 4. The label does not resolve the objection.
The sentence after the label states the premise Plaintiff challenges. Describing the motions as
requests for early discovery does not change the reason the order gives for declining to authorize
them.
Meta also incorporates its arguments from ECF No. 73: that the requests should await the
dismissal motions and that the answers would not help Plaintiff. ECF No. 101 at 4. Those are
alternative grounds, and ECF No. 91 at 5-7 answers them. The seven interrogatories ask where
the two reports originated, what identifying information they contained, and whether they were
connected to any account Plaintiff held. ECF Nos. 15-1, 54-1. Each permits one of three answers.
None asks for the reports. NCMEC states that Plaintiff "does not have access to those reports."
ECF No. 74 at 5. That statement describes the gap: Defendants hold the records and seek dismissal
with prejudice on the ground that the letters' statements are true. ECF No. 91 at 5-6. Plaintiff
requests the answers now because Defendants' motions place the content of those records at issue
before any Scheduling Order will issue. The proposed pleading states its claims without the
answers. ECF No. 91 at 6-7. Whether to authorize the questions and whether any answer may be
considered on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion are separate questions. The Court should authorize the
requests on the existing showing or restore them for determination under Rule 26(d)(l). ECF No.
90 ,r 16(±)-(g).

2


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

II.

Document 102
1043

Filed 10/28/26

Page 3 of 10 PageID#

META DOES NOT RESOLVE THE PENDING COMPARISON AND DEADLINE
OBJECTIONS OR ESTABLISH FUTILITY OF THE PROPOSED PLEADING.
Plaintiff does not dispute the Court's authority to require a comparison document. ECF No.

91 at 11. Plaintiff produced none through October 7. The objections did not stay ECF No. 64. Id. at
13-14. The question is whether denial of ECF No. 59, with the filed proposed pleading and the
existing merits briefing before the Court, was the appropriate consequence. ECF No. 64 issued on
September 9 and set September 11 as the compliance date. ECF No. 64. Plaintiffs declaration
states that actual notice of ECF No. 64 arrived at about 9:09 p.m. on September 11. ECF No. 681 ,r,r 8- 9. On September 13 Plaintiff requested relief from the expired deadline under Rule 6(b )( 1)
(B) and a compliance period keyed to a ruling on the baseline. ECF No. 67 ,r 7. No comparison
followed through October 7. ECF No. 84 at 2. NCMEC called the initial missed deadline
"understandable." ECF No. 74 at 4. ECF No. 84 found "ample opportunity" to comply. ECF No.
84 at 2. It did not separately address the requested deadline relief or the baseline objection when
making that finding. Those circumstances bore on whether denial, rather than a defined compliance
period, was the appropriate response. Meta's opposition does not address them.
Meta's chronology states that "[r]ather than comply with this order, Plaintiff filed Rule
72(a) objections." ECF No. 101 at 2. The deadline expired on September 11. The objections were
submitted on September 13 . ECF No. 67 ,r 5. The weeks of nonproduction that followed are a
separate period, during which the request for deadline relief remained pending.
ECF No. 64 required comparison against the original Complaint, ECF No. 1. ECF No. 59
would replace the First Amended Complaint, ECF No. 5. ECF No. 59 ,r 3. A comparison against
ECF No. 1 combines changes already made in ECF No. 5 with the changes now proposed. That is
the basis for the request to reconsider or clarify the baseline. ECF No. 67 ,r 7. Vogel denied
amendment without prejudice and permitted a renewed motion with clean and marked copies.
