MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF'S MOTION FOR ENTRY OF A
SCHEDULING ORDER AND, AS NECESSARY, AN INITIAL PRETRIAL
CONFERENCE

I.

INTRODUCTION

This action has an operative complaint, appearing Defendants, and pending motions. ECF
5, 10, 21 , 45 . It has no Rule 16(b) scheduling order. NCMEC was served on July 31, 2026, and
appeared on August 12, 2026. ECF 3, 10. Under Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2) and 6(a), the ordinary
deadline for the scheduling order, absent a finding of good cause for delay, was October 13, 2026.
ECF 84 confirmed on October 7, 2026 that no scheduling order existed. ECF 84 at 1-2.
Plaintiff requests three things. First, entry of the scheduling order after the report or
consultation Rule 16(b)(1) requires. Second, an initial scheduling conference where necessary to
obtain that consultation, even if the Court is not prepared to enter the complete schedule at once.
Third, if either step is postponed, an order stating the good cause found under Rule 16(b)(2) and

1


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

the date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed. The third request is not a substitute
for the first two and is not consent to postponement.
This Motion does not seek authorization of particular discovery, adjudication of any
discovery dispute, or reconsideration of any ruling. It asks the Court to establish the timetable for
a pending action.

II.

PROCEDURAL FACTS

applications concerning ECF 84 and ECF 96 remain pending. ECF 89, 90, 93, 97-99. None of
those filings is the subject of this Motion.

III.

RULE 16(b) GOVERNS THIS ACTION, AND ITS ORDINARY DEADLINE RAN
ON OCTOBER 13, 2026.
A.

The action is not exempt.

Rule 16(b)(1) applies "[ e]xcept in categories of actions exempted by local rule." Fed. R.
Civ. P. 16(b)(l). Local Civil Rule 16(A) exempts "[p]roceedings upon a defendant's default and
matters involving habeas corpus petitions, other pro se prisoner petitions, bankruptcy proceedings,

2


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 104
1062

Filed 10/28/26

Page 3 of 10 PageID#

condemnation cases, forfeitures, and reviews from administrative agencies." E.D. Va. L. Civ. R.
16(A). This is a civil action by a non-prisoner asserting claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and
Virginia law. ECF 5. It is in none of the exempt categories. Local Civil Rule 16(B) therefore
applies: "In all other civil actions, as promptly as possible after a complaint or notice of removal
has been filed, the Court shall schedule an initial pretrial conference to be conducted in accordance
with Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)." Local Civil Rule 16(B).
B.

The computation.

Rule 16(b)(2) provides that "unless the judge finds good cause for delay, the judge must
issue it within the earlier of 90 days after any defendant has been served with the complaint or 60
days after any defendant has appeared." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). Local Civil Rule 16(B) sets the
same outer bound: "not later than sixty (60) days from first appearance or ninety (90) days after
service of the complaint." Local Civil Rule 16(B).

Rule 6(a) governs the computation of "any time period specified in these rules ." Fed. R.
Civ. P. 6(a). The 90-day interval is not a second period that opens after the 60-day period closes.
Rule 16(b)(2) selects the earlier of the two. The ordinary Rule 16(b)(2) deadline, absent a finding
of good cause for delay, was October 13, 2026.

3


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

C.

Document 104

Page 4 of 10 PageID#

The command and the exception.

Rule 16(b)(2) states both. The judge "must issue" the scheduling order within the period.
The judge may issue it later upon finding "good cause for delay." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). Plaintiff
does not contend that the lapse affects the Court's jurisdiction or the validity of any order entered
since. Plaintiff does not contend that passage of the deadline itself authorizes service of discovery.
Plaintiff contends that the period has run and that the rule now calls for one of two things: a
scheduling order, or a finding of good cause for a defined delay.
IV.

RULE 16(b)(l) SUPPLIES TWO ROUTES TO THE SCHEDULING ORDER,
AND EITHER CAN BEGIN NOW.
Rule 16(b)( 1) provides two means of proceeding: receipt of the parties' Rule 26( f) report

or consultation with counsel and the unrepresented party at a scheduling conference. Fed. R. Civ.
P. 16(b)(1 )(A)-(B). Plaintiff requests the conference route if a sufficient report is not available.
Local Civil Rule 16(B) permits scheduling without a conference where the federal requirements
are otherwise satisfied; Plaintiff does not invoke it to dispense with both alternatives.
The parties' Rule 26(f) conference is the subject of a separate motion. Plaintiff does not
represent here that the conference is complete, and this Motion does not depend on it.
Where no completed report exists, Rule 16(b)(l)(B) supplies the Court' s own means of
scheduling. Rule 26(f)(l) ties the parties' conference to the Court's calendar: the parties must
confer "at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due
under Rule 16(b)," except "when the court orders otherwise." Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(l). Rule 26(f)
(4) permits a court, by local rule, to require the parties' conference to occur less than 21 days
before the scheduling conference, to shorten the reporting interval, and to excuse the written report
in favor of oral reporting at the Rule 16(b) conference. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(4). Local Civil Rule
26(A)(l) adopts those adjustments for this District. Local Civil Rule 26(A)(l)(a)-(b). A

4


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 104
1064

Filed 10/28/26

Page 5 of 10 PageID#

conference-setting order that shortens the intervals supplies dates the parties can meet after the
order issues. Plaintiff requests that order. Mot. ~ 9(c).
The 2015 amendment to Rule 16(b)(2) shortened the scheduling timetable to reduce delay
at the beginning of litigation. The Advisory Committee recognized that some cases require more
time to prepare a complete schedule, and contemplated that an initial scheduling conference would
ordinarily occur within the timetable even where final scheduling required additional time. Fed.
R. Civ. P. 16 advisory committee's note to 2015 amendment. That distinction supports the separate
request in Motion ~ 10: if the Court determines that the complete scheduling order should await
another development, the Court can still hold the initial conference now and establish the
remaining case-management steps. Plaintiff does not contend that the note entitles Plaintiff to the
particular dates proposed.
The party-to-party conference under Rule 26(f) and the Court's conference under Rule
16(b) are distinct events. Plaintiff does not offer the Court's conference as a finding that the parties'
conference has occurred. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to find that any Defendant has declined
to participate, to require a written-only conference, or to adopt Plaintiffs proposals by default.
Plaintiff asks the Court to set the consultation Rule 16(b)(1 )(B) describes and to direct the
preparatory steps the Court requires.
V.

ECF 84 IDENTIFIED THE ABSENCE OF A SCHEDULING ORDER; THIS
MOTION REQUESTS THE PROCESS WHOSE ABSENCE IT IDENTIFIED.
ECF 84 addressed Plaintiffs motions for limited discovery before the Rule 26(f)

conference and Plaintiffs motion for leave to amend. ECF 15, 54, 59. It denied the discovery
motions "as premature" and stated that "discovery officially begins when the District Judge issues
a Scheduling Order and currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case." ECF 84 at 1-2. ECF

5


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 104
1065

Filed 10/28/26

Page 6 of 10 PageID#

84 did not set a scheduling timetable and did not make a finding of good cause for delay under
Rule 16(b)(2).
ECF 84 relied on the absence of a scheduling order in denying the requests before it.
Plaintiff maintains his objections to that reasoning in the pending review applications. ECF 89, 90,
93. This Motion presents a different request: establish the scheduling process whose absence the
order identified. Continued absence of that process leaves no date for the next ordinary casemanagement step.
If the Court relies on ECF 84 as a reason to defer scheduling itself, Plaintiff requests
identification of that construction and its basis.

VI.

PENDING MOTIONS ARE MANAGED THROUGH THE SCHEDULE, NOT
THROUGH AN UNDEFINED POSTPONEMENT.
Three motions to dismiss are pending. ECF 10, 21, 45. Rule 16(b)(2) measures the ordinary

deadline from service or appearance, not from the filing of an answer. Pending motions may be
relevant to a case-specific finding of good cause for delay, but their existence does not replace that
determination. The first is a docket fact. The second is a determination Rule 16(b)(2) assigns to
the judge.
The First Amended Complaint is the operative pleading. ECF 5. Scheduling proceeds from
the operative pleading. Rule 16(b)(3)(A) requires the scheduling order to "limit the time to join
other parties, amend the pleadings, complete discovery, and file motions." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)
(3)(A). Rule 16(b)(4) permits modification "for good cause and with the judge's consent." Fed. R.
Civ. P. 16(b)(4). Those provisions allow a schedule to be entered while motions are pending and
adjusted when rulings issue. The Court retains its authority to sequence the case through the
schedule it enters.

6


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 104
1066

Filed 10/28/26

Page 7 of 10 PageID#

Plaintiff does not ask the Court to predict the disposition of the pending motions. Plaintiff
asks the Court to establish the timetable governing this action while those motions remain pending.
If the Court determines that a pending motion supplies good cause for delay, Rule 16(b)(2)
accommodates that determination, with the scope and duration of the postponement identified.
This Motion does not request a stay of the motions to dismiss and does not expand any sequencing
request already pending.

VII.

ANY POSTPONEMENT SHOULD STATE ITS BASIS AND THE NEXT
SCHEDULING STEP.
Rule 16(b)(2) predicates delay on a finding of good cause. Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). If the

Court postpones the scheduling conference or entry of the scheduling order, Plaintiff requests that
the order state the good cause found and the date or event on which scheduling will next be
addressed. A stated basis permits the parties to determine what remains required and when the
action will proceed. The request for a stated basis is not consent to postponement and does not
withdraw the request for scheduling now.

VIII. CONCLUSION
Plaintiff requests that the Court: ( 1) enter a scheduling order after the report or consultation
Rule 16(b)( 1) requires, with the preparatory intervals shortened under Rule 26( f)(l ), Rule 26( f)
(4), and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(l); (2) set an initial scheduling conference on a date certain if the
Court requires one to accomplish that consultation, or if the Court determines that the complete
scheduling order should await another development; and (3) if the Court postpones either step,
state the good cause found under Rule 16(b)(2) and the date or event on which scheduling will
next be addressed. Plaintiff requests disposition of each request to the extent the preceding request
is denied or deferred.

PlaintiffMarvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(f)(l)-(3),
and under the Court's case-management authority under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16, for
an order directing the appearing parties to complete the conference Rule 26(f) requires by a date

RULE 26(f) ASSIGNS PLANNING RESPONSIBILITIES TO THE APPEARING
PARTIES.
Rule 26(±)(1) provides that, except in exempted proceedings or "when the court orders

otherwise, the parties must confer as soon as practicable-and in any event at least 21 days before
a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due under Rule 16(b)." Fed. R. Civ.
P. 26(±)(1). This action is not an exempted proceeding under Rule 26(a)(l)(B). Plaintiff has located
no order of this Court directing otherwise. Ballentine Deel. ,-J 10.
Rule 26(±)(2) states what the conference is for and who must arrange it. The parties "must
consider the nature and basis of their claims and defenses and the possibilities for promptly settling
or resolving the case; make or arrange for the disclosures required by Rule 26(a)(l); discuss any
issues about preserving discoverable information; and develop a proposed discovery plan." Fed.
R. Civ. P. 26(±)(2). "The attorneys of record and all unrepresented parties that have appeared in
the case are jointly responsible for arranging the conference, for attempting in good faith to agree
on the proposed discovery plan, and for submitting to the court within 14 days after the conference
a written report outlining the plan." Id. Rule 26(±)(3) lists what the plan must state, including "the
parties' views and proposals" on the subjects of discovery, "whether discovery should be
conducted in phases or be limited to or focused on particular issues," the handling of electronically
stored information, the timing and method for complying with Rule 26(b )(5)(A), changes to
discovery limits, and any other orders the Court should enter under Rule 26( c) or Rule 16(b) and
(c). Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(3)(A)-(F).

3


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 106
1085

Filed 10/28/26

Page 4 of 12 PageID#

Those provisions apply to Plaintiff, who has appeared pro se, and to counsel of record for
NCMEC, Hall, and Meta, each of which has appeared. ECF 10, 21, 45. The obligation is joint.
Rule 26(f)(2) does not assign to Plaintiff alone the task of arranging the conference, and it does
not permit an appearing party to decline participation on its own assessment of timing.
This Motion does not depend on establishing that a particular conference deadline has
already passed. The Rule 16(b)(2) computation is presented in Plaintiffs companion Motion for
Entry of a Scheduling Order and is not repeated here. The request here is prospective: a workable
order setting the dates by which the appearing parties will complete what Rule 26(f) requires.

II.

PENDING MOTIONS TO DISMISS DO NOT, BY THEMSELVES, EXCUSE
PARTICIPATION.
The 1993 Advisory Committee Note expressly addresses pending Rule 12 motions: "The

obligation to participate in the planning process is imposed on all parties that have appeared in the
case, including defendants who, because of a pending Rule 12 motion, may not have yet filed an
answer in the case." Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee's note to 1993 amendment (subdivision
(f)). The same Note contemplates that agreement may not be reached, and that where it is not, the
report should "indicate the competing proposals of the parties" so that the court can resolve them.
Id. The rule's text is the principal authority; the Note explains its application to the circumstance

counsel's reply describes.
Counsel's October 28 reply states three reasons for postponement: the pending motions, if
granted in full, would dispose of all claims; the surviving claims are not yet known; and Plaintiff
might seek leave to amend after a dismissal. Ex. C-1. Each of those is a contingency that the
planning process is designed to address.
First, planning can identify how each contingency affects the proposed schedule. Rule 26(f)
(2) directs the parties to consider "the nature and basis of their claims and defenses" as they stand.

4


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 106
1086

Filed 10/28/26

Page 5 of 12 PageID#

The First Amended Complaint is the operative pleading. ECF 5. The defenses asserted in the
pending motions are known. A plan developed from that record can state the parties' views on
what discovery, if any, should precede the Court's rulings.
Second, Defendants may propose phased discovery, deferral of substantive discovery until
the motions are decided, or other protective terms. Rule 26(f)(3)(B) requires the plan to state the
parties' views on "whether discovery should be conducted in phases or be limited to or focused on
particular issues." Rule 26(f)(3)(F) invites proposals for "any other orders that the court should
issue under Rule 26( c) or under Rule 16(b) and (c). "A Defendant that believes no discovery should
proceed until the motions are decided states that position in the report.
Third, the report places those proposals before the Court for resolution. That is the function
Rule 26(f)(2) assigns it. The Court then decides sequencing with each party's position stated, rather
than with one party's position stated in correspondence and the planning step not performed.
The proposition this Motion rests on is limited: the pendency of the motions to dismiss
does not, by itself, excuse participation in planning. Plaintiff does not contend that every request
for postponement lacks merit. This Motion asks the Court to decide when the conference will
occur. It does not ask the Court to decide any request concerning the sequencing or postponement
of substantive discovery; those requests belong in the report, where each party states its position
for the Court's resolution. The Court retains its authority to modify or defer the process under Rule
26(f)(l) and Rule 16. Nothing in the requested order affects the immunity defenses NCMEC and
Hall have asserted, which they may preserve in the report and in every other filing. The order
sought here would require each Defendant to state its position in the form the Rule prescribes, by
a date the Court sets.

5


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

III.

Document 106
1087

Filed 10/28/26

Page 6 of 12 PageID#

THE CORRESPONDENCE PRESENTS A CURRENT TIMING DISPUTE.

Plaintiff requested responses by October 30, 2026. Ex. A § IV. That date had not passed
when this Motion was filed, and Plaintiff does not contend that any Defendant defaulted on it.
Plaintiff files now because the October 28 reply states a position, not because a deadline expired.
The reply states that a conference is "premature at this juncture" and that "it seems
premature to be planning discovery" until the motions are decided and any further amendment is
known. Ex. C-1. That is a position that planning should await further developments. It identifies
no order of this Court postponing the conference, proposes no date, and does not answer whether
NCMEC or Hall would oppose an order setting a deadline. Ex. C-1. The position is stated by
counsel for NCMEC and Hall. The reply's reference to "Meta and my clients" does not state
Meta's position, and counsel does not represent Meta. Meta's counsel has not responded to
Plaintiffs separate request. Ballentine Decl. ~ 9. Plaintiff does not attribute the reply to Meta.
An order setting a completion date and a report date resolves the dispute the
correspondence presents. It identifies when participation must occur and how any disagreement
reaches the Court. No finding of bad faith is necessary to enter it, and Plaintiff does not request
one.
IV.

A SUBSTANTIVE WRITTEN EXCHANGE CAN PRODUCE THE REQUIRED
REPORT.

Rule 26(±)(2) requires the parties to "confer." The 2000 amendment replaced the earlier
requirement that the parties "meet." The accompanying Note explains that the parties may confer
by means other than a face-to-face meeting, while preserving the court's authority to require faceto-face attendance by order in a particular case. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee's note to
2000 amendment (subdivision (f)). The Note does not establish a right to confer by any particular

Document 106
1088

Filed 10/28/26

Page 7 of 12 PageID#

means, and it does not make an unanswered invitation a completed conference. Plaintiff does not
contend that it does.
Plaintiff requests the Court's approval of a defined written process. The October 16
common agenda identifies the subjects: the nature and basis of claims and defenses and
possibilities for resolution; initial disclosures and any objections to their timing; preservation;
subjects, timing, and phasing of discovery; electronically stored information; privilege and workproduct procedures, including the timing and method for complying with Rule 26(b )(5)(A), which
Rule 26(f)(3)(D) as amended effective December 1, 2025 requires the plan to address; changes to
discovery limits; and protective and scheduling orders. Ex. A § III. The agenda keys each subject
to the provision of Rule 26(f)(2) or (3) that requires it. Id.
The requested order directs substantive exchange on those subjects and reconciliation of
positions before the report is filed. It does not request a finding that transmission of the October
16 materials completed the conference. Plaintiff does not make that contention. The conference
and the report are separate steps. The conference is completed when each appearing party has
stated its position on each required subject and the parties have attempted in good faith to agree.
Substantive disagreement may remain after that exchange; the report records it. Failure to agree
does not itself establish failure to complete the conference. Ex. A § V.
V.

THE REQUESTED ORDER COMPLEMENTS THE RULE 16 MOTION.
Plaintiffs Motion for Entry of a Scheduling Order (ECF _) addresses the Court's

scheduling process under Rule 16(b): the scheduling conference and entry of the scheduling order.
This Motion addresses the parties' obligations under Rule 26(f): participation in the planning

Mot. ,r 9; ECF _ ,r 5.

ECF 84 addressed two motions under Rule 26( d)(l) for leave to serve limited
interrogatories before the Rule 26(f) conference, ECF 15 and 54. The order interpreted them as
"requests for expedited discovery" and denied them as premature because "discovery has not
officially begun in this case" and "discovery officially begins when the District Judge issues a
Scheduling Order and currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case." ECF 84 at 1-2. ECF 84
does not address the parties' conference under Rule 26(f) and does not postpone it. Those motions

THE REQUESTED DEADLINES PROVIDE A DEFINED NEXT STEP.

last stated. The 14-days-after-completion term preserves Rule 26(f)(2)'s ordinary reporting period
where the conference is completed early.
The companion motion requests a Rule 16(b) scheduling conference within 21 days of its
granting order, with the parties' conference no later than seven days before and the report no later

ORDER

This matter comes before the Court on pro se Plaintiffs (i) Motion for Entry of a

Scheduling Order and, as necessary, an Initial Pretrial Conference and (ii) Motion for an Order
Directing Completion of the Rule 26(1) Conference and Submission of a Discovery Plan. (Dkts.
103, 105). Plaintiff seeks multiple forms of relief. First, Plaintiff requests entry of a scheduling
order. Second, Plaintiff requests an order directing the parties to complete a Rule 26(f) conference

and file respective discovery plans. Third, Plaintiff requests an initial pretrial conference. Fourth,
if any of these steps are postponed. Plaintiff requests that the order state the date or event on which
scheduling will next be addressed. In deference to Plaintiffs pro se status, the Court will liberally
construe his filings. See Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007). However, even applying this
liberal standard. Plaintiff has not established that he is entitled to the relief he seeks.

There are three pending motions to dismiss in this matter. The last of which was filed on

September 2, 2026. See Dkts. 10, 21, & 45. “Given that Rule 16 Scheduling Orders initiate
discovery obligations, it is standard for courts to wait until any preliminary motions such as


Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF

Document 108
1115

Filed 10/29/26

Page 2 of 2 PageID#

motions to dismiss or to remand arc resolved to avoid expensive or otherwise burdensome

discovery on potentially frivolous claims.” Giirri Rubio v. MiilUn, No. 25-CV-2756-ABA, 2026
WI. 1194557, at *3 (D. Md. May 1, 2026). Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has

chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.

Accordingly, Plaintiffs Motions (Dkts. 103, 105) arc DKNIKl) without prejudice.
ENTERED this 29lh day of October, 2026.

WILLIAM E. LITZPATRICK

UNITED STA'I'ES MAGISTRATE JUDGE

runs.text: PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR PRIORITY DETERMINATION AND SEQUENCING OF PENDING PROCEEDINGS CONCERNING ECF NO. 96

content.text: Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves before District Judge Rossie D. Alston, Jr. under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 1 and 72(a), 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A), and the Court’s authority to control the disposition of matters on its docket. This Motion concerns the order of judicial consideration of matters already pending. Plaintiff seeks priority determination of this Motion and an order permitting the assigned magistrate judge, Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick, to address the Rule 54(b) reconsideration of ECF No. 96 before the District Judge completes review of the overlapping issues. A Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1). Plaintiff incorporates it by reference.
I.	THE PENDING PROCEEDINGS
1.	ECF No. 86 requested determination of historical financial-interest facts. ECF No. 86 at 4, 6. ECF No. 96 denied that motion as moot following reassignment. ECF No. 96 at 1.
2.	ECF Nos. 97–99 present Rule 72(a) objections and related requests to the District Judge concerning ECF No. 96.

3.	Plaintiff’s Rule 54(b) Motion to Vacate ECF No. 96 and Determine Magistrate Judge Davis’s Ownership of Meta Common Stock (the “Rule 54(b) Motion”), filed November 1, 2026, requests restoration and determination of the historical ownership issues as to the dates on which ECF Nos. 64 and 84 were entered. Rule 54(b) Mot. ¶¶ 10, 17, 20.
4.	ECF No. 93 requests retrospective relief concerning ECF Nos. 64 and 84. ECF No. 93 ¶¶ 5, 10(R2). Ordinary briefing on ECF No. 93 was completed through ECF No. 102, filed October 28, 2026.
II.	GROUNDS FOR PRIORITY AND SEQUENCING

runs.text: II.	GROUNDS FOR PRIORITY AND SEQUENCING

content.text: 5.	The Rule 54(b) Motion seeks determinations concerning facts material to ECF No. 93. ECF No. 93 ¶ 5 lists “the dates of ownership” among “[t]he questions requiring resolution.”

6.	Determination of the Rule 54(b) Motion first would establish what the assigned magistrate judge has decided, declined to decide, or directed for further factual development before district-judge review of the overlapping issues. The “Overlapping ECF No. 96 Issues” are whether ECF No. 96 should be set aside, modified, or given limited effect, ECF No. 97 ¶¶ 7–14, 17–18, 20(4)–(5), and the historical ownership and holding-arrangement facts, with any relief under ECF No. 93 that depends on them, ECF No. 93 ¶¶ 5, 10(R2), 10(R7).
7.	Priority consideration is warranted because ECF No. 93 has completed ordinary briefing and may be adjudicated while the Rule 54(b) Motion remains pending.
III.	RELIEF REQUESTED
8.	Plaintiff requests that this Motion receive priority consideration, be decided on the papers, and receive an express disposition of the sequencing request.

9.	Plaintiff requests an order directing prompt consideration of the Rule 54(b) Motion by the assigned magistrate judge, subject to the District Judge’s determination of the pending referral-authority question. ECF No. 93 ¶ 10(R1); ECF No. 97 ¶¶ 15, 20(6).
10.	Plaintiff requests deferral of final district-judge determination of the Overlapping ECF No. 96 Issues until disposition of the Rule 54(b) Motion or further order.

11.	Plaintiff requests that the order preserve immediate determination of independent or threshold issues. Those issues include the successor designation and independently warranted relief under ECF No. 93. ECF No. 93 ¶ 10(R6); ECF No. 97 ¶¶ 15, 20(6).
12.	Plaintiff requests that the order preserve all pending objections, motions, existing deadlines, and independent requests for relief.

13.	This Motion does not seek a general stay, supplement ECF No. 93, reopen its briefing, or extend or restart any period to object under Rule 72(a). It does not request deferral of ECF Nos. 10, 21, or 45, and Plaintiff maintains ECF No. 93 ¶ 10(R5)(c).

14.	Plaintiff waives oral argument on this Motion only and requests that the Court direct its submission on the papers under Local Civil Rules 7(E) and 7(J) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 78(b). A Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument and Request for Submission on the Papers accompanies this Motion.
15.	Plaintiff relies on the existing docket. No declaration or exhibit accompanies this Motion.
WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter the accompanying Proposed Order.

content.text: ECF No. 86 asked the Court to “state on the record” whether the asset reported as “FB common stock” is common stock of Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. and whether that interest was held on the dates of specified orders. ECF No. 86 at 4. ECF No. 96 denied that motion as moot following reassignment and made no finding on those questions. ECF No. 96 at 1. Plaintiff’s Rule 54(b) Motion to Vacate ECF No. 96 and Determine Magistrate Judge Davis’s Ownership of Meta Common Stock (the “Rule 54(b) Motion”), filed November 1, 2026, asks the assigned magistrate judge to vacate ECF No. 96 and determine ownership on the dates of ECF Nos. 64 and 84. Rule 54(b) Mot. ¶¶ 10, 17, 20.

The District Judge has pending requests concerning the consequences of the challenged participation. ECF No. 93 requests vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84 “upon the statutory findings identified in paragraph 5,” which include “the dates of ownership.” ECF No. 93 ¶¶ 5, 10(R2). Ordinary briefing on ECF No. 93 was completed through ECF No. 102, filed October 28, 2026. ECF Nos. 97–99 are a separate proceeding. They present Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 96 and related requests, which ECF No. 102 does not address. ECF No. 97 ¶ 17 asks the District Judge to decide ECF No. 93 “on its own grounds, resolving the statutory facts to the extent necessary to that decision.” Plaintiff maintains that request. The Rule 54(b) Motion is an additional request. Mem. Supp. Rule 54(b) Mot., Part IV.E.
II.	SEQUENCING IS A PROPER EXERCISE OF CASE-MANAGEMENT AUTHORITY.

content.text: The Federal Rules “should be construed, administered, and employed by the court and the parties to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every action and proceeding.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 1. The power to stay proceedings “is incidental to the power inherent in every court to control the disposition of the causes on its docket with economy of time and effort for itself, for counsel, and for litigants.” Landis v. North American Co., 299 U.S. 248, 254 (1936). How to do so “calls for the exercise of judgment, which must weigh competing interests and maintain an even balance.” Id. at 254–55. An order setting the sequence of related matters within one action falls within that authority.

R. Civ. P. 72(a). The requested sequence follows that structure. It changes no standard of review and removes no matter from the District Judge.

The requested sequence permits the Court to obtain the assigned magistrate judge’s disposition of the pending reconsideration request before completing review of the Overlapping ECF No. 96 Issues defined in the Motion at paragraph 6. It establishes the procedural and factual posture of that request without requiring duplicative consideration, reopening completed briefing, or altering the relief already requested from the District Judge. Any disposition remains subject to timely objection under Rule 72(a).

A party seeking a stay “must make out a clear case of hardship or inequity in being required to go forward, if there is even a fair possibility that the stay for which he prays will work damage to some one else.” Landis, 299 U.S. at 255; see Williford v. Armstrong World Indus., Inc., 715 F.2d 124, 127 (4th Cir. 1983) (requiring “clear and convincing circumstances outweighing potential harm to the party against whom it is operative”). To the extent that standard applies, the requested deferral operates on Plaintiff’s own requests. It imposes no obligation on any Defendant and does not defer ECF Nos. 10, 21, or 45. Without it, two judicial officers could address the same order at the same time, and ECF No. 93 could be decided while the Rule 54(b) Motion remains undetermined.

content.text: PLAINTIFF’S RULE 54(b) MOTION TO VACATE ECF NO. 96 AND DETERMINE MAGISTRATE JUDGE DAVIS’S OWNERSHIP OF META COMMON STOCK

runs.text: PLAINTIFF’S RULE 54(b) MOTION TO VACATE ECF NO. 96 AND DETERMINE MAGISTRATE JUDGE DAVIS’S OWNERSHIP OF META COMMON STOCK

content.text: Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b) to vacate the Order entered October 22, 2026 (ECF No. 96), which denied ECF No. 86 as moot. Plaintiff seeks restoration, for decision, of the historical financial-interest determination requested in Part V and Request A2 of ECF No. 86. Plaintiff moves for a finding that Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis owned common stock of Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) on September 9, 2026, when he entered ECF No. 64, and on October 7, 2026, when he entered ECF No. 84. Plaintiff requests determination of the ownership and holding-arrangement facts necessary to apply 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4). In the alternative, Plaintiff requests an on-record determination of who owned the reported asset on each date and whether the interest fell within § 455(d)(4), after the factual development necessary to decide that question. A Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1). Plaintiff incorporates it by reference.
I.	THE ORDER CHALLENGED

1.	ECF No. 96 denied ECF No. 86 in its entirety. Its operative text reads: “ORDERED that Plaintiff’s Motion is DENIED AS MOOT. The case has been reassigned to Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick.” ECF No. 96 at 1. Magistrate Judge Davis signed it. It was entered October 22, 2026.
2.	An unnumbered docket entry of the same date reads: “Case Reassigned to Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick. Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis no longer assigned to the case.”

3.	ECF No. 96 states one ground: reassignment. It does not determine whether the asset reported as “FB common stock” is Meta common stock. It does not determine whether that asset was owned on any date in 2026. It does not determine the arrangement through which the asset is held. It does not determine whether any divestiture occurred. It makes no finding on any item in ECF No. 86, Part V.

4.	ECF No. 96 is an interlocutory order. No judgment has been entered. Under Rule 54(b), an order that adjudicates fewer than all the claims “may be revised at any time before the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims and all the parties’ rights and liabilities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b).
II.	THE REQUEST TO BE RESTORED

runs.text: II.	THE REQUEST TO BE RESTORED

content.text: 5.	ECF No. 86 was filed October 13, 2026 and entered October 14, 2026. It presented two kinds of requests.

6.	The first kind was prospective. Request A1 sought disqualification of Magistrate Judge Davis. Request A3 sought determination of the motion before further substantive action. Request A4 sought transfer of the referred matters upon disqualification. ECF No. 86 at 5–6 (Part VII).

7.	The second kind was historical. Part V asked the Court to “state on the record” five facts: “(a) whether the asset reported as ‘FB common stock’ on Exhibits A and B is common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.; (b) whether that interest was held on July 30, 2026, and on each date on which ECF Nos. 62, 63, 64, 65, 82, and 84 were entered; (c) the date and manner of any divestiture; (d) whether the interest is held directly or through a mutual or common investment fund within the meaning of 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4)(i); and (e) any other fact the Court considers material to the application of 28 U.S.C. § 455(f).” ECF No. 86 at 4. Request A2 asked the Court to “[s]tate on the record whether the reported interest was held during the challenged participation, the date and manner of any divestiture, and the facts necessary to determine any claimed exception under 28 U.S.C. § 455(f).” ECF No. 86 at 6.

8.	Reassignment answered the first kind of request. Magistrate Judge Davis no longer participates in this action. Plaintiff does not seek his disqualification from further participation. Plaintiff does not seek his reinstatement. Plaintiff raises no objection to Magistrate Judge Fitzpatrick personally. The separately pending challenge to the source and procedure of the successor designation, ECF Nos. 97–99, is maintained and is addressed in Part VI below.

9.	Reassignment did not answer the second kind. Ownership on September 9, 2026 and on October 7, 2026 is a fact about two judicial acts already completed. The identity of the officer who handles later matters does not change that fact.

10.	This Motion seeks restoration of the second kind of request as to two dates. September 9, 2026 is the date ECF No. 64 was entered. ECF No. 64 required a redline against the original Complaint by September 11, 2026. October 7, 2026 is the date ECF No. 84 was entered. ECF No. 84 denied ECF No. 59 for noncompliance with ECF No. 64. It denied ECF No. 15, which sought discovery from Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”), and ECF No. 54, which sought discovery from Meta. ECF No. 84 at 1–2. The Part V requests concerning the dates of ECF Nos. 62, 63, 65, and 82 remain presented in the applications identified in Part VI below. This Motion does not expand them.
III.	GROUNDS FOR RECONSIDERATION

11.	A court may revise an interlocutory order under the same circumstances in which it may depart from the law of the case: “a subsequent trial produc[ing] substantially different evidence,” a change in applicable law, or “clear error causing ‘manifest injustice.’” Carlson v. Boston Scientific Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). Plaintiff invokes the third ground.

runs.text: 11.	A court may revise an interlocutory order under the same circumstances in which it may depart from the law of the case: “a subsequent trial produc[ing] substantially different evidence,” a change in applicable law, or “clear error causing ‘manifest injustice.’”
, 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). Plaintiff invokes the third ground.

content.text: 12.	The error. ECF No. 96 treated reassignment as disposing of the entire motion. Reassignment disposed of the prospective requests. It did not reach the historical requests. A request becomes moot when no effectual relief can follow from granting it. Church of Scientology of Cal. v. United States, 506 U.S. 9, 12 (1992). The historical determination requested in ECF No. 86 can still produce effectual relief. It is the factual predicate of Plaintiff’s pending application for relief from ECF Nos. 64 and 84. ECF No. 93 ¶¶ 5, 10(R2), 10(R7). A change in the officer assigned to future matters did not make the request to determine that predicate moot.

Church of Scientology of Cal. v. United States

, 506 U.S. 9, 12 (1992). The historical determination requested in ECF No. 86 can still produce effectual relief. It is the factual predicate of Plaintiff’s pending application for relief from ECF Nos. 64 and 84. ECF No. 93 ¶¶ 5, 10(R2), 10(R7). A change in the officer assigned to future matters did not make the request to determine that predicate moot.

content.text: 13.	The injustice. ECF No. 96 closed the proceeding in which Plaintiff expressly requested determination of the reported financial interest. It did so without deciding ownership or providing for development of the ownership record. ECF Nos. 64 and 84 remain operative, and ECF No. 93 presents a statutory challenge to those orders. Plaintiff contends that terminating the supported historical inquiry as moot, while its subject remains material to that pending challenge, causes manifest injustice. The pending district-judge applications preserve additional means of correction; they do not supply the determination requested in ECF No. 86.

14.	Plaintiff does not present the financial disclosure reports as new evidence. They were before the Court when ECF No. 96 issued. ECF Nos. 86-2, 86-3. The ground is error in the legal effect given to reassignment.

15.	ECF No. 96 made a legal determination that reassignment rendered ECF No. 86 moot in its entirety. Plaintiff asks the successor magistrate judge to reconsider that determination under Rule 54(b). Plaintiff contends that the blanket mootness disposition constitutes clear error causing manifest injustice for the reasons stated here and in the accompanying Memorandum. The requested reconsideration does not require reweighing a prior ownership finding because no such finding was made.

16.	Authority. This Motion is presented within the existing referral of pretrial matters under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A) and Local Civil Rule 72. It asks the assigned magistrate judge to revise an interlocutory pretrial order entered in that referral. It does not invoke 28 U.S.C. § 636(c). By invoking Rule 54(b), Plaintiff does not concede that ECF No. 96 was entered with authority. Plaintiff maintains in ECF Nos. 97–99 the objection that the reassignment may have ended Magistrate Judge Davis’s authority to adjudicate ECF No. 86 before ECF No. 96 was entered. Seeking reconsideration here does not abandon that objection. The two requests are alternatives. If ECF No. 96 was entered without authority, the District Judge may vacate it on that ground. If it was entered with authority, it is an interlocutory order that the assigned magistrate judge may revise under Rule 54(b).
IV.	THE FINDINGS REQUESTED
17.	Plaintiff requests that the Court find:

(a)	The asset reported as “FB common stock” at Part VII, line 6, of the Financial Disclosure Reports at ECF No. 86-2 at 3 (report page 2) and ECF No. 86-3 at 5 (report page 4) is common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.
(b)	Magistrate Judge Davis owned that stock on September 9, 2026, when he entered ECF No. 64.
(c)	Magistrate Judge Davis owned that stock on October 7, 2026, when he entered ECF No. 84.
(d)	That ownership was a “financial interest” within 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4) and was not excluded by § 455(d)(4)(i).

18.	These are findings Plaintiff asks the Court to make. No prior order has made them. The evidentiary basis is stated in the Memorandum in Support. The same asset appears in two consecutive annual reports. Each report describes it as common stock. Each report places it in the same value range, $15,001 to $50,000. Neither report records a transaction on that line during its reporting period. ECF No. 86-2 at 3; ECF No. 86-3 at 5. The reports document the reported holding at the close of 2024 and at the close of 2025. They do not directly document ownership on September 9 or October 7, 2026. Plaintiff requests a finding of continued ownership from that evidence and, to the extent necessary, completion of the record supporting that finding.

19.	The requested findings are confined to ownership and statutory classification. They do not determine knowledge under § 455(b)(4), the application of § 455(f), or the remedy for any order entered. Those questions are presented in ECF No. 93. They are not requested here.
V.	THE ALTERNATIVE REQUEST FOR DETERMINATION AFTER FACTUAL DEVELOPMENT

runs.text: V.	THE ALTERNATIVE REQUEST FOR DETERMINATION AFTER FACTUAL DEVELOPMENT

content.text: 20.	Alternatively, Plaintiff requests an on-record determination whether the reported asset was owned on September 9 and October 7, 2026, by Magistrate Judge Davis or another holder covered by § 455(b)(4), and whether the interest fell within § 455(d)(4). Plaintiff requests the factual development necessary to decide that question and an opportunity to address the resulting record. This alternative request does not depend on the Court accepting Plaintiff’s inference of continued personal ownership.

21.	The record to be developed is confined to four facts: the issuer and the actual owner of the reported asset; ownership on September 9, 2026 and on October 7, 2026, each date separately; the arrangement through which the asset is held, for purposes of § 455(d)(4)(i); and any disposition of the asset necessary to explain ownership on either date. If the record shows that the asset was owned on either date not by Magistrate Judge Davis individually but by Magistrate Judge Davis as a fiduciary, by his spouse, or by a minor child residing in his household, Plaintiff requests that finding in place of findings (b) and (c). Identification of the holder does not itself determine knowledge under § 455(b)(4) or any other question reserved in paragraph 19.

22.	Plaintiff proposes that the Court obtain a written statement from Magistrate Judge Davis, the relevant records, or both, through a procedure within the Court’s authority, and that the Court set a date for the submission and a period for the parties’ responses. Rule 43(c) permits the Court to hear a motion on affidavits. Plaintiff does not request a deposition of any judicial officer. Plaintiff does not request general financial discovery, unrelated investment records, or any inquiry into judicial deliberations. Plaintiff does not request that nonresponse be treated as establishing ownership.
23.	Obtaining information from Magistrate Judge Davis is not returning adjudication to him. The restored request is to be decided by the assigned magistrate judge.
VI.	RELATED PROCEEDINGS

24.	ECF No. 99 requested that the District Judge determine the historical financial-interest facts in resolving ECF No. 93. Plaintiff maintains that application and the pending objections. Through this Motion, Plaintiff now additionally requests that the assigned successor magistrate judge vacate ECF No. 96, restore the historical component of ECF No. 86, and adjudicate ownership and the statutory character of the reported interest on September 9 and October 7, 2026.

25.	The requested determination would supply a factual record for the District Judge’s consideration of the pending statutory challenge and retrospective relief. This Motion does not ask the successor magistrate judge to decide ECF No. 93 or resolve the objections pending before the District Judge. It asks the successor magistrate judge to decide the restored request in ECF No. 86. Plaintiff seeks a determination of the historical facts, not another reservation of those facts for possible later determination. ECF No. 93, ECF Nos. 89–91, and ECF Nos. 97–99 remain pending before the District Judge. This Motion does not withdraw them, does not transfer them, and does not extend or restart any period to object under Rule 72(a).

26.	This Motion does not request vacatur of ECF No. 64 or ECF No. 84. It does not request that ECF No. 59-1 become the operative pleading. It does not request adjudication of any Defendant’s liability on the underlying claims. Its object is ECF No. 96 and the request ECF No. 96 left undetermined.
VII.	RELIEF REQUESTED
27.	Plaintiff requests an order, in the form of Proposed Order A or, in the alternative, Proposed Order B:
First, vacating ECF No. 96;
Second, restoring for decision the historical financial-interest component of ECF No. 86 identified in Part V and Request A2, as to September 9, 2026 and October 7, 2026;
Third, entering the findings stated in paragraph 17;

Fourth, in the alternative, determining on the record whether the asset reported as “FB common stock” was owned on each of those dates by Magistrate Judge Davis individually or as a fiduciary, by his spouse, or by a minor child residing in his household, and whether the interest on each date was a financial interest within § 455(d)(4), after the factual development described in paragraphs 21 and 22 and an opportunity for the parties to address the resulting record;
Fifth, if the record shows ownership on either date by a holder described in § 455(b)(4) other than Magistrate Judge Davis individually, entering that finding in place of findings (b) and (c);

Sixth, recognizing that further prospective relief against Magistrate Judge Davis under ECF No. 86, Requests A1, A3, and A4, is unnecessary following reassignment, without that recognition disposing of the historical request; and

Seventh, stating the disposition of the vacatur request, the requested ownership findings, and the alternative request for factual development and determination; and, for any request not reached, identifying the ground on which the Court declines to reach it.

28.	Plaintiff submits with this Motion the Memorandum in Support, Proposed Order A, and Proposed Order B. Plaintiff relies on the existing record, including ECF Nos. 64, 84, 86, 86-1 through 86-3, 87, 93, 96, 97, and 99, and the October 22, 2026 reassignment entry. No new declaration accompanies this Motion.
WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter Proposed Order A or, in the alternative, Proposed Order B.

content.text: I.	INTRODUCTION

ECF No. 86 asked one question of fact: whether Magistrate Judge Davis held common stock of Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) while he entered orders in this action. ECF No. 86 at 2. ECF No. 96 answered a different question. It held that reassignment made the motion moot. ECF No. 96 at 1. The question of fact was never decided.

Reassignment ended Magistrate Judge Davis’s participation. It did not change whether he owned Meta stock on September 9, 2026, when he entered ECF No. 64, or on October 7, 2026, when he entered ECF No. 84. Those two orders remain in force. A pending application before the District Judge, ECF No. 93, seeks relief from them on the ground that § 455 required disqualification when they were entered. The ownership facts are the predicate of that application. A disposition that declared the request for those facts moot, without finding them and without providing for their development, is the error this Motion asks the Court to correct.

The Motion asks for three things in sequence. First, vacatur of ECF No. 96 under Rule 54(b). Second, restoration of the historical component of ECF No. 86 for decision. Third, a decision: a finding that Magistrate Judge Davis owned Meta common stock on the two dates or, in the alternative, an on-record determination of who owned the reported asset on each date and whether it was a financial interest under § 455(d)(4), after the factual development needed to answer. The Motion asks the Court to decide the question. It does not ask the Court to reserve it again.

III.	THE GOVERNING STANDARD

A. Rule 54(b). An order that adjudicates fewer than all the claims “may be revised at any time before the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims and all the parties’ rights and liabilities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). A district court “retains the power to reconsider and modify its interlocutory judgments . . . at any time prior to final judgment when such is warranted.” Am. Canoe Ass’n v. Murphy Farms, Inc., 326 F.3d 505, 514–15 (4th Cir. 2003). The discretion “is not limitless.” Carlson v. Boston Scientific Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). A court may revise an interlocutory order under the same circumstances in which it may depart from the law of the case: “a subsequent trial produc[ing] substantially different evidence,” a change in applicable law, or “clear error causing ‘manifest injustice.’” Id. The Fourth Circuit restated the three grounds in Clear Touch Interactive, Inc. v. The Ockers Co., Nos. 25-1304 & 25-1374, slip op. at 22–25 & n.6 (4th Cir. Apr. 1, 2026) (published), and affirmed a revision that corrected a legal error in a prior interlocutory ruling. Clear Touch predates ECF No. 96. Plaintiff cites it for the Rule 54(b) standard, not as an intervening change in law.

content.text: B. The successor judge. Where “the order was entered by one judge and then reviewed by another,” the latter judge “should be hesitant to overrule the earlier determination.” Carlson, 856 F.3d at 325. In U.S. Tobacco Coop. Inc. v. Big South Wholesale of Va., LLC, 899 F.3d 236, 256–60 (4th Cir. 2018), the Fourth Circuit vacated a successor district judge’s reconsideration of a predecessor’s substitution order because the successor neither identified one of the three grounds nor could have satisfied the clear-error ground on that record. The court repeated that a prior decision qualifies for the third ground only if it was “dead wrong.” Id. at 258 (quoting TFWS, Inc. v. Franchot, 572 F.3d 186, 194 (4th Cir. 2009)). U.S. Tobacco rejected a reconsideration that did not satisfy the governing grounds. It did not hold that a predecessor’s ruling is beyond correction when a ground is satisfied. Clear Touch applied the same standard and upheld the correction of a legal error by a judge who had inherited the case from a colleague. Slip op. at 24–25 & n.6.

content.text: C. The magistrate judge’s authority. A district judge “may designate a magistrate judge to hear and determine any pretrial matter pending before the court,” subject to the exceptions listed in the statute. 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). In this District, “[d]uties and cases may be assigned or referred to a magistrate judge by an order entered in the action or on the instructions of a district judge.” Local Civil Rule 72. The District Judge may reconsider a magistrate judge’s pretrial order “where it has been shown that the magistrate judge’s order is clearly erroneous or contrary to law.” 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A); Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a). ECF No. 96 was entered within the referral of pretrial matters. The successor magistrate judge now holds that referral. A Rule 54(b) motion to revise a pretrial order entered within the referral is itself a pretrial matter within it.

content.text: ECF No. 86 presented two kinds of requests. The prospective requests sought to end Magistrate Judge Davis’s participation: disqualification, priority determination, and transfer of the referred matters. ECF No. 86 at 5–6 (Requests A1, A3, A4). Reassignment supplied that relief. Magistrate Judge Davis no longer participates. The prospective requests are moot.

The historical requests sought findings of fact. Part V asked the Court to “state on the record” whether the asset reported as “FB common stock” is Meta common stock, whether it was held on specified dates, the date and manner of any divestiture, and whether it is held directly or through a fund within § 455(d)(4)(i). ECF No. 86 at 4. Request A2 asked the Court to “[s]tate on the record whether the reported interest was held during the challenged participation.” ECF No. 86 at 6. Those requests concern completed events. Whether Magistrate Judge Davis owned Meta stock on September 9, 2026 and on October 7, 2026 is a fact fixed on those dates. Reassignment on October 22, 2026 did not alter it.

Effectual relief remains available on the historical requests. The findings were requested as relief in their own right: ECF No. 86 asked that they be stated “on the record.” ECF No. 86 at 4, 6. They are also the predicate of a pending application. ECF No. 93 seeks vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84 “upon the statutory findings identified in paragraph 5,” which include “the dates of ownership” and the holding arrangement. ECF No. 93 ¶¶ 5, 10(R2). ECF No. 93 ¶ 10(R7) requests a decision record identifying “the period for which [the disqualification ground] is established.” Findings entered on the restored request would become part of the record in this action. They would be available to the District Judge when he decides ECF No. 93. A request whose grant produces findings that a pending application requires is not a request on which no effectual relief can follow.

ECF No. 96 did not distinguish the two kinds of requests. It treated reassignment as disposing of all of them. ECF No. 96 at 1. Reassignment answered the prospective requests only. The determination that it mooted the historical requests was error.
C.	The Error Causes Manifest Injustice Because ECF No. 96 Terminated a Requested Historical Inquiry While Its Subject Remains Material to a Pending Statutory Challenge.

runs.text: C.	The Error Causes Manifest Injustice Because ECF No. 96 Terminated a Requested Historical Inquiry While Its Subject Remains Material to a Pending Statutory Challenge.

content.text: The injustice is traced to ECF No. 96 itself. ECF No. 96 closed the proceeding in which Plaintiff expressly requested determination of the reported financial interest. It did so without deciding ownership and without providing for development of the ownership record. ECF Nos. 64 and 84 remain operative. ECF No. 84 denied leave to amend and denied the discovery motions directed to NCMEC and Meta. ECF No. 84 at 1–2. ECF No. 93 presents a statutory challenge to both orders that depends on the ownership facts. ECF No. 93 ¶¶ 5, 10(R2). Terminating the historical inquiry as moot, while its subject remains material to that pending challenge, leaves the challenge without the findings it requires and leaves the orders in force without any officer having determined the fact on which their validity under § 455 is questioned.

Plaintiff does not contend that an unfavorable order causes manifest injustice by being unfavorable. Plaintiff does not reargue here whether ECF Nos. 64 and 84 were correct when entered. Those questions are presented in ECF Nos. 66, 67, 89–91, and 93. The point here is narrower. The pending district-judge applications preserve additional means of correction. They do not supply the determination requested in ECF No. 86. ECF No. 99 asked the District Judge to resolve the statutory facts “to the extent necessary” to ECF No. 93. ECF No. 99 at 11. That request is conditional on the District Judge’s path to decision. ECF No. 86 requested the findings unconditionally, as relief. ECF No. 96 ended that request without reaching it.
D.	The Successor-Judge Restraint Does Not Bar Correction of a Legal Error in a Mootness Ruling That Made No Finding.

The restraint protects a predecessor’s determinations from re-weighing. ECF No. 96 made a legal determination about mootness and no factual determination about ownership. Correcting the mootness ruling disturbs no finding. It reaches a request that was never decided.

content.text: The referral authorizes the magistrate judge to “hear and determine any pretrial matter pending before the court.” 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). ECF No. 86 was such a matter. It was filed before the magistrate judge, decided by the magistrate judge, and is now presented for revision to the magistrate judge who holds the referral. The findings requested are findings on a referred pretrial motion. They are not advisory because the officer who makes them does not also decide every consequence that follows from them. Section 636 and Rule 72 contemplate magistrate-judge adjudication and fact development within a district-court proceeding, subject to the District Judge’s review. 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A); Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a). Findings entered on the restored request become part of the record in this action. The District Judge may consider them in resolving ECF No. 93. That use does not convert this Motion into a proceeding under Rule 72(b), and Plaintiff does not ask the Court to label the findings a report and recommendation. The request is for a decision within the restored pretrial proceeding. Rule 52(a)(3) dispenses with findings on most motions; it does not prohibit the factual determination requested here, which ECF No. 86 sought as its own relief.

F.	The Reports Support the Requested Findings. If the Court Does Not Draw the Inference of Continued Personal Ownership, It Should Determine the Holder and the Statutory Classification on Each Date.

content.text: The requested findings are stated in the Motion at paragraph 17. The evidence for each follows.

Issuer. Both reports describe line 6 as “FB common stock.” ECF No. 86-2 at 3; ECF No. 86-3 at 5. Both reports identify common stock by trading symbol. ECF No. 87 at 3. “FB” was the Nasdaq trading symbol of the Class A common stock of Facebook, Inc., which changed its name to Meta Platforms, Inc. on October 28, 2021; the symbol changed to “META” in June 2022. ECF No. 86 at 2–3; ECF No. 87 at 3 (identifying the Form 8-K and Forms 10-K that establish those facts). The reports continue to use the former symbol. The description supports the finding that line 6 denotes common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.

Ownership on the two dates. The reports establish the reported holding at the close of 2024 and at the close of 2025. Each report places the holding in the same value range. Neither records a purchase or sale on line 6 during its reporting period. ECF No. 86-2 at 3; ECF No. 86-3 at 5. The 2025 report was certified on May 14 and May 26, 2026. ECF No. 86-2 at 2. The certification dates are not themselves evidence of ownership on those dates; they are evidence of when the year-end 2025 holding was reported. The reports do not directly document ownership on September 9 or October 7, 2026. They support an inference of continuity: an asset held at two consecutive year-ends, in the same value range, with no reported transaction, continued to be held nine and ten months later. Plaintiff advances continued ownership as that inference. ECF No. 86 at 3; ECF No. 93 ¶ 5. Plaintiff asks the Court to draw it and to enter findings (b) and (c). To the extent the Court requires more before drawing it, Part IV.G describes the record to be completed.

Statutory classification. Section 455(d)(4) defines “financial interest” as “ownership of a legal or equitable interest, however small.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4). The exception in § 455(d)(4)(i) applies to “[o]wnership in a mutual or common investment fund that holds securities.” The reports list line 6 as common stock. They list mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, and an individual retirement account as separate line items. ECF No. 87 at 3. On the face of the reports, line 6 is a direct holding. Finding (d) follows from findings (a) through (c) and from the face of the reports, subject to the holding-arrangement fact addressed below.

The holder. The AO Form 10 certification covers “information pertaining to my spouse and minor or dependent children.” ECF No. 86-2 at 2; ECF No. 86-3 at 9. Line 6 does not state whose asset it is. Section 455(b)(4) reaches a financial interest held by the judge “individually or as a fiduciary, or his spouse or minor child residing in his household.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4). ECF No. 93 ¶ 5 did not allege ownership by the Magistrate Judge personally rather than by another covered holder. If the record shows that the asset was owned on either date by Magistrate Judge Davis as a fiduciary, by his spouse, or by a minor child residing in his household, Plaintiff requests that finding in place of findings (b) and (c). A dependent child listed on a disclosure form is not for that reason a minor child residing in the household within § 455(b)(4); the finding must identify the holder by the statutory category. Identification of the holder does not itself establish a violation. Knowledge under § 455(b)(4), the application of § 455(f), and the remedy for any order entered remain reserved to ECF No. 93. Motion ¶ 19.

The alternative request. If the Court does not accept the inference of continued personal ownership on the present record, Plaintiff requests an on-record determination whether the reported asset was owned on September 9 and October 7, 2026 by Magistrate Judge Davis or another holder covered by § 455(b)(4), and whether the interest fell within § 455(d)(4). Motion ¶ 20. That request does not depend on the Court accepting Plaintiff’s inference. It asks the Court to answer the question either way, after the development described next.
G.	The Court May Develop the Ownership Record Through a Procedure Within Its Authority Without Returning Any Adjudication to Magistrate Judge Davis.

runs.text: G.	The Court May Develop the Ownership Record Through a Procedure Within Its Authority Without Returning Any Adjudication to Magistrate Judge Davis.

content.text: Rule 43(c) provides that when a motion relies on facts outside the record, “the court may hear the matter on affidavits or may hear it wholly or partly on oral testimony or on depositions.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 43(c). The rule supplies a method for receiving evidence on a motion. It does not itself establish a successor magistrate judge’s power to compel another judicial officer to produce financial information, and Plaintiff does not cite it for that proposition.

Plaintiff proposes two sources and asks the Court to select the lawful procedure for obtaining them: a written statement from Magistrate Judge Davis addressing the four facts identified in the Motion at paragraph 21, and the records that show ownership of the reported asset on the two dates. Motion ¶ 22. The Court may request the statement. The Court may receive the records. The Court may set a date for the submission and a period for the parties’ responses. Plaintiff does not request a deposition of any judicial officer, general financial discovery, unrelated investment records, or any inquiry into judicial deliberations. Plaintiff does not request that nonresponse be treated as establishing ownership. Motion ¶ 22.

Historical facts about one judge’s participation can be developed before a different judge. In Liljeberg v. Health Services Acquisition Corp., 486 U.S. 847, 850–51 (1988), the court of appeals determined that resolution of a § 455 motion “required factual findings concerning the extent and timing of” the trial judge’s knowledge of a disqualifying interest and “remanded the matter to a different judge for such findings.” The different judge made them, and the case proceeded on that record. Id. at 851. Liljeberg arose on a Rule 60(b)(6) motion after final judgment, and its remedial holding is not invoked here. Plaintiff cites it for what its procedural history shows: a judge other than the one whose interest was questioned found the historical facts about that interest. That is the procedure requested.

Disposition dates are part of that record. If the asset was sold or transferred before either date, the date of the sale or transfer establishes nonownership on that date. If it was sold or transferred after, the date establishes ownership through that point. Plaintiff requests those facts for that purpose. The application of § 455(f), which depends on additional conditions, remains reserved to ECF No. 93.
H.	The Requested Disposition.

Proposed Order A grants reconsideration, vacates ECF No. 96, restores the historical component of ECF No. 86, and enters the four findings on the existing record. It separates ownership on September 9 from ownership on October 7. It separates issuer identity, actual ownership, and statutory classification. It states that the findings become part of the record in this action and do not themselves decide the relief requested in ECF No. 93. It recognizes separately that prospective removal of Magistrate Judge Davis from further participation is unnecessary following reassignment.

Proposed Order B grants reconsideration, vacates ECF No. 96, restores the historical request for decision, and establishes a court-controlled procedure for obtaining the written statement, the records, or both, with a period for the parties to respond. It states the question to be determined so that it encompasses the actual holder and the statutory classification on each date, not only whether Plaintiff’s inference is correct. It retains the request for determination. Its submission and response periods are requested scheduling terms, not preexisting deadlines. It contains no provision closing ECF No. 86, denying the historical request without prejudice, or substituting preservation for adjudication.

Plaintiff also requests that the order disposing of this Motion state the disposition of the vacatur request, the requested ownership findings, and the alternative request for factual development and determination; and, for any request not reached, identify the ground on which the Court declines to reach it. Motion ¶ 27 (Seventh). That is a request concerning the form of the Court’s disposition. It is not an outcome Plaintiff offers as relief.
V.	CONCLUSION

ECF No. 96 determined that reassignment mooted ECF No. 86 in its entirety. Reassignment mooted the prospective requests. It did not moot the request for historical findings about ownership on September 9 and October 7, 2026, which remain the predicate of a pending statutory challenge to ECF Nos. 64 and 84. The determination was clear error, and terminating the historical inquiry on that ground, while its subject remains material, causes manifest injustice. The Court should vacate ECF No. 96, restore the historical component of ECF No. 86, and decide it: by entering the findings stated in the Motion at paragraph 17 or, in the alternative, by determining on a developed record who owned the reported asset on each date and whether it was a financial interest under § 455(d)(4). Plaintiff requests entry of Proposed Order A or, in the alternative, Proposed Order B.

runs.text: PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

content.text: Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2), 15(d), 20(a)(2), and 21 for leave to file the Second Amended Complaint attached as Exhibit A. Under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1), a Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion and states the grounds. Plaintiff incorporates it by reference. A Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine and a Proposed Order also accompany this Motion.
I.	THE SUBMISSION
1.	Exhibit A is the complete proposed Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”). It is one integrated pleading. It incorporates no prior pleading by reference.
2.	Exhibit B is a comparison of Exhibit A against the Complaint (ECF No. 1). It marks each addition and deletion. It is the comparison described in the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order (ECF No. 64).
3.	Exhibit C is a comparison of Exhibit A against the operative First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5). It marks each addition and deletion made to the operative pleading.

4.	Plaintiff submits a complete proposed Second Amended Complaint, together with comparisons against both the original Complaint (ECF No. 1) and the operative First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5), to facilitate the Court’s review of the proposed amendments.
II.	THE PRIOR MOTION AND ITS DISPOSITION

runs.text: II.	THE PRIOR MOTION AND ITS DISPOSITION

content.text: 5.	On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff moved for leave to file a second amended and supplemental complaint (ECF No. 59). On September 9, 2026, the Court ordered Plaintiff to provide a redlined version of the proposed pleading showing the changes made to the Complaint (ECF No. 1), no later than September 11, 2026 (ECF No. 64).

6.	On October 7, 2026, the Court denied ECF No. 59. The Order stated one ground: “Plaintiff was given ample opportunity to comply with the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order [Dkt. No. 64] by producing a redlined Second Amended Complaint but has failed to do so as of the date of this Order.” ECF No. 84 at 2. The Order made no finding of futility, prejudice, bad faith, or undue delay. It did not address the merits of any claim or any argument raised in the pending motions to dismiss.

7.	Defendants Hall and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) requested, in opposing ECF No. 59, “the opportunity to supplement or amend this Opposition, if and when Plaintiff submits the redline version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint.” ECF No. 74 at 4. Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) has stated that “nothing in Magistrate Judge Davis’s order expressly precludes Plaintiff from renewing his request to amend by curing his failure to comply with the Court’s order requiring Plaintiff submit a redlined version of the proposed amended complaint.” ECF No. 101 at 6.
8.	This Motion supplies the comparison. It presents the request for leave anew, on the complete record.
III.	THE PROPOSED PLEADING
9.	The First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) is the operative pleading. The SAC replaces it with one integrated pleading.

10.	The SAC adds one defendant: Panayiota Souras, also known as Yiota G. Souras, NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, sued individually. Ex. A ¶¶ 14, 21, 91–104. The First Amended Complaint identified among the John/Jane Doe Defendants “the NCMEC personnel who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 25. The SAC alleges, on information and belief, that Souras participated in that approval or authorization. The SAC names Souras in Counts I, II, IV, V, and VI. Ex. A, Counts I, II, IV, V, VI.

11.	The SAC adds no cause of action. It retains the six-count structure of the First Amended Complaint. Count I and Count II plead defamation per se and defamation by implication against Hall, Souras, and NCMEC, one count for each of the two April 22, 2026 letters. Count III pleads intentional infliction of emotional distress against Hall and NCMEC. Count IV pleads conspiracy under the first clause of 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) against all Defendants. Count V pleads Virginia common-law conspiracy against all Defendants. Count VI pleads insulting words under Va. Code § 8.01-45 against Hall, Souras, and NCMEC. Ex. A, Counts I–VI.

12.	The SAC pleads additional facts in four categories. First, facts concerning Souras’s responsibilities and her alleged participation in the review, approval, and authorization of the April 22, 2026 letters. Ex. A § J. Second, facts concerning Plaintiff’s legal name and Plaintiff’s Meta accounts, and, on information and belief, the contents of the two CyberTipline reports the letters reference. Ex. A § T. Third, facts concerning the letters’ wording, omitted limitations, and the meaning a reasonable reader would take from them. Ex. A §§ K, L. Fourth, events occurring after the First Amended Complaint was filed: NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum, the August 13, 2026 correspondence with counsel for NCMEC and Hall, Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California, and Hall’s September 2, 2026 filings. Ex. A § P.

13.	The proposed Second Amended Complaint retains federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1), supplemental jurisdiction under § 1367(a), and restores § 1332(a)(1) as an alternative basis for original jurisdiction over the state-law claims, as supported by the citizenship and amount-in-controversy allegations. Ex. A ¶¶ 9–11.

14.	The SAC combines amendment under Rule 15(a)(2) with supplementation under Rule 15(d) in one pleading. The amended matter and the supplemental matter concern the same two April 22, 2026 letters, the same six claims, and the same course of conduct.
IV.	GROUNDS

15.	Rule 15(a)(2) provides that the Court “should freely give leave when justice so requires.” Rule 15(d) permits a supplemental pleading “setting out any transaction, occurrence, or event that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented.” Rule 20(a)(2) permits joinder of a defendant against whom a right to relief is asserted “with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences” where “any question of law or fact common to all defendants will arise in the action.” Rule 21 provides that the Court “may at any time, on just terms, add or drop a party.”
16.	No Defendant has answered. No scheduling order has issued under Rule 16(b). Discovery has not begun. ECF No. 108 at 2. Rule 15(a)(2) alone supplies the standard for amendment.

17.	The claims against Souras arise from the same two letters as every claim in the First Amended Complaint. The questions whether the letters were issued before formal service, what the letters conveyed, whether the imputation was false, and who within NCMEC approved the letters are common to Souras, Hall, and NCMEC.

18.	The amendment prejudices no Defendant. It adds no theory of recovery. It is offered before any answer, before any scheduling order, and before any discovery. Defendants have briefed the subjects the SAC addresses. ECF Nos. 11, 22, 39, 45.

19.	The amendment is not futile. The SAC pleads facts that, accepted as true, state each of the six existing claims, including the claims against Souras. The Memorandum in Support addresses each dismissal theory Defendants have asserted.

20.	The post-filing events in Section P are transactions, occurrences, and events that happened after August 6, 2026. They concern the same letters, the same Defendants, and the same claims. Rule 15(d) permits their inclusion in the operative pleading.
V.	RELATIONSHIP TO PENDING PAPERS

21.	Plaintiff’s pending objections and applications concerning ECF Nos. 64 and 84 remain submitted in their respective proceedings. Granting this Motion would provide the immediate relief of permitting the proposed superseding pleading. Plaintiff requests no determination through this Motion concerning the continued justiciability or disposition of the remaining objections or retrospective-relief requests, which remain subject to the effect of any relief actually granted.
22.	The pending motions to dismiss directed to the First Amended Complaint (ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45) are procedural context. This Motion requests no disposition of those motions.
VI.	RELIEF REQUESTED

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter an order: (a) granting Plaintiff leave under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2), 15(d), 20(a)(2), and 21 to file the Second Amended Complaint attached as Exhibit A, deeming Exhibit A filed as of the date of the order, and deeming it the operative pleading in this action; (b) directing the Clerk, to the extent administratively necessary, to docket the Second Amended Complaint separately as the operative complaint; (c) directing the Clerk to issue a summons for Defendant Panayiota Souras under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(b) upon Plaintiff’s presentation of a completed summons form; (d) providing that Defendants Hall, NCMEC, and Meta shall respond to the Second Amended Complaint within the time prescribed by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a)(3) or such other time as the Court directs, and that Defendant Souras shall respond within the time prescribed by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(a) following service; and (e) granting such further relief as the Court deems just.
Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,
Marvelle J. Ballentine
Plaintiff, pro se
1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847
Alexandria, Virginia 22307
jayballentine@protonmail.com
