runs.text: MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

content.text: Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine submits this Memorandum in Support of his Motion for Leave to File Second Amended Complaint. The proposed pleading is Exhibit A to the Motion. Exhibit B compares Exhibit A against the Complaint (ECF No. 1). Exhibit C compares Exhibit A against the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5). The Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine (“Ballentine Decl.”) accompanies the Motion.
I.	INTRODUCTION

The Court denied Plaintiff’s prior motion for leave (ECF No. 59) for one stated reason: the absence of a redlined comparison. ECF No. 84 at 2. The Order did not find the proposed amendment futile. It did not find prejudice, bad faith, or undue delay. It did not reach the merits of any claim. Meta has said as much: the Court’s orders did not “address the merits of any of Plaintiff’s claims or the arguments raised in Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss,” and nothing in ECF No. 84 “expressly precludes Plaintiff from renewing his request to amend by curing” the omission. ECF No. 101 at 6. NCMEC asked for the chance to respond once a redline was filed. ECF No. 74 at 4. This Motion supplies two comparisons, one against ECF No. 1 and one against ECF No. 5, and presents the request for leave on the complete record.

The proposed Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”) does four things. It names NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, Panayiota Souras, and alleges, on information and belief, that she participated in the approval or authorization described in the First Amended Complaint (“FAC”), which identified among the Doe Defendants “the NCMEC personnel who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 25. It pleads additional facts bearing on falsity, defamatory meaning, and the Defendants’ knowledge. It incorporates events that occurred after August 6, 2026. It keeps the same six counts and the same categories of relief. Leave should be granted under Rules 15(a)(2), 15(d), 20(a)(2), and 21.
II.	BACKGROUND
A.	The Pleadings and the Pending Motions to Dismiss

runs.text: A.	The Pleadings and the Pending Motions to Dismiss

content.text: Plaintiff filed the Complaint on July 30, 2026 (ECF No. 1) and the FAC, as of right, on August 6, 2026 (ECF No. 5). NCMEC moved to dismiss on August 12, 2026 (ECF Nos. 10, 11). Meta moved to dismiss on August 21, 2026 (ECF Nos. 21, 22) and replied on August 31, 2026 (ECF No. 39). Hall moved to dismiss on September 2, 2026, adopting and joining NCMEC’s motion and memorandum (ECF No. 45). No Defendant has answered. No scheduling order has issued. On October 29, 2026, the Court stated that “the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2.
B.	ECF Nos. 59, 64, and 84

On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff moved for leave to file a second amended and supplemental complaint, attaching the complete proposed pleading as Exhibit A (ECF Nos. 59, 59-1, 60). On September 9, 2026, the Court found that it “does not possess sufficient information to issue an Order on this matter” and directed Plaintiff to provide, by September 11, 2026, a redlined version that “must clearly indicate the changes, deletions, and additions that were made to Plaintiff’s Complaint [Dkt. No. 1].” ECF No. 64. NCMEC and Hall opposed ECF No. 59 on September 18, 2026 (ECF No. 74). Meta opposed on September 22, 2026 (ECF No. 83). On October 7, 2026, the Court denied ECF No. 59 on the ground that Plaintiff “was given ample opportunity to comply with the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order [Dkt. No. 64] by producing a redlined Second Amended Complaint but has failed to do so as of the date of this Order.” ECF No. 84 at 2. Plaintiff’s Rule 72(a) objections to ECF Nos. 64 and 84 and related applications remain pending (ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68, 89, 90, 91, 93, 94).
C.	The Proposed Pleading

The SAC is one integrated pleading of 319 numbered paragraphs. It contains a Preliminary Statement, Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, Scope of Allegations, Facts in Sections A through T, six Counts, a Prayer for Relief, and a Demand for Jury Trial. Ex. A.

The SAC adds Souras as a defendant. It alleges that she served as NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer at its Alexandria headquarters; that she was responsible for NCMEC’s legal affairs, including litigation and compliance; that she practiced at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP before joining NCMEC in 2006; that Orrick represented Meta in the two underlying federal actions and received Plaintiff’s April 9, 2026 materials on Meta’s behalf; and that she has performed related functions in prior CyberTipline litigation. Ex. A ¶¶ 21, 91–96. It alleges, on information and belief, that Souras participated in the handling of the April 9, 2026 request, approved the wording of the April 22, 2026 letters, and authorized or directed Hall to issue them before formal service. Ex. A ¶¶ 99–101. It identifies the records, within NCMEC’s control, that would confirm or refute them. Ex. A ¶ 104. It pleads the mental states with which she acted and the purpose her participation served. Ex. A ¶ 102.

The SAC adds facts concerning Plaintiff’s legal name and his Meta accounts, and, on information and belief, the contents of the two CyberTipline reports the letters reference. Ex. A § T; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 3–11. It adds facts concerning the letters’ content defects and the meaning a reasonable reader would take from them. Ex. A §§ K, L. It incorporates events after August 6, 2026: NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum, the August 13, 2026 correspondence with counsel for NCMEC and Hall, Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California, and Hall’s September 2, 2026 filings. III.	GOVERNING STANDARDS
A.	Amendment

Rule 15(a)(2) provides that the Court “should freely give leave when justice so requires.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2). Absent “undue delay, bad faith or dilatory motive on the part of the movant, repeated failure to cure deficiencies by amendments previously allowed, undue prejudice to the opposing party by virtue of allowance of the amendment, futility of amendment, etc.,” leave “should, as the rules require, be ‘freely given.’” Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962). The Fourth Circuit reads Rule 15(a) “to provide that ‘leave to amend a pleading should be denied only when the amendment would be prejudicial to the opposing party, there has been bad faith on the part of the moving party, or the amendment would have been futile.’” Laber v. Harvey, 438 F.3d 404, 426 (4th Cir. 2006) (en banc) (quoting Johnson v. Oroweat Foods Co., 785 F.2d 503, 509 (4th Cir. 1986)). “Delay alone, however, is an insufficient reason to deny the plaintiff’s motion to amend.” Id. at 427. “Rather, the delay must be accompanied by prejudice, bad faith, or futility.” Edwards v. City of Goldsboro, 178 F.3d 231, 242 (4th Cir. 1999).

content.text: B.	Supplementation

Rule 15(d) permits the Court, “[o]n motion and reasonable notice,” to allow a party, “on just terms,” to serve “a supplemental pleading setting out any transaction, occurrence, or event that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d). “The court may permit supplementation even though the original pleading is defective in stating a claim or defense.” Id. The standards governing amendment and supplementation “are nearly identical. In either situation, leave should be freely granted, and should be denied only where ‘good reason exists . . . , such as prejudice to the defendants.’” Franks v. Ross, 313 F.3d 184, 198 n.15 (4th Cir. 2002) (citation omitted).

content.text: Rule 20(a)(2) permits persons to be joined as defendants if “any right to relief is asserted against them jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences” and “any question of law or fact common to all defendants will arise in the action.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 20(a)(2). Rule 21 provides that “[o]n motion or on its own, the court may at any time, on just terms, add or drop a party.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 21. Rule 15(a) governs an amendment that adds a party. Galustian v. Peter, 591 F.3d 724, 730 (4th Cir. 2010) (“While some courts have concluded that Rule 15(a) does not apply to amendments seeking to add parties, . . . most courts, including this one, have concluded otherwise.”). A court deciding such a motion “must consider both the general principles of amendment provided by Rule 15(a) and also the more specific joinder provisions of Rule 20(a).” Hinson v. Norwest Fin. S.C., Inc., 239 F.3d 611, 618 (4th Cir. 2001).

content.text: D.	Futility

“Futility is apparent if the proposed amended complaint fails to state a claim under the applicable rules and accompanying standards.” Katyle v. Penn Nat’l Gaming, Inc., 637 F.3d 462, 471 (4th Cir. 2011). The applicable standard is Rule 12(b)(6). A complaint satisfies it when it pleads “sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)). The Court accepts the well-pleaded facts as true and draws reasonable inferences in the plaintiff’s favor. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Kolon Indus., Inc., 637 F.3d 435, 440 (4th Cir. 2011). The Court does not adopt a defendant’s characterization of a defendant-authored document as established fact at the pleading stage. Goines v. Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd., 822 F.3d 159, 167–69 (4th Cir. 2016).

content.text: 1.	The claims against Hall, NCMEC, and Meta.
The SAC pleads facts addressed to each dismissal theory the Defendants have asserted. ECF Nos. 11, 22, 39, 45.

First, the SAC distinguishes an advance notice of intended subpoenas from formally served compulsory process. The April 9, 2026 transmission was captioned “Advance Notice of Intended Subpoenas — Two Separate Matters,” enclosed signed subpoenas, and stated that formal service would occur after the notice period had run. Neither subpoena was served. No return, proof of service, or court order existed. Plaintiff neither waived service nor requested an early response. Ex. A §§ G, I (¶¶ 54–56, 72–75).

Second, the SAC pleads the voluntary and private issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters. The letters were addressed to Plaintiff alone, were not copied to any court or counsel, and were not filed in either action. They were not CyberTipline reports or referrals and were not undertaken as part of any effort to identify a child victim. Ex. A ¶¶ 79–80. The SAC pleads that the conduct was intentional, was undertaken with actual malice and reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury without legal justification, and served the litigation-directed purpose alleged in Section Q. Ex. A ¶ 80.

Third, the SAC pleads source-level falsity. Plaintiff’s legal name is Marvelle J. Ballentine. Before April 22, 2026, he never used that name to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any Meta account. The Facebook account associated with the July 4, 2022 enforcement event was maintained under the name “Jay Ballentine.” On information and belief, neither report referenced in the letters, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” and neither concerned Plaintiff personally. Ex. A § T; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 3–11.

Fourth, the SAC pleads person-level falsity and defamatory implication. The letters placed Plaintiff’s full legal name in the same sentence as “two CyberTipline reports,” joined Plaintiff’s three search identifiers disjunctively in the order he supplied them, identified no report number, date, provider, or matched identifier, and omitted every limiting statement. Ex. A §§ K, L (¶¶ 105–119). The SAC pleads the meaning a reasonable reader would take from the letters. Ex. A ¶¶ 117, 194.

Fifth, the SAC pleads facts supporting Hall’s knowledge, intent, recklessness, and actual malice as of April 22, 2026: her access to NCMEC’s legal-intake records showing no service; her selection of language characterizing the letters as responses to a subpoena; her disjunctive listing of Plaintiff’s own search terms without disambiguation; and her omission of every source-identifying detail. Ex. A §§ I, K, T; Ex. A ¶¶ 244–246. The later events in Section P are pleaded as bearing on subsequent knowledge, continuing position, the unresolved referent of the letters, and continuing injury, not as proof of what Hall knew on April 22, 2026. Ex. A ¶¶ 173, 185, 188, 289.
Sixth, the SAC pleads Plaintiff’s disclosed survivor status and Hall’s knowledge of it before April 22, 2026. Ex. A §§ C, G (¶¶ 39–45, 60); Ex. A ¶ 283.

Seventh, the SAC pleads the circumstantial facts supporting the alleged agreement: identical materials to NCMEC and to counsel for Meta and Accenture on April 9, 2026; motions on April 21, 2026 directed at the same discovery; imminent depositions; no formal service and no court order requiring a response; two case-keyed letters one day after those motions; issuance before the notice period expired; omission of every source-identifying detail; an unsworn assertion, outside the discovery process, on the subject scheduled for sworn examination; and issuance while the motions remained pending. Ex. A § O (¶¶ 141–151).
Eighth, the SAC pleads the object of the understanding and the deterrence directed at Plaintiff’s attendance as a party and his testimony as a prospective witness. Ex. A § Q (¶¶ 190–196).
Ninth, the SAC pleads overt acts by each Defendant and personal injury with physical manifestation, impaired capacity, and litigation-related consequences. Ex. A §§ R, S (¶¶ 197–213).

Meta’s opposition to ECF No. 59 argued that the allegation concerning Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California “has no relevance whatsoever to Plaintiff’s claims against Meta.” ECF No. 83 at 3. The SAC pleads that filing only as a subsequent fact bearing on Meta’s knowledge, state of mind, and awareness of the relationship between the two proceedings. Ex. A ¶¶ 185, 297. It states that no claim rests on the filing and that liability under Count IV rests on Sections O, Q, and R. Ex. A ¶ 297. The weight of one subsequent-knowledge allegation does not determine whether Count IV states a claim. Count IV rests on the agreement alleged in Section O, the purpose alleged in Section Q, the overt acts alleged in Section R, and the injury alleged in Section S. Ex. A ¶¶ 290–299.
2.	The claims against Souras.

The SAC pleads each element of each count against Souras. For Counts I and II, it pleads her participation in publication by approving the wording and authorizing or directing issuance (Ex. A ¶¶ 235, 259); falsity (¶¶ 242–243, 266–267); negligence and, separately, actual malice, with the facts from which each is inferred (¶¶ 247, 271); and scope of employment (¶¶ 249, 273). For Count IV, it pleads her knowing participation in implementing the agreement, her knowledge of the pending actions and the announced formal service, her sharing of the purpose, and her overt acts (¶¶ 102, 154, 199, 294, 296). For Count V, it pleads her part in the combination and its execution (¶¶ 302–303). For Count VI, it pleads her approval of the words communicated to Plaintiff and her knowledge or reckless disregard of their falsity (¶¶ 311, 316).

NCMEC has invoked 18 U.S.C. § 2258D. ECF No. 11 at 7. That section bars civil claims “against NCMEC, including any director, officer, employee, or agent of NCMEC, arising from the performance of the CyberTipline responsibilities or functions of NCMEC.” 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(a). It does not apply where the officer or employee “engaged in intentional misconduct,” acted “with actual malice,” acted “with reckless disregard to a substantial risk of causing injury without legal justification,” or acted “for a purpose unrelated to the performance of any responsibility or function under this section, section 2258A or 2258C of this title, or section 404 of the Missing Children’s Assistance Act (34 U.S.C. 11293).” 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(b). The SAC pleads, as to Souras, that her review, approval, and authorization “were not part of any effort to identify a child victim,” and that her participation “was intentional, was undertaken with actual malice and reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury without legal justification, and served the litigation-directed purpose alleged in Section Q.” Ex. A ¶ 102. Those allegations track subsection (b). The SAC attaches the facts from which they are inferred: the letters were voluntary correspondence, issued before formal service, without any court order, addressed to Plaintiff alone, keyed to two pending federal actions in which the recipient’s own counsel had moved to stay the same discovery one day earlier. Ex. A §§ G, H, I, J, O. Whether the exception applies is a merits question. At the pleading stage the question is whether the SAC pleads facts that, taken as true, fall within subsection (b). It does.

The allegations of Souras’s participation are pleaded on information and belief, and the SAC says so in each instance. The Fourth Circuit has held that factual “allegations pled on information and belief are not categorically insufficient to state a claim for relief where the proof supporting the allegation is within the sole possession and control of the defendant or where the belief is based on sufficient factual material that makes the inference of culpability plausible.” Lowy v. Daniel Defense, LLC, No. 24-1822, slip op. at 34–35 (4th Cir. Feb. 11, 2026) (citation omitted). Such allegations “may not be wholly conclusory,” and must be “supported by . . . well-pled facts that exist independent of [the plaintiff’s] legal conclusions.” Kashdan v. George Mason Univ., 70 F.4th 694, 701 (4th Cir. 2023). The SAC satisfies both conditions. It pleads the facts on which the belief rests: Souras’s responsibility for NCMEC’s litigation and compliance matters; her documented performance of related functions in CyberTipline litigation; her former employment at Orrick, which represented Meta in both actions and received the April 9, 2026 materials for Meta; the arrival of the request at NCMEC’s Legal Department; the issuance of the response by Hall, as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel, on NCMEC letterhead in two pending federal actions; and the chronology in Sections G through I. Ex. A ¶¶ 91–98; Ex. A §§ G–I. It states that the identities of other reviewers, the internal routing, the communications, and any approval records are maintained in NCMEC’s records and cannot be reached without discovery. Ex. A ¶ 104. Those are well-pleaded facts independent of the legal conclusion. The inference that NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer reviewed and approved case-captioned legal correspondence issued by her office in two pending federal actions is plausible on those facts.

The SAC pleads, with the factual basis, that neither report as received identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine” and that neither concerned Plaintiff personally. Ex. A ¶¶ 228–232. Ex. A ¶¶ 176, 178–179, 215. Those allegations are accepted as true on a futility inquiry. Kolon, 637 F.3d at 440.

content.text: Section P pleads events after August 6, 2026: NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum stating that NCMEC “responded to the subpoenas without awaiting formal service” and that the linkage may involve “a person with the same name”; Plaintiff’s August 13, 2026 question to counsel and counsel’s response; Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California citing this action; and Hall’s September 2, 2026 filings adopting NCMEC’s positions. Ex. A ¶¶ 175–189. Count III pleads that the severe emotional distress on which it rests continued after the FAC was filed while the referent of the letters remained unresolved. Ex. A ¶ 289. Each is a “transaction, occurrence, or event that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d). Each concerns the same letters, the same Defendants, and the same claims. Each bears on knowledge, state of mind, the referent of the letters, or continuing injury. The Scope of Allegations limits their use: court filings are pleaded “solely as facts establishing timing, notice, knowledge, coordination, and admissions,” and “[n]one is conduct on which any claim rests.” Ex. A ¶ 25.

One integrated pleading serves efficient adjudication. Defendants respond to one pleading. The Court adjudicates one set of allegations. Rule 15(d) exists to permit that result, and the Fourth Circuit treats a pleading that both amends and supplements under the same standard. Franks, 313 F.3d at 198 n.15.

Deciding leave first permits the Court to adjudicate one complete pleading once.

content.text: PLAINTIFF’S PROPOSED SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT
DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy against my Facebook account and cut off the contracts I performed through it. I sued them in September 2025. Meta filed a motion to dismiss. Meta did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion.

When Meta’s co-defendants’ lawyers asserted that a “legitimate violation by Ballentine is consistent with the facts” while repeatedly putting my name beside the words “child sexual exploitation” in their papers, I sued them in February 2026. Defendants filed motions to dismiss. Defendants did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

I sent Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas to NCMEC in April concerning those two cases, and their attorney, Ms. Hall, sent me two letters associating my full legal name, “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” with two CyberTipline reports. I sued them in May 2026 because I have never even used my full legal name to operate any social media account. NCMEC and Hall filed motions to dismiss. NCMEC and Hall did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

I served Meta on July 31, 2026 concerning its role in the drafting, transmission, and delivery of the letters. It filed a motion to dismiss. Once again, it did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion. Meta substituted the CyberTipline report with a chronicle of my prior lawsuits, their captions, and their procedural history.

I have sworn that I never used my full legal name to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any Meta product or service that I used. The defense may move to dismiss this complaint. Whether or not they staple a CyberTipline report to the motions is to be determined.
That matters because the two letters signed by Hall on behalf of NCMEC stated:
“In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its written responses as detailed below.

NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.”

So, that leaves the remaining questions up for determination: Where did my legal name come from? How and why did it arrive on those letters? Did either of the two asserted CyberTipline reports, as originally received by NCMEC, actually identify “Marvelle J. Ballentine”? Did Meta submit either report? Why did NCMEC and Hall act before formal service? Why did they not wait the five days until April 27, when one court temporarily stayed discovery, or the nine days until May 1, when discovery in the other action was temporarily stayed? Where did the urgency come from?

I bring six counts: conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and Virginia law against all Defendants, for letters sent to frighten me out of my own lawsuits; defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and insulting words against Hall and NCMEC, for what the letters said and to whom. This Complaint adds NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, Panayiota Souras, who, on information and belief, approved the wording of the letters and authorized Hall to send them before formal service. The defamation and insulting-words counts are also asserted against Souras; Count III remains against Hall and NCMEC.
JURISDICTION AND VENUE
This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1). Count IV arises under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2).

This Court has supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) over the claims for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, common-law conspiracy, and insulting words. Those claims arise from the same nucleus of operative fact as Count IV: the preparation, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of the April 22, 2026 letters. They form part of the same case or controversy.

In the alternative, this Court has original jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1) over Counts I, II, III, V, and VI if complete diversity exists. Plaintiff is a citizen of the State of Florida. NCMEC, a District of Columbia non-profit corporation with its principal place of business in Virginia, is a citizen of the District of Columbia and Virginia. Meta, a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in California, is a citizen of Delaware and California. At all relevant times, Hall and Souras worked at NCMEC’s headquarters in Alexandria, Virginia. On information and belief, each is domiciled in, and therefore is a citizen of, a State other than Florida. Plaintiff cannot presently allege the citizenship of John/Jane Does 1-6, whose identities are unknown. This basis applies only if no Defendant is a citizen of Florida and each Doe Defendant’s citizenship is alleged or no Doe Defendant remains a party. The amount in controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.

Venue is proper in this district under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2). A substantial part of the events giving rise to the claims occurred here. Hall prepared or approved, signed, and issued the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s office in Alexandria, Virginia, within the Alexandria Division of this district. The letters were transmitted to Plaintiff’s commercial mail-receiving address in Alexandria, Virginia, where they were opened and processed.

This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Hall under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). Hall performed the challenged acts in Virginia. She prepared or approved, signed, issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s Alexandria headquarters. The first third-party publication alleged in this Complaint occurred in Alexandria, when the commercial mail-receiving agency opened, reviewed, and scanned the letters. Each claim against Hall arises from her Virginia conduct.

This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Souras under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). Souras served as Chief Legal Officer of NCMEC at its Alexandria, Virginia headquarters. On information and belief, Souras reviewed, approved, and authorized the April 22, 2026 letters in the course of her work for NCMEC, and the letters issued from NCMEC’s Alexandria office and were transmitted to Plaintiff’s Alexandria address as a result. Each claim against Souras arises from that Virginia conduct.

This Court has general personal jurisdiction over NCMEC, a corporation with its principal place of business in Alexandria, Virginia. This Court also has specific personal jurisdiction over NCMEC under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). The April 22, 2026 letters were prepared or approved, signed, and issued from NCMEC’s Alexandria headquarters, and each claim against NCMEC arises from that Virginia conduct.

This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Meta Platforms, Inc. under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3) and the conspiracy-based attribution of forum contacts. Sections O through R allege the conspiracy. Meta knowingly participated through one or more authorized representatives or intermediaries. NCMEC and Hall committed the Virginia acts alleged in this Complaint in furtherance of that conspiracy. Meta received the April 9, 2026 materials directed to NCMEC’s Legal Department in Alexandria, Virginia. The understanding alleged in Section O contemplated that Hall would issue the case-specific correspondence from that Virginia office. Plaintiff’s claim against Meta arises from those Virginia acts.
The exercise of personal jurisdiction over each Defendant comports with the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
PARTIES

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine, also known as Jay Ballentine, is an adult citizen of the State of Florida. At all relevant times Plaintiff maintained a mailing address at 1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847, Alexandria, Virginia 22307. A commercial mail-receiving agency operates that address and is authorized to receive and process mail on Plaintiff’s behalf.

Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) is a District of Columbia non-profit corporation. Its principal place of business is 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. NCMEC operates the CyberTipline under federal authorization in connection with 18 U.S.C. § 2258A. At all relevant times NCMEC employed Defendant Katie Hall as its Corporate Counsel. Hall was responsible for legal correspondence NCMEC issued in response to claimed legal process. NCMEC is sued for its own conduct, undertaken through Hall and one or more additional personnel. NCMEC is also sued vicariously for the conduct of Hall and Souras within the scope of their employment.

Defendant Katie Hall is an individual. At all relevant times she served as Corporate Counsel of NCMEC at 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. On information and belief, Hall is domiciled in a State other than Florida and is a citizen of that State. Hall prepared or approved, signed, issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters. Hall is sued individually for her own tortious conduct.

Defendant Panayiota Souras, known publicly as Yiota G. Souras, is an individual. At all relevant times she served as Chief Legal Officer of NCMEC at 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. On information and belief, Souras is domiciled in a State other than Florida and is a citizen of that State. Souras was responsible for NCMEC’s legal affairs, including litigation and compliance, and managed NCMEC’s legal operations. Souras is sued individually for her own alleged participation in reviewing, approving, and authorizing the April 22, 2026 letters.

Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) is a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in Menlo Park, California. Meta was a defendant in the 376 Action and in the 286 Action, each identified in Section A, at all relevant times. Meta is an electronic service provider subject to the reporting duties of 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.
Meta owns and operates Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.

Defendants John/Jane Does 1-6 are persons not yet identified who participated in the communications, authorization, approval, preparation, or transmission alleged in this Complaint. Their roles include: the Meta representative or representatives who communicated with NCMEC concerning Plaintiff, the identifiers, the intended subpoenas, or the two federal actions; any Accenture representative who knowingly joined or implemented the understanding alleged in this Complaint; any NCMEC personnel, other than Hall and Souras, who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters; and any intermediary, including counsel or other agents acting for Meta, Accenture, or NCMEC, through whom the alleged communications occurred. Meta, Accenture, NCMEC, and their representatives hold the records that identify the Doe Defendants. Plaintiff will seek leave to amend when those identities are ascertained.
SCOPE OF ALLEGATIONS

This Complaint predicates no liability on the filing of any motion, brief, or other paper in any court. Court filings identified here are alleged solely as facts establishing timing, notice, knowledge, coordination, and admissions. The claims do not challenge NCMEC’s receipt, maintenance, or lawful referral of CyberTipline reports. The claims challenge the extra-judicial agreement alleged below and the preparation, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of external legal correspondence that falsely invoked compulsory process and served the litigation-directed purposes alleged below. No claim against Meta seeks liability for the July 4, 2022 account-level enforcement, for any content-related decision, for any failure to restore Plaintiff’s account, or for any treatment of third-party content. Those matters are alleged only to establish the subject matter of the pending federal actions, Defendants’ knowledge, Meta’s interest in whether a CyberTipline report exists, and the testimony Defendants sought to deter. The same is true of the memorandum, motion to stay, and opposition filed in the 1341 Action and the August 13, 2026 filing in the 376 Action, each identified in Section P. Each is alleged as an admission and as a fact establishing timing, coordination, and knowledge. None is conduct on which any claim rests.
FACTS
A.	The Federal Proceedings and Plaintiff’s Role as Party and Prospective Witness

B.	The Contested CyberTipline Question

One question has been contested since October 2025: whether Meta, or any person acting in connection with the July 4, 2022 account-enforcement event, transmitted a CyberTipline report under 18 U.S.C. § 2258A concerning Plaintiff or his account identifiers.
Before April 22, 2026, no CyberTipline report concerning Plaintiff had been identified, produced, or attributed to any provider in any forum.

Plaintiff’s first substantive act in the 376 Action was a motion for leave to serve a single early request for admission. The request asked whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff’s account. The court denied the motion.
From that denial forward, the defendants in the 376 Action knew what Plaintiff’s discovery would target: the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report.

The operative complaint in the 376 Action alleged that Meta filed no CyberTipline report. Its prayer sought a declaration that no CyberTipline report was filed regarding the July 4, 2022 enforcement event.

On April 9, 2026, Meta moved to dismiss the 376 Action (ECF No. 85). Meta described Plaintiff’s allegation that a CyberTipline report had been submitted and disseminated as “hypothetical (and elsewhere contradicted).” Meta identified the contradiction as Plaintiff’s allegation that “Meta filed no CyberTipline report.”
In the 286 Action, the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report bore on the claims then pending, including the falsity and factual basis of the statements challenged in that action.

The letter opened with this sentence: “In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its written responses as detailed below.”

The ruling dates the movants themselves had requested had not arrived: April 24, 2026 in the 286 Action, April 27, 2026 in the 376 Action.

L.	Statutory Imputation and Defamatory Meaning

runs.text: L.	Statutory Imputation and Defamatory Meaning

content.text: Section 2258A of Title 18 requires an electronic service provider to report to NCMEC’s CyberTipline after obtaining actual knowledge of facts or circumstances from which there is an apparent violation of specified federal child-exploitation statutes. The CyberTipline also receives reports from other sources concerning suspected child exploitation.

The statutes enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A include 18 U.S.C. § 2251 (sexual exploitation of children), § 2251A (selling or buying of children), § 2252 (certain activities relating to material involving the sexual exploitation of minors), § 2252A (certain activities relating to material constituting or containing child pornography), and § 2422(b) (coercion and enticement of minors).

In the context alleged, a reader of the letter would understand the statement that NCMEC had received two CyberTipline reports “concerning” Plaintiff’s full legal name and identifiers to convey that NCMEC had received two reports associating Plaintiff personally with suspected child-exploitation conduct and that the reported matter could be made available to law enforcement.

By linking Plaintiff’s full legal name to two CyberTipline reports, the letter imputes to Plaintiff conduct constituting offenses involving moral turpitude. If the imputation were true, Plaintiff could be indicted and punished for those offenses.
The imputation is false. Plaintiff has not engaged in conduct constituting, or reasonably appearing to constitute, a violation of any statute enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.

content.text: Each letter was transmitted to Plaintiff’s commercial mail-receiving agency address at 1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847, Alexandria, Virginia 22307.

To create and maintain the mailbox account, Plaintiff had to supply identifying information, including his full legal name and photographic identification. USPS Form 1583, authorizing the agency to receive and process mail on Plaintiff’s behalf, was on file.

The agency maintains a mail-management system. That system associates incoming mail, scanned mail images, account records, Plaintiff’s verified identity, Plaintiff’s full legal name, and Plaintiff’s photographic identification with Plaintiff’s mailbox account.
In the ordinary course of business, the agency opens incoming envelopes, scans the contents, and uploads digital images to the mail-management system.

On or about April 28, 2026, an agency employee opened the envelope containing the two letters. To perform the scan service, the employee necessarily reviewed the contents of each letter. The employee scanned each letter and uploaded a digital reproduction of each to the mail-management system.

That employee was an independent commercial mail-processing employee, authorized only to perform routine mail-processing services. The employee had no role in Plaintiff’s litigation or legal affairs. The employee had no attorney-client, fiduciary, or personal relationship with Plaintiff.
The employee viewed, handled, and scanned the contents of each letter in the ordinary course of the agency’s commercial mail-processing business.

Hall selected the transmission channel. As Corporate Counsel, she knew or had reason to know that a commercial mail-receiving agency operated the address, and that delivery through that channel required third-party employees to open, review, scan, digitize, and process the contents before Plaintiff could access them.

Hall directed transmission of the letters to the commercial mail-receiving agency address rather than to the clerk of court in either Middle District of Florida action, to any party’s counsel of record, or to a secure transmission channel.
After scanning and upload, the agency forwarded the physical envelope containing both letters to Plaintiff’s designated local mailbox in the ordinary course of its mail-forwarding operations.

The administrator of both the commercial mail-receiving agency account and the local mailbox account opened the forwarded envelope and read both letters in the ordinary course of her administrative duties.
That administrator is a person distinct from Plaintiff. She read the letters while administering the two mailbox accounts.
The digital reproductions of the letters remain stored in the agency’s mail-management system. They are outside Plaintiff’s possession and control.
The mail-management system associates those reproductions with Plaintiff’s verified identity, Plaintiff’s full legal name, Plaintiff’s mailbox account, and Plaintiff’s photographic identification.

On information and belief, administrators, employees, contractors, and other persons with system-level access to the mail-management system can access the account records and scanned mail images associated with Plaintiff’s mailbox account.
Plaintiff does not know the identities of all persons with administrative or system-level access to that system.

Plaintiff does not control that system. He does not control its access permissions, administrative access, audit logs, retention practices, or internal dissemination of scanned mail images associated with his mailbox account.

content.text: On June 16, 2026, NCMEC and Hall jointly moved to dismiss the complaint in the 1341 Action. Their supporting memorandum (1341 Action, ECF No. 5) stated that NCMEC “did not await formal service of the subpoenas.”

As of July 15, 2026, Plaintiff had served no interrogatory, no request for production, no request for admission, and no deposition notice in the 1341 Action. No discovery response was due from anyone. The only discovery-related activity pending was planning under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(f).
On July 15, 2026, NCMEC and Hall jointly moved to stay pre-answer discovery and Rule 26 obligations in the 1341 Action (1341 Action, ECF No. 11).
The motion stated that NCMEC “has reason to be concerned that information provided in discovery in this matter could give rise to further litigation from Mr. Ballentine.”
No declaration or affidavit accompanied the motion. The motion identified no specific discovery request and no particularized burden of responding to any request.

Plaintiff opposed the motion on July 16, 2026. By order dated July 17, 2026, the Court granted the motion and stayed discovery pending resolution of Defendants’ motion to dismiss (1341 Action, ECF Nos. 13, 15).

On July 27, 2026, Plaintiff moved in the 1341 Action for leave to file an amended and supplemental complaint. The proposed pleading added Meta and Doe Defendants and asserted a claim under the first clause of 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) (1341 Action, ECF No. 18).
Meta was not then a party to the 1341 Action. Meta had not appeared in it.

On July 29, 2026, NCMEC and Hall jointly opposed that motion (1341 Action, ECF No. 20). Counsel for NCMEC and Hall signed and filed the opposition. No attorney had appeared for Meta in the 1341 Action.
The opposition stated that the 1341 Action “arises out of two subpoenas sent, but not formally served.”

The opposition stated that “NCMEC responded exactly as instructed in the subpoenas.” It characterized the letters as reflecting “a subpoena recipient following, to a ‘t,’ the instructions in the subpoenas.”

The opposition stated that Hall “was clearly acting in the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas,” that Hall “was working within the course and scope of her employment,” and that Hall “is entitled to the same defenses as the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.”

Under the heading “There is No Basis to Include the Proposed New Defendants in this Matter,” the opposition stated that, absent the alleged conspiracy, “there would be no claim asserted as to John or Jane Does, or Meta Platforms, Inc.”
As of July 29, 2026, NCMEC and Hall had told the Court, in filed papers, that the letters followed Plaintiff’s subpoena instructions exactly.

As of July 29, 2026, NCMEC and Hall had also told the Court, in filed papers, that NCMEC “has reason to be concerned that information provided in discovery in this matter could give rise to further litigation from Mr. Ballentine.”
Neither the July 15, 2026 motion nor the July 29, 2026 opposition identified what information about the letters, if provided in discovery, could give rise to further litigation.

Q.	The Objective and the Means of Intimidation

runs.text: Q.	The Objective and the Means of Intimidation

content.text: The purpose of the understanding was to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from continuing to attend the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party, and from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully as a prospective witness in those pending federal proceedings, including on the CyberTipline-reporting question.

The intimidation targeted Plaintiff’s continued attendance as a party in the two pending federal actions and his prospective sworn testimony concerning his account, the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the absence of any law-enforcement contact with him, and his damages.

Defendants knew that Plaintiff was pro se. They knew the noticed depositions depended on his personal preparation and examination. They knew the CyberTipline issue was central to the noticed examinations. They knew Plaintiff was a prospective witness concerning his account, the enforcement event, and his damages.

content.text: The letters bore the letterhead of the federally designated clearinghouse for CyberTipline reporting. They carried the signature of its Corporate Counsel. They called themselves responses to subpoenas before formal service. They associated Plaintiff’s full legal name, alternate name, and email identifier with CyberTipline reports. They omitted the reporting provider, report dates, report numbers, matched identifier, platform, account connection, and disposition. They were keyed to the two federal actions by caption. They issued while the depositions remained imminent and the protective motions remained pending. They were addressed to Plaintiff alone.

A reasonable reader would take the letters to communicate this: NCMEC possessed reports generated in connection with apparent violations of federal child-exploitation statutes; those reports associated one or more of Plaintiff’s identifiers with the reported matter; and those reports could be available to law enforcement.

Plaintiff understood the letters to mean that federal reporting records connected his identity to suspected child-exploitation conduct and that law enforcement could treat him as a subject of investigation.

Defendants intended that fear of investigation, arrest, or prosecution would cause Plaintiff to dismiss or withdraw from the two federal actions. That would deter Plaintiff, as a party, from continuing to attend those proceedings. It would deter Plaintiff, as a prospective witness, from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully. Abandonment of the contemplated CyberTipline discovery and impairment of Plaintiff’s preparation were intended and foreseeable consequences of that deterrence.
R.	Overt Acts
In furtherance of the understanding, Hall signed each of the two April 22, 2026 letters. On information and belief, she prepared or approved their wording and authorized their transmission.
In furtherance of the understanding, Hall issued the two case-keyed letters and caused them to be mailed to Plaintiff.

In furtherance of the understanding, on information and belief, Souras reviewed the proposed response, approved the wording associating Plaintiff’s identifiers with two CyberTipline reports, and authorized or directed Hall to issue the letters before formal service.
The letters issued and were mailed before formal service of either subpoena, before the announced notice period had run, and before adjudication of the April 21, 2026 motions.

In furtherance of the understanding, NCMEC, acting through Hall and one or more additional personnel, approved the issuance of the two letters and authorized the use of NCMEC’s name, letterhead, and institutional identity in each.
S.	Injury
Plaintiff’s injury began on April 28, 2026, when he read the two letters. He vomited. He wept.

Plaintiff understood the letters to mean that federal reporting records connected his identity to suspected child-exploitation conduct and that law enforcement could treat him as a subject of investigation. Plaintiff has engaged in no conduct constituting or appearing to constitute a violation of any statute enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A. He nonetheless lived in acute fear of imminent governmental investigation, arrest, search, and prosecution. He believed that continuing the two actions and pressing the CyberTipline issue could expose him to those consequences. That fear persisted in acute form in the days after April 28, 2026.

Plaintiff feared that Hall and NCMEC had sent copies of the letters to counsel for the defendants in the two actions. He feared that the letters, each bearing a federal caption, would be filed on the public dockets of those actions, placing on a public federal docket a statement from the federally designated clearinghouse for CyberTipline reporting that associated his legal name with two CyberTipline reports. He feared that family members following those dockets, including family members with children, would distance themselves from him if the letters were filed.

Each letter was created for one pending action. Each bore that action’s caption. Each purported to answer discovery directed at the CyberTipline issue. Plaintiff therefore understood the asserted reports as consequences connected to his continued pursuit of that issue in the two actions. He believed that dismissing the actions and abandoning the contemplated discovery would end the proceedings through which the asserted reports had surfaced and would reduce the perceived risk of further governmental attention.

The fear caused Plaintiff an acute psychological and functional injury beginning April 28, 2026. His sleep was disrupted. His eating was disrupted. He suffered intrusive fear of contact by law enforcement. He suffered recurrent involuntary recollections of his own childhood sexual abuse. He could not sustain attention on litigation materials. He lost productive and income-producing time.
During the acute period, Plaintiff distanced himself from his own children. He expected to be taken into custody.

On reading the letters, Plaintiff immediately considered dismissing both federal actions. He believed that continuing to litigate the CyberTipline issue exposed him to criminal investigation or prosecution. On multiple occasions in the days after April 28, 2026, Plaintiff refrained from dismissing the two actions only by deliberate effort.

During the acute period, the letters’ assertion that two CyberTipline reports existed dominated Plaintiff’s attention. He did not examine the letters’ stated procedural predicate. Days later, on reviewing the letters again, he recognized that no subpoena had been served. He understood then that the letters were voluntary correspondence, not responses compelled or authenticated through judicial process. From that realization, the letters’ perceived official and compulsory force diminished, and Plaintiff’s acute fear of imminent arrest began to subside.

The letters’ assertion stands unretracted and uncorrected. The digital reproductions persist in the agency’s mail-management system, outside Plaintiff’s possession and control. Apprehension concerning the asserted reports recurred while the two actions remained pending.

Plaintiff continued to prosecute the two actions despite the acute impairment. He did so by deliberate effort and at materially diminished capacity. That diminished capacity affected his responses to the then-pending stay and protective-order motions, his evaluation and pursuit of the contemplated NCMEC discovery, and his administration of the canceled deposition sittings, including his communications with the court reporter and videographer he had retained.
Plaintiff ultimately refused to dismiss the two actions.

The acts undertaken in furtherance of the understanding injured Plaintiff in his person. They materially impaired his continued attendance as a party in the federal proceedings. They materially impaired his ability to testify freely, fully, and truthfully as a prospective witness. The injuries alleged in this Section, including the impairment of Plaintiff’s litigation preparation, are consequences of that deterrence.
The conduct alleged in this Complaint caused Plaintiff humiliation, embarrassment, mental suffering, injury to reputation, and severe emotional distress.

As of the filing of this Complaint, Plaintiff does not know which of the three identifiers listed in the letters, if any, appears in or otherwise identifies a person in either of the two CyberTipline reports the letters reference.
The depositions noticed for April 28, April 29, and April 30, 2026 did not occur.
Plaintiff has obtained no sworn testimony answering whether Meta submitted a CyberTipline report in connection with his Facebook account or the July 4, 2022 enforcement event.
The 376 Action remains pending in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California as Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL.

This Count is pleaded in the alternative under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(d)(2).

On or about April 28, 2026, Hall caused the April 22, 2026 letter referencing Case No. 6:26-cv-00376-AGM-DCI to be published to third parties through the transmission and processing described in Section M of the Facts. On information and belief, Souras participated in that publication by approving the wording of the letter and by authorizing or directing its issuance through Hall.

Publication first occurred in Virginia. It occurred when the commercial mail-receiving agency employee opened, reviewed, scanned, and uploaded the letter in the ordinary course of the transmission channel Hall selected. Further circulation occurred when the administrator of Plaintiff’s mailbox accounts later opened and read the forwarded letter.

The digital reproduction of the letter, created by the agency on April 28, 2026, remains in the agency’s mail-management system. That system associates the reproduction with Plaintiff’s verified identity, Plaintiff’s full legal name, Plaintiff’s mailbox account, and Plaintiff’s photographic identification.
The letter is of and concerning Plaintiff. It identifies him as “Marvelle J. Ballentine” and “Jay Ballentine” and by the email address jaychizza@icloud.com.

The letter is defamatory per se. It imputes to Plaintiff the commission of a criminal offense involving moral turpitude for which Plaintiff, if the imputation were true, could be indicted and punished.

Hall, writing as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel and on NCMEC letterhead, associated Plaintiff’s full legal name with two CyberTipline reports. The CyberTipline receives reports concerning suspected online child sexual exploitation, including the mandatory electronic-service-provider reports required by 18 U.S.C. § 2258A. A reasonable reader would understand the association to convey that NCMEC had received reports linking Plaintiff personally to suspected child-exploitation conduct and that the reported matter could be available to law enforcement.

In the alternative, if the letter is not defamatory per se on its face, it is defamatory by implication. Hall used the word “concerning.” She placed Plaintiff’s full legal name in the same sentence as “two CyberTipline reports.” She included no limiting language. The letter does not state that the reports might match only one identifier, might concern a different person, might have been submitted by a non-Meta provider, might be unrelated to Plaintiff’s Facebook account, or might not have resulted in any law-enforcement referral. Those omissions caused the letter to convey that the reports concern Plaintiff personally. Hall intended the letter to convey that meaning. On information and belief, Souras, by approving that wording, intended or endorsed the same meaning. The letter conveyed that meaning to the third parties who reviewed and read it.

The imputation, whether per se or by implication, is false. Plaintiff has not engaged in conduct constituting, or reasonably appearing to constitute, a violation of any statute enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.

On information and belief, neither report referenced in the letter concerned Plaintiff personally. On information and belief, neither report, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine.”

Hall acted, at a minimum, negligently. She issued the letter without verifying whether the subpoena had been formally served and without an internal review process adequate to determine the status of formal service or the absence of any obligation to respond at that time.
Hall knowingly characterized the letter as issued “[i]n response to” a subpoena before formal service. Plaintiff had not waived service. Plaintiff had not requested an early response.

Hall acted with actual malice as to the defamatory implication. She had obvious reasons to doubt that the information before her established that two reports concerned Plaintiff personally. Plaintiff had supplied the three identifiers. The letter linked them disjunctively. The letter identified no report-specific match and no disambiguation. Hall nonetheless chose wording that placed Plaintiff’s full legal name in the same sentence as “two CyberTipline reports,” and she omitted any clarification that a report might match only a different identifier, person, provider, platform, or event. Hall knew the implication was false or recklessly disregarded whether it was false. Hall intended the recipients to understand that the reports concerned Plaintiff personally. Hall also knew, or recklessly disregarded, the falsity of the source-level and person-level allegations pleaded in Section T.

On information and belief, Souras failed to exercise reasonable care in determining whether the referenced reports concerned Plaintiff personally, as distinguished from a report matching another identifier or concerning another person, before approving the wording of the letter. Souras acted, at a minimum, negligently. Separately, on information and belief, Souras acted with actual malice as to the defamatory implication. The April 9, 2026 materials and the letter itself, as alleged in Section J, showed that Plaintiff had supplied the three identifiers, that the request sought only a document sufficient to show whether any report concerning them existed, and that formal service was announced to follow. She approved wording that placed Plaintiff’s full legal name in the same sentence as “two CyberTipline reports,” linked the identifiers disjunctively, and identified no report-specific match. On information and belief, Souras knew the implication was false or recklessly disregarded whether it was false.

Hall performed every act alleged in this Count within the scope of her employment as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel and in performance of her responsibility for legal correspondence NCMEC issues in response to claimed legal process. She acted under her NCMEC title, on NCMEC letterhead, and from NCMEC’s Alexandria offices. NCMEC is liable for her conduct alleged in this Count.
On information and belief, Souras performed the acts alleged in this Count within the scope of her employment as NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer. NCMEC is liable for her conduct alleged in this Count.
NCMEC, acting through Hall, through Souras, and through one or more additional personnel, approved the wording of the letter and authorized its issuance and transmission.
Because the letter is defamatory per se, Plaintiff is entitled under Virginia law to presumed damages without proof of actual injury. Plaintiff is a private-figure plaintiff.
Plaintiff has also suffered actual damages: humiliation, embarrassment, mental suffering, and injury to reputation.
The digital reproduction of the letter persists in the agency’s mail-management system, outside Plaintiff’s possession and control.
That system associates the reproduction with Plaintiff’s verified identity, Plaintiff’s full legal name, Plaintiff’s mailbox account, and Plaintiff’s photographic identification.

Plaintiff does not control that system’s access permissions, administrative access, audit logs, retention practices, or internal dissemination of scanned mail images associated with his mailbox account.

Hall acted willfully, wantonly, and in conscious disregard of Plaintiff’s rights. She issued the letter knowing its pre-service process characterization and knowing, or recklessly disregarding, its defamatory implication. She has refused to correct it. She has defended it as accurate and proper. On information and belief, Souras approved the letter’s wording and authorized its issuance with the same knowledge or reckless disregard. NCMEC approved the letter’s issuance and has not withdrawn, corrected, or retracted it. NCMEC’s filings in the 1341 Action are alleged only as evidence that, after notice of Plaintiff’s claims, NCMEC continued to maintain that the letter was accurate and proper. Plaintiff is entitled to punitive damages against Hall, Souras, and NCMEC to the extent permitted by law, subject to Va. Code § 8.01-38.1.

COUNT III
INTENTIONAL INFLICTION OF EMOTIONAL DISTRESS
(Against Defendants Katie Hall and NCMEC)

Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement, Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections, and Sections A, B, C, G, H, I, K, N, P, S, and T of the Facts, as if fully set forth herein.

On April 22, 2026, Hall directed two letters at Plaintiff. Each was keyed by caption to a pending federal action. Each associated Plaintiff’s legal name, alternate name, and account identifier with two CyberTipline reports. Each called itself a response to a subpoena before formal service. No subpoena had been served. Plaintiff had not requested or authorized an early response. No court order required a response. A motion to stay discovery had been filed in each referenced action the day before. Hall issued the letters when no rule, order, or obligation required it, before the ruling dates the movants had requested and before the noticed depositions. Hall directed the case-keyed letters to Plaintiff alone. This Count rests on Hall’s direct transmission of that targeted correspondence to Plaintiff. It does not depend on third-party publication or reputational injury.

Hall knew, before she issued the letters, that Plaintiff is a disclosed survivor of childhood sexual abuse. Section C alleges the disclosures. Hall understood the criminal and law-enforcement significance of associating a named individual with CyberTipline reports. She understood that invoking subpoena process before formal service would lend the assertion added official force. Hall directed at Plaintiff a communication associating his legal name with reporting concerning child sexual exploitation, the subject of the abuse he had disclosed. Hall knew, or recklessly disregarded, that directing that combination at a disclosed survivor of childhood sexual abuse created a high probability of acute emotional distress. Hall knew that the association, so directed, was substantially certain to cause Plaintiff acute emotional distress. She acted with intent to cause that distress, or in reckless disregard of the substantial certainty that it would result.

Directing at a disclosed survivor of childhood sexual abuse a false and unauthenticated association between that person and child-exploitation reporting offends the generally accepted standards of decency and morality and exceeds the bounds of what a civilized community tolerates.

Hall performed every act alleged in this Count within the scope of her employment as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel and in performance of her responsibility for legal correspondence NCMEC issues in response to claimed legal process. NCMEC, acting through Hall and one or more additional personnel, approved the wording of the letters and authorized their issuance and transmission. NCMEC is liable for the conduct alleged in this Count.

Hall’s conduct directly and proximately caused Plaintiff severe emotional distress. Upon reading the letters on April 28, 2026, Plaintiff vomited. He suffered recurrent involuntary recollections of his own childhood sexual abuse. He lived in acute fear of imminent arrest and prosecution. Expecting to be taken into custody, he distanced himself from his own children. His sleep and eating were disrupted. He could not sustain attention on his work. That distress persisted in acute form until, days later, he recognized that no subpoena had been served. The distress was severe. It was beyond what a reasonable person could be expected to endure.

The severe emotional distress on which this Count rests arises from Hall’s direct transmission of the letters to Plaintiff and from their content. It does not arise from any apprehension that the letters would be published to, or read by, any other person.

As a direct and proximate result of the conduct alleged in this Count, Plaintiff sustained compensatory damages for mental anguish, severe emotional distress, physical manifestation, functional impairment, lost productive capacity, and loss of capacity for the enjoyment of life. Count III seeks no recovery for reputational injury.

COUNT IV

Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement, Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections, and Sections A through K, Sections N through P, and Sections Q through T of the Facts, as if fully set forth herein.

Meta, Hall, Souras, and NCMEC are separate and legally distinct persons. Meta is a corporation. Hall is an individual. Souras is an individual. NCMEC is a non-profit corporation. Neither Hall nor Souras is an officer, employee, agent, or authorized representative of Meta. NCMEC is not an affiliate, agent, or representative of Meta. The agreement alleged in Section O was reached between Meta, acting through one or more of its own officers, employees, agents, or authorized representatives, on one side, and Hall and NCMEC on the other. On information and belief, Souras participated in implementing that agreement on the NCMEC side. The combination alleged in this Count comprises at least two separate and legally distinct persons.

Defendants reached the agreement alleged in Section O of the Facts. Section O pleads the facts on which that allegation rests, including the identical materials received by NCMEC and by counsel for Meta and Accenture, the April 21, 2026 motions directed at the same discovery, and the two letters, each keyed to a separate federal action, issued the next day before formal service and before any court ruled.

The purpose of the agreement was to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from continuing to attend the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party, and from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully as a prospective witness in those pending federal proceedings, as alleged in Section Q of the Facts. The letters, on NCMEC letterhead and over the signature of its Corporate Counsel, associated Plaintiff’s full legal name with two CyberTipline reports, and they issued while the noticed depositions were imminent and the protective motions were pending.

One or more Defendants committed acts in furtherance of the agreement, as alleged in Section R of the Facts. Hall signed and transmitted the letters. On information and belief, Souras approved their wording and authorized or directed their issuance. NCMEC approved their issuance and authorized the use of its name, letterhead, and institutional identity.

The acts in furtherance of the agreement injured Plaintiff in his person and materially impaired his attendance and testimony as a party and prospective witness, as alleged in Section S of the Facts. He became physically ill. He feared arrest and prosecution. He distanced himself from his children. He could not sustain attention on litigation materials.

Meta knowingly joined the agreement through one or more authorized representatives or intermediaries. Hall knowingly joined and implemented the agreement by preparing or approving the letters, signing them, and authorizing their transmission. On information and belief, Souras knowingly joined and implemented the agreement by approving the wording of the letters and authorizing or directing their issuance before formal service, with knowledge that the 376 Action and the 286 Action were pending, that Plaintiff’s April 9, 2026 request had been directed to NCMEC, that formal service of the subpoenas was announced to follow, and of the litigation-directed purpose of the agreement alleged in Section Q. NCMEC knowingly joined and implemented the agreement, acting through Hall, through Souras, and through one or more additional personnel who approved the issuance of the letters. Each Doe Defendant is liable only to the extent the evidence establishes that the Doe knowingly joined or implemented the common plan.

Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the 376 Action, alleged in Section P, is pleaded as a subsequent fact bearing on Meta’s knowledge, Meta’s state of mind, Meta’s awareness of the relationship between this action and the 376 Action, and the circumstantial allegations supporting this Count. It is not an independent basis for liability. Liability under this Count rests on the conduct alleged in Sections O, Q, and R of the Facts.
Defendants’ conduct directly and proximately caused the injuries alleged in this Complaint.
Defendants acted intentionally and with conscious disregard for Plaintiff’s federally protected status as a party and prospective witness, warranting punitive damages.
COUNT V
COMMON-LAW CONSPIRACY
(Against All Defendants)

Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement, Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections, and Sections A through O and Sections Q through T of the Facts, as if fully set forth herein.
This Count arises under the common law of Virginia.

Hall, Souras, NCMEC, Meta, and one or more Doe Defendants combined through the understanding alleged in Section O of the Facts. Meta is separate and legally distinct from Hall, from Souras, and from NCMEC, as this Complaint alleges. The combination comprised at least two separate and legally distinct persons.

The combination was carried out through the preparation, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of the two April 22, 2026 letters. On information and belief, Souras approved their wording and authorized or directed their issuance. The publication of each letter constituted the defamation alleged in Counts I and II.

The participants understood and intended that the letters would travel through the selected commercial mail channel. They understood and intended that the third-party publication alleged in Counts I and II would occur in carrying out the understanding.
The participants committed the overt acts alleged in Section R of the Facts. The publications alleged in Counts I and II occurred.
The participants acted intentionally, purposefully, and without lawful justification.

As a direct and proximate result of the combination and the acts in furtherance of it, Plaintiff sustained the damages alleged in Section S of the Facts and in Counts I and II: presumed damages, humiliation, embarrassment, mental suffering, and injury to reputation. INSULTING WORDS — VA. CODE § 8.01-45

Hall directed each of the two April 22, 2026 letters to Plaintiff personally, at Plaintiff’s mailing address. On information and belief, Souras approved the words of each letter and authorized or directed that they be communicated to Plaintiff.

The words of each letter associated Plaintiff’s full legal name, alternate name, and email identifier with two CyberTipline reports, on NCMEC letterhead, over the signature of NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel, and framed as a response to subpoena process before formal service. Those words, in their usual construction and common acceptation, are insults that tend to violence and breach of the peace. In the context alleged in Section L of the Facts, the words convey the imputation described in that Section.
The imputation each letter conveys is false. Plaintiff has not engaged in conduct constituting, or reasonably appearing to constitute, a violation of any statute enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.

On information and belief, neither report referenced in the letters concerned Plaintiff personally. On information and belief, neither report, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine.”

Hall selected the words of each letter. She knowingly selected language stating that each letter responded to a subpoena before formal service, when Plaintiff had not waived service or requested an early response. She acted with knowledge or reckless disregard of the falsity of the imputation each letter conveyed.

On information and belief, Souras approved the words of each letter with knowledge that Plaintiff had supplied the identifiers, that the request sought only a document sufficient to show whether any report existed, and that formal service had not occurred, and acted with knowledge or reckless disregard of the falsity of the imputation each letter conveyed.

Hall performed every act alleged in this Count within the scope of her employment as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel. On information and belief, Souras performed the acts alleged in this Count within the scope of her employment as NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer. NCMEC, acting through Hall, through Souras, and through one or more additional personnel, approved the wording of the letters and authorized their issuance and transmission. NCMEC is liable for the conduct alleged in this Count.

As a direct and proximate result of the conduct alleged in this Count, Plaintiff sustained the damages alleged in Section S of the Facts: humiliation, embarrassment, mental suffering, and severe emotional distress.
Hall, Souras, and NCMEC acted willfully, wantonly, and in conscious disregard of Plaintiff’s rights, warranting punitive damages subject to Va. Code § 8.01-38.1.

content.text: Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56(a) and Local Civil Rule 56 for partial summary judgment on one part of Counts I, II, III, and VI of the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5). In the alternative, Plaintiff requests an order under Rule 56(g). This Motion renews the motion filed at ECF No. 6, which the Court denied without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time. ECF No. 12. A Memorandum in Support under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1), the Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine with Exhibits 3 through 5, Proposed Order A, and Proposed Order B accompany this Motion.
I.	THE DETERMINATION REQUESTED

1.	Plaintiff requests summary judgment on the following part of Counts I, II, III, and VI against Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”): that Defendant Katie Hall acted as NCMEC’s employee and agent, within the course and scope of her employment, when she signed and issued on NCMEC’s behalf the two letters dated April 22, 2026 that appear at ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3 (the “letters”).

2.	The First Amended Complaint sues NCMEC “vicariously for the conduct of Hall committed within the scope of her employment.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 21. Counts I, II, III, and VI each allege that Hall acted within the scope of her employment as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel. Id. ¶¶ 195, 216, 230, 258. The requested determination resolves the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under those counts.

runs.text: 2.	The First Amended Complaint sues NCMEC “vicariously for the conduct of Hall committed within the scope of her employment.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 21. Counts I, II, III, and VI each allege that Hall acted within the scope of her employment as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel.
¶¶ 195, 216, 230, 258. The requested determination resolves the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under those counts.

content.text: 3.	The determination concerns Hall’s relationship with NCMEC. It does not concern any relationship between Hall and any other Defendant. It does not resolve whether Hall’s conduct was tortious, whether any privilege or immunity applies, whether NCMEC authorized or ratified any particular act, whether Hall performed any function described in 18 U.S.C. § 2258D, or any count other than Counts I, II, III, and VI.
II.	THE COURT’S AUTHORIZATION TO RENEW

runs.text: II.	THE COURT’S AUTHORIZATION TO RENEW

content.text: 4.	Plaintiff filed the original motion on August 6, 2026. ECF Nos. 6, 7. The Court denied it on August 12, 2026, “without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time.” ECF No. 12 at 1.
