III.	THE CHANGED RECORD
6.	NCMEC, Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”), and Hall have each responded to the First Amended Complaint. ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45. Those motions remain pending.

7.	NCMEC’s memorandum in support of its motion states that NCMEC “responded to the subpoenas without awaiting formal service via two substantively-identical letters signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC,” and that Hall “at all times relevant was an employee of NCMEC.” ECF No. 11 at 2, 5 n.2. ECF No. 11 was docketed on August 12, 2026, before ECF No. 12. ECF No. 12 denied the original motion because responses were not yet due; it did not address the merits. Hall’s adoption of ECF No. 11 (ECF No. 45, Sept. 2, 2026) and Plaintiff’s two declarations (ECF Nos. 31, 59-2) came after ECF No. 12.
8.	Hall “adopts and joins in” NCMEC’s motion and memorandum and describes herself in that filing “as an employee of NCMEC.” ECF No. 45 at 1. Hall’s filing came after ECF No. 12.

9.	Plaintiff has filed two declarations under 28 U.S.C. § 1746 concerning the names under which he operated Meta accounts and the reason his legal name appears in the April 9, 2026 materials he transmitted to NCMEC. ECF No. 31 (filed August 24, 2026); ECF No. 59-2 (executed September 7, 2026; filed September 8, 2026). Both came after ECF No. 12.

10.	ECF No. 5 remains the operative pleading, and this Motion rests on it. The declarations are offered as record evidence under Rule 56(c)(1)(A). Their consideration does not depend on adoption of the proposed pleading attached to ECF No. 59, for which leave was denied. ECF No. 84.

11.	The denial of ECF No. 59 is the subject of Plaintiff’s pending objections (ECF Nos. 90, 91, 102). Plaintiff also files concurrently a renewed motion for leave to file a Second Amended Complaint. The proposed pleading retains the claims against Hall and NCMEC to which this Motion’s agency-and-scope request relates. Should leave be granted before determination of this Motion, Plaintiff requests consideration of the corresponding issue under the resulting operative pleading, following any supplemental briefing the Court deems necessary, rather than denial solely because the First Amended Complaint has been superseded.
IV.	THE ALTERNATIVE REQUEST UNDER RULE 56(g)

runs.text: IV.	THE ALTERNATIVE REQUEST UNDER RULE 56(g)

content.text: 12.	If the Court does not grant all the relief requested in Part I, Plaintiff requests that the Court consider under Rule 56(g): (a) the agency-and-scope determination described in Part I, if the Court finds that determination not genuinely disputed but declines the form of judgment requested; and (b) the material facts numbered 1 through 17 in Part III of the Memorandum in Support, each considered separately. Plaintiff requests an order stating which of those facts are not genuinely in dispute and treating each such fact as established in this action.

13.	The numbered facts concern: (a) Hall’s employment and the capacity in which the letters issued; (b) the April 9, 2026 transmission and the absence of formal service before issuance; (c) the identifiers listed in Plaintiff’s Schedule A and the identifiers used in the letters; (d) Plaintiff’s account-name history, including that Plaintiff did not use “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to operate any Meta account he used before April 22, 2026, and that he operated the Facebook account involved in Meta’s July 4, 2022 enforcement action under the name “Jay Ballentine”; and (e) what the letters do not identify. The facts in categories (b) through (e) are material to Counts I, II, III, and VI. Not all of them are necessary to the agency-and-scope determination. Plaintiff presents them as alternative relief for that reason.
14.	A dispute concerning one numbered fact does not place any other numbered fact in dispute. Plaintiff requests separate consideration of each.
V.	TREATMENT UNDER RULE 56(e)(2)

15.	Plaintiff requests that, as to any numbered fact that is properly supported by Plaintiff and not properly addressed under Rule 56(c), the Court exercise its discretion under Rule 56(e)(2) and Local Civil Rule 56(B) to consider the fact undisputed for purposes of this Motion. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to treat any fact as established in this action on that basis alone. The Court retains its discretion under Rule 56(e)(1) to permit a party to address a fact, and under Rule 56(e)(4) to issue any other appropriate order.
VI.	WHAT THIS MOTION DOES NOT SEEK

runs.text: VI.	WHAT THIS MOTION DOES NOT SEEK

content.text: 16.	This Motion seeks no determination concerning: the existence, contents, source, or accuracy of any CyberTipline report; the truth or falsity of the letters’ report-existence statement as applied to Plaintiff personally; any agreement among Defendants; any Defendant’s motive or state of mind; damages; the litigation privilege; immunity under 18 U.S.C. § 2258D or 34 U.S.C. § 20505; NCMEC’s direct liability for its own conduct; or any claim against the Doe Defendants. It seeks no liability determination against Meta. It requests no discovery. It does not ask the Court to modify any order concerning scheduling or discovery.
VII.	DEFERRAL AND STATEMENT OF REASONS

runs.text: VII.	DEFERRAL AND STATEMENT OF REASONS

content.text: 17.	If the Court concludes that adjudication of this Motion should await disposition of the pending motions to dismiss or another event, Plaintiff requests that the Court defer ruling to that identified event, whether under Rule 56(d)(1) on any Defendant’s showing or under the Court’s authority to manage its docket, rather than deny the Motion without prejudice. Plaintiff further requests that the Court state on the record the reasons for its ruling, consistent with Rule 56(a).
VIII.	RELIEF REQUESTED
WHEREFORE, Plaintiff requests that the Court:

(1)	grant partial summary judgment, in the form of Proposed Order A, determining that Hall acted as NCMEC’s employee and agent, within the course and scope of her employment, when she signed and issued the two April 22, 2026 letters on NCMEC’s behalf, and that the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI is established;

(2)	in the alternative, if the relief in paragraph (1) is not granted in full, enter an order under Rule 56(g), in the form of Proposed Order B, addressing the agency-and-scope determination and stating which of the material facts numbered 1 through 17 in the Memorandum in Support are not genuinely in dispute, and treating each such fact as established in this action;

(3)	consider undisputed for purposes of this Motion, under Rule 56(e)(2) and Local Civil Rule 56(B) and within the Court’s discretion, each numbered fact that is properly supported by Plaintiff and not properly addressed under Rule 56(c);
(4)	consider each numbered fact separately, so that any showing of a need for discovery concerning one fact is evaluated as to that fact;

(5)	if the Court elects to postpone its ruling, defer ruling to an identified event, whether under Rule 56(d)(1) on any Defendant’s showing or under the Court’s authority to manage its docket, rather than deny the Motion without prejudice;
(6)	state on the record the reasons for its ruling, consistent with Rule 56(a); and
(7)	grant such further relief as is just.

content.text: I.	NCMEC AND HALL DESCRIBE THE APRIL 22, 2026 LETTERS AS HALL’S WORK FOR NCMEC

runs.text: I.	NCMEC AND HALL DESCRIBE THE APRIL 22, 2026 LETTERS AS HALL’S WORK FOR NCMEC

content.text: NCMEC has told this Court how the two April 22, 2026 letters came to be. “On April 22, 2026, NCMEC responded to the subpoenas without awaiting formal service via two substantively-identical letters signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC.” ECF No. 11 at 2. Hall “adopts and joins in” that memorandum. ECF No. 45 at 1. The letters bear NCMEC’s letterhead. Each carries Hall’s signature above the title “Corporate Counsel.” ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. In the earlier action over the same letters, NCMEC and Hall, through the counsel who represents both of them here, told this Court that Hall “was clearly acting in the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas.” ECF No. 7-4 at 7.

Plaintiff renews the request the Court denied on August 12, 2026, “without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time.” ECF No. 12 at 1. The request is narrow. Plaintiff asks the Court to determine under Rule 56(a) that Hall acted as NCMEC’s employee and agent, within the course and scope of her employment, when she signed and issued the two letters on NCMEC’s behalf. That determination resolves the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI. ECF No. 5 ¶ 21. It resolves nothing else.

If the Court does not grant that relief in full, Plaintiff asks the Court to consider, under Rule 56(g), the same determination and seventeen numbered facts. The facts concern Hall’s employment, the April 9, 2026 transmission, the absence of formal service, the wording of the letters, what the letters omit, and the names under which Plaintiff operated Meta accounts. Each rests on a document in the record, a statement of NCMEC or Hall, or Plaintiff’s sworn testimony about his own conduct.

The Motion does not ask what any CyberTipline report contains. It does not ask whether the letters were true, whether any privilege or immunity applies, whether Defendants agreed with one another, or what anyone intended. The submitted issue is the capacity in which Hall acted. The evidence on that issue comes from NCMEC and Hall.
II.	THE RESPONSE POSTURE AND THE EVIDENTIARY RECORD HAVE CHANGED SINCE AUGUST 12, 2026

runs.text: II.	THE RESPONSE POSTURE AND THE EVIDENTIARY RECORD HAVE CHANGED SINCE AUGUST 12, 2026

content.text: A.	The August 12 Order.

The Court denied the original motion “without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time.” ECF No. 12 at 1. The Order identified two circumstances. Plaintiff had filed the First Amended Complaint and the motion on the same day. And “Defendants’ answers or other responses to the Original Complaint are not due until August 21, 2026.” Id. The Order found the motion premature on that basis.

Plaintiff had filed the First Amended Complaint and the motion on the same day. And “Defendants’ answers or other responses to the Original Complaint are not due until August 21, 2026.”
The Order found the motion premature on that basis.

content.text: B.	What has happened since.

table: Original motion and supporting evidence filed
NCMEC moves to dismiss; its memorandum describes Hall’s capacity and states that the letters issued before formal service
Original motion denied without prejudice to renewal

content.text: ECF No. 11 was docketed on August 12, 2026, before ECF No. 12. ECF No. 12 denied the original motion because responses were not yet due; it did not address the merits. Hall’s adoption of ECF No. 11 (ECF No. 45, Sept. 2, 2026) and Plaintiff’s two declarations (ECF Nos. 31, 59-2) came after ECF No. 12.

The change since August 12 is not the passage of time. The response posture the Order identified has changed: each appearing Defendant has responded. And the record has expanded. NCMEC’s memorandum states the capacity in which Hall acted and states that NCMEC issued the letters before formal service. ECF No. 11 at 2, 5 n.2. Hall adopted those statements. ECF No. 45 at 1. Plaintiff’s declarations supply testimony, on personal knowledge, about the names he used on Meta’s services and the reason his legal name appears in the April 9 materials. ECF No. 31 ¶¶ 2–7; ECF No. 59-2 ¶¶ 2–10. The letters, the April 9 materials, and the earlier joint filing of NCMEC and Hall were before the Court in August and remain in the record. ECF Nos. 7-4, 7-5, 7-6.
C.	Local Civil Rule 56.

Rule 56(b) permits a motion for summary judgment “at any time until 30 days after the close of all discovery” unless “a different time is set by local rule or the court orders otherwise.” Local Civil Rule 56(A) sets a different time for this District and displaces that default. “The time provisions of Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(b) shall not apply in this District.” The Court’s Order supplies the operative instruction here: renewal “at an appropriate time.” ECF No. 12 at 1. Local Civil Rule 56(C) requires leave of Court for separate motions for summary judgment on separate grounds. This Motion renews the one ground presented in ECF No. 6. Its alternative request under Rule 56(g) concerns the same submission and is not a separate ground.

The timing argument is this. The Court reserved renewal. The parties whose relationship is at issue have since responded and have described that relationship to the Court. The record now includes those descriptions and Plaintiff’s testimony. That is the record on which the submitted component can be assessed. The pending Rule 12 motions test the sufficiency of the pleading; this Motion asks the Court to determine one component on the record.
D.	The Motion rests on the operative pleading and seeks no change to any discovery or scheduling disposition.

content.text: ECF No. 5 is the operative pleading. The Motion rests on it. The declaration at ECF No. 59-2 was filed as an exhibit to a motion for leave to amend, ECF No. 59, which the Court denied. ECF No. 84. The Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine filed with this Motion (“Ballentine Decl.”) restates that testimony. The Motion requests no discovery. It seeks adjudication on existing evidence, and it asks the Court to modify no order concerning scheduling or discovery.

ECF No. 108 states that “the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. This Motion is consistent with ECF Nos. 84 and 108. It seeks no discovery. It rests on documents already docketed, on testimony Plaintiff has already sworn, and on statements NCMEC and Hall made in their own filings. It asks the Court to modify neither order. The Fourth Circuit has identified the risk of early summary judgment where the facts are “exclusively in the control of the opposing party.” Harrods Ltd. v. Sixty Internet Domain Names, 302 F.3d 214, 247 (4th Cir. 2002) (quotation marks and citation omitted); see Part VIII. The facts on the submitted component are in the control of NCMEC and Hall, and NCMEC and Hall have stated them. A party that has stated a fact in its own brief does not need discovery to learn it.

runs.text: A.	Rule 56(a) and the burden of a plaintiff-movant.

content.text: A party may move for summary judgment on “each claim or defense — or the part of each claim or defense — on which summary judgment is sought.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). The Court “shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Id. A fact is material if it “might affect the outcome of the suit under the governing law.” Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986). A dispute is genuine if “the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party.” Id. The question is whether the evidence presents a sufficient disagreement to require submission to a jury or is so one-sided that one party must prevail as a matter of law. Id. at 251–52. Credibility determinations, the weighing of evidence, and the drawing of legitimate inferences are jury functions, and the nonmovant’s evidence is believed with justifiable inferences drawn in its favor. Id. at 255.

content.text: B.	The evidentiary foundations.

Rule 56(c)(1)(A) permits a fact to be supported by citing particular parts of the record, including documents, declarations, and admissions. Rule 56(c)(4) requires a declaration to be made on personal knowledge, to set out facts that would be admissible in evidence, and to show the declarant’s competence. Plaintiff’s facts rest on four foundations, and each does a different job.

First, authentication. Plaintiff’s declarations identify the earlier joint filing of NCMEC and Hall, the letters, and the April 9 materials as true and correct copies obtained from identified sources. ECF No. 7-1 ¶¶ 4–6; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 2–4. The copies of the letters in the record are reproduced from the exhibits NCMEC and Hall themselves filed in the earlier action. ECF No. 7-1 ¶ 5; Ballentine Decl. ¶ 3. Authentication establishes what a document is. It does not establish the truth of every assertion in the document.
Second, document contents. The letters and the April 9 materials are in the record. ECF Nos. 7-5, 7-6. Their wording is a fact about them.

Third, opposing-party representations. The statements of NCMEC and Hall in ECF Nos. 11 and 45, and in the joint filing reproduced at ECF No. 7-4, are statements of the parties whose relationship is at issue.
Fourth, personal-knowledge testimony. Plaintiff’s declarations state what Plaintiff did. ECF No. 31 ¶¶ 1, 8; ECF No. 59-2 ¶ 1.

content.text: “[A]n employer is liable for the tortious act of his employee if the employee was performing his employer’s business and acting within the scope of his employment.” Parker v. Carilion Clinic, 296 Va. 319, 335, 819 S.E.2d 809 (2018) (citation omitted). The inquiry asks whether “the service itself, in which the tortious act was done, was within the ordinary course of [the employer’s] business.” Id. at 336 (citation omitted). The act must have been “within the scope of the duties of the employment and in the execution of the service for which the employee was engaged.” Id. at 338–39 (quotation marks and citation omitted). The employee must have committed the act “while actively engaged in a job-related service.” Id. at 339. Presence at work, use of the employer’s property, and the employer’s time are not enough. Id.

content.text: A.	The sequence under Rule 56(c) and Rule 56(e).

content.text: Rule 56(c)(1) requires a party asserting that a fact cannot be or is genuinely disputed to support the assertion by citing particular parts of the record, or by showing that the materials cited do not establish the absence or presence of a genuine dispute, or that an adverse party cannot produce admissible evidence to support the fact. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(1)(A)–(B). Rule 56(c)(2) permits an objection that cited material cannot be presented in a form that would be admissible in evidence. Local Civil Rule 56(B) requires an opposing brief to include a specifically captioned section listing the material facts the opponent contends are genuinely in issue, with citations to the parts of the record relied on. The local rule then provides: “In determining a motion for summary judgment, the Court may assume that facts identified by the moving party in its listing of material facts are admitted, unless such a fact is controverted in the statement of genuine issues filed in opposition to the motion.”

The sequence is this. First, Plaintiff must support each asserted fact. Part III does so. Second, an opposing party may challenge the evidence: its sufficiency to establish the proposition, its admissibility, or its materiality. A legal argument that the cited materials do not establish the proposition is a proper response under Rule 56(c)(1)(B). An objection under Rule 56(c)(2) is a proper response. A showing of immateriality is a proper response. Third, a bare contradiction without record support is not sufficient. Fourth, where a fact is properly supported and not properly addressed, the Court may give an opportunity to address it, consider it undisputed for purposes of the Motion, or issue another appropriate order. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(e)(1), (2), (4). Fifth, any establishment of a fact in the action, beyond this Motion, requires separate consideration under Rule 56(g).
B.	Motion-specific treatment and case-wide treatment are different.

runs.text: B.	Motion-specific treatment and case-wide treatment are different.

content.text: Rule 56(e)(2) permits the Court to consider a fact undisputed “for purposes of the motion.” Local Civil Rule 56(B) permits the same assumption in determining the Motion. Neither establishes a fact for trial. Rule 56(g) reaches further. When the Court does not grant all the relief requested by the motion, it “may enter an order stating any material fact . . . that is not genuinely in dispute and treating the fact as established in the case.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(g). Plaintiff requests the two forms of treatment in that order and keeps them distinct.

A Defendant may accept a fact for purposes of this Motion only. Rule 56(c)(1)(A) recognizes stipulations “made for purposes of the motion only.” Plaintiff’s express request under Rule 56(g) gives notice that each numbered fact is offered for establishment in the action. That notice does not convert a limited acceptance into an unlimited one. A Defendant that accepts a fact for the Motion only may say so in its statement of genuine issues, and the Court may take that limitation into account in deciding whether to establish the fact under Rule 56(g). Plaintiff does not contend that any Defendant’s earlier briefing operates as a response to this Motion. The oppositions to this Motion are where each fact is to be addressed.

runs.text: VIII.	ANY CLAIMED NEED FOR DISCOVERY SHOULD BE EVALUATED AGAINST THE PARTICULAR DETERMINATION IT AFFECTS

content.text: As a general rule, summary judgment is appropriate only after adequate time for discovery. Harrods Ltd. v. Sixty Internet Domain Names, 302 F.3d 214, 244 (4th Cir. 2002). Rule 56(d) supplies the mechanism. A nonmovant that cannot present facts essential to its opposition may show that by affidavit or declaration, “for specified reasons,” and the Court may defer considering the motion, deny it, allow time for discovery, or issue any other appropriate order. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(d). The Fourth Circuit gives such a showing great weight. Harrods, 302 F.3d at 244. The court has also recognized that a nonmovant’s objections may serve as the functional equivalent of an affidavit where they adequately inform the district court of the discovery needed and the nonmovant has not been lax in pursuing it. Id. at 244–45; see Pledger v. Lynch, 5 F.4th 511, 526 (4th Cir. 2021) (applying that principle to the objections of a pro se prisoner). Harrods applied the predecessor of current Rule 56(d). Plaintiff does not ask the Court to hold any Defendant to a form. He asks that any claimed need be stated for the fact it affects.

  II.      STANDARD OF REVIEW

           Under Rule 15(a), leave to amend is to be granted freely, "absent bad faith, undue

  prejudice to the opposing party, or futility of amendment." Hardee v. Mun . Jail Va. Beach

  Sheriff's Off, 2025 U.S . Dist. LEXIS 184735, *5 (E.D. Va. 2025) (quoting United States v.

  Pittman, 209 F.3d 314,317 (4th Cir. 2000)); Save Our Sound OBX, Inc. v. NC. DOT, 914 F.3d

  213 , 228 (4th Cir. 2019) (same). A proposed amendment is futile "when it is clearly insufficient

  or frivolous on its face .. . [or[ if the claim it presents would not survive a motion to dismiss."

  Id.; United States ex rel. Wilson v. Kellogg Brown & Root, Inc., 525 F.3d 370,375 (4th Cir.

  2008).

           Under Rule 20, multiple persons may be joined in one action as defendants if:

  "(A) any right to relief is asserted against them jointly, severally, or in the alternative with

  respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or

  occurrences; and (B) any question of law or fact common to all defendants will arise in the

  action." Fed. R. Civ. P. 20(a)(2); Ellis v. Werfel, 86 F.4th 1032, 1035 (4th Cir. 2023).

         Additionally, the proposed FAC's additional causes of action appear unlikely to survive a

  Rule 12(b)( 6) motion, as well, and as such are futile . As to proposed Count III-Intentional

  Infliction of Emotional Distress as to Defendant Hall-Plaintiff fails to state a claim upon which

  relief may be granted. In order to succeed on such a claim under Virginia law, a plaintiff must

  show four elements of proof: (1) the conduct was intentional or reckless; (2) the conduct was

  "outrageous or intolerable;" (3) there was a casual connection between the conduct and the

  resulting emotional distress; and (4) the resulting emotional distress was severe. Super Valu, Inc.

  v. Johnson , 276 Va. 356, 370 (2008); Almy v. Grisham , 273 Va. 68 (2007); Young v. Wilson , 2026

  U.S. Dist. LEXIS 147023, *10 (E.D. Va. 2026) (quoting Almy). "[O]nly where the conduct has

  been so outrageous in character, and so extreme in degree, as to go beyond all possible bounds of

  decency, and to be regarded as atrocious, and utterly intolerable in a civilized community" can a

  claim survive. Young, 2026 U.S . Dist. LEXIS at *10 (quoting Russo v. White, 241 Va. 23 , 27

  (1991)). This is an exacting standard-as noted by the Virginia Supreme Court in Russo v.

  White, even if a defendant intended to inflict emotional distress, and acted in a fashion that could

  support an award of punitive damages for another tort, the conduct must be utterly intolerable.

  241 Va. 23 , 27 (1991).

         The proposed FAC falls well short of that standard. Again, this is about Plaintiff sending

  subpoenas to NCMEC, and NCMEC responding without waiting to be formally served. It

  cannot be said that NCMEC responding to those subpoenas, using the exact language specified

  by Plaintiff, is "outrageous," "extreme," goes "beyond all possible bounds of decency," or is

           A claim for relief under 42 U.S .C. § 1985(2) requires a plaintiff to "plausibly allege an

  agreement or 'meeting of minds' among the alleged conspirators." Simmons v. Poe, 47 F.3d

  13 70, 13 77 (4th Cir. 1995). Plaintiff's proposed FAC falls well short of that threshold, and

  would not survive a motion to dismiss, as both the existence of, and alleged aim of, the

  conspiracy are entirely predicated on nonsensical conclusory allegations. In the Fourth Circuit,

  "allegations of parallel conduct and a bare assertion of a conspiracy are not enough for a claim to

  proceed" under 42 U.S.C. § 1985 . Thomas v. Salvation Army S. Terr., 841 F.3d 632, 637 (4th Cir.

  2016); A Society Without a Name v. Virginia, 655 F.3d 342, 347 (4th Cir. 2011).

           B. There is No Basis to Include the Proposed New Defendants in this Matter.

           Finally, Plaintiff's proposed FAC seeks to add Meta Platforms, Inc. and six John or Jane

  Doe defendants. For reasons unclear-and despite the fact that Defendant Hall is and was an

  employee of the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, who was clearly acting in

  the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas-Plaintiff seeks to drop

  the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, add persons who allegedly

  communicated and conspired with Defendant Hall, and add Meta Platforms, Inc. as a defendant

  under the 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) claim.

           As to the exclusion of the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, its

  removal from the lawsuit would have no effect on the pending motion to dismiss, or viability of

  Plaintiff's claims. Defendant Hall was working within the course and scope of her employment,

  and is entitled to the same defenses as the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.

         Further, under Rule 20, multiple defendants can be joined in one action only if any right

  to relief is asserted against them "with respect to or arising out of the same transaction,

  occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences, and any question of law or fact common to

  all defendants will arise in the action." Fed. R. Civ. P. 20(a)(2). Absent Plaintiff's conclusory

  and imaginary conspiracy-whereby NCMEC responded to subpoenas, precisely as requested,

  supposedly in order to further a common scheme to intimidate Plaintiff out of testifying-there is

  no transaction, occurrence, or series thereof common to all defendants. (To wit, there would be

  no claim asserted as to John or Jane Does, or Meta Platforms, Inc.)

  IV.    CONCLUSION

         In light of the foregoing, NCMEC respectfully submits that Plaintiffs' Motion for Leave

  to File an Amended Complaint should be denied as futile . The new allegations, and new counts,

  in the proposed FAC are conclusory, lacking factual support, and those counts fail to state a

  claim upon which relief may be granted. Further, the only basis by which there is any common

  transaction, occurrence, or series thereof would be if Plaintiff were to plausibly assert the

  existence of a conspiracy under 42 U.S .C. § 1985(2), which the proposed FAC fails to do . As

  such, NCMEC respectfully requests that Plaintiff's Motion for Leave be denied, and that this

  matter proceed to the hearing set for August 7, 2026 on NCMEC's Motion to Dismiss.

runs.text: [PROPOSED] ORDER A — GRANTING PARTIAL SUMMARY JUDGMENT ON THE AGENCY-AND-SCOPE COMPONENT

content.text: This matter is before the Court on Plaintiff’s Renewed Rule 56 Motion for Partial Summary Judgment (the “Motion”). The Motion concerns the two letters dated April 22, 2026, signed by Defendant Katie Hall on the letterhead of Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”), that appear in the record at ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3 (the “Letters”). The Court has considered the Motion, the Memorandum in Support, the parties’ submissions, if any, and the record.

The Court finds as follows. The Letters bear NCMEC’s letterhead and Hall’s signature above the title “Corporate Counsel.” ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. Each Letter states that NCMEC provides its written responses. Id. NCMEC has stated in this action that the Letters were “signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC,” and that Hall “at all times relevant was an employee of NCMEC.” ECF No. 11 at 2, 5 n.2. Hall has adopted that memorandum and has described herself as an employee of NCMEC. ECF No. 45 at 1. In an earlier action concerning the same Letters, NCMEC and Hall, through common counsel, stated that Hall “was clearly acting in the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas.” ECF No. 7-4 at 7. No party has identified record evidence that Hall acted outside the scope of her employment, or on a motive of her own, when she signed and issued the Letters.

content.text: Under Virginia law, an employer is liable for the tortious act of its employee if the employee was performing the employer’s business and acting within the scope of employment, and the inquiry asks whether the service in which the act was done was within the ordinary course of the employer’s business and within the scope of the duties for which the employee was engaged. Parker v. Carilion Clinic, 296 Va. 319, 335–39, 819 S.E.2d 809 (2018). On this record, no reasonable jury could find that Hall was performing other than NCMEC’s business, or acting outside the scope of her employment, when she signed and issued the Letters. There is no genuine dispute as to the material facts stated above, and Plaintiff is entitled to judgment as a matter of law on the part of Counts I, II, III, and VI of the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) identified below. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). Accordingly, it is hereby

content.text: ORDERED that the Motion is GRANTED as to the agency-and-scope component identified in Part I of the Motion, as follows:
1.	Hall was an employee of NCMEC and served as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel when she signed and issued the Letters.
2.	Hall signed and issued the Letters on NCMEC’s behalf, as NCMEC’s agent, within the course and scope of her employment, in the execution of the service for which NCMEC employed her.

3.	The agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI of the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 21, 195, 216, 230, 258) is established. Whether Hall’s conduct in signing and issuing the Letters was tortious, and whether NCMEC is liable for that conduct under any count, remain for later adjudication.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that, if leave to file a Second Amended Complaint has been granted, the determination in paragraphs 1 through 3 above applies to the corresponding claims under the resulting operative pleading.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that this Order does not determine: whether any element of Counts I, II, III, or VI other than the component stated above is established; any defense asserted or available to Hall or NCMEC, including the litigation privilege and any immunity under 18 U.S.C. § 2258D or 34 U.S.C. § 20505; NCMEC’s direct liability for its own conduct; the existence, contents, source, or accuracy of any CyberTipline report; the truth or falsity of any statement in the Letters; the existence of any agreement among Defendants; any Defendant’s motive or state of mind; any claim against Meta Platforms, Inc. or the Doe Defendants; or any question of damages or other remedy. All such matters are reserved.
It is FURTHER ORDERED that this Order does not determine the material facts numbered 1 through 17 in Part III of the Memorandum in Support, except to the extent stated in paragraphs 1 and 2 above.
It is FURTHER ORDERED that this Order is not a final judgment and does not direct the entry of judgment under Rule 54(b).
IT IS SO ORDERED. The Clerk is directed to provide a copy of this Order to Plaintiff at his address of record and to counsel of record.

runs.text: [PROPOSED] ORDER B — ESTABLISHING MATERIAL FACTS UNDER FEDERAL RULE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE 56(g)

content.text: This matter is before the Court on Plaintiff’s Renewed Rule 56 Motion for Partial Summary Judgment (the “Motion”). The Motion concerns the two letters dated April 22, 2026, signed by Defendant Katie Hall on the letterhead of Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”), that appear in the record at ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3 (the “Letters”). The Court has considered the Motion, the Memorandum in Support, the parties’ submissions, if any, and the record.

The Court has applied the standard of Rule 56(a) to the agency-and-scope component identified in Part I of the Motion. The Court does not grant the Motion’s request for partial summary judgment under Rule 56(a) in the form requested, for the reasons stated by the Court on the record. Because the Court does not grant all the relief requested by the Motion, the Court has considered under Rule 56(g) each material fact listed in Part III of the Memorandum in Support, the parties’ statements of genuine issues, if any, and the opportunity of each affected party to oppose establishment of each fact. The Court finds that the facts stated below are not genuinely in dispute. Accordingly, it is hereby

ORDERED that the following facts are established in this action and shall be treated as established in all further proceedings. Each numbered provision is severable. The Court’s omission of any proposed fact from this Order does not establish any contrary proposition and leaves that matter for later proceedings.
A.	Hall’s employment and the Letters

runs.text: A.	Hall’s employment and the Letters

content.text: 1.	Katie Hall was an employee of NCMEC and served as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel when she signed and issued the Letters.
2.	Hall signed each of the two Letters. Each Letter is on NCMEC letterhead. The signature block of each Letter identifies Hall as “Corporate Counsel.”

3.	The first sentence of the body of each Letter states: “In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) provides its written responses as detailed below.” The reference line of one Letter identifies the matter as “Marvelle Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al.” The reference line of the other identifies the matter as “Marvelle Ballentine v. Devin S. Anderson, et al.”
B.	The April 9, 2026 materials and formal service

runs.text: B.	The April 9, 2026 materials and formal service

content.text: 4.	On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted to NCMEC’s Legal Department a letter giving advance notice of intended subpoenas in two separate matters, together with two signed subpoena forms and a Schedule A for each. The letter stated that each notice was accompanied by a signed copy of the draft subpoena “that will be formally served after the notice period has run.” NCMEC received the materials.
5.	No subpoena had been formally served on NCMEC when NCMEC issued the Letters.

6.	Schedule A to each subpoena form directed production of a document sufficient to show whether NCMEC received or maintains any CyberTipline report, referral, or submission concerning three identifiers. Schedule A listed the identifiers as “(1) Marvelle J. Ballentine,” “(2) Jay Ballentine,” and “(3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com,” and joined them with “and/or.”

7.	Each Letter states that NCMEC has received two CyberTipline reports “concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com.” The three identifiers and the connector “and/or” in that sentence are the identifiers and connector that appear in Schedule A.
C.	Plaintiff’s account-name history

8.	Before April 22, 2026, Plaintiff did not use the name “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any product or service owned or operated by Meta Platforms, Inc. that Plaintiff used.

9.	Before April 22, 2026, Plaintiff did not use “Marvelle J. Ballentine” as a username, profile name, display name, account name, or other identity by which he identified himself on Facebook, Instagram, Threads, WhatsApp, Oculus, Meta Quest, or any other Meta product or service that he used.

Ballentine” to Meta Platforms, Inc. as the name identifying him for purposes of any Meta account that he created, maintained, or operated, or as the name identifying any such account. content.text: INTRODUCTION

ECF No. 105 requested participation and reporting, not discovery responses. ECF No. 108 denied that request based on postponement of discovery. The Order states: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2.

Plaintiff asks the Court to reconsider that application under Rule 54(b). The Court can direct the parties’ planning conference and report and determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after considering the report. Rule 26(a)(1)(C) and Rule 34(b)(2)(A) permit the Court to set a different time for the consequences a conference ordinarily triggers. The Court’s authority under Rules 16 and 26 over the timing and sequence of discovery permits it to make that determination after the parties have conferred. Proposed Order A directs the conference and report and does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. The question on reconsideration is whether postponing the planning steps remains warranted on those terms. If the Court concludes that planning remains postponed, Plaintiff asks that the postponement be stated, its source identified to the extent the Court relies on a direction of the District Judge, and the procedure after the dismissal rulings established. That is Proposed Order B.

Three distinctions govern this Memorandum. First, the denial of the conference request and the explanation for it are different things. The dispute concerns the basis and the continuing effect of the denial, not whether a ruling exists. Second, the Court’s authority to postpone planning and its exercise of that authority are different things. Plaintiff challenges the application of the discretion to the request presented, not the existence of the discretion. Third, an error in the original ruling and a reason to modify it now are different things. The narrowed terms in Proposed Order A support modification now. They do not by themselves prove that ECF No. 108 was erroneous when entered.

content.text: Rule 54(b) provides that an order adjudicating fewer than all the claims or the rights of fewer than all the parties “may be revised at any time before the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims and all the parties’ rights and liabilities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). The Fourth Circuit has held that “[m]otions for reconsideration of interlocutory orders are not subject to the strict standards applicable to motions for reconsideration of a final judgment.” Am. Canoe Ass’n v. Murphy Farms, Inc., 326 F.3d 505, 514 (4th Cir. 2003). A district court “retains the power to reconsider and modify its interlocutory judgments, including partial summary judgments, at any time prior to final judgment when such is warranted.” Id. at 514–15. That power is committed to the court’s discretion, and the law-of-the-case doctrine guides that discretion. Id. at 515. American Canoe addressed an interlocutory standing determination treated as a partial summary judgment. Id. at 514–16. Plaintiff does not contend that its reasoning imposes a heightened duty here.

content.text: The discretion has limits. Rule 54(b) allows more flexibility to revise interlocutory orders before final judgment than Rule 59(e) allows after it, but “the discretion Rule 54(b) provides is not limitless.” Carlson v. Boston Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). The Fourth Circuit treats interlocutory rulings as law of the case and permits revision in three circumstances: “(1) a subsequent trial producing substantially different evidence; (2) a change in applicable law; or (3) clear error causing manifest injustice.” Id. (internal quotation marks and alteration omitted). U.S. Tobacco Cooperative applied the same three circumstances and confirmed that the clear-error ground requires more than disagreement with the ruling. U.S. Tobacco Coop. Inc. v. Big S. Wholesale of Va., LLC, 899 F.3d 236, 256–58 (4th Cir. 2018).

A ruling is not clearly erroneous because a different procedure would have been preferable. Plaintiff bears the burden on this Motion. The Order states that Plaintiff “has not established that he is entitled to the relief he seeks.” ECF No. 108 at 1. Plaintiff accepts that burden. Plaintiff must identify an error in the ruling as entered and a consequence that the error works. Plaintiff addresses each separately. Plaintiff then addresses the narrowed terms that support modification now whether or not the Court finds the original error.
A.	The asserted error: the Order treated the conference and report as the commencement of discovery.

content.text: ECF No. 108 rests on the postponement of discovery. Its quoted rationale concerns scheduling orders that “initiate discovery obligations” and the avoidance of “expensive or otherwise burdensome discovery on potentially frivolous claims.” ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Its case-specific ground is the District Judge’s choice “to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2.

ECF No. 105 did not ask the Court to begin discovery. It asked the Court to set the dates for the planning conference and the report. ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(a)–(b). It left every proposal to postpone discovery to the report. ECF No. 105 ¶¶ 6, 11(b); ECF No. 106 at 5. A Defendant that believed no discovery should proceed until the motions were decided could state that position in the report, and the Court would then decide sequencing with each party’s position before it. ECF No. 106 at 5. The request contained the mechanism by which the discovery-postponement decision would be honored.

The Rules separate the conference from discovery. Rule 26(d)(1) places the conference before discovery. Rule 26(a)(1)(C), Rule 26(d)(2)(B), and Rule 34(b)(2)(A) each permit the Court to set a different time for the consequences a conference triggers. The asserted error is that ECF No. 108 applied the discovery-postponement decision as if the conference were the commencement of discovery. The distinction between planning and discovery was presented in ECF No. 105 ¶¶ 6 and 8 and ECF No. 106 at 4–5 and 7–8. Plaintiff does not present it as new. Plaintiff asserts that the Order did not apply it.

ECF No. 108 is an order of this Court. It is not counsel’s assessment of timing, and Plaintiff does not treat it as one. Rule 26(f)(1) permits the Court to order otherwise. Pending dismissal motions do not themselves create an exemption from planning. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 1993 amendment (subdivision (f)). A court may nevertheless direct postponement in the particular action. The question is whether the ground ECF No. 108 states supports postponing planning when the planning order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. On the Order’s own terms, the reason to wait is the burden of discovery. Part V.G addresses that reason as applied to the narrowed procedure.
B.	The asserted consequence: court-directed planning deferred for the pendency of the motions, without implementation terms.

runs.text: B.	The asserted consequence: court-directed planning deferred for the pendency of the motions, without implementation terms.

content.text: The consequence Plaintiff asserts is limited to what the record supports. When Plaintiff executed the declaration accompanying ECF No. 105, the parties had not completed the conference, and no report containing agreed and competing proposals existed. ECF No. 107 ¶¶ 10–11. The denial defers court-directed planning while three motions to dismiss remain pending. The Order identifies the event that ends the postponement of discovery: resolution of the pending motions to dismiss. ECF No. 108 at 2. It does not state whether the conference and report are postponed with discovery, whether initial disclosures are postponed, what step follows the dismissal rulings, what happens if the rulings issue on different dates, or what happens if a dismissal permits amendment rather than ending the action.

Plaintiff does not assert that evidence has been lost. Plaintiff does not assert an inability to oppose the motions to dismiss. Plaintiff does not assert that the Order prohibits voluntary consultation among the parties. Plaintiff does not assert that procedural uncertainty is, by itself, manifest injustice. The injustice Plaintiff asserts is the postponement of a planning process that the Order’s stated ground did not require to be postponed, for the full pendency of the dismissal motions, if the Court accepts the error stated in Part III.A. If the Court does not accept that error, the implementation terms remain useful, and Proposed Order B supplies them.

Those terms support modification now. They are not evidence of what ECF No. 105 already requested, and Plaintiff does not present them as such. ECF No. 108 denied ECF No. 105 without prejudice. Plaintiff does not read it as an invitation to renew the request before the motions to dismiss are decided. If the Court declines to find error in the original disposition, Plaintiff asks that the Court consider the narrowed terms as a renewed request and decide it on its own merits under Rule 26(f)(1) and Rule 16. Reconsideration remains the principal vehicle. Renewal is a subordinate characterization of the same confined relief.
IV.	RULE 26(f) PERMITS PLANNING WHILE THE COURT CONTROLS DISCOVERY TIMING

runs.text: IV.	RULE 26(f) PERMITS PLANNING WHILE THE COURT CONTROLS DISCOVERY TIMING

content.text: A.	The appearing parties share the planning obligation, subject to the Court’s order.

runs.text: A.	The appearing parties share the planning obligation, subject to the Court’s order.

content.text: Rule 26(f)(1) provides: “Except in a proceeding exempted from initial disclosure under Rule 26(a)(1)(B) or when the court orders otherwise, the parties must confer as soon as practicable—and in any event at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due under Rule 16(b).” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(1). Rule 26(f)(2) places the obligation jointly on “[t]he attorneys of record and all unrepresented parties that have appeared in the case.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(2). The 1993 Advisory Committee Note states that the obligation “is imposed on all parties that have appeared in the case, including defendants who, because of a pending Rule 12 motion, may not have yet filed an answer in the case.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 1993 amendment (subdivision (f)). Plaintiff relies on the Note for that proposition. Plaintiff does not rely on the Note’s description of deadlines that later amendments replaced.

Two propositions follow. Pending dismissal motions do not themselves exempt a party from planning. The Court may nevertheless postpone planning in a particular action by ordering otherwise. ECF No. 108 is such an order to the extent it postpones the conference. The question on reconsideration is whether that postponement remains warranted when the planning order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay.
B.	The report may present competing proposals, including proposals to defer.

runs.text: B.	The report may present competing proposals, including proposals to defer.

content.text: Rule 26(f)(3) requires the discovery plan to state “the parties’ views and proposals” on the timing and form of disclosures; on the subjects and timing of discovery and “whether discovery should be conducted in phases or be limited to or focused on particular issues”; on electronically stored information; on claims of privilege and trial-preparation protection; on changes to the limits on discovery; and on “any other orders that the court should issue under Rule 26(c) or under Rule 16(b) and (c).” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(3)(A)–(F). Rule 26(f)(3)(D), as amended effective December 1, 2025, requires the plan to address “the timing and method for complying with Rule 26(b)(5)(A).” The conference may establish a method for later discovery without requiring immediate production of documents. Plaintiff’s common agenda keys each subject to the provision that requires it. It includes the Rule 26(f)(3)(D) subject. ECF No. 107-1 (Ex. A) § III.

The rule requires good-faith consideration of each subject. It does not require agreement. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(2). The 1993 Note contemplates that the parties may not agree and that the report then indicates their competing proposals. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 1993 amendment (subdivision (f)). A Defendant may propose that no discovery proceed until the motions are decided. That proposal is a view on the subjects Rule 26(f)(3)(B) and (F) identify. The report records it.

Plaintiff does not contend that every planning subject is independent of which claims survive. The scope of preservation, the sources of electronically stored information, and the privilege issues that arise may each depend on the surviving claims. The parties can nevertheless discuss methods and state conditional proposals now, and identify in the report the matters that depend on the dismissal rulings. Proposed Order A requires that engagement. A party may, as to any subject, propose deferral, explain why the subject cannot usefully be resolved before the dismissal rulings, state a conditional proposal, or record a disagreement. Each party must still consider each subject and state its position. A single sentence repeated under every heading is not the participation Rule 26(f)(2) describes.

The 1993 Note also contemplates a report that describes incomplete participation. Id. Plaintiff cannot supply another party’s views. Plaintiff cannot convert an unanswered invitation into that party’s participation. A report describing nonparticipation does not establish that the conference Rule 26(f) requires occurred. Proposed Order A therefore provides for a status report if the conference remains incomplete at the reporting deadline, and provides that a status report does not complete the conference. That provision is a reporting safeguard. It is not an assertion that no other reporting mechanism exists.

content.text: Rule 26(f)(2) requires the parties to “confer.” The 2000 amendment changed the rule “to require only a ‘conference’ of the parties, rather than a ‘meeting.’” The accompanying Note contemplates other means of conferring, while stating that there are “important benefits to face-to-face discussion,” and the court retains authority to require attendance in person. Plaintiff does not claim one. Proposed Order A directs substantive written exchange on each subject and permits any other format the participants agree on or the Court directs. Silence does not complete the conference. Transmission of proposals does not complete it. The conference is complete when each participant has stated its position on each subject and the participants have attempted in good faith to agree. ECF No. 107-1 (Ex. A) §§ I, V; ECF No. 106 at 7.

If every claim is dismissed without leave to amend, that work will not be used. The task is limited. The participants are four. Plaintiff’s proposals and agenda already exist. ECF No. 107 ¶¶ 3–4. A Defendant that believes a subject cannot usefully be addressed before the rulings may say so and state a conditional proposal. The report then shows the Court which subjects can be resolved now and which await the rulings. That is the function Rule 26(f)(2) assigns the report. The cost of a report on those terms is the preparation of positions. It is not the cost the Order’s quoted rationale identifies, which is the expense and burden of discovery itself.

content.text: ECF No. 108 attributes the postponement of discovery to a choice by the District Judge. ECF No. 108 at 2. It does not identify the order or instruction that records the choice. Local Civil Rule 72 recognizes that matters may be referred to a magistrate judge on a district judge’s instructions, and such an instruction may not appear as a separately entered order. Plaintiff does not contend that the absence of a docketed order establishes that no instruction exists. Plaintiff does not request internal communications or deliberations. Plaintiff requests identification of the operative direction, to the extent the Court relies on one, so that its scope is known to the parties.

It states the postponement, identifies the direction and its scope, and sets the procedure that follows the dismissal rulings. Second, a direction may concern substantive discovery and leave planning available. If so, planning is available for the Court’s consideration under Rule 26(f)(1) on the narrowed terms. Availability does not compel a planning order. Plaintiff asks the Court to exercise its own judgment on those terms. Third, the attribution may reflect an inference from the procedural posture of three pending motions to dismiss and no scheduling order. If so, the Court’s own determination under Rule 26(f)(1) governs, and Plaintiff asks the Court to make it on the narrowed terms.

In no case does Plaintiff ask the Magistrate Judge to countermand a direction of the District Judge. The Motion operates within the authority referred under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). Each form of relief requested is consistent with whichever source operated.

VI.	THE PROPOSED ORDERS ADDRESS PLANNING WITHOUT DECIDING DISCOVERY PROPOSALS

runs.text: VI.	THE PROPOSED ORDERS ADDRESS PLANNING WITHOUT DECIDING DISCOVERY PROPOSALS

content.text: A.	Proposed Order A.

Proposed Order A modifies ECF No. 108 as to ECF No. 105 only. The participants are Plaintiff and counsel for NCMEC, Hall, and Meta. The Doe Defendants, unidentified and unserved, are not included. ECF No. 105 ¶ 1. The conference is to be completed within 14 days after entry, by substantive written exchange on the subjects in Rule 26(f)(2)–(3) or by another format the participants agree on or the Court directs. The report is due within 14 days after completion and no later than 18 days after entry. The 14-day period after completion tracks Rule 26(f)(2). The 14-day completion period and the 18-day outer limit are requested terms. To the extent the outer limit requires the report sooner than 14 days after completion, the order shortens the reporting interval under Rule 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1)(b).

The report states agreements as agreements and disagreements as separately attributed positions. Counsel for NCMEC and Hall identifies whether those Defendants adopt a position jointly. ECF No. 107-1 (Ex. A) § V. Plaintiff circulates a proposed report for counsel’s review. The responsibility for the report remains joint under Rule 26(f)(2), and the order adds no interim deadline. If the conference remains incomplete at the reporting deadline, the parties file a status report, or a party unable to obtain a joint report files its own, identifying the participation, the exchanges, and the remaining obstacle. A status report does not complete the conference, extend the completion deadline, or excuse further participation.

Proposed Order A does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. The timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. Any party requesting postponement, phasing, or modification of discovery or disclosure obligations may state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination. Nothing in the order decides whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed a discovery stay or modifies any other applicable order. The Court may determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after consideration of the report. Existing preservation duties remain unchanged, and the order imposes no new preservation obligation. The disposition of ECF No. 103, ECF No. 84, and every other order remain unchanged. Every pending motion, objection, and application remains pending on its own grounds.
B.	Proposed Order B.

Proposed Order B is the alternative if the Court determines that planning must remain postponed. It grants reconsideration only to state and implement the postponement. It denies the request for an immediate conference deadline without prejudice. It states that the parties’ conference and report are postponed pending disposition of ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45. It states that initial disclosures are not due until a date set by further order and that any postponement of discovery is limited to the scope the Court states. It reserves one paragraph for the Court’s statement of the source and scope of any direction of the District Judge on which the postponement rests, or of the Court’s own determination under Rule 26(f)(1). Plaintiff has not drafted that paragraph. Plaintiff cannot state a direction the record does not contain.

Proposed Order B then sets the procedure that follows the dismissal rulings. Within 14 days after disposition of the last of ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45, unless a final judgment has ended the action, Plaintiff and counsel for the parties remaining in the action file a status report identifying the remaining claims and parties, any leave to amend and its deadline, proposed dates for the conference, the report, and initial disclosures, and any continuing request for postponement. A party unable to obtain a joint report files its own. After a ruling on fewer than all three motions, any party may move for earlier planning as to the claims and parties that remain. That motion does not itself impose planning obligations on a party whose motion remains undecided. The filing of a status report does not commence discovery. The phrase “unless a final judgment has ended the action” covers a dismissal with leave to amend, in which the action continues and awaits an amended pleading.
C.	Local Civil Rule 37(E).

The Motion seeks reconsideration of a case-management ruling. It does not seek an order compelling a disclosure or a response to a discovery request. content.text: Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b) for reconsideration of the Order signed and filed October 29, 2026 and entered on the docket October 30, 2026 (ECF No. 108), insofar as it denied Plaintiff’s Motion for Entry of a Scheduling Order and, as Necessary, an Initial Pretrial Conference (ECF No. 103). Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick entered ECF No. 108. This Motion asks the Magistrate Judge to reconsider that Order. The ground asserted is clear error causing manifest injustice. Carlson v. Boston Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). Under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1), a Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion, with Proposed Order A and Proposed Order B.

Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick entered ECF No. 108. This Motion asks the Magistrate Judge to reconsider that Order. The ground asserted is clear error causing manifest injustice.
, 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). Under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1), a Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion, with Proposed Order A and Proposed Order B.

content.text: I.	GROUNDS

1.	ECF No. 103 requested three forms of relief. First, entry of a scheduling order after the report or consultation Rule 16(b)(1) requires. ECF No. 103 ¶ 9, at 3. Second, if the complete scheduling order should await disposition of a pending matter, a determination whether an initial scheduling conference could proceed now to establish the remaining case-management steps. ECF No. 103 ¶ 10, at 3. Third, if either step was postponed, a statement of the good cause found under Rule 16(b)(2) and the date or event on which scheduling would next be addressed. ECF No. 103 ¶ 11, at 4. ECF No. 103 did not seek immediate interrogatory responses, document production, or depositions. ECF No. 103, Part II, at 3.

2.	The ordinary Rule 16(b)(2) date for the scheduling order was October 13, 2026, subject to a finding of good cause for delay. Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) was served July 31, 2026. ECF No. 3 at 2. NCMEC appeared August 12, 2026. ECF No. 10 at 1. Sixty days after August 12, 2026 was Sunday, October 11, 2026. Monday, October 12, 2026 was a legal holiday. The period ran to Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(1)(C), 6(a)(6)(A), 16(b)(2). The Memorandum sets out the computation.

3.	ECF No. 108 denied ECF No. 103 on the following stated ground: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. ECF No. 108 identified the initial-conference request. ECF No. 108 at 1. It denied that request through the same discovery-postponement rationale applied to the scheduling order. It did not separately explain that application. It contains no express finding under Rule 16(b)(2). Its reasons may be read as an implicit determination that good cause exists to delay the scheduling order. Plaintiff challenges whether those reasons support postponing the initial-conference alternative. ECF No. 108 identifies no order or instruction as the source of the decision it attributes to the District Judge.

4.	A decision to postpone discovery bears on whether the complete scheduling order should be entered now. Judicial consultation at a Rule 16(b) scheduling conference is not itself document production, deposition testimony, or an interrogatory response. Preparatory steps for that conference can affect disclosure and discovery timing. The Court can address those consequences expressly while deciding whether judicial scheduling should proceed. Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(3)(B)(i)–(ii), 16(c)(2)(F). ECF No. 108 applied a rationale directed to discovery to withhold judicial consultation without addressing whether that consultation could proceed while discovery remained deferred. That application is the error asserted.

5.	The source and scope of the decision attributed to the District Judge bear on that application. The District Judge’s entries of record are ECF Nos. 12, 25, 48, 50, and 70. None addresses the Rule 16(b) schedule. Local Civil Rule 72 permits a magistrate judge to act on the instructions of a district judge. The local rule does not itself establish that such an instruction exists in this action or what it says. Plaintiff requests identification of any operative order or instruction to the extent necessary to determine the scheduling obligations in this action and the scope of the authority referred.

6.	Plaintiff requests correction of the disposition or, in the alternative, a stated basis and scope for its continuation and a defined next step. Neither form of relief compels immediate merits discovery. Rule 54(b) permits revision of ECF No. 108 at any time before final judgment. ECF No. 108 was entered Friday, October 30, 2026. This Motion is submitted Sunday, November 1, 2026.
II.	SCOPE

7.	This Motion concerns only the denial of ECF No. 103. It does not seek reconsideration of the denial of ECF No. 105. It does not renew the requests denied in ECF No. 84. It does not seek authorization of interrogatories, document requests, depositions, or any other discovery. It does not seek a determination concerning the successor designation. Plaintiff’s pending applications remain pending on their own terms. None is withdrawn or expanded by this Motion. This Motion does not replace any separate objection required to obtain review of ECF No. 108.
III.	RELIEF REQUESTED
8.	Plaintiff requests that the Court:
(a)	reconsider ECF No. 108 insofar as it denied ECF No. 103, and modify that disposition;
(b)	establish a Rule 16(b) scheduling procedure for this action;

(c)	set a scheduling conference under Rule 16(b)(1)(B) and Local Civil Rule 16(B) on a date certain within 21 days after entry of the order, unless a sufficient Rule 26(f) report filed before that date permits earlier entry of the scheduling order without a conference;

(d)	direct the parties’ preparatory conference and written report on calendar dates fixed by the Court, each falling after entry of the order, with the intervals shortened under Rules 26(f)(1) and 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1) as requested in ECF No. 103 ¶ 9(c), at 3, and provide that a qualifying conference and report already completed satisfy that direction;

(e)	hold the initial conference and establish the remaining case-management steps even if the Court determines that completion of the scheduling order should await disposition of the pending motions to dismiss; and

(f)	in the alternative, if the Court continues to postpone both the scheduling order and the initial conference, identify any operative order or instruction on which the postponement rests and its application to each of those steps; state the Court’s basis for the continued postponement under Rule 16(b)(2); and establish a procedure under which the Court will take the next scheduling step within 14 days after disposition of the last pending motion to dismiss, if the action remains pending, with authority to proceed earlier where an individual disposition permits.

9.	The 21-day, seven-day, three-day, and 14-day periods are requested case-management terms. The rules do not impose them. The alternative request in paragraph 8(f) is not consent to postponement. ECF No. 103 ¶ 12, at 4.
10.	Proposed Order A and Proposed Order B are submitted with this Motion. Plaintiff relies on the existing record.

content.text: I.	ECF NO. 108 APPLIED A DISCOVERY-POSTPONEMENT RATIONALE TO JUDICIAL SCHEDULING RELIEF

runs.text: I.	ECF NO. 108 APPLIED A DISCOVERY-POSTPONEMENT RATIONALE TO JUDICIAL SCHEDULING RELIEF

content.text: ECF No. 108 denied judicial scheduling relief because the District Judge had chosen to postpone discovery. Plaintiff seeks reconsideration of that rationale as applied to the initial-conference alternative.

ECF No. 108 states its ground in one sentence: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. On that ground, it denied Plaintiff’s Motion for Entry of a Scheduling Order and, as Necessary, an Initial Pretrial Conference (ECF No. 103) without prejudice. ECF No. 108 at 2.

ECF No. 103 requested a scheduling order. ECF No. 103 ¶ 9, at 3. It separately requested that, if the complete scheduling order should await disposition of a pending matter, the Court determine whether an initial scheduling conference could proceed now to establish the remaining case-management steps. ECF No. 103 ¶ 10, at 3. This Memorandum refers to that second request as the initial-conference alternative. ECF No. 108 identified it. ECF No. 108 at 1. It denied the initial-conference request through the same discovery-postponement rationale applied to the scheduling order. It did not separately explain that application.

content.text: Rule 16(b)(1) applies “[e]xcept in categories of actions exempted by local rule.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(1). Local Civil Rule 16(A) exempts “[p]roceedings upon a defendant’s default and matters involving habeas corpus petitions, other pro se prisoner petitions, bankruptcy proceedings, condemnation cases, forfeitures, and reviews from administrative agencies.” Local Civil Rule 16(A). content.text: Rule 54(b) provides that an order “that adjudicates fewer than all the claims or the rights and liabilities of fewer than all the parties does not end the action as to any of the claims or parties and may be revised at any time before the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims and all the parties’ rights and liabilities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). ECF No. 108 denied case-management requests without prejudice. It adjudicated no claim. It is an interlocutory order within Rule 54(b).

The Fourth Circuit recognizes the authority Rule 54(b) describes. “[A] district court retains the power to reconsider and modify its interlocutory judgments, including partial summary judgments, at any time prior to final judgment when such is warranted.” Am. Canoe Ass’n v. Murphy Farms, Inc., 326 F.3d 505, 514–15 (4th Cir. 2003). Motions to reconsider interlocutory orders “are not subject to the strict standards applicable to motions for reconsideration of a final judgment.” Id. at 514.

content.text: A.	Scheduling can proceed while discovery remains regulated.

runs.text: A.	Scheduling can proceed while discovery remains regulated.

content.text: Three propositions describe the relationship between judicial scheduling and discovery. Plaintiff relies on all three.

First, judicial consultation at a scheduling conference is not itself document production, deposition testimony, or an interrogatory response. Rule 16(b)(1)(B) describes the conference as “consulting with the parties’ attorneys and any unrepresented parties at a scheduling conference.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(1)(B). Rule 16(a) states the purposes a pretrial conference serves, including “establishing early and continuing control so that the case will not be protracted because of lack of management” and “discouraging wasteful pretrial activities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(a)(2)–(3).

Second, preparatory steps can affect disclosure and discovery timing. Rule 26(f)(1) requires the parties to confer “at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due under Rule 16(b),” except “when the court orders otherwise.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(1). Rule 26(a)(1)(C) sets initial disclosures “at or within 14 days after the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference unless a different time is set by stipulation or court order.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(C). Rule 26(d)(1) restricts discovery before the parties’ conference, subject to exceptions that include a court order. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1). It does not provide that discovery proceeds after the conference regardless of court orders. Setting a scheduling conference calls for a parties’ conference. The parties’ conference carries timing consequences for disclosures and discovery unless the Court orders otherwise. Plaintiff does not contend otherwise.

Third, the Court can address those consequences expressly while deciding whether judicial scheduling should proceed. The scheduling order “may” “modify the timing of disclosures under Rules 26(a) and 26(e)(1)” and “modify the extent of discovery.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(3)(B)(i)–(ii). At any pretrial conference the Court “may consider and take appropriate action on” “controlling and scheduling discovery, including orders affecting disclosures and discovery under Rule 26 and Rules 29 through 37.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(c)(2)(F). Local Civil Rule 16(B) permits the Court to proceed by scheduling order in addition to, or in lieu of, the initial conference. A court that intends to defer discovery until the dismissal rulings can state that in the order that follows the conference, or in a direction entered before it.

A complete scheduling order and an interim case-management direction are different things. The scheduling order “must limit the time to join other parties, amend the pleadings, complete discovery, and file motions.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(3)(A). An interim direction that establishes sequencing and the next step is not a scheduling order unless it contains those limits. Plaintiff requests the complete order where it can be entered. Where it cannot, Plaintiff requests the interim direction. A decision to postpone discovery bears on the first. It bears less directly on the second. ECF No. 108 applied it to both without distinguishing them.

It sets no separate deadline for a preliminary conference. The question is the reach of the stated reasons. Read as a good-cause determination, those reasons address discovery burden and the complete schedule. Plaintiff acknowledges four points. Ballentine moves under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(a) for an order clarifying one passage of the Order signed and filed October 29, 2026 and entered October 30, 2026 (ECF No. 108), and correcting that passage only if an oversight, omission, or unintended ambiguity prevents it from expressing the determination the Court intended when it issued the Order. Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick signed ECF No. 108. This Motion is presented to him. Plaintiff does not request a different determination. Plaintiff requests that the written Order conform to the determination actually made on October 29, 2026. A Memorandum in Support under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) and a Proposed Order accompany this Motion.
I.	THE PASSAGE AND THE REQUESTED CORRECTION

runs.text: I.	THE PASSAGE AND THE REQUESTED CORRECTION

content.text: 1.	ECF No. 108 denied without prejudice Plaintiff’s Motion for Entry of a Scheduling Order and, as Necessary, an Initial Pretrial Conference (ECF No. 103) and Plaintiff’s Motion for an Order Directing Completion of the Rule 26(f) Conference and Submission of a Discovery Plan (ECF No. 105). ECF No. 108 at 1–2.

2.	ECF No. 108 states: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. The attribution immediately precedes the denial and supplies a stated premise for it.
3.	The passage identifies the District Judge as the officer who made the described choice. The passage does not identify the order, instruction, or other action on which that attribution rests.

4.	The passage describes a choice concerning “any discovery.” Page 1 of ECF No. 108 identifies four requests: entry of a scheduling order; an order directing completion of a Rule 26(f) conference and the filing of discovery plans; an initial pretrial conference; and, for any postponed step, a statement of the date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed. ECF No. 108 at 1. The Order does not state whether the attributed choice was understood to concern substantive discovery only or also the scheduling and planning steps the Order identifies.
II.	GROUNDS

5.	Plaintiff has examined the District Judge’s docketed orders and notices in this action: ECF Nos. 12, 25, 48, 50, and 70. Each addresses a subject other than the timing of discovery, the Rule 26(f) conference, or the Rule 16(b) schedule.

6.	ECF No. 84 addresses discovery timing. It states that “discovery has not officially begun in this case” and that “currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2. Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis signed ECF No. 84.

7.	The documents Plaintiff reviewed do not identify the action described in ECF No. 108. Plaintiff does not treat that absence as proof that no instruction existed. Local Civil Rule 72 recognizes assignment and referral “by an order entered in the action or on the instructions of a district judge.” An instruction need not appear in a separately entered order.

8.	Rule 60(a) permits the Court to correct “a mistake arising from oversight or omission” in an order. The Fourth Circuit reads that phrase to include an inconsistency between the text of an order and the court’s intent when it entered the order, and “an unintended ambiguity that obfuscates the court’s original intent.” Sartin v. McNair Law Firm PA, 756 F.3d 259, 265–66 (4th Cir. 2014). The power is limited by the court’s original intent. Id. at 266. Plaintiff seeks correction only if the wording fails, through a qualifying oversight, omission, or unintended ambiguity, to express that intent.
