content.text: ECF No. 108 attributes to the District Judge a choice “to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. The Order does not identify the order, instruction, or other action on which that attribution rests. The District Judge’s docketed orders and notices address other subjects. The one earlier docketed order that addresses discovery timing was signed by the previously assigned magistrate judge.

The same passage carries a second question of original meaning. Page 1 of the Order identifies four requests: a scheduling order, a Rule 26(f) conference and discovery plans, an initial pretrial conference, and a statement of the next scheduling event. ECF No. 108 at 1. Page 2 resolves them through a statement about “any discovery.” The Order does not state whether the attributed choice was understood to reach the scheduling and planning steps it identifies, or substantive discovery alone.

Plaintiff requests clarification of the action and scope the Court intended the passage to describe, and correction of the text only if a qualifying oversight, omission, or unintended ambiguity prevents the text from expressing that intent. Plaintiff seeks conformity between the words of the Order and the determination the Court made on October 29, 2026. Plaintiff does not seek a different determination.
II.	RULE 60(a) PERMITS CORRECTION OF EXPRESSION, NOT RECONSIDERATION OF AN INTENTIONAL DETERMINATION

runs.text: II.	RULE 60(a) PERMITS CORRECTION OF EXPRESSION, NOT RECONSIDERATION OF AN INTENTIONAL DETERMINATION

content.text: A.	The Rule.

Rule 60(a) provides: “The court may correct a clerical mistake or a mistake arising from oversight or omission whenever one is found in a judgment, order, or other part of the record. The court may do so on motion or on its own, with or without notice.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(a). The Rule applies to an “order.” This Motion invokes subdivision (a) alone. It does not invoke the grounds for relief from a final judgment in subdivision (b).
B.	Sartin.

The Fourth Circuit has fixed the scope of subdivision (a). “Rule 60(a) is not confined just to fixing typographical and other clerical errors.” Sartin v. McNair Law Firm PA, 756 F.3d 259, 265 (4th Cir. 2014). A mistake arising from oversight or omission “occurs when there is an inconsistency between the text of an order or judgment and the district court’s intent when it entered the order or judgment.” Id. at 265–66. The phrase “also includes an unintended ambiguity that obfuscates the court’s original intent.” Id. at 266. The power “is circumscribed by the court’s intent when it issued the order or judgment.” Id. A court may not use the Rule to change its mind about the determination it made. Id. at 265. Original intent “may be ascertained through consideration of contemporaneous documents, such as a memorandum opinion or transcript, and by the presiding judge’s own subsequent statements regarding his intent.” Id. at 266 (internal quotation marks and citation omitted). The Fourth Circuit treated the issuing judge’s subsequent explanation as reliable evidence of that intent and examined whether the contemporaneous record supported it. Id. at 266–67. The Fourth Circuit resolved the validity of an earlier Rule 60(a) clarification order while deciding the causation element of a malpractice appeal. Id. at 263–67.

C.	Chavez-Deremer.

The Fourth Circuit has also fixed the boundary. “[A] court is not authorized to use Rule 60(a) to reconsider an issue that has already been decided, or to revisit the court’s decisions already made.” Chavez-Deremer v. Medical Staffing of America, LLC, Nos. 23-2176, 23-2284, slip op. at 69 (4th Cir. July 17, 2025) (published), reported at 147 F.4th 371, 416 (citing Sartin, 756 F.3d at 265). A party may not relabel a substantive ruling as a clerical mistake to obtain further litigation of it. Id., slip op. at 69–70. The movant there sought further litigation of damages determinations the district court had already made. Id. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the denial. Id., slip op. at 70–71.

content.text: D.	The threshold applied.

The two decisions state one test. Rule 60(a) asks whether the words of the order express what the issuing court intended when it entered the order. It does not ask whether the court should have intended something else. This Motion asks the first question only.

The threshold carries an acknowledgment. An unexplained attribution is not necessarily an inadvertent one. An omitted citation does not itself establish a correctable mistake. An intentional inference is not a drafting error because it may be disputed. The Court “is not required to state findings or conclusions when ruling on a motion under Rule 12 or 56 or, unless these rules provide otherwise, on any other motion.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 52(a)(3). This Motion does not rest on an entitlement to additional reasons. If the passage accurately expresses the original determination and contains no qualifying oversight, omission, or unintended ambiguity, Rule 60(a) requires no expanded statement, and Plaintiff requests none. The Motion is directed to the possibility that the passage does not express that determination, and to the means Rule 60(a) supplies if it does not.
E.	Presentation to the issuing magistrate judge.

runs.text: V.	CLARIFICATION SHOULD IDENTIFY THE ORIGINALLY INTENDED REACH OF THE SAME PASSAGE

content.text: ECF No. 108 at 1 identifies the four requests before it: “First, Plaintiff requests entry of a scheduling order. Second, Plaintiff requests an order directing the parties to complete a Rule 26(f) conference and file respective discovery plans. Third, Plaintiff requests an initial pretrial conference. Fourth, if any of these steps are postponed, Plaintiff requests that the order state the date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed.” The underlying motions described their own scope. ECF No. 103 sought “initial case management” and disclaimed any contention that passage of the scheduling deadline “authorizes service of discovery.” ECF No. 103 ¶¶ 7–8. ECF No. 105 sought “participation and reporting” and disclaimed any request for “answers to interrogatories, production of documents.” ECF No. 105 ¶ 8.

The passage resolves those requests through a statement concerning “any discovery.” That treatment presents a question about the reach originally intended for the statement. Plaintiff does not characterize the Order as inconsistent with itself. The Order can intentionally deny scheduling and planning relief on the ground that substantive discovery has been deferred. Whether that reasoning suffices is a reconsideration or review question and is not presented here. What is presented is whether the words “any discovery” were intended to describe a decision about substantive discovery alone, or a decision that also reached entry of a scheduling order, the initial pretrial conference, the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference, and the discovery-plan report.

A related question of original operation attaches. Both motions were denied without prejudice. That disposition is not unclear. The question is whether ECF No. 108 was intended only to deny the requested orders, or also to recognize or direct a postponement of the planning steps requested in ECF No. 105. The Order identifies “resolution of the pending motions to dismiss” as the relevant event. ECF No. 108 at 2. The uncertainty concerns which steps the attributed decision was understood to cover before that event occurs.

Plaintiff asks what the Order meant. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to enter a stay, to make a good-cause finding, to decide any present deadline, to establish a resumption procedure, or to rule that planning must proceed. Any clarification describes the Order’s original operation. It does not create a new postponement.
VI.	THE LIMITED CLARIFICATION MATTERS WITHOUT DECIDING THE MERITS

runs.text: VI.	THE LIMITED CLARIFICATION MATTERS WITHOUT DECIDING THE MERITS

content.text: Accurate attribution distinguishes an order that implements a direction of the District Judge from an order that states the Magistrate Judge’s own inference or determination. Accurate scope distinguishes denial of two requested orders from an intended direction concerning the planning steps themselves. Each distinction concerns what the Order is, not whether the Order was right. Plaintiff does not contend that every party’s present obligations turn on this one sentence. Other rules and orders may bear on them. Plaintiff contends only that the sentence should say what the Court meant it to say.

This Motion does not argue that pending dismissal motions cannot support postponement. It does not address the Rule 16(b)(2) date or the sufficiency of good cause. It does not challenge the general proposition the Order quotes from another district court. ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Those matters are reconsideration or review questions and are not presented here. This Motion does not extend, and does not substitute for compliance with, the Rule 72(a) objection period applicable to ECF No. 108.
VII.	CONCLUSION AND RELIEF

Plaintiff requests entry of the accompanying Proposed Order, which (1) to the extent necessary to address a qualifying omission or unintended ambiguity, clarifies whether the passage at ECF No. 108 at 2 describes an order or instruction of the District Judge, an inference or determination by the Magistrate Judge, or another identified judicial action, and identifies any order or instruction by date and docket citation or by its operative terms; (2) clarifies how that action was understood, when ECF No. 108 issued, to relate to the scheduling order, the initial pretrial conference, the Rule 26(f) conference, and the discovery-plan report, and whether ECF No. 108 was intended only to deny the requested orders without prejudice or also to recognize or direct postponement of the planning steps requested in ECF No. 105; (3) corrects the identified passage by stating replacement language only if the existing text fails to express the determination actually intended on October 29, 2026; and (4) leaves the denial without prejudice of ECF Nos. 103 and 105 unchanged, creates no new obligation, and resolves no separately filed application.

The Order attributes a decision to the District Judge and applies it to the requests before the Court. Rule 60(a), as the Fourth Circuit construes it, permits the issuing judge to confirm that the text expresses that determination and to conform the text if it does not. Plaintiff requests that order, with the denial unchanged.

runs.text: I.	RULE 201 REQUIRES NOTICE OF A COURT RECORD WHOSE EXISTENCE AND TEXT ARE NOT SUBJECT TO REASONABLE DISPUTE

content.text: Federal Rule of Evidence 201(b)(2) permits the Court to notice a fact that “can be accurately and readily determined from sources whose accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned.” Rule 201(c)(2) provides that the Court “must take judicial notice if a party requests it and the court is supplied with the necessary information.” Rule 201(d) provides that notice may be taken “at any stage of the proceeding.” Plaintiff has requested notice. Exhibit A supplies the information.

The Fourth Circuit has stated that “[t]he most frequent use of judicial notice of ascertainable facts is in noticing the content of court records.” Colonial Penn Ins. Co. v. Coil, 887 F.2d 1236, 1239 (4th Cir. 1989) (quoting 21 C. Wright & K. Graham, Federal Practice and Procedure: Evidence § 5106, at 505 (1977)). The same opinion recognized that “federal courts, in appropriate circumstances, may take notice of proceedings in other courts, both within and without the federal judicial system, if those proceedings have a direct relation to matters at issue.” Id. (quoting St. Louis Baptist Temple, Inc. v. FDIC, 605 F.2d 1169, 1172 (10th Cir. 1979)). Colonial Penn applied those principles on appeal, to state-court guilty pleas entered after the district court’s judgment. Id. at 1239–40. A filing on a federal docket, bearing that court’s electronic filing header on every page, is a court record of the same kind.

content.text: ECF No. 152 is pleaded in the proposed Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint. ECF No. 59-1 ¶¶ 164–169. Paragraph 165 quotes the portion of footnote 3 that describes this action. The Court’s ability to compare the pleaded quotation with the source record serves the determination of those motions.

Meta and NCMEC have invoked the same mechanism in this action. Meta’s memorandum states that, on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, a court may consider “matters of which the court may take judicial notice.” ECF No. 22 at 8 (citations and internal quotation marks omitted).  3          This case arises out of Meta Platforms, Inc.’s (“Meta”) policy against “Child Sexual

15   III.    LEGAL STANDARD
16           To survive a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), a complaint must include “sufficient
17   factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Nayab v.
18   Cap. One Bank (USA), N.A., 942 F.3d 480, 495–96 (9th Cir. 2019) (quoting Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556
19   U.S. 662, 678 (2009)). “The plausibility standard … asks for more than a sheer possibility that a
20   defendant has acted unlawfully.” Id. at 496. Although well-pleaded factual allegations are assumed
21   to be true, “the court is not required to accept as true allegations that are merely conclusory,
22   unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.” Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.,
23   899 F.3d 988, 1008 (9th Cir. 2018) (citation modified). And while pro se pleadings are construed
24   “liberally,” a pro se plaintiff must still allege “factual matter” sufficient “to state a claim to relief
25   that is plausible on its face.” Johnson v. Lucent Techs., Inc., 653 F.3d 1000, 1010–11 (9th Cir.
26   2011) (citation omitted). Where an amended complaint “omits previously-pled material information
27   that harms Plaintiff’s case,” the Court may consider the prior pleadings because the allegations are
28   “appropriately characterized as judicial admissions.” Jackson v. Loews Hotels, Inc., No. ED CV

 5   IV.    ARGUMENT
 6          Plaintiff’s claim fails as a matter of law. First and foremost, Plaintiff’s claim is barred by
 7   Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act because it seeks to hold Defendants liable for a
 8   protected publication decision. Plaintiff cannot circumvent that bar by conspicuously replacing his
 9   allegations from prior complaints regarding the disablement of his Facebook account with vague
10   allegations that Defendants interrupted his ability to perform third-party contracts. Further,
11   Plaintiff’s claim also fails for the independent reason that he does not plead any facts that plausibly
12   support his assertion that Defendants acted because of his race, as Section 1981 requires. And the
13   SAC fails as to each of the Vendor Defendants because it improperly asserts claims against the
14   Vendor Defendants collectively, without specifying which of the Vendor Defendants were
15   responsible for the specific acts alleged in the SAC. The Court should dismiss Plaintiff’s claim with
16   prejudice.
17          A.      Plaintiff’s Claims Against Each Defendant Are Barred By Section 230
18          Plaintiff’s SAC fails because it is barred in its entirety by Section 230(c)(1) of the
19   Communications Decency Act (“CDA”), 47 U.S.C. § 230. Section 230(c)(1) states that “[n]o
20   provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of
21   any information provided by another information content provider.” 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1). Section
22   230(e)(3) further states that “[n]o cause of action may be brought and no liability may be imposed
23   under any State or local law that is inconsistent with this section.” 47 U.S.C. § 230(e)(3). The Ninth
24   Circuit has accordingly held that, under Section 230(c)(1), an interactive computer service provider
25   or user cannot be held liable for removing content published on its services by a third party. See
26   Fair Hous. Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommates.com, LLC, 521 F.3d 1157, 1170–71 (9th
27   Cir. 2008) (“[A]ny activity that can be boiled down to deciding whether to exclude material that
28   third parties seek to post online is perforce immune under section 230.”). And where it is apparent

 2   e.g., SAC ¶ 79 (alleging that Plaintiff used his Facebook account to “source[ ] … customers and
 3   leads”); see also FAC ¶ 53 (“Plaintiff began marketing his RV repair business on Facebook.”).
 4   Here, Plaintiff’s claims all stem from the alleged disablement of his Facebook account, and he does
 5   not allege any Defendant played any role in developing the content posted via that Facebook
 6   account. The second Section 230 requirement is satisfied.
                   3.     The SAC Seeks to Hold Each Defendant Liable for Its Purported
 7
                          Exercise of a Publisher’s Traditional Editorial Function
 8          Section 230(c)(1)’s final requirement is met because Plaintiff’s allegations seek to treat
 9   Defendants as a “publisher” of third-party content. Under Section 230(c)(1), a claim treats a
10   defendant as a “publisher” if it seeks to hold the defendant liable for its purported exercise of
11   traditional “editorial functions”—such as deciding “whether to publish, withdraw, postpone or alter
12   content created by third parties.” Murphy v. Twitter, Inc., 60 Cal. App. 5th 12, 17 (2021). “[A]ny
13   activity that can be boiled down to deciding whether to exclude material that third parties seek to
14   post online is perforce immune under section 230.” Fair Hous. Council, 521 F.3d at 1170–71. What
15   matters here is not the “name of the cause of action,” but “whether the duty that the plaintiff alleges
16   the defendant violated derives from the defendant’s status or conduct as a ‘publisher or speaker.’ If
17   it does, [S]ection 230(c)(1) precludes liability.” See Barnes v. Yahoo!, Inc., 570 F.3d 1096, 1101–
18   02 (9th Cir. 2009); Sikhs for Just. “SFJ”, Inc. v. Facebook, Inc., 144 F. Supp. 3d 1088, 1095 (N.D.
19   Cal. 2015) (holding that “removing content is something publishers do” and that Section 230 barred
20   a discrimination claim) (citation omitted), aff’d 697 F. App’x 526 (9th Cir. 2017).
21          Here, all of Plaintiff’s claims arise out of the alleged disablement of Plaintiff’s Facebook
22   account, which is “precisely the kind of activity for which [S]ection 230 was meant to provide
23   immunity.” Fair Hous. Council, 521 F.3d at 1170 (footnote omitted). Courts in this district and
24   beyond have routinely dismissed claims, such as those here, premised on a defendant’s decision to
25   suspend or terminate a user’s account, restricting their ability to post or otherwise access their
26   account. See, e.g., King v. Facebook, Inc., 572 F. Supp. 3d 776, 795 (N.D. Cal. 2021) (holding that
27   “Facebook has CDA immunity … to the extent that [plaintiff’s] claim is based on Facebook’s
28   disabling of [plaintiff’s] account”); Castronuova, 2025 WL 1914860, at *4 (holding that complaint
                                                                   DEFS’ MOT. TO DISMISS SECOND AM. COMPL.
                                                       9                              NO. 3:26-CV-5939-RFL

Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL         Document 152         Filed 08/13/26        Page 18 of 25



 1   based    on   defendants     alleged   “decisions     to   remove    or     exclude,   including   by
 2   suspending … plaintiff’s accounts” for politically discriminatory reasons was barred by Section
 3   230); Elansari v. Meta, Inc., No. 22-3060, 2024 WL 163080, at *1–2 (3d Cir. Jan. 16, 2024)
 4   (recognizing that Section 230 bars claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 alleging that Meta disabled
 5   accounts for racially discriminatory reasons).
 6           Accordingly, all three requirements of Section 230 are met, and Plaintiff’s claim should be
 7   dismissed in its entirety with prejudice.
 8           B.     Plaintiff Cannot Plead Around Section 230 in His SAC by Omitting Material
 9                  Allegations from the FAC
             The Court should consider Plaintiff’s allegations in the FAC in construing the allegations
10
     in the SAC. In an apparent attempt to creatively plead around the application of Section 230 to bar
11
     his claim, the SAC omits several material allegations necessary to understand Plaintiff’s factual
12
     allegations. In particular, the SAC bases Plaintiff’s entire case on (1) a “Notice” he allegedly
13
     received from Meta on July 4, 2022, which purportedly interrupted his ability to perform third-
14
     party contracts through Facebook; and (2) a Vendor Defendant’s alleged decision to uphold the
15
     Notice on appeal. But the SAC is silent on the content of the alleged Notice, and for obvious
16
     reasons. The FAC clearly alleges that the Notice informed Plaintiff that Meta had disabled his
17
     account for violating Meta’s CSE policy and, when Plaintiff tried to appeal the account
18
     disablement, an unnamed Vendor Defendant upheld it. FAC ¶¶ 54–57. Because claims based on
19
     such account disablement decisions are squarely barred by Section 230, each Defendant moved to
20
     dismiss the FAC in its entirety under Section 230. Plaintiff responded by trying to excise all
21
     references to the account disablement and Meta’s CSE policy from his SAC. But removing
22
     allegations from an amended complaint does not “simply erase those allegations from the case[,]”
23
     and the court “may consider” Plaintiff’s original “allegations as part of its context-specific inquiry
24
     into whether the [SAC] plausibly suggests an entitlement to relief . . . .” In re YogaWorks, Inc. Sec.
25
     Litig., No. CV 18-10696, 2020 WL 2549290, at *3 (C.D. Cal., Apr. 23, 2020) (citation modified);
26
     see also Cole, 2010 WL 532428, at *4 (same).
27
             Similarly, whereas the FAC plainly alleged that Plaintiff “market[ed] his RV repair business
28

                                                      10                              NO. 3:26-CV-5939-RFL

Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL         Document 152         Filed 08/13/26      Page 19 of 25



 1   on Facebook” (FAC ¶ 53), the SAC now omits any reference to content posted by Plaintiff through
 2   his Facebook account, instead referring to the Facebook account only as “the instrument through
 3   which Plaintiff performed [] third-party contracts.” SAC ¶ 30. Again, this omission is a blatant
 4   attempt to evade the application of Section 230, which, as set forth above, applies when the
 5   plaintiff’s claims treat the defendant as the publisher or speaker of content that the defendant itself
 6   did not provide.
 7          As a result of these omissions, the SAC, if considered alone, presents an incomplete and
 8   confusing picture of Plaintiff’s factual allegations and obscures Plaintiff’s allegations that his
 9   Facebook account was disabled and that he advertised his business on his Facebook account.
10   Because the SAC omits key factual allegations necessary to understand Plaintiff’s claims, and does
11   not explain the omissions or contradict those prior allegations, the Court should consider the FAC’s
12   factual allegations to properly evaluate Plaintiff’s allegations and claim in the SAC. See, e.g., J.
13   Edwards Jewelry Distrib., LLC v. Wells Fargo & Co., No. 18-cv-03886, 2019 WL 2329248, at *4
14   (N.D. Cal. May 31, 2019) (holding that the “fact that Plaintiff has now eliminated these allegations
15   and this exhibit from its SAC does not impact the Court’s analysis” because the “‘Court does not
16   ignore the prior allegations in determining the plausibility of current pleadings.’” (quoting
17   Stanislaus Food Prods., Co. v. USS-POSCO Indus., 782 F. Supp. 2d 1059, 1075 (E.D. Cal. 2011))).
18          Plaintiff’s attempt to creatively plead around Section 230 in his SAC by omitting prior
19   allegations about the advertising content posted on his Facebook account and by framing the alleged
20   disablement of his Facebook account simply as the sending of a “Notice” that interrupted his ability
21   to perform contracts and access his account-resident property therefore does not change the
22   outcome. See Lee v. Fin. Recovery Servs., No. 5:24-cv-00861, 2024 WL 5439275, at *2 (C.D. Cal.
23   Nov. 14, 2024) (noting that plaintiff “cannot … avoid dismissal simply by eliminating
24   allegations … especially where she fails to explain why she decided to omit such adverse facts in
25   the amended complaint”). No matter how Plaintiff frames his allegations, at bottom, Plaintiff’s
26   claim is premised on Meta’s alleged decision to disable Plaintiff’s Facebook account and an
27

28

Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL         Document 152         Filed 08/13/26      Page 20 of 25



 1   unnamed Vendor Defendant’s decision to uphold that disablement.6 Courts have rejected similar
 2   attempts to “circumvent the CDA’s protections through ‘creative’ pleading.” Kimzey v. Yelp! Inc.,
 3   836 F.3d 1263, 1265–66 (9th Cir. 2016) (affirming dismissal of complaint under Section 230,
 4   rejecting plaintiff’s “artful skirting” of Section 230 based on plaintiff’s “apparent[] hope[] to plead
 5   around the CDA to advance the same basic argument that the statute plainly bars”); see also Barnes,
 6   570 F.3d at 1102 (noting that, for purposes of Section 230 immunity, “what matters is whether the
 7   cause of action inherently requires the court to treat the defendant as the ‘publisher or speaker’ of
 8   content provided by another”).
 9          C.      Plaintiff Fails to State a Claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1981
10          Even beyond the deficiencies described above, Plaintiff’s claim still fails as a matter of law.
11   To state a claim under § 1981, a plaintiff must “allege (1) he is a member of a protected class, (2)
12   he attempted to contract for certain services, and (3) he was denied … the right to make or enforce
13   a contract.” Knight v. Wells Fargo Bank N.A., 459 F. Supp. 3d 1288, 1291 (N.D. Cal. 2019).
14   “Because claims brought under § 1981 are grounded in the Equal Protection Clause of the
15   Fourteenth Amendment, an ‘essential element’ of a valid § 1981 action is that the defendant ‘acted
16   with the intent to discriminate on the basis of race.’” Floyd v. Saber Fitness Hegenberger, LLC,
17   No. 24-cv-01278, 2024 WL 2971669, at *7 (N.D. Cal. June 11, 2024) (emphasis omitted) (quoting
18   McKenzie v. City of Milpitas, 738 F. Supp. 1293, 1301 (N.D. Cal. 1990)). “Thus, to establish a
19   claim under § 1981, the plaintiff must show overt acts by the defendant, ‘coupled with some direct
20   evidence that the defendant’s conduct was motivated by racial animus.’” Id. (citation omitted).
21   “Mere conclusory allegations of intentional discrimination will not suffice.” Gray v. Apple Inc.,
22   No.16-cv-04421, 2017 WL 1709327, at *3 (N.D. Cal. May 3, 2017) (citation omitted).
23          Plaintiff fails to sufficiently plead a § 1981 claim because he does not plead any facts that
24   plausibly support his assertion that Meta disabled his Facebook account or that any of the Vendor
25   Defendants upheld the disablement because of his race. To the contrary, the SAC’s assertion that
     6
26     Even if the Court does not interpret the SAC’s vague allegations of a Notice that interrupted
     Plaintiff’s ability to perform contracts against the backdrop of the SAC, which makes clear Plaintiff
27   is referring to Meta’s disablement of his Facebook account, other allegations in the SAC clarify
     that this is what Plaintiff is referring to. For example, the purported “Comparator” allegations show
28   that underlying conduct involved alleged account suspensions and “return[s] to account access.”
     SAC ¶¶ 61-62.

                                                       12                             NO. 3:26-CV-5939-RFL

Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL         Document 152        Filed 08/13/26      Page 21 of 25



 1   Defendants’ alleged actions were racially motivated is based solely on the SAC’s allegations that
 2   (i) when a reviewer from one of the Vendor Defendants adversely decided Plaintiff’s appeal, the
 3   reviewer was potentially able to see Plaintiff’s profile picture and his government-issued
 4   identification, see SAC ¶ 84, and (ii) Meta restored accounts for a handful of “[w]hite [Facebook]
 5   account-holders” who allegedly received similar notices. Id. ¶ 82.7
 6          But the mere fact that a Vendor Defendant (or Meta) had access to Plaintiff’s photos and
 7   thus arguably had constructive notice that Plaintiff is Black does nothing to establish that any
 8   Defendant was motivated by race when Meta allegedly disabled Plaintiff’s Facebook account
 9   pursuant to its CSE policy and a Vendor Defendant allegedly upheld the disablement on appeal.
10   See Mir v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., No. 2:19-cv-03960, 2019 WL 8355841, at *2 (C.D. Cal.
11   Sept. 19, 2019) (“Mere knowledge of Plaintiff’s ethnicity coupled with a conclusory assertion of
12   discriminatory animus for Defendant’s action does not create a plausible inference necessary” for
13   § 1981 claim “to survive a 12(b)(6) motion”); Austin v. ABC Legal, No. 21-cv-09076, 2022 WL
14   1606293, at *1, 3 (N.D. Cal. May 20, 2022) (dismissing § 1981 claim because allegations that
15   defendant “knew plaintiff was a black man due to … Pictures (for ID verification) … and via self-
16   identification” were insufficient to show discriminatory intent).
17          Similarly, Plaintiff’s allegation that—out of over 105.9 million CSE actions and over 8,100
18   reversals,8 FAC ¶¶ 94, 97—there exist a handful of white users whose Facebook accounts were
19   restored after being flagged under the same CSE policy does not raise a plausible inference of any
20   type of discrimination, much less the intentional discrimination that Section 1981 claims require.
21
     7
       Elsewhere in his SAC, Plaintiff attempts to fault several of the Defendants for affirmatively
22   evaluating their practices and tools for potential racial disparities. See SAC ¶¶ 71-76. For example,
     Plaintiff alleges that Meta commissioned an external Civil Rights Audit and conducted internal
23   research where the results allegedly suggested “concerns regarding algorithmic bias in Meta’s
     enforcement systems” and “racial disparities in enforcement outcomes. Id. ¶¶ 72-74. Similarly, the
24   SAC alleges that Accenture’s “public Responsible AI position has acknowledged that algorithmic
     review” could “produce[] differential error rates by race.” Id. ¶ 71. At most, these allegations show
25   that Defendants were actively trying to detect and address potential racial disparities.
     8
26     The FAC’s allegations regarding the total number of CSE actions and reversals illustrated that a
     sample set of five alleged reversals is wholly inadequate to plausibly suggest a pattern. Because
27   these now-omitted allegations harmed Plaintiff’s claim, the Court may consider them in deciding
     the present motion. See, e.g., Cole, 2010 WL 532428, at *4. Even without this background,
28   however, Plaintiff’s alleged comparator set is too small and lacking in details to support an
     inference of racial discrimination, as set forth herein.

 1   See SAC ¶¶ 59–63 (identifying five white Facebook users whose accounts were allegedly restored
 2   following appeal); see also Gray, 2017 WL 1709327, at *3 (holding that allegations that “a white
 3   customer” successfully completed the same transaction Plaintiff attempted “during the same time”
 4   did not suffice to support a § 1981 claim); Davis v. Valon Mortg. Inc., No. CV-22-01510, 2023 WL
 5   4661789, at *2–3 (D. Ariz. July 20, 2023) (holding plaintiff failed to sufficiently plead race
 6   discrimination where he was allegedly required to interview for a lateral position and a white
 7   woman was not).
 8          Moreover, Plaintiff fails to allege any details about the alleged identified comparators which
 9   would allow “the court [to] reasonably infer that racial animus accounts for the difference in
10   treatment.” Snoqualmie Indian Tribe v. City of Snoqualmie, 186 F. Supp. 3d 1155, 1163 (W.D.
11   Wash. 2016) (citation modified). Here, Plaintiff does not allege any details about the content posted
12   on his Facebook account, nor does he include any allegations demonstrating that the alleged
13   comparators are similarly situated to him in any respect. Indeed, the SAC does not even allege that
14   the “account-level notices” received by the five alleged comparator accounts concerned the same
15   subject matter as Plaintiff’s “Notice,” because the SAC fails to allege the content of any of the
16   alleged notices. Compare SAC ¶ 58 (alleging that “Meta has returned white Facebook account-
17   holders to third-party contracting capacity following account-level notices arising from identified
18   factual predicates”) with FAC ¶ 69 (alleging that the same identified five comparator accounts “was
19   enforced within Meta’s sexual content and [CSE] enforcement family”). And, if the Court considers
20   the FAC’s more detailed allegations regarding the alleged comparators, those allegations suggest
21   that the purported comparators are not, in fact, similarly situated.9
22          Because Plaintiff has failed to plead any facts supporting a plausible inference that any
23   Defendant intentionally discriminated against him, his § 1981 claims must be dismissed. See Ray
24   v. Am. Airlines, Inc, 755 F. Supp. 3d 1277, 1281 (C.D. Cal. 2024) (dismissing claims because “[t]he
25   mere intersection of plaintiff’s race and his alleged mistreatment by a defendant … is not enough
26   to nudge plaintiff’s claim of racial discrimination across the line from conceivable to plausible”
     9
27     See, e.g., FAC ¶¶ 69–70 (alleging that comparator account named “Steven Ertelt” is an
     “Organization/Business account” that was “flagged under the CSE policy for a medical C-section
28   video”); id. ¶ 69 (table) (identifying alleged comparator “COMP-1” as an individual account, while
     identifying Plaintiff’s account as a “Business Owner” page).

 1   (citation modified)); Gueye v. Wells Fargo Bank, No. 3:22-cv-08904, 2024 WL 1024740, at *3–4
 2   (N.D. Cal. Mar. 7, 2024) (dismissing pro se plaintiff’s Section 1981 claim for lack of but-for
 3   causation because his allegation that defendants “star[ed] down at him” did not support his
 4   conclusion that he had “been subjected to racial profiling, racial slurs, derogatory comments,
 5   suspicion, unequal treatment and humiliation”).
 6          D.      Plaintiff’s Allegations Improperly Group the Vendor Defendants Together
 7          Finally, the SAC fails as to each of the Vendor Defendants because it improperly asserts
 8   claims against the Vendor Defendants collectively, without specifying which of the Vendor
 9   Defendants were responsible for the specific acts alleged in the SAC. See TEEC Angel Mgmt, LLC
10   v. Tsingyuan Ventures LLC, No. 24-cv-08991, 2026 WL 1660035, at *1–2 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 27 2026)
11   (dismissing complaint based on finding that “Plaintiffs engage[d] in improper group pleading”
12   where plaintiff referred to defendants “collectively without attributing conduct to any particular
13   Defendant” or otherwise “distinguishing what each entity did”); Beluca Ventures LLC v.
14   Aktiebolag, 622 F. Supp. 3d 806, 816 (N.D. Cal. 2022) (holding that “the Complaint improperly
15   engages in undifferentiated pleading that fails to make clear what allegations are being made
16   against” each defendant where “[a]lmost all of the allegations in the Complaint are made against”
17   one entity, defined to include all the defendants). Here, although the SAC asserts the Section 1981
18   claim against all the Vendor Defendants, it fails to clearly specify which Vendor Defendant that
19   Plaintiff alleges reviewed his Facebook account, or whether Plaintiff is merely guessing that one
20   of the Vendor Defendants reviewed the Facebook account. See SAC ¶¶ 84, 86 (alleging that a
21   “Codefendant,” defined to include Accenture, Genpact and TaskUs, “decided Plaintiff’s appeal”
22   and “but for Plaintiff’s race, the Codefendant would not have decided Plaintiff’s appeal adversely”);
23   see also Beatport LLC v. SoundCloud, Ltd., No. CV 19-847, 2020 WL 3977602, at *5 (C.D. Cal.
24   July 13, 2020) (“It is a basic pleading defect for a complaint to ‘lump’ parties together and to fail
25   to distinguish between named defendants.” (citation omitted)). Accordingly, Plaintiff’s Section
26   1981 claim against the Vendor Defendants is independently subject to dismissal for failure to allege
27   specific conduct as to each Vendor Defendant.
28

 1           E.        Plaintiff Should Not Be Granted Leave to Amend
 2           Leave to amend is inappropriate where amendment would be futile. See Chinatown
 3   Neighborhood Ass’n v. Harris, 794 F.3d 1136, 1144 (9th Cir. 2015). Plaintiff has already amended
 4   his Complaint twice in the instant action, and has filed more than ten complaints overall against
 5   some combination of the Defendants in various actions arising out of the parties’ dispute. See Dkt
 6   No. 148 at 5. Despite all of Plaintiff’s attempts, none of his complaints has successfully stated any
 7   claim against any defendant, as demonstrated by Defendants’ prior motions to dismiss. Thus, any
 8   additional attempt will be futile, including because Plaintiff is challenging the alleged decision to
 9   disable his Facebook account and so his claims will be barred by Section 230(c)(1) no matter what
10   additional facts he pleads. See, e.g., Reaud v. Facebook, Inc., No. 23-cv-06329, 2024 WL 4126066,
11   at *5 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 9, 2024) (denying leave to amend where plaintiff could not “allege additional
12   plausible facts to escape Section 230”).
13      V.        CONCLUSION
14           For the foregoing reasons, Defendants respectfully request that the Court dismiss the SAC
15   with prejudice.

content.text: Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) for leave to file the Notice of Subsequent Record Development attached as Exhibit A. A Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion.
I.	GROUNDS
1.	Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) provides that “[n]o further briefs or written communications may be filed without first obtaining leave of Court.”

2.	ECF No. 93 (Motion for Targeted Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84, Withdrawal or Modification of the Magistrate-Judge Referral, and Related Interim Relief) and ECF Nos. 97–99 (Rule 72(a) Objections to ECF No. 96 and related requests) are pending before the District Judge. Plaintiff’s consolidated reply in support of ECF Nos. 90 and 93 was filed October 28, 2026. ECF No. 102.

content.text: INTRODUCTION

THE COMPLAINT SAYS “ONE MAN, WITHOUT A LAWYER.”
THE COURT’S FIRST ORDER SAYS “HER.”

runs.text:
THE COMPLAINT SAYS “ONE MAN, WITHOUT A LAWYER.”
THE COURT’S FIRST ORDER SAYS “HER.”

content.text: On August 6, 2026, Plaintiff filed his First Amended Complaint, ECF No. 5. That pleading contains fifty-one masculine references to Plaintiff: forty-two masculine pronouns, four references to “man,” three references to “Mr. Ballentine,” and one reference each to “father” and “husband.” The identification begins in the opening paragraphs. Paragraph 2 refers to “a man’s name.” Paragraph 3 identifies Plaintiff as “one man, without a lawyer.” Paragraphs 4 and 6 repeat the reference to a man. ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 2–4, 6. On the same day, Plaintiff filed his Motion for Partial Summary Judgment, ECF No. 6, and supporting memorandum, ECF No. 7. The motion’s two references to “her” concern Defendant Katie Hall, not Plaintiff. The accompanying memorandum separately describes Plaintiff as the person who provided advance notice of subpoenas “he intended to serve.” ECF No. 7 at 1. Six days later, District Judge Alston entered ECF No. 12, stating that Plaintiff filed “her Amended Complaint” and “her Motion for Partial Summary Judgment,” and directing the Clerk to provide the order to Plaintiff at “her last known address.” ECF No. 12 at 1. The Court thus referred to Plaintiff as female three times in its first order adjudicating his motion, notwithstanding the contrary identifying information in the operative pleading and accompanying memorandum. The order denied the motion as premature before any Defendant had opposed it. The discrepancy raises a question apparent from the documents themselves: whether the identifying information expressly provided in the materials before the Court was consulted or verified before the order issued.

Plaintiff has testified that he did not use his full legal name to operate any Meta account he used. NCMEC’s April 22, 2026 letters associated that name, an alternate name, and an email identifier, joined by “and/or,” with two CyberTipline reports. Neither letter identifies which identifier appeared in either underlying report. NCMEC knows which. He does not. On April 22, 2026, NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel typed the name onto NCMEC letterhead directly after the words “two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning” and mailed it to him twice. The CyberTipline exists to catch people who hurt children. There is no reader in this country who does not know what those words mean next to a man’s name. For six months he has tried to ask one question: is his name in those reports?

He first tried in May, in this courthouse, in a case he brought over the letters. He served no discovery. He filed no discovery motion. He did what Rule 26 asks of every party and proposed a planning conference. NCMEC went to the Court and asked that there be no discovery at all, because information provided in discovery “could give rise to further litigation from Mr. Ballentine.” The Court stayed discovery two days later. When he brought this action, NCMEC’s counsel wrote in August that if he so much as requested a meet-and-confer, counsel would move for a stay. He asked three yes-or-no questions instead. NCMEC answered that he “simply cannot possibly know.” The Court said discovery had not begun. He asked for discovery to begin. The Court said it must wait for the motions to dismiss, the same motions that say he cannot know. The stay motion NCMEC promised was never filed. It was never needed.

The magistrate judge who said discovery had not begun, and who denied the amendment, had, according to his own financial disclosures, reported Meta common stock through the end of last year. Mr. Ballentine asked him to say on the record whether he still held it when he ruled, and whether the law permitted him to rule at all. He never answered. Instead the case was reassigned, by a process that appears nowhere on the docket and was never explained to the plaintiff, and the judge whose interest was in question signed the order declaring the question moot. The new magistrate judge’s first act in the case was to deny a scheduling order and relieve every defendant of the Rule 26(f) conference the rules require of them, before any defendant had moved for it. In two cases and six months, every door closed before a defendant had to push on it. The question of whose name is in the reports has still not been answered by anyone.
ARGUMENT
I.	LEAVE IS REQUIRED, AND THE COURT HAS AUTHORITY TO GRANT IT.

runs.text: I.	LEAVE IS REQUIRED, AND THE COURT HAS AUTHORITY TO GRANT IT.

content.text: Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) permits no further briefs or written communications without leave of Court. Exhibit A is a written communication to the Court that is not a brief on a pending motion. Plaintiff therefore asks for leave. The Court’s authority to receive a record document on its own docket is not in question. The only question is whether Exhibit A serves a purpose the Rules recognize. It does.

Rule 72(a) provides that a party “may not assign as error a defect in the order not timely objected to.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a). Objections to ECF Nos. 63, 64, 65, 84, and 96 are on file. ECF Nos. 66, 89, 97. Each remains undecided. Exhibit A places those orders, the objections to them, the rule each objection invokes, and the consequence of each in one chronology. On any appeal, the record consists of the papers and exhibits filed in this Court. Fed. R. App. P. 10(a)(1). A document that collects the preserved objections in sequence is a record document in the ordinary sense.
II.	ONE DOCUMENT SERVES THE COURT BETTER THAN NINE.

runs.text: II.	ONE DOCUMENT SERVES THE COURT BETTER THAN NINE.

content.text: On October 30, 2026, nine of Plaintiff’s motions and objections were pending with no disposition on the docket. Exhibit A, Part XI. The orders they address were entered by two magistrate judges across seven weeks. Exhibit A, Part II. The District Judge, in deciding the objections, and any reviewing court, in deciding an appeal, would otherwise reconstruct the sequence from more than one hundred docket entries and three separate objection packages. Exhibit A does that work once. Every quotation in it is reproduced from the docketed document cited, with a page citation, so that each entry can be checked against the docket in a minute. Declaration ¶ 3.
III.	NO DEFENDANT IS PREJUDICED.

Exhibit A requests no relief. It adds no ground to any pending objection or motion. It renews no argument. It moves no deadline and requires no response. A Defendant who disputes any entry in it may say so in one page. Leave to file costs the Defendants nothing, and denial of leave would leave the District Judge to assemble the same chronology without it.
CONCLUSION
Plaintiff requests that the Court grant leave to file Exhibit A and direct the Clerk to docket it as a separate entry.
Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,
Marvelle J. Ballentine
Plaintiff, pro se
1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847
Alexandria, Virginia 22307
jayballentine@protonmail.com

content.text: PLAINTIFF’S CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF PROCEDURAL IRREGULARITIES AND JUDICIAL ACTIONS

runs.text: PLAINTIFF’S CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF PROCEDURAL IRREGULARITIES AND JUDICIAL ACTIONS

content.text: Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine submits this Statement. The Statement places the Court’s orders, the Clerk’s entries, the submissions those orders addressed, and the dispositions that followed in one chronology. The Statement runs through October 30, 2026, the date ECF No. 108 was entered. The Statement requests no relief.
I.	SCOPE, SOURCES, AND METHOD

1.	The sources of this Statement are the docket of this action, the orders and notices entered on it, and the filings cited by ECF number. Quoted language is reproduced from the docketed document. Page citations refer to the pages of the cited docketed document. Entries that carry no ECF number are identified by date and subject.

2.	This Statement uses two defined terms. A “judicial action” is an order, notice, or docket entry made by the Court or by the Clerk. A “procedural irregularity” is a judicial action for which the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, the Local Civil Rules of this Court, and the orders on the docket supply no stated authority, or a judicial action taken outside a deadline or requirement those sources state. The Statement also identifies discrepancies between judicial descriptions of the record and the filings to which those descriptions refer. Such discrepancies are documented as record-accuracy issues, whether or not they independently constitute violations of a procedural rule. Each sequence below identifies the governing rule and states what the rule provides. Where the rule supplies no authority for the action, the Statement says so. Where the rule supplies authority, the Statement says that instead.

3.	Each sequence is presented in a fixed order: the judicial action, with its date, ECF number, and operative language; the procedural context, meaning what was pending and what the applicable rule or order required; the subsequent action, meaning what Plaintiff filed or what the Court did next; and the procedural consequence.

4.	Part II is a ledger of every judicial action entered through October 30, 2026. Parts III through IX present seven sequences drawn from that ledger. Part X states the aggregate record in numbers. Part XI lists the matters pending on October 30, 2026.
II.	LEDGER OF JUDICIAL ACTIONS

content.text: 7.	On August 6, 2026, Plaintiff filed his First Amended Complaint, ECF No. 5. The pleading contains fifty-one masculine references to Plaintiff, comprising thirty uses of “his,” six of “he,” four of “him,” two of “himself,” four of “man,” three of “Mr. Ballentine,” and one each of “father” and “husband.” These references include quotations reproduced in the pleading. The identification appears at the beginning: paragraph 2 refers to “a man’s name”; paragraph 3 states “I was the plaintiff — one man, without a lawyer”; paragraph 4 refers to “everything a man would need to test it”; and paragraph 6 refers to “what that name does to a man.” ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 2–4, 6. Subsequent factual allegations repeatedly refer to Plaintiff using “he,” “him,” and “his,” including the allegations concerning Plaintiff’s prospective testimony, account history, and alleged injuries. ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 31, 33, 41, 43, 159–160, 163, 170, 172, 174–175, 178, 180, 227–228, 231, 239.

8.	On the same date, August 6, 2026, Plaintiff filed his Motion for Partial Summary Judgment under Rule 56(a), with an alternative request under Rule 56(g), concerning whether Defendant Katie Hall acted as NCMEC’s agent and within the scope of her employment when issuing the two April 22, 2026 letters. ECF No. 6. The motion contains two uses of the feminine pronoun “her,” both referring to Defendant Hall’s employment, and none referring to Plaintiff. Its supporting memorandum expressly describes Plaintiff as having provided advance notice of subpoenas “he intended to serve.” ECF No. 7 at 1. The memorandum, a declaration, and eight exhibits accompanied the motion. ECF No. 7. The Clerk docketed the motion on August 7, 2026.

It further directs the Clerk to provide a copy “to pro se Plaintiff at her last known address.” ECF No. 12 at 1. Those are three feminine references to Plaintiff, notwithstanding the fifty-one masculine references in the operative complaint and the additional masculine reference in the memorandum supporting the motion under consideration. The order states that Defendants’ responses to the original Complaint “are not due until August 21, 2026,” concludes that the motion “is premature,” and denies it “without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time.” Id.

content.text: 10.	Local Civil Rule 56(A) displaces the timing provisions of Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(b) in this District. Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) ordinarily provides fourteen calendar days for an opposing brief unless otherwise directed by the Court. ECF No. 12 issued six days after Plaintiff filed his motion and five days after the Clerk docketed it. No Defendant had filed an opposition. NCMEC’s motion to dismiss was docketed the same day as the order. ECF Nos. 10–12. On August 12, 2026, Plaintiff submitted a notice setting the motion for hearing on September 18, 2026. The Clerk docketed the notice on August 13. ECF No. 13. On August 17, 2026, the Clerk entered a notice stating that “the hearing will not be set pursuant the Order entered on 8/12/2026 denying on the Motion.” Unnumbered entry of August 17, 2026.

11.	The first order adjudicating Plaintiff’s motion referred to him as female three times despite fifty-one masculine references in the operative complaint and one in the supporting memorandum. Four references to “man” appeared within the complaint’s first six paragraphs, including Plaintiff’s express self-identification in paragraph 3. The inconsistency was not confined to an incidental passage of the order: it appeared both in the description of the filings under review and in the directive for service. The order does not establish what materials were personally reviewed before its entry. The documented discrepancy permits a reasonable observer to question whether the complaint’s opening identification of Plaintiff was consulted or verified. The Court resolved the motion on procedural timing before opposition, did not reach the agency-and-scope issue, and specified neither a date nor a triggering event for renewal. ECF No. 12 at 1.

At this time, the Court cannot issue an order concerning Plaintiff’s Motions because discovery has not officially begun in this case. Pursuant to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, discovery officially begins when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order and currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2.

Rule 26(d)(1) provides: “A party may not seek discovery from any source before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f), except in a proceeding exempted from initial disclosure under Rule 26(a)(1)(B), or when authorized by these rules, by stipulation, or by court order.” The rule authorizes discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference “by court order.” Each motion asked for that order. ECF Nos. 15, 54. The order states that the Court “cannot issue an order” because discovery had not begun. ECF No. 84 at 1. The rule’s text supplies the authority the order states the Court lacked. The order cites no provision of the Federal Rules for the proposition that discovery “officially begins when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2.

Rule 16(b)(2) provides: “The judge must issue the scheduling order as soon as practicable, but unless the judge finds good cause for delay, the judge must issue it within the earlier of 90 days after any defendant has been served with the complaint or 60 days after any defendant has appeared.” Local Civil Rule 16(B) provides that “not later than sixty (60) days from first appearance or ninety (90) days after service of the complaint, the Court shall enter an order fixing the cut-off dates for the respective parties to complete the processes of discovery, the date for a final pretrial conference and, whenever practicable, the trial date.”

content.text: 39.	On October 13, 2026, Plaintiff moved under 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) and § 455(a) for the disqualification of Magistrate Judge Davis and for priority determination. ECF No. 86. The motion attached Magistrate Judge Davis’s financial disclosure reports for calendar years 2024 and 2025. Each report identifies “FB common stock” at Part VII, line 6, with no transaction reported on that line. ECF No. 86 at 2; ECF Nos. 86-2, 86-3. The motion states that “FB” was the Nasdaq trading symbol for the Class A common stock of Facebook, Inc., which changed its name to Meta Platforms, Inc. on October 28, 2021. ECF No. 86 at 2–3.

40.	The motion requested that the Court state on the record: whether the reported asset is common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.; whether the interest was held on July 30, 2026, and on each date on which ECF Nos. 62, 63, 64, 65, 82, and 84 were entered; the date and manner of any divestiture; whether the interest was held directly or through a fund within 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4)(i); and any fact material to 28 U.S.C. § 455(f). ECF No. 86 at 4–5. The motion stated that it “alleges no bias, hostility, improper motive, bad faith, or intentional nondisclosure” and “rests on two signed financial disclosure reports and the docket.” ECF No. 86 at 2.

41.	Section 455(b)(4) provides that a magistrate judge “shall also disqualify himself” where “[h]e knows that he, individually or as a fiduciary, or his spouse or minor child residing in his household, has a financial interest in the subject matter in controversy or in a party to the proceeding.” Section 455(e) provides that no magistrate judge “shall accept from the parties to the proceeding a waiver of any ground for disqualification enumerated in subsection (b).” Section 455(f) permits a judge who learns of a financial interest after “substantial judicial time has been devoted to the matter” to continue if the interest is divested.

The order states that three motions to dismiss are pending, quotes a District of Maryland decision for the proposition that courts commonly wait for resolution of preliminary motions before entering a Rule 16 order, and then states: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.
